metadata.scope: e_germany (1326 baronies across k_andalusia, k_badajoz, k_bavaria, k_burgundy, k_castille, k_east_francia, k_england, k_frisia, k_hungary, k_italy, k_leon, k_lotharingia, k_navarra, k_pomerania, k_romagna, k_sardinia, k_sorbia, k_spanish_galicia, k_valencia, x_script_3965, x_script_4328)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.vanilla_ck3_name: Exact English localisation string from CK3 titles_l_english.yml.
schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/standard English display name of the audited settlement or holding (stripped of key prefixes and parenthetical notes).
schema_notes.modern_name_note: Optional administrative parent, alternate designation, or native-script qualifier extracted from modern_name; null if none.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.anachronism_type: Mutually exclusive historicity category: attested_pre_867 | fictional_placeholder | post_867_eponym | renamed_post_867 | modern_anachronism | early_modern_foundation | high_late_medieval_attestation | unattested_indigenous_or_minor.
schema_notes.is_historical_at: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'}: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= that bookmark year.
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation for the audited name (negative values = BCE; null if unattested).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.eponym: Structured eponym object {year, post_867, type, details} when named after a person, saint, ruler, deity, or dynasty/tribe; null otherwise.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.historical_names: List of distinct pre-867 attested names for the same site or immediate predecessor: [{name, native_script, language, attested_from, attested_to, source, relationship, notes}].
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_alarcos.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a papal bull of Pope Gregory VIII on 4 November 1187 confirming the castles of the Order of Calatrava, and famous for the Battle of Alarcos in 1195 CE.

morphemes.translation: Alarcos (from pre-Roman Iberian root, possibly related to Lacar/Lacu-)

b_alarcos.etymology_analysis: The name Alarcos derives from Andalusi Arabic al-Arak, which likely adapted a pre-Roman Iberian or Celtiberian toponym associated with the hillfort overlooking the Guadiana River.

b_almader.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 12th-century Islamic and Castilian sources as Ḥiṣn al-Ma'din ('fortress of the mine'), captured by Alfonso VII in 1151 CE.
b_almader.etymology_analysis: Almadén derives directly from Andalusi Arabic al-ma'din ('the mine'), referring to the world's largest cinnabar and mercury deposits exploited there since antiquity.

historical_names.name: Sisapo
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE); also Strabo, Geographica (c. 20 CE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Sisapo, located nearby at La Bienvenida in the Alcudia Valley, served as the Roman cinnabar-mining center before medieval settlement consolidated around Almadén.

b_jaen.first_mention_attestation: Attested by Pliny the Elder in his Naturalis Historia (77 CE) as Aurgi, and later in early Islamic sources from the 8th century as Jayyān.
b_jaen.etymology_analysis: The modern name Jaén derives via Andalusi Arabic Jayyān, most commonly traced to a late Roman estate name Villa Gaiena ('estate of Gaius'), which superseded the older Iberian-Roman name Aurgi.

historical_names.name: Aurgi
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE)
historical_names.notes: Known in Roman antiquity as Aurgi (Municipium Flavium Aurgitanum) and in 8th-century Islamic sources as Jayyān.

b_andujar.first_mention_attestation: First clearly attested in 888 CE when Umayyad Emir Abd Allah ordered the fortification of the stronghold of Andūyar against insurgents.
b_andujar.etymology_analysis: Andújar derives from Andalusi Arabic Andūyar, which reflects a pre-Roman Iberian or Roman toponym adapted into Arabic after the population of nearby Isturgi relocated to the river crossing.

historical_names.name: Isturgi
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE)
historical_names.notes: The Iberian and Roman town of Isturgi (Visigothic Sturgi) lay at nearby Los Villares de Andújar before its inhabitants moved to the site of modern Andújar.

historical_names.name: Sturgi
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE)
historical_names.notes: The Iberian and Roman town of Isturgi (Visigothic Sturgi) lay at nearby Los Villares de Andújar before its inhabitants moved to the site of modern Andújar.

b_ubeda.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Andalusi chronicles as Ubbadat al-'Arab, refounded and fortified during the reign of Umayyad Emir Abd al-Rahman II (822–852 CE).
b_ubeda.etymology_analysis: Úbeda derives from Andalusi Arabic Ubbadat al-'Arab, the name given to the settlement refounded under Emir Abd al-Rahman II in the mid-9th century.

b_calatrava.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Arabic chronicles as early as 785 CE (and again in 853 CE) as the Umayyad frontier fortress of Qal'at Rabāḥ.
b_calatrava.etymology_analysis: Calatrava derives from Andalusi Arabic Qal'at Rabāḥ ('Fortress of Rabah'), named after an 8th-century Arab commander who held the Guadiana crossing, with 'la Vieja' ('the Old') added after the Order of Calatrava moved its seat in 1217.

b_tomelloso.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1243 CE in the records of the Military Order of Calatrava after settlers from nearby villages consolidated around the castle.
b_tomelloso.etymology_analysis: Valdepeñas is a Spanish topographic compound meaning 'valley of rocks/crags' (Val de Peñas), describing the stony depression in southern La Mancha where the town was established in the 13th century.

b_mentesa.first_mention_attestation: The Castilian fortress name La Guardia (later La Guardia de Jaén) arose after Ferdinand III's conquest of the site in 1244 CE (constituted as a lordship in 1331 CE), succeeding ancient Mentesa Bastia (77 CE).
b_mentesa.etymology_analysis: The modern Spanish name La Guardia de Jaén refers to its role as a frontier watchtower guarding Jaén; it replaced the ancient Iberian-Roman name Mentesa Bastia (Arabic Mantīsa).

historical_names.name: Mentesa Bastia
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Iberian and Roman city of Mentesa Bastia, which served as the early Islamic capital of the kūra under the name Mantīsa before its transfer to Jaén.

historical_names.name: Mantīsa
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Iberian and Roman city of Mentesa Bastia, which served as the early Islamic capital of the kūra under the name Mantīsa before its transfer to Jaén.

b_cordoba.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Corduba in Polybius's Histories (mid-2nd century BCE) and later in Strabo and Livy following its Roman foundation in 169/152 BCE.
b_cordoba.etymology_analysis: Córdoba derives from Latin Corduba (via Andalusi Arabic Qurṭuba), a Romanization of an Old Iberian or Tartessian place name of uncertain meaning.

b_cantillana.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Catiliana (whence Cantillana) in Isidore of Seville's Etymologiae (c. 630 CE), succeeding the Roman river port of Naeva (77 CE).
b_cantillana.etymology_analysis: Cantillana derives from a Late Roman estate name Cantilliana (recorded as Catiliana by Isidore of Seville), formed from the Roman family name Cantillus with the possessive suffix -āna, which replaced the earlier name Naeva.

historical_names.name: Naeva
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE); Isidore of Seville, Etymologiae (c. 630 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman fluvial port of Naeva, renamed Catiliana/Cantilliana in Late Antiquity.

b_guadiato.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written documents as Fuente Ovejuna in 1315 CE, reflecting its medieval sheep-herding economy.
b_guadiato.etymology_analysis: Fuente Obejuna means 'sheep spring' in Spanish (historically spelled Fuente Ovejuna), referring to the pastoral wool market of the area rather than a popular folk etymology linking it to Roman Fons Mellaria.

historical_names.name: Mellaria
historical_names.source: Strabo, Geographica (c. 20 CE); Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE)
historical_names.notes: The Roman town of Mellaria lay roughly 8 km from the modern urban center of Fuente Obejuna.

b_pedroche.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Biṭrawsh (capital of the kūra of Faḥṣ al-Ballūṭ) in 10th-century Andalusi geographical works such as Aḥmad al-Rāzī (d. 955 CE).
b_pedroche.etymology_analysis: Pedroche derives from Andalusi Arabic Biṭrawsh, itself adapted from a Late Latin or Mozarabic form (often linked to petrosus, 'stony', or personal name Petrus), and gave its name to the surrounding Los Pedroches comarca.

b_almeria.first_mention_attestation: Founded and walled as a medina in 955 CE by Caliph Abd al-Rahman III under the name al-Mariyyat Bayyāna ('watchtower of Bayyāna').
b_almeria.etymology_analysis: Almería derives from Andalusi Arabic al-Mariyya ('the watchtower'), shortened from al-Mariyyat Bayyāna, the coastal watchtower and port serving the inland town of Bayyāna (Pechina).

historical_names.name: Urci
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE, for Urci)
historical_names.notes: Roman Urci and early Islamic Bayyāna (modern Pechina) served as the regional urban predecessors prior to Almería's 955 CE foundation.

historical_names.name: Bayyāna
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE, for Urci)
historical_names.notes: Roman Urci and early Islamic Bayyāna (modern Pechina) served as the regional urban predecessors prior to Almería's 955 CE foundation.

b_lorca.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Eliocroca in the Antonine Itinerary (c. 300 CE) as a station on the Via Augusta and shortly thereafter as an early Christian bishopric.
b_lorca.etymology_analysis: Lorca derives via Andalusi Arabic Lūrqa from the Roman name Eliocroca (possibly from a pre-Roman Iberian or Greco-Latin compound).

b_baza.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Basti by Pliny the Elder in Naturalis Historia (77 CE) and in Strabo and Ptolemy as the capital of the Iberian Bastetani.
b_baza.etymology_analysis: Baza derives from the ancient Iberian toponym Basti (capital of the Bastetani), which passed through Roman Basti and Andalusi Arabic Basṭa into modern Spanish Baza.

b_cabra.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Roman Igabrum by Pliny the Elder in Naturalis Historia (77 CE) — following Livy's earlier Licabrum — and as the Visigothic episcopal see of Egabro at the Council of Elvira (c. 306 CE).
b_cabra.etymology_analysis: Cabra derives from Roman Igabrum (earlier Licabrum, Visigothic Egabro, Arabic Qabra), reshaped by popular etymology toward Spanish cabra ('goat', Latin capra).

b_antequera.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Anticaria (Antikaria) in the Antonine Itinerary (c. 300 CE) and Roman inscriptions.

morphemes.translation: Roman city name (possibly 'old/ancient place' from antiqua)

b_antequera.etymology_analysis: Antequera derives from Roman Anticaria (Arabic Antaqīra), likely related to Latin antiqua ('ancient') or an Iberian substrate adapted into Latin.

b_granada.first_mention_attestation: While the ancient Iberian-Roman city of Iliberri (77 CE; Arabic Elvira) lay nearby, the city of Gharnāṭa (Granada) rose to prominence in 1013 CE when the Zirid emirs moved their capital from Medina Elvira to the Albaicín hill.

morphemes.translation: Granada (possibly from Latin granata 'pomegranate/red' or pre-Roman root)

b_granada.etymology_analysis: Granada derives from Andalusi Arabic Gharnāṭa, variously explained from Latin grānāta ('pomegranate' or 'scarlet/red', referring to the reddish soil) or a pre-Roman/Berber root.

historical_names.name: Iliberri
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE)
historical_names.notes: Iberian and Roman Iliberri (Elvira), later Arabic Ilbīra and Gharnāṭa.

historical_names.name: Iliberris
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE)
historical_names.notes: Iberian and Roman Iliberri (Elvira), later Arabic Ilbīra and Gharnāṭa.

historical_names.name: Elvira
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE)
historical_names.notes: Iberian and Roman Iliberri (Elvira), later Arabic Ilbīra and Gharnāṭa.

b_quesada.first_mention_attestation: First documented in medieval Reconquista chronicles around its 1157 CE capture by Alfonso VII, and in late Andalusi sources as Qayshāṭa.

morphemes.translation: Quesada (possibly from Latin casa/capsa or Arabic phrase)

b_quesada.etymology_analysis: Quesada derives from Andalusi Arabic Qayshāṭa, whose exact origin is debated between a Romance/Latin substrate and an Arabic compound.

b_guadiz.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Acci (Julia Gemella Acci) in Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia (77 CE) and Ptolemy's Geographia.
b_guadiz.etymology_analysis: Guadix derives from Andalusi Arabic Wādī Āsh ('River of Acci'), combining Arabic wādī with the Arabicized form of the Roman colony name Acci.

historical_names.name: Acci
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman colony of Acci at Guadix el Viejo (6 km northwest), renamed Wādī Āsh after 711 CE.

historical_names.name: Julia Gemella Acci
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman colony of Acci at Guadix el Viejo (6 km northwest), renamed Wādī Āsh after 711 CE.

b_malaga.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Malaka in Strabo's Geographica (c. 20 CE) and Malaca in Pliny the Elder (77 CE), continuing the Phoenician colony founded c. 770 BCE.
b_malaga.etymology_analysis: Málaga derives from Phoenician Malaka (mlkʾ), commonly linked to the Semitic root for 'salt' in reference to its ancient fish-salting industry, via Latin Malaca and Arabic Mālaqa.

b_nerja.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 10th-century and later Andalusi sources as Nārīsha, with no written attestation of the settlement prior to 867 CE.
b_nerja.etymology_analysis: Nerja derives from Andalusi Arabic Nārīsha, meaning 'abundant spring', referring to the water sources around the coastal settlement.

b_motril.first_mention_attestation: Attested in medieval Andalusi sources from the 10th century onward as Muṭrayil, with no written attestation prior to 867 CE.
b_motril.etymology_analysis: Motril most likely derives from Latin Murtētum ('place of myrtles'), evolving through Mozarabic and Andalusi Arabic Muṭrayil into Spanish Motril.

b_algeciras.first_mention_attestation: Refounded in 711 CE as al-Jazīra al-Khaḍrā' (whence Algeciras) on the site of Roman Iulia Traducta (attested by Pliny the Elder in 77 CE).
b_algeciras.etymology_analysis: Algeciras derives from Andalusi Arabic al-Jazīra al-Khaḍrā' ('The Green Island'), which shortened to al-Jazīra and passed into Spanish as Algeciras.

historical_names.name: Iulia Traducta
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman Iulia Traducta, refounded in 711 CE as al-Jazīra al-Khaḍrā'.

b_arcos.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Madīnat Arkuš in 10th–11th century Andalusi chronicles (later capital of the Taifa of Arcos), with no written attestation prior to 867 CE.
b_arcos.etymology_analysis: Arcos derives from Latin Arx/Arcis ('citadel/fortress on high ground') via Andalusi Arabic Arkuš, with 'de la Frontera' added after its 13th-century Castilian conquest on the Granadan frontier.

b_moron.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Mawrūr (capital of a caliphal kūra) in 10th-century Andalusi geography such as Aḥmad al-Rāzī, with no written attestation prior to 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: Morón (from Latin Maurōrum 'of the Moors' or pre-Roman morr 'rocky hill')

b_moron.etymology_analysis: Morón derives from Andalusi Arabic Mawrūr, usually traced to Late Latin Maurōrum ('of the Moors') or a pre-Roman root morr ('rocky hill'), with 'de la Frontera' added after Ferdinand III's conquest in 1240.

b_cadiz.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Gḗdeira in Herodotus's Histories (c. 440 BCE) and on Phoenician coins as Gadir (ʾgdr).
b_cadiz.etymology_analysis: Cádiz derives from Phoenician Gadir (ʾgdr, 'walled stronghold'), which became Greek Gadeira, Latin Gades, and Andalusi Arabic Qādis.

b_tarifa.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Islamic conquest chronicles recording the 710 CE landing of Umayyad commander Ṭarīf ibn Mālik, after whom the town (Jazīrat Ṭarīf) was named.

morphemes.translation: personal name of Ṭarīf ibn Mālik (710 CE)

b_tarifa.etymology_analysis: Tarifa is named after Ṭarīf ibn Mālik, the Berber/Umayyad commander who led a reconnaissance raid across the strait in 710 CE (Jazīrat Ṭarīf).

b_jerez.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Sharīsh in 10th-century Andalusi chronicles, with no written attestation of the modern urban site prior to 867 CE.
b_jerez.etymology_analysis: Jerez derives from Andalusi Arabic Sharīsh (Old Spanish Xerez, source of the English word 'sherry'), with 'de la Frontera' added during the 13th-century Castilian-Granadan frontier period.

historical_names.name: Asta Regia
historical_names.source: Strabo, Geographica (c. 20 CE); Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Asta Regia (Mesas de Asta, ~11 km from Jerez) was the main pre-Islamic urban center of the area.

b_moura.first_mention_attestation: First clearly documented around its 1166 CE Christian conquest by Portugal, having served in the 11th–12th centuries as the Islamic fortress of al-Manīja.
b_moura.etymology_analysis: Moura means 'Moorish woman' in Portuguese (from Latin Maura), traditionally linked to the legend of the 12th-century Moorish princess Salúquia during the 1166 conquest.

b_serpa.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written historical records during its 1166 CE capture by Afonso Henriques of Portugal, with no written attestation prior to 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: from Latin serpens 'serpent' or pre-Roman root

b_serpa.etymology_analysis: Serpa is traditionally associated with Latin serpens ('serpent', reflected in the town's medieval heraldic wyvern), though it may preserve a pre-Roman substrate.

b_niebla.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Ilipla in Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia (77 CE) and later as Visigothic Elepla and Arabic Labla.
b_niebla.etymology_analysis: Niebla derives from ancient Iberian-Roman Ilipla via Visigothic Elepla and Andalusi Arabic Labla (with Romance initial n- from the Arabic/Latin preposition or article).

b_huelva.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Onoba in Strabo's Geographica (c. 20 CE) and Onuba Aestuaria in Pliny the Elder (77 CE).
b_huelva.etymology_analysis: Huelva derives from the pre-Roman Tartessian-Phoenician name Onoba (Latin Onuba), which evolved through Andalusi Arabic Walba into modern Spanish Huelva.

b_ayamonte.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Ayamonte in 1239–1240 CE in King Sancho II of Portugal's charter granting the conquered castle to the Order of Santiago.
b_ayamonte.etymology_analysis: Ayamonte is commonly explained as a tautological hybrid of a pre-Roman root aya ('hill/height') and Latin-Romance monte ('mount/hill').

b_zafra.first_mention_attestation: First documented in mid-13th century Reconquista charters during the Castilian-Portuguese campaigns in the Sierra Morena.
b_zafra.etymology_analysis: Aracena is plausibly derived from a Roman villa name such as Villa Aretiana or Arciana, formed from a Roman personal name with the estate suffix -āna.

b_sevilla.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Hispalis in Julius Caesar's Bellum Civile and Bellum Hispaniense (c. 45 BCE), continuing the older Tartessian settlement Spal.
b_sevilla.etymology_analysis: Seville (Spanish Sevilla) derives from Tartessian Spal/Ispal via Roman Hispalis and Andalusi Arabic Ishbīliya.

b_carmona.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Carmo in Julius Caesar's Bellum Civile (2.19, c. 49 BCE) as the strongest city of Hispania Ulterior.
b_carmona.etymology_analysis: Carmona derives from the pre-Roman Turdetanian and Roman name Carmo (accusative Carmōnem), via Andalusi Arabic Qarmūna.

b_almonte.first_mention_attestation: Attested as the fortress of al-Munt in Ibn Ḥayyān's al-Muqtabis for the 10th century, with no written attestation prior to 867 CE.
b_almonte.etymology_analysis: Almonte derives from Andalusi Arabic al-Munt, a hybrid of the Arabic definite article al- with Mozarabic munt (from Latin mons, 'hill/mount').

b_triana.first_mention_attestation: First documented in Castilian Reconquista records around 1247 CE, reflecting the late Andalusi fortress name Ḥiṣn al-Qullār.
b_triana.etymology_analysis: Aznalcóllar derives from Andalusi Arabic Ḥiṣn al-Qullār ('Fortress of al-Qullar'), with ḥiṣn regularly evolving into Spanish Aznal-.

b_cuenca.first_mention_attestation: Documented as the Andalusi stronghold of Qūnkah (Cuenca), founded/fortified around 999 CE under al-Manṣūr and described by 11th–12th century geographers.
b_cuenca.etymology_analysis: Cuenca derives from Latin conca ('bowl/basin'), referring to the deep gorge between the Júcar and Huécar rivers, adapted into Arabic as Qūnkah.

b_altotajo.first_mention_attestation: First documented around its 1175–1177 CE conquest by Alfonso VIII of Castile (and its 1190 fuero), after serving as an Andalusi stronghold named Walma.
b_altotajo.etymology_analysis: Huélamo derives from Andalusi Arabic Walma (Walmu), which in turn may reflect an earlier Latin or pre-Roman toponym such as Olano.

b_zurita.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Andalusi chronicles as the alcazaba of Zurayṭa built under Emir Muḥammad I (r. 852–886 CE), with its Castilian fuero granted in 1180 CE.
b_zurita.etymology_analysis: Zorita derives from Andalusi Arabic Zurayṭa, while 'de los Canes' ('of the Dogs') was added in the medieval Castilian period.

historical_names.name: Reccopolis
historical_names.source: John of Biclaro, Chronicle (c. 590 CE, recording its 578 CE foundation by Leovigild)
historical_names.notes: The Visigothic royal city of Reccopolis, founded in 578 CE by King Leovigild, lies within the municipality of Zorita de los Canes.

b_huete.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 10th-century Andalusi chronicles as the madīna and fortress of Wabda (Alcazaba de Wabda) in the kūra of Santaver.
b_huete.etymology_analysis: Huete derives from Andalusi Arabic Wabda, which is generally traced to the pre-Roman and Roman toponym Opta.

b_madrid.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Ibn Ḥayyān's al-Muqtabis as the Umayyad frontier fortress (ḥiṣn) of Mayrīṭ/Majrīṭ founded by Emir Muḥammad I around 865 CE.
b_madrid.etymology_analysis: Madrid derives from Andalusi Arabic Mayrīṭ/Majrīṭ, a hybrid combining Arabic majrā ('watercourse/conduit') with the Romance collective suffix -īṭ (Latin -ētum), denoting a place rich in streams and underground water.

b_gudalajara.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 9th-century Andalusi chronicles as Madīnat al-Faraj and Wādī al-Ḥijāra, where an Umayyad alcázar was built by the mid-9th century.
b_gudalajara.etymology_analysis: Guadalajara derives from Andalusi Arabic Wādī al-Ḥijāra ('River/Valley of Stones'), possibly translating the nearby pre-Roman name Arriaca (Basque arri, 'stone').

historical_names.name: Madīnat al-Faraj
historical_names.source: Andalusi chronicles (mid-9th century CE)
historical_names.notes: Known in the 9th century as Madīnat al-Faraj and Wādī al-Ḥijāra; Roman Arriaca lay nearby on the Henares.

b_villarejodesalvanes.first_mention_attestation: First documented on 23 April 1099 CE when King Alfonso VI of León donated the valley of Salvanés to the Church of Toledo.
b_villarejodesalvanes.etymology_analysis: Villarejo de Salvanés combines Spanish villarejo ('small hamlet') with the valley name Salvanés, traditionally linked to Latin silva ('forest/woodland').

b_arganda.first_mention_attestation: First documented in the late 11th century following the Christian conquest of the Taifa of Toledo (1085 CE) within the domain of Alcalá.

morphemes.translation: from Celtiberian Arkanta or Latin area canda ('white area')
of the King (granted royal villa status by Philip II)

b_arganda.etymology_analysis: Arganda is variously derived from Celtiberian Arkanta or Latin area canda ('white/bright ground'), with 'del Rey' added after Philip II granted it the title of royal villa.

b_malagon.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a papal bull of Pope Gregory VIII on 4 November 1187 CE confirming the castles of the Order of Calatrava.
b_malagon.etymology_analysis: Malagón preserves a medieval toponym of uncertain pre-Roman or Andalusi origin, first recorded in late 12th-century charters of the Order of Calatrava.

b_cabaneros.first_mention_attestation: Documented from the 13th century as part of the Montes de Toledo lands owned by the city of Toledo, with no written attestation prior to 867 CE.
b_cabaneros.etymology_analysis: Cabañeros derives from Spanish cabaña ('hut/cabin') with the suffix -eros, referring to the seasonal huts built by shepherds and charcoal-burners in the Montes de Toledo.

b_lajara.first_mention_attestation: Documented from the 13th century during the Castilian repopulation of the western Montes de Toledo, with no written attestation prior to 867 CE.
b_lajara.etymology_analysis: La Jara derives from Spanish jara ('rockrose/scrubland', borrowed from Andalusi Arabic sha'rā'), naming the Mediterranean scrubland comarca of western Toledo.

b_lapueblademontalban.first_mention_attestation: La Puebla de Montalbán is first documented as an established settlement by 1387, having developed after the dissolution of the Templar commandery of Montalbán in 1312 and the transfer of its territory to the Fernández Coronel family.

morphemes.translation: planned settlement, repopulated town (from Latin populus)

b_lapueblademontalban.etymology_analysis: The toponym combines Spanish 'la puebla' (a medieval repopulation settlement, from Latin 'populus') with 'de Montalbán', referring to the nearby fortress of Montalbán, whose name derives from Latin 'mons albus' ('white mountain').

b_molina.first_mention_attestation: Molina de Aragón is first attested in the late 11th century (c. 1080s) as the seat of the Islamic Taifa of Molina (Arabic Malīna) under the Banu Khazraj, before receiving its Castilian fuero from Manrique Pérez de Lara in April 1154.

morphemes.translation: Aragon (referring to the Kingdom of Aragon)

b_molina.etymology_analysis: Molina derives from Latin 'molina' ('mill', ultimately from 'mola', 'millstone'), reflected in the millstones on the town's coat of arms; 'de Aragón' was later appended to distinguish it from other towns named Molina due to its proximity and historical ties to the Crown of Aragon.

b_ablanque.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Ablanque; the village developed within the medieval Lordship of Molina (Señorío de Molina), organized under regional fueros from the 12th century onward.

morphemes.translation: uncertain root, possibly related to Latin albus ('white') or a pre-Roman toponymic base

b_ablanque.etymology_analysis: The etymology of Ablanque is uncertain; local toponymic tradition often connects it by folk etymology to 'blanco' (from Germanic/Latinized 'blanq'/'albus', 'white'), though it may reflect a pre-Roman or Mozarabic substrate name.

b_medinaceli.first_mention_attestation: While the hilltop site was the Celtiberian town of Ocilis (153–152 BCE), the Islamic madina of Madīnat Sālim (whence Medinaceli) was established in the 8th–10th centuries and became the capital of the Middle March in 946 CE.

morphemes.translation: Salim (referring to the Berber Banū Sālim lineage)

b_medinaceli.etymology_analysis: The modern name Medinaceli derives from Andalusi Arabic 'Madīnat Sālim' ('City of Salim'), named after the Berber Banū Sālim clan of the Masmuda tribal group that settled the strategic hilltop fortress during the Islamic period.

historical_names.name: Ocilis
historical_names.source: Appian, Iberike (Second Celtiberian War, 153–152 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Celtiberian town of the Arevaci/Belli borderlands and later Roman municipium on the same hilltop site.

historical_names.name: Occilis
historical_names.source: Appian, Iberike (Second Celtiberian War, 153–152 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Celtiberian town of the Arevaci/Belli borderlands and later Roman municipium on the same hilltop site.

b_siguenza.first_mention_attestation: Sigüenza is attested in Classical Antiquity as the Celtiberian town of Segontia, mentioned by Livy in his account of Cato the Elder's campaign against the Celtiberians in 195 BCE.
b_siguenza.etymology_analysis: Sigüenza evolved phonetically from the Latinized Celtiberian name 'Segontia' (from Celtic *sego- 'strength, victory', meaning 'the strong/victorious place' or 'dominating over the valley').

b_ucles.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Uclés; its fortress was constructed in the late 9th century (c. 890) by al-Fath ibn Musa ibn Dhi-l-Nun, and the town is documented under Cordobese authority by the 920s.
b_ucles.etymology_analysis: The Spanish name Uclés derives from Andalusi Arabic 'Uqlīsh', itself an Arabized form of an earlier pre-Roman or Roman-era local toponym.

historical_names.name: Segobriga
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE)
historical_names.notes: The Roman municipium of Segobriga (Cabeza del Griego, ~12 km south) served as the classical urban center and episcopal see of the area before its decline and the rise of Uclés.

b_mora.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Mora; the fortress and settlement are first recorded in 10th-century Andalusi sources (from 927 CE) during the Emirate/Caliphate of Córdoba.

morphemes.translation: uncertain: possibly from Latin mora ('delay/station') or pre-Roman *mor- ('stone/hill')

b_mora.etymology_analysis: The toponym Mora is of disputed origin, variously traced by Spanish toponymists to a pre-Roman root *mor- ('heap of stones, rocky hill'), Latin 'mora' ('halting place, station'), or medieval Romance 'mora' ('Moorish woman' in later folk association).

b_ocana.first_mention_attestation: While identified with the Roman vicus of Vicus Cuminarius (c. 215 CE), medieval Ocaña is first attested in Christian sources when the Order of Calatrava established an encomienda there in 1176 CE.
b_ocana.etymology_analysis: Ocaña is generally derived from the Celtiberian root 'olca-' ('fertile ground, plowed field') via *Olcania > Ocania > Ocaña, though some scholars (such as Nieto Ballester) propose a pre-Roman non-Celtic Indo-European origin.

historical_names.name: Vicus Cuminarius
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (early 3rd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman mansio/vicus identified with the site of Ocaña.

b_quintanar.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Quintanar de la Orden; the settlement was repopulated by the Order of Santiago and received its charter (carta puebla) during the reign of Ferdinand III of Castile (1217–1252).

morphemes.translation: place of the fifth part or fifth-mile marker (from Latin quintana)
of the Order (referring to the Order of Santiago)

b_quintanar.etymology_analysis: Quintanar derives from Latin 'quintana' ('one-fifth', referring either to a tenant's fifth-share rent or a five-mile marker from a Roman road station), with 'de la Orden' added to denote its governance by the Military Order of Santiago (replacing the earlier 'de la Encina').

b_toledo.first_mention_attestation: Toledo is first attested in written history as Toletum, a fortified city of the Carpetani tribe, in Livy's account of Marcus Fulvius Nobilior's victory over a Celtiberian-Carpetanian coalition in 193 BCE.
b_toledo.etymology_analysis: Toledo derives from Latin 'Toletum' (Arabic 'Ṭulayṭulah'), a Latinized pre-Roman toponym likely rooted in a Celtic or Iberian stem meaning 'elevated place' or 'height', fitting its defensible hill above the Tagus.

b_maqueda.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Maqueda; its Moorish fortress (Castillo de la Vela) is first securely recorded in 981 CE when Almanzor expanded and fortified it.

morphemes.translation: Maqueda (from Arabic maq'ad 'seat/post' or a pre-Arabic toponym)

b_maqueda.etymology_analysis: Maqueda reflects an Andalusi Arabic form (Maqqada/Makkada), traditionally linked either to an Arabic noun denoting a fortified post or resting station, or to an Arabized pre-Roman place name.

b_talavera.first_mention_attestation: Talavera de la Reina is first attested as Aebura (in Carpetania) in Livy's account of Quintus Fulvius Flaccus's siege and defeat of the Celtiberians in 181 BCE, later becoming Roman Caesarobriga.

morphemes.translation: of the Queen (added after 14th-century royal grants)

b_talavera.etymology_analysis: Talavera derives from Andalusi Arabic 'Talabayra', an adaptation of the Visigothic 'Elbora'/'Ebora' (Celtiberian 'Aebura'), while 'de la Reina' ('of the Queen') was added in the 14th century when the town was granted to Castilian queens.

historical_names.name: Aebura
historical_names.source: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita (siege of Aebura, 181 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Pre-Roman ford settlement (Aebura), Roman municipium (Caesarobriga), and Visigothic town (Elbora/Ebora) on the same site.

historical_names.name: Caesarobriga
historical_names.source: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita (siege of Aebura, 181 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Pre-Roman ford settlement (Aebura), Roman municipium (Caesarobriga), and Visigothic town (Elbora/Ebora) on the same site.

b_faro.first_mention_attestation: The ancient Roman port of Ossonoba (23 CE) was renamed Santa Maria Ibn Harun (later Harun, whence Faro) under the Banu Harun dynasty of the Taifa of Santa Maria del Algarve in the 11th century (c. 1026 CE).

morphemes.translation: Faro (from Andalusi Arabic Hārūn, from Santa Maria Ibn Hārūn)

b_faro.etymology_analysis: After the 10th-century Islamic period, Ossonoba was renamed Santa Maria Ibn Hārūn after a local Muslim ruler; Portuguese 'Faro' evolved from the shortened Arabic/Romance form 'Faarun'/'Hārūn' (unrelated to 'farol', 'lighthouse').

historical_names.name: Ossonoba
historical_names.source: Strabo, Geography (c. 23 CE); Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE)
historical_names.notes: Phoenician-founded and Roman port city and late-antique episcopal see on the same site.

b_mertola.first_mention_attestation: Mértola is attested in Classical Antiquity as Myrtilis (or Myrtilis Iulia), recorded by Strabo in his Geography (c. 23 CE) and Pliny the Elder (77 CE) as a major Guadiana river port.
b_mertola.etymology_analysis: Mértola evolved from the pre-Roman/Lusitanian toponym 'Myrtilis' (Roman 'Myrtilis Iulia') through Andalusi Arabic 'Mārtula' into modern Portuguese 'Mértola'.

b_silves.first_mention_attestation: Although Roman-era remains exist at Silves, no written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for the name Silves (or Arabic Shilb); it enters written records in the 11th century (1027 CE) as the capital of the Moorish Taifa of Silves.

morphemes.translation: Silves (from Andalusi Arabic Shilb, from Latin silva 'forest/woods' or pre-Roman Cilpes)

b_silves.etymology_analysis: Portuguese 'Silves' derives from Andalusi Arabic 'Shilb', which in turn likely reflects either Latin 'silva' ('woodland') or a pre-Roman settlement name.

b_ourique.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Ourique; it is first recorded in medieval chronicles in connection with the Battle of Ourique fought on 25 July 1139.

morphemes.translation: Ourique (likely from a pre-Roman or Arabized toponym)

b_ourique.etymology_analysis: The origin of Ourique is uncertain; it is attested in medieval Portuguese/Arabic sources in the 12th century and likely derives from a pre-Roman or Mozarabic-Arabic place name.

b_lagos.first_mention_attestation: Lagos is attested in Classical Antiquity as Lacobriga (Laccobriga), recorded by Strabo (c. 23 CE) and Pomponius Mela, and associated with the Sertorian War (1st century BCE).
b_lagos.etymology_analysis: Lagos derives from the Celtic-Latin toponym 'Lacobriga' (combining *lako- 'lake/lagoon' and *-briga 'fortress'), which evolved into Portuguese 'Lagos' (reinforcing the association with 'lakes/lagoons').

b_badajoz.first_mention_attestation: Badajoz was founded in 875 CE by the muwallad leader Ibn Marwan al-Jilliqi under the Arabic name Baṭalyaws (after the 867 CE baseline).

morphemes.translation: Badajoz (of uncertain pre-Arabic or Latinized origin)

b_badajoz.etymology_analysis: Spanish 'Badajoz' evolved from Andalusi Arabic 'Baṭalyaws', the name given to the city upon its foundation in 875 CE; its deeper root remains debated among linguists.

b_olivienza.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Olivenza; the settlement originated around 1230 CE when the Knights Templar established a commandery there after the Leonese conquest of Badajoz.
b_olivienza.etymology_analysis: Olivenza (Portuguese Olivença) is a medieval Romance toponym derived from 'oliva' ('olive tree', from Latin 'oliva'), reflecting olive cultivation in the Guadiana valley.

b_ilerena.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Llerena; it is first recorded in Christian sources in 1243 when the Order of Santiago under Pelay Pérez Correa conquered the Andalusi settlement of Ellerina.
b_ilerena.etymology_analysis: Llerena derives from the medieval Andalusi/Mozarabic name 'Ellerina' (or 'Ellerena'), recorded at the time of the 13th-century Castilian conquest.

b_caceres.first_mention_attestation: Cáceres is attested in Classical Antiquity as the Roman colony Norba Caesarina (founded c. 34 BCE) and in late-antique documents (3rd–4th century CE, Ravenna Cosmography) under the ablative form Castris.

morphemes.translation: in/at the military camps (ablative plural of castrum)

b_caceres.etymology_analysis: Cáceres derives from Latin 'castris' ('at the camps', shortened from Castra Caecilia / Norba Caesarina), transmitted through Andalusi Arabic 'Qāṣras' (ḥiṣn Qāṣras) into Spanish 'Cáceres'.

b_alcantara.first_mention_attestation: The site of Alcántara is attested in 106 CE by the Latin dedicatory inscription of the Roman Alcántara Bridge built over the Tagus by Gaius Julius Lacer in honor of Emperor Trajan.
b_alcantara.etymology_analysis: Alcántara derives from Andalusi Arabic 'al-qanṭarah' ('the bridge' or 'the arch'), referring directly to the monumental Roman stone arch bridge spanning the Tagus.

b_zalaca.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Sagrajas (Zalaca); the site enters written history with the Battle of Sagrajas (az-Zallāqah) fought on 23 October 1086 between Yusuf ibn Tashfin and Alfonso VI.
b_zalaca.etymology_analysis: Zalaca comes from Arabic 'az-Zallāqah' ('slippery ground'), a name associated in Islamic historiography with the blood-soaked terrain of the 1086 battle; the modern Spanish name is Sagrajas.

b_medellin.first_mention_attestation: Medellín was founded in 75 BCE by the Roman general Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius as the military base Metellinum during the Sertorian War.

morphemes.translation: Metellus (Roman gens/cognomen of Q. Caecilius Metellus Pius)

b_medellin.etymology_analysis: Medellín derives from Latin 'Metellinum', named after its 75 BCE Roman founder Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius.

b_donllorente.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Don Llorente; it was a late medieval hamlet near the Guadiana whose inhabitants relocated in the 15th century to found Don Benito due to recurring floods.

eponym.details: Named after a medieval local founder or landowner styled Don Llorente, traditionally paired with the founder of neighboring Don Benito.

b_donllorente.etymology_analysis: The toponym combines the Spanish honorific 'Don' (from Latin 'dominus') with the medieval personal name 'Llorente' (from Latin 'Laurentius'), referring to an early landowner or founder.

b_hornachos.first_mention_attestation: The modern town of Hornachos is first documented in Christian chronicles in 1235 CE when Ferdinand III granted it to the Order of Santiago, though its Andalusi name Furnayuš reflects the nearby Roman oppidum Fornacis.
b_hornachos.etymology_analysis: Hornachos derives from Latin 'fornacis' ('furnaces', via Andalusi Arabic 'Furnayuš'), referring to ancient silver and iron smelting furnaces in the Sierra Grande de Hornachos.

historical_names.name: Fornacis
historical_names.source: Ptolemy, Geography II.5.7 (c. 150 CE)
historical_names.notes: Ptolemy's Fornacis is identified archaeologically with the nearby oppidum at Cerro de Hornachuelos (~9 km away), abandoned around the late 1st century CE.

b_merida.first_mention_attestation: Mérida was founded in 25 BCE by Emperor Augustus as the Roman colonia Augusta Emerita (Emerita Augusta) to settle veteran soldiers of the Cantabrian Wars.
b_merida.etymology_analysis: Mérida derives from Latin 'Emerita' (from 'Augusta Emerita'), referring to the discharged Roman veteran soldiers ('emeriti') settled there in 25 BCE, transmitted via Arabic 'Māridah'.

b_trujillo.first_mention_attestation: Trujillo is attested in Classical Antiquity as Turgalium, a stipendiary town and prefecture of Augusta Emerita recorded in Roman sources (Pliny the Elder, c. 77 CE, and the Antonine Itinerary).

morphemes.translation: Trujillo (Latinized pre-Roman Turaca/Turacia, adapted via Arabic Targhālah)

b_trujillo.etymology_analysis: Trujillo evolved from Roman 'Turgalium' (likely from a pre-Roman root *Turaca/*Turacia) through Andalusi Arabic 'Targhālah' and medieval Castilian 'Trugillo'.

b_castilblanco.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Castilblanco; its medieval castle and settlement date to the early 12th century during the campaigns of Alfonso VII in Extremadura.
b_castilblanco.etymology_analysis: Castilblanco is a transparent medieval Spanish compound meaning 'white castle', combining 'castil' (from Latin 'castellum') and 'blanco' ('white').

b_hervas.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Hervás; the town originated in the late 12th century (with a municipal charter in 1186 CE) around a Templar settlement in the Ambroz valley.

morphemes.translation: Hervás (from Santihervás, after Saints Gervasius and Protasius, or Latin herba 'grass')

b_hervas.etymology_analysis: Hervás is commonly traced to 'Santihervás' (a contraction of San Gervasio, referring to the early church/hermitage of Saints Gervasius and Protasius), though folk etymology also links it to 'herbazal' (grassy pasture).

b_coira.first_mention_attestation: Coria (CK3 b_coira in Plasencia) is attested in Classical Antiquity as the Vettonian and Roman municipium of Caurium (Caurenses), recorded by Pliny the Elder (77 CE) and Ptolemy (c. 150 CE).
b_coira.etymology_analysis: Coria (medieval Leonese/Portuguese 'Coira') evolved from the Roman municipium 'Caurium', a Latinization of an indigenous Vettonian settlement name.

b_almaraz.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Almaraz; although prehistoric and Celtiberian finds exist in the territory, the medieval town enters records in the post-867 Andalusi and Castilian periods.

morphemes.translation: watchtower, guard post (or maraz 'place of encounters/pasture')

b_almaraz.etymology_analysis: Almaraz derives from Andalusi Arabic 'al-maḥras' ('the guard post/watchtower') or 'al-maraz' ('meeting place'), reflecting its strategic position guarding the Tagus crossing.

b_alcacerdosal.first_mention_attestation: Alcácer do Sal is attested in Classical Antiquity as Salacia (Urbs Imperatoria Salacia), recorded by Pliny the Elder (77 CE) and Ptolemy as an important Roman port and salt-trade center on the Sado River.
b_alcacerdosal.etymology_analysis: Alcácer do Sal combines Portuguese 'Alcácer' (from Arabic 'al-qaṣr', 'the fortress', itself from Latin 'castrum') with 'do Sal' ('of the salt'), preserving the memory of its ancient salt pans.

b_montemor.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Montemor-o-Novo; the town is first recorded in March 1203 when King Sancho I of Portugal granted its first royal charter (foral).
b_montemor.etymology_analysis: Montemor-o-Novo means 'the New Great Mount', from Latin 'mons maior' ('great hill') plus Portuguese 'o Novo' ('the New') to distinguish it from Montemor-o-Velho in northern Portugal.

b_vianadoalento.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Viana do Alentejo; it is first recorded in 1313 CE when King Dinis of Portugal granted it a foral and ordered the construction of its castle.

morphemes.translation: Viana (medieval Portuguese settlement name, possibly from Latin/Celtic Viana or transferred from northern Viana)

b_vianadoalento.etymology_analysis: The settlement was originally called 'Viana' (attested in 1313) and later received the regional qualifier 'do Alentejo' ('beyond the Tagus') to distinguish it from Viana do Castelo.

b_avis.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Avis; the fortress and town were founded in 1211 CE by the Knights of the Order of Aviz.

morphemes.translation: bird (from Latin avis, linked to the foundation legend of two eagles)

b_avis.etymology_analysis: According to medieval Portuguese tradition, the name Avis derives from Latin 'avis' ('bird'), commemorating two eagles observed perched on an oak tree when the Knights of Évora chose the site in 1211.

b_evora.first_mention_attestation: Évora is attested in Classical Antiquity as Ebora (Ebora Liberalitas Julia), recorded by Strabo (c. 23 CE) and Pliny the Elder (77 CE) as a Roman municipium in Lusitania.
b_evora.etymology_analysis: Évora derives from the pre-Roman Celtic toponym 'Ebora' (from Proto-Celtic *eburos, 'yew tree'), later styled 'Ebora Liberalitas Julia' by the Romans.

b_beja.first_mention_attestation: Beja was established as the Roman colony Pax Julia by Julius Caesar in 48 BCE when he concluded peace with the Lusitanians, becoming a major conventus capital of Lusitania.

morphemes.translation: peace (shortened in Visigothic to Paca, Arabic Bāja)

b_beja.etymology_analysis: Beja derives from Latin 'Pax' (in 'Pax Julia'/'Pax Augusta'), which was shortened in Visigothic times to 'Paca', adapted into Arabic as 'Bāja' (as Arabic lacks the /p/ phoneme), and evolved into Portuguese 'Beja'.

b_elvas.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Elvas; while unproven hypotheses link it to Roman Alba, the earliest archaeological remains and Andalusi records (as Yalbash) date to the 10th century.

morphemes.translation: Elvas (from an uncertain pre-Arabic root, possibly Helvia or Alba)

b_elvas.etymology_analysis: Portuguese 'Elvas' derives from Andalusi Arabic 'Yalbash', whose pre-Islamic origin is uncertain (sometimes speculatively linked to Latin 'Alba' or 'Helvia', though unconfirmed by inscriptions).

b_nisa.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Nisa; the town was established in the late 13th century (c. 1290) by the Knights Templar, succeeding the nearby earlier settlement of Nisa-a-Velha.

morphemes.translation: Nisa (likely transferred from Nice / Nissa in Provence by 12th–13th century settlers)

b_nisa.etymology_analysis: Nisa (earlier spelled 'Nissa') is traditionally attributed to Provençal/French settlers (from Occitan 'Nissa', Nice) who participated in the 12th–13th century repopulation of the upper Alentejo.

b_crato.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Crato; it enters written records in 1232 CE when King Sancho II donated it to the Knights Hospitaller and Prior Mendo Gonçalves granted its foral.

morphemes.translation: Crato (of uncertain pre-Roman or medieval origin)

b_crato.etymology_analysis: The etymology of Crato is uncertain; it is first documented in 13th-century Portuguese charters and likely preserves a pre-Roman or medieval local place name.

b_lisboa.first_mention_attestation: Lisbon is attested in Classical Antiquity as Olisipo, fortified by Decimus Junius Brutus Callaicus in 138 BCE and later mentioned by Strabo, Pomponius Mela, and Pliny the Elder.
b_lisboa.etymology_analysis: Lisbon (Portuguese Lisboa) evolved from the pre-Roman name 'Olisipo' (bearing the southwestern Iberian '-ippo' suffix), adapted into Andalusi Arabic as 'al-Ishbūnā' and into Portuguese as 'Lisboa'.

b_santarem.first_mention_attestation: Santarém is attested in Classical Antiquity as Scallabis (later Scallabis Praesidium Iulium), occupied by the Romans from 138 BCE and raised to a conventus capital.

morphemes.translation: Irene (Saint Irene of Tomar, martyred c. 653 CE)

b_santarem.etymology_analysis: Santarém derives from Late Latin 'Sancta Irene' (Arabic 'Shantarīn'), replacing the ancient name Scallabis in honor of Saint Irene of Tomar.

historical_names.name: Scallabis
historical_names.source: Roman occupation of Scallabis (138 BCE); Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia
historical_names.notes: Ancient hillfort and Roman conventus capital on the Tagus.

historical_names.name: Scallabis Praesidium Iulium
historical_names.source: Roman occupation of Scallabis (138 BCE); Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia
historical_names.notes: Ancient hillfort and Roman conventus capital on the Tagus.

b_setubal.first_mention_attestation: Setúbal is attested in Classical Antiquity as Caetobriga (Cetóbriga), recorded in Roman sources (including Ptolemy, c. 150 CE) as a Lusitanian fish-salting port on the Sado estuary.
b_setubal.etymology_analysis: Setúbal evolved from the pre-Roman Celtic name 'Caetobriga' (adapted in Andalusi Arabic as 'Shaṭūbar'), combining a root *caeto- with '-briga' ('fortified settlement').

b_schongau.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Schongau; the original Welf settlement (modern Altenstadt) and Hohenstaufen town of Schongau are first attested in the 12th century (e.g., Welf VI's 1179 transfer to Frederick Barbarossa).
b_schongau.etymology_analysis: Schongau derives from 'Schönach-Gau', combining the local stream name Schönach ('clear/beautiful water') with Old High German 'gouwe'/'gau' ('district, territory').

b_peiting.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Peiting; it is first mentioned in 1055 CE in connection with the Welf fortress (Burg Peiting, later recorded in 1101 as 'nova arx Bitengoe').
b_peiting.etymology_analysis: Peiting (medieval 'Bitengoe') is an early Bavarian '-ing' settlement name formed from a Germanic personal name (Bito/Pito) plus the patronymic/locative suffix '-ing'.

b_hohenschwangau.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Hohenschwangau; the medieval Schwanstein castle of the Lords of Schwangau is first reliably attested in the 12th century (an alleged 1090/97 mention is considered a modern forgery).
b_hohenschwangau.etymology_analysis: Hohenschwangau means 'Upper Schwangau', adding 'Hohen-' ('high/upper') to the 12th-century territorial name 'Schwangau' ('swan district' or 'pasture district').

b_augsburg.first_mention_attestation: Augsburg was founded in 15 BCE by the Romans under Augustus as the military camp and provincial capital Augusta Vindelicorum.
b_augsburg.etymology_analysis: Augsburg combines 'Augs-' (a contraction of Latin 'Augusta', from 'Augusta Vindelicorum') with Old High German 'burg' ('fortified city').

b_friedberg.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Friedberg; Friedberg Castle was built in 1257 CE and the town was founded in 1264 CE by Duke Ludwig II and Konradin as a border toll station.
b_friedberg.etymology_analysis: Friedberg is a high-medieval German castle name meaning 'peace hill' or 'protective fortress' (Middle High German 'vride' + 'berc').

b_lechrain.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for the regional name Lechrain; although the Lech river is attested in antiquity, the region's name is documented in modern historiography starting with Johann Georg von Lori's Geschichte des Lechrains (1765).
b_lechrain.etymology_analysis: Lechrain combines the ancient river name 'Lech' with Old High German 'rein' ('border, boundary ridge'), denoting the historic borderland between Bavaria and Swabia along the Lech.

historical_names.name: Licus
historical_names.source: Roman inscriptions of 8/7 BCE and classical geography (Ptolemy's Likios)
historical_names.notes: The Lech river itself is attested in 8/7 BCE, though the compound regional name Lechrain is post-867.

historical_names.name: Licca
historical_names.source: Roman inscriptions of 8/7 BCE and classical geography (Ptolemy's Likios)
historical_names.notes: The Lech river itself is attested in 8/7 BCE, though the compound regional name Lechrain is post-867.

b_kaufbeuren.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1112 CE through the noble family of the Freiherren von Buron/Beuren; although a Carolingian royal manor (Reichshof) is presumed to have existed in the mid-8th century, no contemporary written attestation survives before 1112 CE.
b_kaufbeuren.etymology_analysis: Originally attested as Buron (from Old High German būr, 'dwelling' or 'settlement', in the dative plural), the name later gained the prefix Kauf- ('market, trade') to reflect its medieval status as a chartered market town and Imperial city.

b_burgau.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1147 CE with the mention of Bruno von Burgau, an official of Duke Welf VI.
b_burgau.etymology_analysis: A compound of Old High German burg ('fortress, castle') and ouwa ('water-meadow, riverine floodplain'), describing a fortified settlement situated in the floodplain of the Mindel river.

b_kirchberg.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1087 CE when Otto de Chirchperg witnessed a donation to the monastery in Schaffhausen; although a Roman castrum stood at Unterkirchberg around 40 CE, its ancient name is unattested.
b_kirchberg.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1087 CE as Chirchperg, combining Old High German kirihha ('church') and berg ('hill'), referring to a church-crowned hill overlooking the Iller valley. The modern municipal prefix Iller- was added in 1972 upon merging Ober- and Unterkirchberg.

b_kempten.first_mention_attestation: First attested around 50 BCE by the Greek geographer Strabo as Kambodunon, a town of the Celtic Estiones, and later rebuilt as Roman Cambodunum after 15 BCE.
b_kempten.etymology_analysis: Derived from Celtic *Kambodūnon ('fortress at the river bend', referring to the bend of the Iller), Latinized as Cambodunum and subsequently adapted through Old High German sound shifts into Kempten.

b_marsetten.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1050 CE when the Counts of Marstetten built a castle above Aitrach as vassals of Kempten Abbey.
b_marsetten.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old High German marah ('horse') or mari ('marsh, boundary') compounded with steti (dative plural of stat, 'place, stead'), denoting a fortified estate or horse-station in the Iller valley.

b_memmingen.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1128 CE under the form Mammingin in a monastic charter.
b_memmingen.etymology_analysis: Formed from the Alemannic personal name Mammo with the Germanic associative suffix -ingun ('among the people of Mammo'), yielding Mammingin and later umlauted Memmingen.

b_ravensburg.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1088 CE as Ravenspurch, a castle seat of the Welf dynasty.
b_ravensburg.etymology_analysis: Compounded from a Low/Central-influenced or personal form of *hraban ('raven') and Middle High German burc ('castle'), meaning 'castle of Hraban' or 'raven's castle'.

b_bregenz.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the early 1st century CE by Strabo, who names the Celtic Brigántioi and their chief town Brigantium on Lake Constance, conquered by Rome in 15 BCE.
b_bregenz.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Celtic root *brigant- ('high, elevated', also the ethnonym of the Brigantii) via the Latinized town name Brigantium, which developed through Alemannic sound changes into Bregenz.

b_eschenlohe.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1246 CE through Count Berthold III of Eschenlohe, whose comital family held the castle above the Loisach valley.
b_eschenlohe.etymology_analysis: A compound of Old High German esca ('ash tree') and lōh ('grove, clearing, woodland'), meaning 'ash-tree grove'.

b_tolz.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1155 CE under the form Tolnze.
b_tolz.etymology_analysis: Attested as Tolnze in 1155 CE, likely derived from a Bavarian personal name Tollo with a possessive/locative suffix, or from a pre-Germanic substrate; the prefix Bad ('spa') was officially granted in 1899.

b_falkenstein.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1115 CE with Reginolt de Valchensteine, ancestor of the Bavarian Counts of Falkenstein near Flintsbach am Inn.
b_falkenstein.etymology_analysis: Composed of Old High German falko ('falcon') and stein ('rock, crag'), a classic High Medieval castle name denoting a fortress perched on a rocky crag.

b_marquardstein.first_mention_attestation: Built and first attested around 1075 CE under Count Marquart II of Hohenstein as his family's new residence in the Achen valley.

eponym.details: Named after Count Marquart II of Hohenstein (fl. c. 1075 CE), who built Marquartstein Castle.

b_marquardstein.etymology_analysis: Named for its founder, Count Marquart II of Hohenstein, combined with Middle High German stein ('rock, stone castle'), meaning 'Marquart's rock-castle'.

b_frontenhausen.first_mention_attestation: First documented around 1100 CE through the comital family of the Counts of Frontenhausen.
b_frontenhausen.etymology_analysis: Formed from the Old High German personal name Franto and hūson (dative plural of hūs, 'house'), meaning 'at the houses of Franto'.

b_dornberg.first_mention_attestation: First documented around 1074 CE when Dietmarus de Dornberch witnessed donations by Archbishop Gebhard of Salzburg to Admont Abbey.
b_dornberg.etymology_analysis: Compounded from Old High German dorn ('thorn, thornbush') and berg ('hill'), referring to the thorn-covered hill near Erharting on which the castle stood.

b_ortenburg.first_mention_attestation: First attested around 1120 CE when Rapoto I of Sponheim built Ortenberg Castle, styling himself Count of Ortenberg by 1134 CE.
b_ortenburg.etymology_analysis: Originally Ortenberg, from Old High German ort ('point, spur, corner') and berg/burc ('hill/fortress'), referring to the castle's position on a projecting ridge; later standardized to -burg.

b_burghausen.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1025 CE as an Imperial estate (Reichsgut) named Burghausen.
b_burghausen.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old High German burg ('fortress, castle') and hūson ('at the houses'), denoting the settlement beneath the hilltop fortress overlooking the Salzach.

b_geisenhausen.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 980 CE in a Bavarian charter.
b_geisenhausen.etymology_analysis: Formed from the Old High German personal name Gīso and hūson ('at the houses'), meaning 'settlement of Gīso'.

b_erding.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 788 CE as Ardeoingas, referring to the Carolingian royal manor (Königshof) at Altenerding.
b_erding.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Bavarian personal name Ardeo plus the Germanic associative suffix -ingas ('settlement of the people of Ardeo'), attested as Ardeoingas in 788 CE and later contracted to Erding.

b_ingolstadt.first_mention_attestation: First documented on 6 February 806 CE in Charlemagne's Divisio Regnorum as Ingoldes stat.
b_ingolstadt.etymology_analysis: From Old High German Ingoldes stat, meaning 'the place/stead of Ingold', combining the personal name Ingold in the genitive with stat ('place').

b_munchsmunster.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a Benedictine monastery by Duke Tassilo III of Bavaria in the late 8th century (c. 788 CE), around which the settlement grew.
b_munchsmunster.etymology_analysis: Compounded from Middle High German münch ('monk') and münster ('monastery, minster', from Latin monasterium), literally 'monks' monastery'.

b_niederschonenfeld.first_mention_attestation: First documented on 9 January 1241 CE when the Bishop of Augsburg confirmed the transfer of a Cistercian nunnery to Schoenenveldt.
b_niederschonenfeld.etymology_analysis: Literally 'lower fair field', combining Middle High German schœne ('fair, pleasant') and velt ('field') with the later qualifier Nieder- ('lower') to distinguish it from nearby Oberschönenfeld.

b_munchen.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1158 CE in the Augsburger Schied (arbitration of Emperor Frederick Barbarossa) as Munichen, following Henry the Lion's establishment of a toll bridge over the Isar.
b_munchen.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old/Middle High German Munichen, the dative plural of munih ('monk'), meaning 'at/by the monks', referring to the monks of Tegernsee Abbey who maintained a nearby settlement.

b_aheim.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1226 CE under the name Aheim am Würmsee (modern Starnberg); the nearby fishing hamlet Achheim was attested earlier in 948 CE as Ouiheim, still after 867 CE.
b_aheim.etymology_analysis: The historical name Aheim derives from Old High German aha ('water, stream') or ouwa ('floodplain') and heim ('homestead, settlement'), referring to the settlement at the northern end of Lake Starnberg (formerly Würmsee).

b_wolfratshausen.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1003 CE as Wolveradeshusun.
b_wolfratshausen.etymology_analysis: Attested as Wolveradeshusun in 1003 CE, combining the Germanic personal name Wolfrat (Wolverad) in the genitive with Old High German hūson ('at the houses').

b_passau.first_mention_attestation: Attested around 150 CE in Ptolemy's Geography as Boiodurum and in late Roman sources (Notitia Dignitatum, c. 400 CE) as Batavis, from which the modern name Passau derives.
b_passau.etymology_analysis: Derived from the late Roman fort name Castra Batava / Batavis (named after the Batavian auxiliary unit garrisoned at the confluence of the Danube, Inn, and Ilz), which evolved via Old High German sound shifts into Passau.

b_waldkirchen.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1203 CE as a settlement in the Bavarian Forest.
b_waldkirchen.etymology_analysis: Compounded from German Wald ('forest') and Kirche ('church', in the dative plural), literally '(at the) church in the forest'.

b_scharding.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 806 CE as Scardinga, a farmstead belonging to the Bishopric of Passau.
b_scharding.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Bavarian personal name Scardo with the Germanic -inga suffix ('settlement of the people of Scardo'), attested as Scardinga in 806 CE.

b_deggendorf.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1002 CE in a charter for Niedermünster Abbey in Regensburg.
b_deggendorf.etymology_analysis: Formed from an Old High German personal name (Dekko or Teggo) and dorf ('village'), meaning 'village of Dekko'.

b_regensburg.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 179 CE on the Roman building inscription of Castra Regina, the legionary fortress of Legio III Italica founded under Emperor Marcus Aurelius.
b_regensburg.etymology_analysis: Derived from the river Regen (Latin Regana, whence Roman Castra Regina, 'fortress on the Regen') combined with Old High German burg ('fortress, walled town').

historical_names.name: Castra Regina
historical_names.source: Castra Regina building inscription (179 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman legionary camp Castra Regina founded in 179 CE; also attested in early medieval sources as Radasbona.

historical_names.name: Radasbona
historical_names.source: Castra Regina building inscription (179 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman legionary camp Castra Regina founded in 179 CE; also attested in early medieval sources as Radasbona.

b_tegernheim.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 901 CE under the name Tegernheim.
b_tegernheim.etymology_analysis: Compounded from Old High German tegar ('large, wide') and heim ('homestead, settlement'), meaning 'large settlement'.

b_abensberg.first_mention_attestation: First documented around 1138 CE as Abensberg.
b_abensberg.etymology_analysis: Named after the river Abens combined with German Berg ('hill'), referring to the fortified hill settlement overlooking the Abens.

b_leonsberg.first_mention_attestation: First attested around 1200 CE when a branch of the Counts of Altendorf established themselves in the Isar valley near Pilsting as the Counts of Leonsberg.
b_leonsberg.etymology_analysis: Compounded from the personal name Leo (or Middle High German lewe/leo, 'lion') and berc ('hill'), designating the hilltop castle of the Counts of Leonsberg.

b_rothenburg.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1256 CE as Rottenburg in Lower Bavaria.
b_rothenburg.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German rōt ('red') and burc ('castle'), referring to a red-roofed or red-brick/stone castle above the Große Laber river.

b_freising.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 724 CE with Saint Corbinian's mission to the Agilolfing ducal seat (Frigisinga), with the diocese formally organized by Saint Boniface in 739 CE.
b_freising.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Germanic personal name Frigiso (or Friso) with the associative suffix -inga ('settlement of the kin of Frigiso'), attested in Latinized form as Frigisinga.

b_ilmunster.first_mention_attestation: First documented in a contemporary written record in 921 CE; although later Tegernsee Abbey tradition attributes the monastery's founding to 746 or 762 CE, historians regard those 8th-century dates as unverified.
b_ilmunster.etymology_analysis: Compounded from the river name Ilm and Old High German munistiri ('monastery, minster', from Latin monasterium), denoting the abbey on the Ilm.

b_kammersberg.etymology_analysis: Named after the parish church dedicated to Saint Peter, located on the Kammersberg ('chamber hill', from Middle High German kamer, denoting a lordly or episcopal domain).

b_murau.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1250 CE as Murowe.
b_murau.etymology_analysis: Attested as Murowe in 1250 CE, combining the river name Mur with Middle High German ouwe ('water-meadow, floodplain').

b_irdning.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1140 CE under the forms Idenich and Ydnich.
b_irdning.etymology_analysis: Attested as Idenich/Ydnich in 1140 CE, originating from an Alpine Slavic toponym in -ik that was later Germanized with the -ing ending.

b_tamsweg.etymology_analysis: Likely a hybrid or Germanized compound of an early personal or local name (Tams-) and Middle High German wëc ('way, road'), reflecting Tamsweg's position on a Lungau transit route.

b_klagenfurt.first_mention_attestation: First documented between 1192 and 1199 CE as Forum Chlagenvurth.
b_klagenfurt.etymology_analysis: Attested as Forum Chlagenvurth in 1192–1199 CE; scholars link the first element to a Romance or Slovene water-sprite/water-crossing term (cf. Slovene Celovec), folk-etymologized into German Klage ('lament') + Furt ('ford').

b_sankt_veit.first_mention_attestation: First documented in an 1131 CE deed mentioning the Saint Vitus Church.
b_sankt_veit.etymology_analysis: Named for the church of Saint Vitus (Sankt Veit), with the river locator an der Glan ('on the Glan', from Celtic *glanos, 'clear, bright').

b_wolfsberg.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1178 CE as Wolfsperch (referring to the castle above the town) in a deed of St. Paul's Abbey in the Lavanttal.

morphemes.translation: of the wolf (or personal name Wolf)

b_wolfsberg.etymology_analysis: Attested as Wolfsperch in 1178 CE, from Middle High German wolf ('wolf', or a personal name Wolf) and berc ('mountain, hill').

b_knittelfeld.etymology_analysis: Compounded from Middle High German knüttel ('cudgel, club', or a personal/field name) and velt ('field, plain'), describing the settlement on the Aichfeld plain.

b_judenburg.first_mention_attestation: First documented in a 1074 CE staple-right deed as mercatum Judinburch.
b_judenburg.etymology_analysis: Attested as mercatum Judinburch in 1074 CE, from Middle High German jude ('Jew') and burc ('borough, fortified town'), reflecting the prominent role of Jewish merchants in the medieval trading settlement.

b_admont.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 859 CE as Ademundi (predating the 1074 CE foundation of Admont Abbey).
b_admont.etymology_analysis: Derived from Latin ad montes ('at the mountains'), describing the settlement's location in a valley basin surrounded by the Ennstaler Alps.

b_villach.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 878 CE as ad pontem Uillach ('at the bridge of Villach') in a charter of King Carloman, eleven years after the 867 CE baseline.
b_villach.etymology_analysis: Derived from a Gallo-Roman estate name *Villanum or *Villiacum (from Latin villa, 'country estate', with the Celtic-Latin -acum suffix), attested as Uillach in 878 CE.

b_feldkirchen.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 888 CE as Ueldchiricha ('Church in the Fields') in a charter of Arnulf of Carinthia, post-dating the 867 CE baseline.
b_feldkirchen.etymology_analysis: Attested as Ueldchiricha in 888 CE, from Old High German feld ('field') and kirihha ('church'), literally 'church in the fields'.

b_spittal.first_mention_attestation: First documented in an 1191 CE deed issued by the Archbishop of Salzburg, following the foundation of a hospital (Spital) by the Counts of Ortenburg.
b_spittal.etymology_analysis: Named after the medieval hospice (Middle High German spitāl, from Latin hospitale) founded at the crossing of the Lieser and Drava (Drau) rivers.

b_kranj.first_mention_attestation: Attested in late antique written sources from the 5th century and around 670 CE in the Ravenna Cosmography as Carnium.
b_kranj.etymology_analysis: Borrowed into Slavic (*Kornь) from Late Latin/Romance Carnium, which derives from the Celtic tribe of the Carnī (ultimately from Celtic *karno-, 'peak, hill, stone pile').

b_krsko.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 895 CE when Emperor Arnulf of Carinthia granted Krško (with Brestanica) to his retainer Valtun, post-dating the 867 CE baseline; the nearby Roman port of Neviodunum (modern Drnovo) was founded in the 1st century CE.
b_krsko.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Slovene river name Krka (itself from a pre-Slavic hydronym, cf. German Gurkfeld) with the Slavic adjectival/toponymic suffix -sko.

historical_names.name: Neviodunum
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder / Roman inscriptions (1st century CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman municipium and river port of Neviodunum at nearby Drnovo, founded in the 1st century CE.

b_kamnik.first_mention_attestation: The name Kamnik is first mentioned in the 11th century (1061 CE), and the settlement was first documented as a town in 1229 CE as a trading post between Ljubljana and Celje.

morphemes.translation: toponymic suffix denoting a place characterized by

b_kamnik.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Slovene noun kamen ('stone'), originally Proto-Slavic *kam(en)ьnikъ referring to a rocky or stony place; its historical German name Stein ('stone') is a direct semantic calque.

b_ljubljana.first_mention_attestation: Ljubljana is first attested in written records in the first half of the 12th century, appearing in 1144 CE under its German name Laibach and in 1146 CE as Luwigana.
b_ljubljana.etymology_analysis: The exact origin of Ljubljana is debated among linguists, with leading hypotheses deriving it either from the Slavic root ljub- ('to love, dear') via an earlier river or personal name (*Ljubovid / Ljubija), or from a pre-Slavic substrate adapted into Slavic and German (Laibach).

historical_names.name: Emona
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (c. 77 CE); Roman colony founded c. 14–15 CE
historical_names.notes: The Roman castrum and colonia of Emona stood on the site of modern Ljubljana before being abandoned after the 6th century.

historical_names.name: Colonia Iulia Aemona
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (c. 77 CE); Roman colony founded c. 14–15 CE
historical_names.notes: The Roman castrum and colonia of Emona stood on the site of modern Ljubljana before being abandoned after the 6th century.

b_dobovec.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Dobovec (Municipality of Trbovlje); while prehistoric mound graves exist in the area, the settlement itself is unattested in early medieval records.
b_dobovec.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Slovene adjective dobov, itself from Common Slavic *dǫbъ ('oak, deciduous tree'), combined with the toponymic suffix -ec, referring to local oak woodland.

b_rudolfswerde.first_mention_attestation: First attested on 7 April 1365 CE as Růdolfswerde, when Habsburg Duke Rudolf IV of Austria founded the town and granted it municipal rights.

eponym.details: Named Rudolfswerde (later Rudolfswerth) after Rudolf IV, Duke of Austria (1339–1365), who founded and chartered the town on 7 April 1365.

morphemes.translation: river island, peninsula, elevated land by water

b_rudolfswerde.etymology_analysis: The historical German name Rudolfswerde combines the personal name of Duke Rudolf IV of Austria with Middle High German werd ('island, peninsula'), referring to the bend of the Krka River; the modern Slovene name Novo Mesto literally means 'new town'.

b_ribnica.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written documents in 1220 CE as Rewenitz (later Reiwencz in 1241 and Reiuenz in 1263).
b_ribnica.etymology_analysis: Originally a hydronym derived from Slovene riba ('fish') with the suffix -nica, denoting a stream abounding in fish and, by extension, the settlement established along its banks (adapted into German as Reifnitz).

b_eichtstad.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 741 CE as the regio Eihstat, when Saint Willibald was sent by Saint Boniface to establish the Diocese of Eichstätt on the site of a former Roman station.
b_eichtstad.etymology_analysis: From Old High German Eihstat, compounding eih ('oak') and stat ('place, site'), meaning 'oak place' or 'settlement by the oaks'.

b_hirschberg.first_mention_attestation: Built between 1170 and 1200 CE by the Counts of Grögling-Dollnstein, Hirschberg is first attested in 1205 CE when the family styled themselves Grafen von Hirschberg.
b_hirschberg.etymology_analysis: A German topographic name combining Middle High German hirz/hirsch ('stag') and berc ('hill, mountain'), referring to the ridge above Beilngries where the castle was erected.

b_neue_weissenburg.first_mention_attestation: The name Weißenburg is first attested in a royal deed in 867 CE (as Wizinburg), on the site of the earlier Roman fort Biriciana.
b_neue_weissenburg.etymology_analysis: From Old High German Wizinburg, compounding wîz ('white') and burg ('fortress, stronghold'), referring to the light-colored limestone fortifications or remains of the Roman fort.

historical_names.name: Biriciana
historical_names.source: Tabula Peutingeriana (4th century CE); Roman fort founded c. 90 CE
historical_names.notes: Roman border fort and settlement on the Limes, recorded as Biriciana on the Tabula Peutingeriana.

b_hohenburg.first_mention_attestation: The castle was constructed around 1000 CE in the Nordgau march, and the name Hohenburg is first documented in 1080 CE with Ernst von Hohenburg.
b_hohenburg.etymology_analysis: From Old High German hôch ('high') and burg ('castle, fortress'), describing the elevated hilltop fortification above the Lauterach valley.

b_cham.first_mention_attestation: Benedictine monks from St. Emmeram's Abbey in Regensburg founded the monastery at Chammünster in 748 CE; the fortified settlement was later attested as civitas Camma in 976 CE.
b_cham.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Celtic hydronym *kambos ('bend, curvature'), referring to the winding Chamb stream that joins the Regen River near Cham.

b_wenzenbach.first_mention_attestation: Attested in undated Regensburg traditions as Menzinpah under Bishop Ambricho of Regensburg (r. 864–891 CE); because the charter cannot be dated specifically to <= 867 CE, it is placed c. 880 CE.
b_wenzenbach.etymology_analysis: From Old High German Menzinpah, combining the personal name Manzo with pah ('brook, stream'), meaning 'at Manzo's brook', which later evolved into Wenzenbach.

b_leuchtenburg.first_mention_attestation: Leuchtenberg is first attested in written charters in 1124 CE as the seat of the Landgraves of Leuchtenberg.
b_leuchtenburg.etymology_analysis: A German hilltop name combining a root related to Middle High German liuhten ('to shine, bright') with berg ('hill, mountain'), referring to a prominent, visible peak.

b_kulmbach.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Kulma in a deed of gift recorded in the Alcuin Bible between 1028 and 1040 CE (traditionally dated c. 1035 CE).
b_kulmbach.etymology_analysis: Derived from the stream name Culmin-aha (later Culmna, and reinterpreted as Kulmbach with -bach 'brook'), meaning 'stream descending from the mountain peak'.

b_bayreuth.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1194 CE as Baierrute in a document issued by Bishop Otto II of Bamberg.
b_bayreuth.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German Baierrute, combining Baier ('Bavarian', referring to settlers from Bavaria) with -rute / -reuth ('forest clearing'), meaning 'clearing of the Bavarians'.

b_parsberg.first_mention_attestation: First reliably attested in 1205 CE as Castrum Bartesperch; earlier 933 CE references in Rüxner's 1530 tournament book are spurious.
b_parsberg.etymology_analysis: From Old High German Bartesperch, combining the personal name Barto with berg ('hill, mountain'), referring to the fortified hill of Barto.

b_lengenfeld.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1123 CE as Lengenfelt in a charter of Ensdorf Abbey, and as castrum Lengenvelt in 1205 CE.
