b_lengenfeld.etymology_analysis: From Old High German *ze demo langîn velde ('at the long field'), describing the broad open plain along the Naab River, later prefixed with Burg- ('castle') in the 14th century.

b_sulzbach.first_mention_attestation: Counts of Sulzbach are first documented in royal charters in 1007 CE (with a legendary foundation date of 1024 CE), although archaeological excavations show castle occupation from the 8th century.
b_sulzbach.etymology_analysis: From Old High German sulz ('brine, salty/mineral water') and bach ('brook, stream'), naming the settlement after the mineral-rich stream at the foot of the castle rock; Rosenberg was merged in 1934.

b_neumarkt.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a written document in 1135 CE as a planned market settlement in the Upper Palatinate.
b_neumarkt.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German niuwe market ('new market'), referring to a planned high-medieval market town established along the trade route between Nuremberg and Regensburg.

b_amstetten.first_mention_attestation: The first written mention of Amstetten itself dates to 1111 CE, following the earlier nearby settlement of Ulmerfeld (attested 995 CE).
b_amstetten.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old High German an den stetten ('at the homesteads/places'), a locative dative plural construction denoting a cluster of settlements.

b_waidhofen.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written sources in 1186 CE as an economic center of the Ybbstal region.
b_waidhofen.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German weide ('pasture, meadow, or hunting ground') and hofen ('at the farmsteads/manors'), denoting estates situated on pastureland along the Ybbs River.

b_freistadt.first_mention_attestation: Founded before 1220 CE as a Babenberg border town, Freistadt is first attested in writing in 1241 CE as Frienstat (and in 1277 as Vreinstat).
b_freistadt.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German vrî stat ('free town'), reflecting the tax and trade privileges granted to attract settlers to the Bohemian frontier.

b_spitz.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written records in 830 CE in the Wachau valley along the Danube.
b_spitz.etymology_analysis: From Old High German spizzi ('pointed, sharp spur'), referring to the pointed terrain or spur where the Spitzer stream meets the Danube.

b_zwettl.first_mention_attestation: Founded by the knights of Kuenring, Zwettl is first attested in a monastery record of Zwettl Abbey in October 1139 CE.
b_zwettl.etymology_analysis: Borrowed into German from Slavic *světьla ('bright place, clearing, glade'), referring to a cleared area in the wooded Waldviertel.

b_gmund.first_mention_attestation: The site is first documented in a boundary charter of 1179 CE as concursus duorum rivulorum ('confluence of two streams'), with the town founded in the late 12th or early 13th century and recorded as a market in 1278 CE.
b_gmund.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German gemünde ('confluence, river mouth'), referring to the meeting of the Lainsitz and Braunaubach streams.

b_hohenau.first_mention_attestation: Although the settlement was established between 1043 and 1050 CE, its first written attestation dates to 1148 CE in a record of its parish church.
b_hohenau.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German hôhen ouwe ('high water-meadow'), referring to elevated meadowland along the March (Morava) River.

b_laa.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written records in 1150 CE as a settlement at a ford across the Thaya River, before being acquired by the Babenbergs around 1190 CE.
b_laa.etymology_analysis: From Old High German lâ (cognate with Middle High German lôch/lâ, 'marsh, boggy meadow'), describing the wet floodplain along the Thaya River.

b_mistelbach.first_mention_attestation: First attested in official deeds around 1130 CE in the Weinviertel region of Lower Austria.
b_mistelbach.etymology_analysis: A German hydronym combining Middle High German mistel ('mistletoe') and bach ('brook'), naming the settlement after the local stream.

b_krems.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 995 CE as Chremisa in an imperial charter issued by Emperor Otto III.
b_krems.etymology_analysis: Named after the Krems River (Chremisa), an ancient pre-Germanic or Celtic hydronym commonly linked to either wild garlic (*krem-) or stony/gravelly water.

b_wild.first_mention_attestation: First attested around 1135 CE as Prvnn (with the constituent village Dappach also attested in 1135 CE); the surrounding forest region is called Die Wild.
b_wild.etymology_analysis: Named after Die Wild, the forested region in the Waldviertel from Middle High German wilde ('wilderness, dense forest').

b_horn.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the mid-11th century (c. 1050 CE) as Hornarun, referring to the church settlement near St. Stephen's.
b_horn.etymology_analysis: From Old High German horn ('horn, projecting spur or river bend'), referring to the curved bend of the Taffa stream or a wedge-shaped terrain feature.

b_haugsdorf.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written documents in 1108 CE in the Pulkau valley of Lower Austria.
b_haugsdorf.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German Hûgesdorf, combining the personal name Hûg (Hugo) with dorf ('village'), meaning 'Hugo's village'.

b_sankt_polten.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 799 CE as Treisma (and in the 823 CE Confirmatio Ludovici Pii), identifying the early medieval settlement and monastery at St. Pölten along the Traisen River.
b_sankt_polten.etymology_analysis: Derived from Saint Hippolytus of Rome, to whom the abbey was dedicated (attested as monasterium Sti Ypoliti in 976 CE), clipped through Sand Pelten (1297) to St. Pölten; the earlier 799 CE name Treisma derives from the Traisen River.

historical_names.name: Aelium Cetium
historical_names.source: Roman municipium charter under Hadrian (c. 122 CE) and Itinerarium Antonini
historical_names.notes: The Roman city of Aelium Cetium stood on the site of the historic center of St. Pölten from the 2nd to 4th centuries CE.

historical_names.name: Cetium
historical_names.source: Roman municipium charter under Hadrian (c. 122 CE) and Itinerarium Antonini
historical_names.notes: The Roman city of Aelium Cetium stood on the site of the historic center of St. Pölten from the 2nd to 4th centuries CE.

b_mariazell.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1157 CE when the Benedictine monk Magnus established a chapel with a statue of the Virgin Mary in the Zellertal.
b_mariazell.etymology_analysis: From Maria ('Virgin Mary') and Zell (Latin cella, 'monastic cell or chapel'), meaning 'Mary in the cell', referring to the 1157 CE pilgrimage chapel.

b_wieselburg.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 976 CE when a castle (Zwisila) was erected at the confluence of the Great and Little Erlauf rivers.
b_wieselburg.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old High German zwisila ('fork, confluence', referring to the junction of the Great and Little Erlauf rivers), later folk-etymologized with -burg ('castle') into Wieselburg.

b_vienna.first_mention_attestation: First attested in medieval sources in 881 CE as Wenia in the Annales iuvavenses (Salzburg Annals), recording a battle against the Magyars.
b_vienna.etymology_analysis: The German name Wien (attested as Wenia in 881 CE, Latinized as Vienna) derives from the Wien River, ultimately from Celtic *Vedunia ('forest river').

historical_names.name: Vindobona
historical_names.source: Ptolemy, Geographia (c. 150 CE); Roman legionary camp built c. 97 CE
historical_names.notes: Roman military camp and municipium on the site of Vienna's first district, abandoned in the 5th century.

b_ernstbrunn.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written documents in 1045 CE as Ernustisprunnin.
b_ernstbrunn.etymology_analysis: From Old High German Ernustisprunnin, combining the personal name Ernust (Ernst) with brunno ('spring, fountain'), meaning 'at Ernst's spring'.

b_floridsdorf.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1786 CE when Floridus Leeb, Provost of Klosterneuburg Abbey, granted land east of Am Spitz to settlers and the new settlement was named Floridsdorf in his honor.

eponym.details: Named after Floridus Leeb (1731–1799), Provost of Klosterneuburg Abbey, who granted land to settlers in 1786.

b_floridsdorf.etymology_analysis: A modern German compound combining the personal name Floridus (after Provost Floridus Leeb) with dorf ('village').

b_padun.first_mention_attestation: The Germanic name Padun is first attested in 869 CE when King Carloman held court at the palatinate there.
b_padun.etymology_analysis: From Old High German Padun (dative plural of bad, 'at the baths'), directly translating the Roman name Aquae in reference to the town's thermal sulfur springs.

historical_names.name: Aquae
historical_names.source: Itinerarium Antonini (c. 300 CE); Roman spa settlement established under Claudius (41–54 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman thermal bath settlement known as Aquae ('the waters'), directly translated into Old High German as Padun.

b_bruck.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written documents in 1074 CE as Aschirichesprucca.

morphemes.translation: personal name Aschirich (dropped in later form)

b_bruck.etymology_analysis: Originally attested as Aschirichesprucca ('Aschirich's bridge'), referring to a bridge crossing the Leitha River, later shortened to Bruck an der Leitha.

b_berchtesgaden.first_mention_attestation: First attested between 1102 and 1105 CE as berthercatmen in connection with the foundation of Berchtesgaden Priory.
b_berchtesgaden.etymology_analysis: From Old High German berthercatmen, combining the personal name Berhther with gadem ('chamber, house, enclosed dwelling'), meaning 'Berchther's house/enclosure'.

b_laukental.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1150 CE as in Liuckentale in a charter mentioning the church of St. Johann in Tirol.

morphemes.translation: valley/river root (possibly personal or stream name)

b_laukental.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German Liuckental, combining the regional/stream element Liuchin- with tal ('valley'), designating the valley of the Großache in Tyrol.

b_kitzbuhel.first_mention_attestation: First attested between 1178 and 1182 CE as Chizbuhel in a Chiemsee Abbey charter naming a Marchwardus de Chizbuhel.
b_kitzbuhel.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German Chizbuhel, combining the Bavarian clan name Chizzo with bühel ('hill, mound'), meaning 'hill of the Chizzo clan'.

b_hallstatt.first_mention_attestation: Despite prehistoric salt mining dating back to the Neolithic and Iron Age, no early medieval written attestation survives; Hallstatt is first documented in 1311 CE when it received market rights.
b_hallstatt.etymology_analysis: A classic Alpine salt-mining toponym combining hall ('salt, saltworks') with stat ('place, site'), meaning 'salt-mining place'.

b_liezen.first_mention_attestation: First attested around 1130 CE as Luecen in a property register of Admont Abbey.
b_liezen.etymology_analysis: Adapted into German from a Slavic toponym (related to *luža, 'wet meadow, bog, moor'), describing the marshy Enns valley floor.

historical_names.name: Stiriate
historical_names.source: Itinerarium Antonini / Tabula Peutingeriana (Roman road station)
historical_names.notes: Roman road and relay station (mansio) located in the Liezen area along the Pyhrn Pass route.

b_wels.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 776 CE as Castrum Uueles in early medieval written records, succeeding the Roman city of Ovilava.

morphemes.translation: settlement on the bend (of the Traun River)

b_wels.etymology_analysis: Possibly of Celtic origin (meaning 'settlement on the bend of the Traun River'), recorded in 776 CE as Castrum Uueles and evolving into modern German Wels.

historical_names.name: Ovilava
historical_names.source: Roman municipal grant under Emperor Hadrian (c. 120 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman provincial capital of Noricum on the site of modern Wels.

historical_names.name: Municipium Ovilava
historical_names.source: Roman municipal grant under Emperor Hadrian (c. 120 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman provincial capital of Noricum on the site of modern Wels.

historical_names.name: Colonia Aurelia Antoniana Ovilabis
historical_names.source: Roman municipal grant under Emperor Hadrian (c. 120 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman provincial capital of Noricum on the site of modern Wels.

b_linz.first_mention_attestation: The name Linz is first attested in a charter dated 20 June 799 CE (together with St. Martin's Church).
b_linz.etymology_analysis: Evolved from Roman Lentia, itself derived from the Celtic root *lentos ('bent, curved'), referring to the bend in the Danube River at Linz.

b_steyr.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 980 CE as Styraburg, a fortress erected above the Steyr River by the Traungau counts.
b_steyr.etymology_analysis: Named after the Steyr (Stiria) River, a hydronym of Celtic origin.

b_leonfelden.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the early 13th century (c. 1200 CE) as Lobenwelt, and granted market rights before 1356 CE.
b_leonfelden.etymology_analysis: First recorded as Lobenwelt, combining an uncertain first element (later reinterpreted via Saint Leonard as Leon-) with Middle High German velt ('field, clearing'); Bad ('spa') was added in the modern era.

b_salzburg.first_mention_attestation: The German name Salzburg is first attested in 739 CE in Willibald's report on the organization of the Bavarian dioceses by Saint Boniface.
b_salzburg.etymology_analysis: From Old High German salz ('salt') and burg ('settlement, city'), referring to the salt barges taxed along the Salzach River.

historical_names.name: Iuvavum
historical_names.source: Roman municipal grant under Emperor Claudius (45 CE) and Pliny the Elder (c. 77 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman municipium on the site of Salzburg, later revived by Saint Rupert around 696 CE.

historical_names.name: Municipium Claudium Iuvavum
historical_names.source: Roman municipal grant under Emperor Claudius (45 CE) and Pliny the Elder (c. 77 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman municipium on the site of Salzburg, later revived by Saint Rupert around 696 CE.

b_braunau.first_mention_attestation: Braunau is first attested in writing in 1120 CE under the spelling Prounaw, receiving town rights in 1260 CE.
b_braunau.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German brûn ('brown', or a personal name) and ouwe ('water-meadow, floodplain'), denoting a floodplain along the Inn River.

historical_names.name: Ranshofen
historical_names.source: Charter of 788 CE (first written mention of Rantersdorf / Ranshofen)
historical_names.notes: Ranshofen (now a district of Braunau am Inn) was already attested in 788 CE as a Carolingian royal estate.

historical_names.name: Rantersdorf
historical_names.source: Charter of 788 CE (first written mention of Rantersdorf / Ranshofen)
historical_names.notes: Ranshofen (now a district of Braunau am Inn) was already attested in 788 CE as a Carolingian royal estate.

b_traunstein.first_mention_attestation: Traunstein is first documented in 1245 as Trauwenstein in a manuscript of the Baumburg monastery, referring to a fortified lordly residence on the Traun River.

morphemes.translation: Traun River (from Old High German Truna)

b_traunstein.etymology_analysis: The toponym combines the hydronym of the Traun River (attested in 790 CE as Truna) with Middle High German stein ('stone' or 'stone castle'), denoting a fortified seat overlooking the river.

historical_names.name: ad Trun
historical_names.source: Salzburg church records (790 CE) listing possessions 'ad Trun'
historical_names.notes: Church possessions along the Traun River are recorded as 'ad Trun' in 790 CE, prior to the 1245 mention of the castle town Trauwenstein.

b_hallein.first_mention_attestation: Salt mining at the site is first documented in a 1198 CE deed, with the name Hallein appearing in the early 13th century.
b_hallein.etymology_analysis: Hallein belongs to the South German and Austrian group of Hall- toponyms associated with salt extraction, combining hall ('saltworks') with a diminutive suffix (-lîn / -ein) to distinguish it from nearby Reichenhall.

b_laufen.first_mention_attestation: Laufen is first mentioned in a Bavarian charter of 748 CE as a settlement beside the rapids of the Salzach River.
b_laufen.etymology_analysis: The name derives from Old High German loufa ('rapids' or 'watercourse'), referring to the narrow bend and rapids of the Salzach River where salt barges had to be unloaded.

b_schaumberg.first_mention_attestation: Schaunberg (also spelled Schaumberg) is first attested in 1160 CE in a document naming Heinricus de Scovenberch.
b_schaumberg.etymology_analysis: Derived from Middle High German schouwen ('to look/watch') and berc ('hill/mountain'), the name means 'lookout hill' and refers to the strategic castle ridge overlooking the Danube plain.

historical_names.name: Ovilava
historical_names.source: Roman imperial inscriptions and Tabula Peutingeriana (2nd–4th century CE) for nearby Wels
historical_names.notes: Roman Ovilava (modern Wels), elevated to a municipium under Hadrian in the 2nd century CE, served as the regional urban center in Upper Austria prior to the high medieval rise of Schaunberg.

b_strasswalchen.first_mention_attestation: Straßwalchen is first documented on 11 April 799 CE as Strazzuualaha in early Salzburg records.
b_strasswalchen.etymology_analysis: The Old High German compound Strazzuualaha combines strazza ('paved road', from Latin strata) with walaha ('Romance-speakers'), denoting a surviving Romanized population living along the old Roman road.

b_ried.first_mention_attestation: Ried is first mentioned on 13 November 1136 CE as a castle of the Bavarian sovereign and seat of the noble house of Ried.

morphemes.language: Old High German / Middle High German

b_ried.etymology_analysis: The name derives from Old High German riet ('reed' or 'marshland'), referring to the reedy banks at the confluence of the Oberach and Breitsach streams.

b_graz.first_mention_attestation: Graz is first documented in 1128 CE as a settlement and fortress in Styria under the Babenberg margraves.
b_graz.etymology_analysis: The German name Graz is adapted from Slovene Gradec, a diminutive of grad ('castle, stronghold'), meaning 'small castle', referring to the early Slavic hillfort on the Schlossberg.

b_koflach.first_mention_attestation: The area of Köflach is first recorded in 1103 CE when Duke Henry III of Carinthia granted rights in the Piber valley to St. Lambrecht Abbey, and the village was elevated to a market in 1170.
b_koflach.etymology_analysis: Derived from Alpine German Kofel ('crag, rocky summit') with the collective suffix -ach, denoting a settlement situated among rocky foothills.

b_kapfenberg.first_mention_attestation: The church of St. Martin at Kapfenberg is first mentioned in 1096 CE, while Oberkapfenberg Castle is documented in 1173 as Castrum chaffenberch.
b_kapfenberg.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German kapfen ('to gaze, watch') and berc ('hill'), the name means 'lookout mountain', describing the strategic hilltop castle overlooking the Mürz valley.

b_leoben.first_mention_attestation: Leoben is first attested in historical sources in 904 CE under the name Liupina.
b_leoben.etymology_analysis: The name originates from the Slavic root ljub- ('beloved, dear', or a personal name derived from it) with the suffix -ina, yielding Liupina (904 CE), later Germanized to Liuben and Leoben.

b_feldbach.first_mention_attestation: Feldbach is first mentioned in 1188 CE under the form Velwinbach during the medieval German colonization of eastern Styria.
b_feldbach.etymology_analysis: The earliest attested form Velwinbach (1188) derives from Middle High German velwe ('willow') and bach ('stream'), meaning 'willow brook', later reinterpreted by folk etymology as Feld-bach ('field brook').

b_liebnitz.first_mention_attestation: Leibnitz is first documented as Lipnizza in an imperial charter issued by Emperor Otto the Great on 7 March 970 CE.
b_liebnitz.etymology_analysis: The early form Lipnizza derives from Slavic lipa ('linden tree') and the locative suffix -nica, meaning 'place of linden trees', which was later Germanized to Leibnitz.

historical_names.name: Flavia Solva
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE), and Roman Noricum municipal inscriptions
historical_names.notes: The Roman municipium of Flavia Solva, chartered under the Flavian emperors in the 1st century CE, stood immediately adjacent to modern Leibnitz at Wagna.

b_maribor.first_mention_attestation: Maribor is first mentioned in 1164 CE as the castle Marchburch ('border castle') on Pyramid Hill in the March of Styria.
b_maribor.etymology_analysis: Originally attested as Middle High German Marchburch ('border castle', later Marburg), the name referred to the frontier fortress of the Styrian march; the modern Slovene name Maribor was adapted from Marburg in the 19th century.

b_windische_buhel.first_mention_attestation: Ljutomer is first attested in written records in 1211 CE as Lvtenwerde, with the fortified town recorded as Lvtenberch in 1249.

morphemes.translation: from German Lut(t)en- (possibly personal name or Slavic *ljutŭ 'fierce')

b_windische_buhel.etymology_analysis: First attested in German forms (Lvtenwerde 1211, Lvtenberch 1249, later Luttenberg), the name combines a personal or Slavic-borrowed stem with -werd ('river island') or -berg ('hill'); the modern Slovene name Ljutomer was coined in the 19th century.

b_murzzuschlag.first_mention_attestation: The settlement of Mürzzuschlag in the Duchy of Styria is first documented in 1227 CE.
b_murzzuschlag.etymology_analysis: The toponym pairs the hydronym Mürz (from Slavic Morica, 'little Mur') with Middle High German zuoslac ('woodland clearing' or 'allotment'), referring to a medieval clearing along the upper Mürz River.

b_ostfurstenfeld.first_mention_attestation: Fürstenfeld was founded around 1170 CE by Margrave Ottokar IV of Styria as a frontier fortress against Hungary.
b_ostfurstenfeld.etymology_analysis: Composed of Middle High German vürste ('prince') and velt ('field, plain'), the name literally means 'the prince's field', reflecting its foundation as a princely border stronghold.

b_pitten.first_mention_attestation: Pitten is first mentioned in a donation charter of 869 CE as ad Putinnu, confirming a grant by the nun Peretcunda to the Bishopric of Freising.
b_pitten.etymology_analysis: Attested in 869 CE as ad Putinnu (later Putina), the name is traced to a pre-Slavic root *Buda meaning 'reed' or 'sedge', referring to the once-marshy valley floor of the Pitten River.

b_oberwart.first_mention_attestation: Oberwart is first mentioned in historical documents in 1327 CE under the Latinized name Superior Eör as a Hungarian border-guard settlement.
b_oberwart.etymology_analysis: The German name Oberwart ('upper watchpost') is a direct translation of the Hungarian Felsőőr (attested in Latin as Superior Eör in 1327), referring to the upper guard settlement of the Hungarian gyepű border system.

b_brixen.first_mention_attestation: Brixen is first mentioned in 901 CE as Prihsna in a charter issued by King Louis the Child granting the territory to the Bishop of Säben.

morphemes.translation: root of uncertain pre-Germanic origin (possibly 'meadow' or 'fortified height')

b_brixen.etymology_analysis: The earliest attested form Prihsna (901 CE, later Prixina) is of pre-Roman (likely Celtic or Rhaetic) origin, whose exact root remains debated among toponymists; it evolved into German Brixen and Italian Bressanone.

historical_names.name: Sabiona
historical_names.source: Late Antique and early medieval episcopal records (Bishopric of Sabiona attested from the late 6th century CE)
historical_names.notes: The Bishopric of Sabiona (Säben), perched on a cliff near Klausen about 14 km southwest of Brixen, was the pre-867 episcopal seat before the bishops transferred their residence to Brixen around 960–1000 CE.

historical_names.name: Säben
historical_names.source: Late Antique and early medieval episcopal records (Bishopric of Sabiona attested from the late 6th century CE)
historical_names.notes: The Bishopric of Sabiona (Säben), perched on a cliff near Klausen about 14 km southwest of Brixen, was the pre-867 episcopal seat before the bishops transferred their residence to Brixen around 960–1000 CE.

b_bruneck.first_mention_attestation: Bruneck is first attested in 1256 CE as apud Bruneke, named after its founder Bishop Bruno von Kirchberg of Brixen.

eponym.details: Named after Bruno von Kirchberg (d. 1288), Prince-Bishop of Brixen, who founded the town and castle around 1256 CE.

morphemes.translation: Bruno (personal name of Bishop Bruno von Kirchberg)

b_bruneck.etymology_analysis: Bruneck combines the personal name of Bishop Bruno von Kirchberg with Middle High German ecke ('corner, rocky spur'), designating the fortified spur overlooking the Rienz valley.

b_innsbruck.first_mention_attestation: Innsbruck is first mentioned in a charter of 1180 CE as a market settlement on the Inn River, receiving town privileges in 1239.
b_innsbruck.etymology_analysis: The name combines the Celtic-derived hydronym Inn (Roman Aenus) with Middle High German brucke ('bridge'), literally meaning 'bridge over the Inn'.

historical_names.name: Veldidena
historical_names.source: Roman Itinerarium Antonini and 4th-century military records (Veldidena), later early medieval Wilten
historical_names.notes: The Roman army station Veldidena (modern Wilten, now a southern district of Innsbruck) was established by the 3rd–4th century CE and served as the primary settlement at the Inn crossing before Innsbruck's 12th-century foundation.

historical_names.name: Wilten
historical_names.source: Roman Itinerarium Antonini and 4th-century military records (Veldidena), later early medieval Wilten
historical_names.notes: The Roman army station Veldidena (modern Wilten, now a southern district of Innsbruck) was established by the 3rd–4th century CE and served as the primary settlement at the Inn crossing before Innsbruck's 12th-century foundation.

b_bozen.first_mention_attestation: Meran (Italian: Merano) is first mentioned in an 857 CE deed as Mairania.
b_bozen.etymology_analysis: The 857 CE form Mairania reflects a Romance/Latin estate name (praedium Marianum or Mairania), likely derived from the Roman personal name Marius or Latin major ('larger estate').

b_kufstein.first_mention_attestation: A church at Caofstein (Kufstein) is first mentioned in a 788 CE deed issued by Bishop Arno of Salzburg.

morphemes.translation: cup, hollow, or rounded crag (from kuofa)

b_kufstein.etymology_analysis: First attested as Caofstein (788 CE), the name likely combines Old High German kuofa ('vat, hollow') or a related terrain term with stein ('rock'), referring to the prominent limestone crag rising above the Inn valley.

b_lienz.first_mention_attestation: Lienz is first mentioned around 1030 CE as Luenzina in a deed issued by the Bishop of Brixen.
b_lienz.etymology_analysis: The 1030 CE form Luenzina is derived either from a Slavic hydronym/toponym (*Lončьnica, 'meadow/bend') or a pre-Roman substrate name, later contracted in German to Lienz.

historical_names.name: Aguntum
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE) for Roman Aguntum; Tassilo III foundation charter (769 CE) for Innichen
historical_names.notes: Roman Aguntum (attested by Pliny the Elder in 77 CE) lay 4 km east of Lienz, while Innichen Abbey (founded 769 CE) served as the primary early medieval center in the upper Drava/Puster valley.

historical_names.name: Innichen
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE) for Roman Aguntum; Tassilo III foundation charter (769 CE) for Innichen
historical_names.notes: Roman Aguntum (attested by Pliny the Elder in 77 CE) lay 4 km east of Lienz, while Innichen Abbey (founded 769 CE) served as the primary early medieval center in the upper Drava/Puster valley.

b_obervallach.first_mention_attestation: Vellach (Velach) is first documented in the second half of the 10th century (c. 957–993, commonly dated c. 967 CE) in a charter of Bishop Abraham of Freising.
b_obervallach.etymology_analysis: Obervellach pairs German Ober- ('upper', distinguishing it from Untervellach) with Velach, a Germanized Slavic toponym derived from *běl- ('white, bright') or *vel- ('great').

b_matrei.first_mention_attestation: The settlement of Matereie (Matrei in Osttirol) is first mentioned in an 1170 CE deed.
b_matrei.etymology_analysis: Attested as Matereie in 1170 CE, the name is of pre-Roman (likely Celtic or Alpine substrate) origin, possibly linked to *matra ('mother' or a mountain/water deity) or a pre-Indo-European mountain root.

b_feurs.first_mention_attestation: Feurs is attested in antiquity as Forum Segusiavorum by Ptolemy in his Geographia (c. 150 CE) and in Gallo-Roman inscriptions.
b_feurs.etymology_analysis: The modern French name Feurs is a direct phonetic contraction of Latin Forum (Segusiavorum) ('forum of the Segusiavi'), which also gave its name to the surrounding Forez region.

b_montbrison.first_mention_attestation: Montbrison is first securely documented in 1096 CE in Forez charters noting the castle and a hospital founded by Count William IV.

morphemes.translation: broken, crumbled (from briser), or personal name Briso

b_montbrison.etymology_analysis: Derived from Latin mons ('hill') combined with either Old French/Arpitan briser ('crumbled', referring to the fractured basalt hill) or a Germanic personal name Briso.

historical_names.name: Aquae Segetae
historical_names.source: Tabula Peutingeriana (4th century CE) for Moingt within modern Montbrison
historical_names.notes: The Gallo-Roman thermal town of Aquae Segetae (modern Moingt, now part of Montbrison) is recorded on the 4th-century Tabula Peutingeriana.

b_roanne.first_mention_attestation: Roanne is first attested as Rodumna in Ptolemy's Geographia (c. 150 CE) and later on the Tabula Peutingeriana.
b_roanne.etymology_analysis: The name derives from Gaulish *Rod-onna ('flowing water'), Latinized as Rodumna, which evolved through medieval Rouhanne into modern Roanne.

b_lyon.first_mention_attestation: Lyon was founded as the Roman colony of Lugdunum in 43 BCE by Lucius Munatius Plancus, and is attested in contemporary Roman sources and Strabo's Geographia.
b_lyon.etymology_analysis: Lyon descends from Gaulish *Lugudunon (Latinized as Lugdunum), meaning 'fortress of Lugus', which underwent regular French phonological reduction to Lyon.

b_villars.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the medieval castle and lordship of Villars-les-Dombes emerged in the 10th to 11th centuries.
b_villars.etymology_analysis: Villars derives from Late Latin villare ('dependent farmstead or hamlet' of a villa), with the regional qualifier les-Dombes added to distinguish it among French communes.

b_beaujeu.first_mention_attestation: Beaujeu is first attested in the mid-10th century (c. 950–967 CE) with Bérard, the first recorded Lord of Beaujeu (de Bello Joco).

morphemes.translation: play, pass, or hillock (Latinized as Bellus Jocus / Jugum)

b_beaujeu.etymology_analysis: Medieval Latin charters render the name Bello Joco ('fair play'), though toponymists often interpret the second element as Latin jugum ('mountain ridge or pass'), yielding 'fair ridge'.

b_monteil.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE for Montélimar itself; the medieval castle of Monteil (Monteil-Adhémar, later Montélimar) developed from the 10th century onward.

eponym.details: Montélimar (Monteil-Adhémar) takes its second element from the Adhémar (Aymar) family, lords of the castle from the 10th–12th centuries.

b_monteil.etymology_analysis: The name combines Occitan monteil ('small hill', from Latin monticulus) with the personal name Adhémar (Aymar), reflecting the medieval lordship of Monteil-Adhémar.

historical_names.name: Acunum
historical_names.source: Itinerarium Burdigalense (333 CE) and Tabula Peutingeriana
historical_names.notes: In Gallo-Roman antiquity, the site of Montélimar was a road station named Acunum (Mansio Acunum) at the crossing of the Roubion.

historical_names.name: Mansio Acunum
historical_names.source: Itinerarium Burdigalense (333 CE) and Tabula Peutingeriana
historical_names.notes: In Gallo-Roman antiquity, the site of Montélimar was a road station named Acunum (Mansio Acunum) at the crossing of the Roubion.

b_die.first_mention_attestation: Dea Augusta Vocontiorum (modern Die) is attested in 2nd–3rd century Roman inscriptions and in 325 CE when Bishop Nicaise of Die attended the Council of Nicaea, as well as in the 333 CE Bordeaux Itinerary.
b_die.etymology_analysis: The French name Die derives directly from Latin Dea ('Goddess') in the Roman civic title Dea Augusta Vocontiorum, capital of the northern Vocontii.

b_valence.first_mention_attestation: Valence is attested as the Roman colony of Valentia by Pliny the Elder in his Naturalis Historia (77 CE) and later by Ptolemy (c. 150 CE).
b_valence.etymology_analysis: Named Valentia ('strength, vigor') upon its foundation as a Roman colony in the 1st century BCE, the Latin toponym evolved regularly into French Valence.

b_grenoble.first_mention_attestation: Grenoble is first attested as Cularo in 43 BCE in a letter from Lucius Munatius Plancus to Cicero, and was renamed Gratianopolis in 381 CE under Emperor Gratian.
b_grenoble.etymology_analysis: Grenoble derives from Late Latin Gratianopolis ('city of Gratian'), the honorific name given in 381 CE to the older Gaulish-Roman settlement of Cularo.

historical_names.name: Cularo
historical_names.source: Letter of Lucius Munatius Plancus to Cicero (43 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Cularo was the original Gaulish and early Roman name of the settlement prior to its renaming to Gratianopolis in 381 CE.

b_vienne.first_mention_attestation: Vienne is attested as Vienna in Julius Caesar's Commentarii de Bello Gallico (c. 52 BCE) as the chief city of the Allobroges.

morphemes.translation: pre-Roman Gaulish toponym of uncertain root (possibly 'white' or 'sacred')

b_vienne.etymology_analysis: The French name Vienne continues the ancient Gaulish-Roman toponym Vienna (attested in Caesar), whose pre-Roman root is preserved without clear Indo-European consensus.

b_chartreuse.first_mention_attestation: The Carthusian nunnery of Chartreuse de Prémol in Vaulnaveys-le-Haut was founded in 1234 CE, following the 1084 foundation of the Grande Chartreuse.
b_chartreuse.etymology_analysis: Chartreuse refers to a monastery of the Carthusian Order (named after the Cartusia massif where Saint Bruno settled in 1084), while Prémol derives from Latin pratum molle ('soft or damp meadow').

b_romans.first_mention_attestation: Romans-sur-Isère was founded in 838 CE when Saint Barnard, Archbishop of Vienne, established a Benedictine abbey (later the Collegiate Church of Saint-Barnard) at a ford on the Isère River.

morphemes.translation: Romanus (possibly a personal name or reference to Romans)

b_romans.etymology_analysis: The town's name (attested as Romanis in 9th-century charters) is generally linked to a personal name Romanus or a local Romanized settlement, qualified in modern French by its position on the Isère River.

b_viviers.first_mention_attestation: Viviers (Latin: Vivarium) became the episcopal seat of the Helvii in the 5th century CE (c. 475 CE) after the decline of Alba Helviorum.
b_viviers.etymology_analysis: The name derives from Latin vivarium ('fishpond' or 'enclosure'), which became Viviers in French and gave its name to the Vivarais region.

historical_names.name: Alba Helviorum
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE), and Roman inscriptions
historical_names.notes: Alba Helviorum (modern Alba-la-Romaine), about 12 km northwest of Viviers, was the Roman civitas capital and original bishopric before the see was transferred to Viviers in the 5th century.

b_annonay.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; while Roman coins indicate ancient occupation, Annonay is first documented in high medieval charters as a pilgrimage stop.

morphemes.translation: Annonius (Roman personal name) or annona ('grain supply')

b_annonay.etymology_analysis: Annonay derives from a Gallo-Roman form *Annoniacum, interpreted either as the estate (-iacum) of a Roman landowner named Annonius or as a grain depot of the praefectus annonae.

b_cuneo.first_mention_attestation: Cuneo was founded on 23 July 1198 CE by local inhabitants who declared it a free commune.
b_cuneo.etymology_analysis: The name derives from Latin cuneus ('wedge'), describing the wedge-shaped plateau between the Stura di Demonte and Gesso rivers where the city was built.

historical_names.name: Pedona
historical_names.source: Early medieval abbey and parish records of San Dalmazzo di Pedona (7th century CE)
historical_names.notes: Pedona (modern Borgo San Dalmazzo), located immediately southwest of Cuneo, was a Roman and early medieval abbey center documented from the 7th century CE.

b_saluzzo.first_mention_attestation: The castle of Saluzzo (Castel soprano) is first mentioned in 1028 CE in the foundation charter of the Abbey of Caramagna.

morphemes.translation: uncertain pre-Roman or Latin root (possibly *sal- 'salt/stream' or personal name)

b_saluzzo.etymology_analysis: Medieval forms such as Salutium (1028) point to a Gallo-Roman or Ligurian-Latin estate name whose exact root remains uncertain, yielding Piedmontese Salusse and Italian Saluzzo.

b_mondovi.first_mention_attestation: Mondovì was founded on a hilltop in 1198 CE by survivors of nearby destroyed villages under the name Mont ëd Vico (Monte di Vico).

morphemes.translation: of Vico (from Latin de Vico, referring to Vicoforte)

b_mondovi.etymology_analysis: Mondovì contracts Piedmontese Mont ëd Vico ('Mount of Vico'), referring to the hill above the older village of Vico (Vicoforte) where the 1198 commune was established.

b_asti.first_mention_attestation: Asti is attested in Roman antiquity as Hasta (becoming a Roman colonia in 89 BCE and municipium in 49 BCE) and recorded by Pliny the Elder in his Naturalis Historia (77 CE).

morphemes.translation: spear (Latin hasta), or pre-Roman Ligurian root

b_asti.etymology_analysis: The Italian name Asti derives from Roman Hasta, either reflecting Latin hasta ('spear') or a Latinized pre-Roman Ligurian toponym.

b_alba_di_monferrato.first_mention_attestation: Alba is attested as the Roman city of Alba Pompeia by Pliny the Elder in his Naturalis Historia (77 CE), having been founded c. 89 BCE under consul Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo.
b_alba_di_monferrato.etymology_analysis: Alba continues the first element of Roman Alba Pompeia, where pre-Roman *alb- ('height, town') was paired with the gentilicium of consul Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo (89 BCE).

b_acqui.first_mention_attestation: Acqui Terme is attested in antiquity as Aquae Statiellae by Strabo in his Geographia (c. 20 CE) and Pliny the Elder in his Naturalis Historia (77 CE).
b_acqui.etymology_analysis: Acqui derives from Latin Aquae ('thermal waters', in the locative/ablative Aquis), shortened from Aquae Statiellae ('waters of the Statielli'); Terme ('baths') was added in 1956.

b_novara.first_mention_attestation: Novara is attested as ancient Novaria by Pliny the Elder in his Naturalis Historia (77 CE) and Tacitus in his Historiae (c. 105 CE).
b_novara.etymology_analysis: Novara descends directly from Roman Novaria, a name of Celto-Ligurian or Latin origin built on *nouo- ('new') with the toponymic suffix -aria.

b_biella.first_mention_attestation: Biella is first attested in a written document of 10 July 826 CE as Bugella, in a donation charter of Emperors Louis the Pious and Lothair to Count Boso.

morphemes.translation: early medieval toponym of uncertain pre-Roman origin

b_biella.etymology_analysis: The 826 CE form Bugella (later Buiella and Biella) is of pre-Roman (likely Celtic or Ligurian) origin, though its exact etymon remains uncertain.

b_vercelli.first_mention_attestation: Vercelli is attested in antiquity as Vercellae by Strabo in his Geographia (c. 20 CE) and Pliny the Elder in his Naturalis Historia (77 CE), and was the site of the 101 BCE Battle of Vercellae.

morphemes.translation: pre-Roman tribal/mining center of the Libici

b_vercelli.etymology_analysis: The Italian name Vercelli continues the ancient Celto-Ligurian toponym Vercellae, which some scholars connect to a pre-Roman term for a mining settlement at a river confluence.

b_turin.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Taurasia, chief town of the Celto-Ligurian Taurini, captured by Hannibal in 218 BCE (recorded by Polybius and Livy); refounded as the Roman colony Julia Augusta Taurinorum after 28 BCE.
b_turin.etymology_analysis: The name Turin (Italian Torino) derives from Latin (Augusta) Taurinorum, meaning 'Augusta of the Taurini', named after the Celto-Ligurian Taurini tribe whose pre-Roman oppidum Taurasia was sacked by Hannibal in 218 BCE.

b_chieri.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned by Pliny the Elder in his Naturalis Historia (c. 77 CE) as Carreum quod Potentia cognominatur, a Roman municipium in Cisalpine Gaul.
b_chieri.etymology_analysis: Chieri evolves from the Roman toponym Carreum (Potentia), attested by Pliny the Elder in the 1st century CE. The root *karr- is a pre-Roman Celtic or Ligurian element meaning 'stone' or 'rock', later palatalized in Piedmontese and Italian to Chieri.

b_santhia.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 990 CE in the travel diary of Archbishop Sigeric of Canterbury along the Via Francigena as Sca Agath (Sancta Agatha), and in a 999 CE imperial diploma of Otto III to the Bishop of Vercelli.
b_santhia.etymology_analysis: The Piedmontese and Italian name Santhià is a contracted vernacular development of Medieval Latin Sancta Agatha, referring to the local pieve (parish church) dedicated to Saint Agatha of Sicily (martyred c. 251 CE).

b_forcalquier.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a charter dated 1018–1032 CE as in castro Furnocalcario, and around 1103 CE as castel de Fornchalcerii.
b_forcalquier.etymology_analysis: Forcalquier derives from the Medieval Latin compound Furnus Calcarius ('lime kiln'), referring to the Roman-era and medieval quicklime kilns operated in the limestone hills around the site.

b_apt.first_mention_attestation: Chief town of the Gallic Vulgientes, destroyed by Rome c. 125 BCE and restored by Julius Caesar around 45 BCE as Colonia Apta Julia Vulgientium (attested by Pliny the Elder and Strabo).
b_apt.etymology_analysis: Apt continues the Roman colonial name Apta (Julia), conferred in the mid-1st century BCE under Julius Caesar, likely Latinizing an earlier Gallic settlement name or referencing its strategic suitability along the Via Domitia.

b_embrun.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the early 1st century CE by Strabo, on the Vicarello Goblets, and later by Ptolemy (iii.1) as Ebrodunum / Eburodunum, chief town of the Caturiges.
b_embrun.etymology_analysis: Embrun derives from the Gaulish compound *Eburodunum (Latinized as Ebrodunum), combining eburo- ('yew') and -dunum ('fortified hilltop'), describing the settlement's commanding rocky promontory above the Durance valley.

b_gap.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Roman itineraries (the 3rd-century CE Antonine Itinerary and the Vicarello Goblets) as Vapincum / Vappincum, later shortened to Vappum and Gap.
b_gap.etymology_analysis: Gap descends from the ancient Celto-Ligurian toponym Vappincum, which was clipped to Vappum in Late Antiquity and underwent Germanic-influenced phonetic shift of initial v- > w- > g- (yielding Gap).

b_briancon.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned by Strabo (early 1st century CE) as Brigantium on the road to the Cottian Alps, and recorded on the Vicarello Goblets and in Ptolemy.
b_briancon.etymology_analysis: Briançon comes from the Gaulish toponym Brigantio (Latinized as Brigantium), built on the Celtic root *brig- ('height, hill'), reflecting its position as a high-altitude Alpine fortress.

b_nice.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 350 BCE by Phocaean Greek colonists from Massalia under the name Nikaia (Νίκαια), attested in classical Greek and Roman historiography (Polybius, Strabo).
b_nice.etymology_analysis: Nice derives from Ancient Greek Níkaia (Latinized as Nicaea), named by Phocaean Greek settlers from Massalia in honor of Nike, the goddess of victory, commemorating a triumph over the neighboring Ligurians.

b_grasse.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a charter dated 15 October 1040 CE in the Cartulary of Saint-Victor of Marseille, signed by Guillelmus de Grassa.
b_grasse.etymology_analysis: Grasse (Occitan Grassa) is first recorded in 1040 CE; its etymology is uncertain, commonly explained as a shortening of Medieval Latin Podium Grassum ('broad/fertile hill'), referring to the limestone hill on which the town was built.

b_barcelonnette.first_mention_attestation: Founded and named in 1231 CE by Ramon Berenguer IV (V), Count of Provence, who granted the new town a charter.

morphemes.translation: Barcelona (ancestral city of the House of Barcelona)

b_barcelonnette.etymology_analysis: Barcelonnette ('Little Barcelona') was coined in 1231 CE by Count Ramon Berenguer IV (V) of Provence, a member of the House of Barcelona, to honor his ancestral Catalan homeland.

historical_names.name: Rigomagensium
historical_names.source: Notitia Galliarum (c. 400 CE), listing Civitas Rigomagensium in the Ubaye valley
historical_names.notes: Roman-era civitas capital of the Ubaye valley prior to the 1231 CE foundation of Barcelonnette.

historical_names.name: Civitas Rigomagensium
historical_names.source: Notitia Galliarum (c. 400 CE), listing Civitas Rigomagensium in the Ubaye valley
historical_names.notes: Roman-era civitas capital of the Ubaye valley prior to the 1231 CE foundation of Barcelonnette.

b_puget.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the 11th century CE under the form Pogit (from Latin pogittum), and later in 1346 CE as Pugetum Tenearum.
b_puget.etymology_analysis: Puget derives from Occitan puget (Medieval Latin pogittum, a diminutive of podium), meaning 'little hill', with the determinant -Théniers referring to its historical territorial district.

b_digne.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 1st century CE by Pliny the Elder (Naturalis Historia) and Ptolemy as Dinia, capital of the Bodiontici; recorded as Digna by 780 CE.
b_digne.etymology_analysis: Digne descends from Roman Dinia, either from a Gaulish hydronymic root *din- ('water', referring to its thermal springs) or from a Gallo-Roman personal name Din(n)ius; '-les-Bains' was officially added in 1988.

b_toulon.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 3rd-century CE Antonine Itinerary and the Notitia Dignitatum as Telo Martius, a Roman imperial purple-dyeing port.

morphemes.translation: local god of springs Telo (or base of a hill)

b_toulon.etymology_analysis: Toulon derives from the Roman name Telo Martius, combining Telo (likely a local Celtic-Ligurian spring deity or topographic term) with Martius ('of Mars'), evolving through Medieval forms Tholon and Tolon.

b_dragugnian.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 909 CE in medieval charters under the Latinized form Dragonianum (also Draconianum).
b_dragugnian.etymology_analysis: Draguignan derives from the Gallo-Roman estate name *Draconianum, formed from the Roman personal name Draconius and the possessive suffix -anum; local medieval folklore later reinterpreted it via Latin draco ('dragon').

b_castellane.first_mention_attestation: First attested under the name Petra Castellana between 965 and 977 CE.
b_castellane.etymology_analysis: Castellane comes from Medieval Latin (Petra) Castellana, combining Occitan pèira ('rock') and castel + -ana ('fortified/castle-bearing'), referring to the fortified medieval settlement on the Roc above the Verdon.

historical_names.name: Sinaca
historical_names.source: Recorded in 813 CE as Sinaca for the fortified Roc site above Castellane
historical_names.notes: Earlier recorded name of the hilltop settlement on the Roc prior to its attestation as Petra Castellana in 965–977 CE.

b_marseille.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 600 BCE as the Phocaean Greek colony of Massalia (Μασσαλία), attested in early Greek historiography and periploi from Hecataeus and Herodotus onward.
b_marseille.etymology_analysis: Marseille descends from Latin Massilia, adapted from Ancient Greek Massalia, the name of the colony founded c. 600 BCE by Phocaean Greeks, likely incorporating a pre-existing Ligurian or Celtic coastal name.

b_aix.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 123 BCE by the Roman consul Gaius Sextius Calvinus as Aquae Sextiae, attested in Livy, Strabo, and Velleius Paterculus.
b_aix.etymology_analysis: Aix derives from Latin Aquae ('waters'), shortened from Aquae Sextiae ('Waters of Sextius'), named after the thermal springs and the Roman consul Gaius Sextius Calvinus who founded the settlement in 123 BCE.

b_arles.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 49 BCE by Julius Caesar (Commentarii de Bello Civili) as Arelate, and by Strabo as Areláte (Ἀρελάτη).
b_arles.etymology_analysis: Arles derives from the Gaulish compound Arelate, formed from are- ('near, by') and *late ('marsh, wetland'), describing its ancient position amidst the marshes of the Rhône delta.

b_orange.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the Roman Republic in connection with the Battle of Arausio (105 BCE), and in Strabo, Pliny the Elder, and Pomponius Mela as Arausio.

morphemes.translation: name of a local Celtic water deity or settlement

b_orange.etymology_analysis: Orange descends from Latin Arausio, the name of a Celtic settlement and local water god; its modern spelling was influenced by folk association with the Old French word for the orange fruit (orange).

b_avignon.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 1st century CE by Strabo (IV.1.11) as Aueniṑn (Ἀυενιών), by Pomponius Mela, and by Pliny the Elder as Avennio Cavarum.
b_avignon.etymology_analysis: Avignon continues the ancient Celto-Ligurian name Avennio (Greek Auenion), derived from a pre-Latin root *ab-ēn- (linked either to the Rhône river or the Rocher des Doms) with the suffix -iōn.

b_vaison.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 1st century CE by Pomponius Mela, Pliny the Elder, and Ptolemy as Vasio (Vocontiorum), a federated civitas capital.
b_vaison.etymology_analysis: Vaison derives from the Gallo-Roman name Vasio (Vasio Vocontiorum), of pre-Roman Celtic or Ligurian origin; the modern epithet '-la-Romaine' was added in 1924 to highlight its extensive Roman ruins.

b_aosta.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 25 BCE by Aulus Terentius Varro Murena as the Roman colony Augusta Praetoria Salassorum, attested in Strabo and Pliny the Elder.
b_aosta.etymology_analysis: Aosta is a phonological reduction of Latin Augusta, shortened from Augusta Praetoria Salassorum, the Roman veteran colony founded in 25 BCE under Emperor Augustus.

b_martigny.first_mention_attestation: While the Celtic-Roman settlement was attested as Octodurus (57–56 BCE) and Forum Claudii Vallensium (41–47 CE), the medieval name Martiniacum (whence Martigny) is first attested in 1018 CE.
b_martigny.etymology_analysis: The modern name Martigny derives from a Gallo-Roman estate name *Martiniacum ('estate of Martinius'), which replaced the earlier Celtic-Roman names Octodurus and Forum Claudii Vallensium.

historical_names.name: Octodurus
historical_names.source: Julius Caesar, Commentarii de Bello Gallico (57–56 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Attested as Octodurus in 57–56 BCE and refounded as Forum Claudii Vallensium in 41–47 CE before the medieval form Martigny prevailed.

historical_names.name: Forum Claudii Vallensium
historical_names.source: Julius Caesar, Commentarii de Bello Gallico (57–56 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Attested as Octodurus in 57–56 BCE and refounded as Forum Claudii Vallensium in 41–47 CE before the medieval form Martigny prevailed.

b_ivrea.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a Roman colony in 100 BCE under the name Eporedia, attested in Strabo, Pliny the Elder, and Velleius Paterculus.
b_ivrea.etymology_analysis: Ivrea evolves from the Roman name Eporedia (Gaulish *Epo-redia, 'horse-chariot' or 'good horse-drivers'), reflecting the Celtic equestrian culture of the Salassi before Roman colonization in 100 BCE.

b_pinerolo.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 981 CE as a possession under the jurisdiction of the Bishop of Turin (and in 996 CE in an imperial diploma).
b_pinerolo.etymology_analysis: Pinerolo (Piedmontese Pinareul) derives from Late Latin *Pinarolium, a diminutive formation based on pinus ('pine tree'), referring to pine woods on the Alpine foothills.

b_canavese.first_mention_attestation: The regional name derives from the medieval curtis of Canava near the Orco river, first attested in a diploma of Berengar II in 951 CE.
b_canavese.etymology_analysis: Canavese is a territorial choronym formed with the Italian suffix -ese from Canava, a 10th-century royal curtis near Cuorgnè whose name is traditionally linked to hemp (canapa) cultivation or a storehouse.

historical_names.name: Eporedia
historical_names.source: Roman colony of Eporedia (modern Ivrea), founded 100 BCE
historical_names.notes: Eporedia (Ivrea) served as the Roman and early medieval urban center of the territory later known as Canavese.

b_geneva.first_mention_attestation: Attested by Julius Caesar in Commentarii de Bello Gallico (58 BCE) as Genava, the northernmost fortified town of the Allobroges.

morphemes.translation: bend, knee, river mouth, or inlet

b_geneva.etymology_analysis: Geneva derives from Celtic *Genawa (Latinized as Genava), from Proto-Celtic *genu- ('knee, bend, mouth'), referring to the outlet where the Rhône flows out of Lake Geneva.

b_annecy.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 867 CE as Anesciacum (villa Anniciaca) in a royal diploma of Lothair II granting the estate to his wife Teutberga; preceded in the plain by the Roman vicus of Boutae (1st–3rd centuries CE).
b_annecy.etymology_analysis: Annecy derives from the Gallo-Roman estate name *Aniciacum (attested as Anesciacum in 867 CE), formed from the Roman gentilicium Anicius and the Celtic-derived property suffix -acum.

historical_names.name: Boutae
historical_names.source: Gallo-Roman inscriptions of the 1st–3rd centuries CE (vicus of Boutae)
historical_names.notes: Roman vicus located on the plain of Les Fins within modern Annecy before settlement shifted to the hill of Anesciacum.

b_thonon_les_bains.first_mention_attestation: First reliably attested in 1191 CE as Thonuns in the Régeste genevois ('Factum apud Thonuns').
b_thonon_les_bains.etymology_analysis: Thonon is generally traced to a Gaulish root *dunon ('fortress, hill') overlooking Lake Geneva; the thermal qualifier '-les-Bains' was officially added by decree in 1890.

b_faucigny.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the late 11th century CE (e.g., 1083 CE charter of Guy of Faucigny, Bishop of Geneva) under the Latinized forms Focignacum and Fulcignacum; the castle is first explicitly named in 1119 CE.

morphemes.translation: Roman personal name Falcinius or Fulcinius

b_faucigny.etymology_analysis: Faucigny derives from a Gallo-Roman estate name *Falciniacum or *Fulciniacum, combining a Roman gentilicium (Falcinius or Fulcinius) with the possessive suffix -iacum.

b_moutiers.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Roman antiquity as Darantasia on the Tabula Peutingeriana and in the Antonine Itinerary (3rd century CE), before being called Monasterium from 996 CE onward.
b_moutiers.etymology_analysis: Moûtiers derives from Medieval Latin Monasterium ('monastery', via Old French Moustiers), which replaced the ancient Celtic-Roman name Darantasia in the late 10th century.

historical_names.name: Darantasia
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary and Tabula Peutingeriana (3rd–4th centuries CE)
historical_names.notes: Capital of the Celtic Ceutrones and Roman provincial center prior to its renaming as Monasterium (Moûtiers) in 996 CE.

b_saint_michel_de_maurienne.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1112 CE as Beati Michaelis in the Cartulaire de Maurienne (and Sancti Michaelis in 1181 CE).
b_saint_michel_de_maurienne.etymology_analysis: Named after the Archangel Michael (Sanctus Michael), with the valley determinant '-de-Maurienne' officially added by decree in 1953.

b_chambery.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1016 CE in the Cartulary of Saint-André as Camefriacum, and in 1029 CE as Camberiaco.
b_chambery.etymology_analysis: Chambéry derives from Gallo-Roman Camberiacum, formed either from a personal name *Camberius/*Cambarius with the estate suffix -iacum, or from Gaulish *cambo- ('river bend').

b_belley.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the 2nd century CE in a Gallo-Roman inscription mentioning the Vicani Bellicenses ('inhabitants of the vicus of Bellicus'), and as an episcopal see (Ecclesia Belicensis) in 567 CE.
b_belley.etymology_analysis: Belley derives from the Gallo-Roman estate or vicus name *Bellicium, formed from the Latin personal cognomen Bellicus.

b_biel.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a written document in 1142 CE as Apud Belnam (before the fortified town was built c. 1225–1230 by Bishop Heinrich von Thun).

morphemes.translation: possibly related to the Celtic god Belenus (or bright/shining spring)

b_biel.etymology_analysis: Biel (French Bienne) derives from the medieval form Belna, hypothesized by toponymists to reflect a sanctuary or spring dedicated to the Celtic deity Belenus.

historical_names.name: Petinesca
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (3rd century CE) for the nearby Roman road station Petinesca
historical_names.notes: Roman-era settlement and road station in the immediate vicinity (with a 4th-century guard station at Mett within modern Biel/Bienne).

b_lucerne.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a charter of 840 CE under the name Luciaria, referring to the settlement around the Benedictine monastery of St. Leodegar founded c. 750 CE.

morphemes.translation: uncertain; possibly linked to St. Leodegar or Latin lucerna ('lamp/light')

b_lucerne.etymology_analysis: Lucerne (German Luzern) is first attested as Luciaria in 840 CE; its etymology is uncertain, variously linked to the abbey's patron Saint Leodegar, a Latin personal name, or folk-etymologically to Latin lucerna ('lantern').

b_bern.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1191 CE by Duke Berthold V of Zähringen on the Aare peninsula and attested in contemporary charters thereafter.

morphemes.translation: cleft/gap (Celtic) or bear (folk etymology) or Verona

b_bern.etymology_analysis: While medieval legend attributes the name Bern to a bear (Bär) slain by Berthold V, modern scholarship links it either to a pre-existing Celtic toponym *berna ('cleft/fissure') or to Verona (Dietrich von Bern).

historical_names.name: Brenodor
historical_names.source: Gallo-Roman inscription (Engehalbinsel, 2nd century CE) naming the vicus Brenodor
historical_names.notes: Celtic oppidum and Roman vicus on the Engehalbinsel peninsula immediately north of medieval Bern.

b_lausanne.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 2nd-century CE Roman inscriptions as vikanor[um] Lousonnensium and in 280 CE as lacu Lausonio (later civitas Lausanna c. 400 CE).
b_lausanne.etymology_analysis: Lausanne descends from the Gallo-Roman name Lousonna, of Celtic or pre-Celtic origin, originally denoting the lakeside settlement at Vidy before residents relocated up the hill.

b_thun.first_mention_attestation: The town of Thun is first explicitly attested in 1133 CE as Tuno (though the surrounding region and lake appear in the 7th-century Chronicle of Fredegar).
b_thun.etymology_analysis: Thun derives from the Celtic word *dūnon ('fortress, fortified town'), Latinized as Dunum and reflected in Old High German as Tuno.

historical_names.name: Lacus Dunensis
historical_names.source: Chronicle of Fredegar (7th century CE), mentioning the region/lake of Thun
historical_names.notes: The region and lake are attested in the 7th century prior to the first written mention of the town itself in 1133 CE.

b_neuchatel.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a charter of 1011 CE in which King Rudolf III of Burgundy donated Novum Castellum ('new castle') to his wife Irmengard.
b_neuchatel.etymology_analysis: Neuchâtel is the French reflex of Medieval Latin Novum Castellum ('new castle'), first recorded in 1011 CE as a royal Burgundian residence.

b_pontarlier.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 3rd-century CE Antonine Itinerary and on the Tabula Peutingeriana as Ariolica (a road station between Urba and Vesontio), before taking the medieval form Pontarlum / Punterli in the 13th century.
b_pontarlier.etymology_analysis: Pontarlier combines French pont ('bridge') with -arlier (from the ancient Gaulish station name Ariolica, preserved in the plain of Chaux d'Arlier), meaning 'bridge of Arlier'.

historical_names.name: Ariolica
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary and Tabula Peutingeriana (3rd–4th centuries CE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Gallo-Roman road station on the Doubs crossing prior to the 13th-century compound Pontarlum / Pontarlier.

b_besancon.first_mention_attestation: Attested by Julius Caesar in Commentarii de Bello Gallico (58 BCE) as Vesontio, chief oppidum of the Sequani.

morphemes.translation: uncertain root (possibly related to *ves- 'mountain/height' or bison)

b_besancon.etymology_analysis: Besançon descends from Latin Vesontio (via Late Latin Besantio), the ancient Gaulish oppidum name recorded by Julius Caesar in 58 BCE.

b_vesoul.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a written document in 899 CE as Castrum Vesulium, referring to the hilltop fortress on La Motte.
b_vesoul.etymology_analysis: Vesoul derives from Medieval Latin Vesulium, built on a pre-Roman oronymic root *ves- ('height, hill'), referring to the prominent limestone hill of La Motte.

b_morteau.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1105 CE in the Latinized form Mortua Aqua.
b_morteau.etymology_analysis: Morteau derives from Latin Mortua Aqua ('dead/stagnant water'), describing the slow, flat stretch of the Doubs river flowing through the Morteau valley.

b_ornans.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1092 CE as Ornens, and in a 1151 CE charter.

morphemes.translation: possibly 'ash tree' (Latin ornus) or personal name

b_ornans.etymology_analysis: Ornans (attested as Ornens in 1092 CE) combines a Gallo-Roman or Germanic stem with the Burgundian-influenced toponymic suffix -ans (from *-ingōs).

b_gy.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1093 CE when Count Renaud of Burgundy sold his lands in the pays gyssois to his brother Hugh, Archbishop of Besançon.
b_gy.etymology_analysis: Gy derives from the Gallo-Roman estate name *Gaiacum, formed from the Latin personal name Gaius and the Celtic-derived possessive suffix -acum.

b_bourg.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1187 CE in the Latinized form Burgo (and in 1272 CE as Burgo in Bressia).
b_bourg.etymology_analysis: Bourg-en-Bresse derives from Franco-Provençal bôrg (Late Latin burgus, 'fortified town/market'), with the regional determinant 'en-Bresse' officially added in 1955.

b_champagnole.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the 10th century CE as Campanola in pago scodiensium (and in 1130 CE in a donation by the Archbishop of Besançon).
b_champagnole.etymology_analysis: Champagnole derives from Late Latin *Campaniola, a diminutive of campania ('plain, open field'), describing the plateau plain at the foot of Mont Rivel.

b_dole.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the 11th century as Dolla (in the Vita Brunonis of Bishop Bruno of Langres, d. 1016 CE), with its castle documented in the late 11th century.

morphemes.translation: river bend, low valley, or hill/eminence

b_dole.etymology_analysis: Dole (attested as Dola / Dolla) derives from a pre-Latin or Celtic root *dola (meaning 'valley, meadow, or river meander') or *tŭll- ('height'), referring to its site overlooking a bend in the Doubs river.

b_quingey.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1135 CE as Quingiaco in regional Burgundian charters recorded by Jean Courtieu, though local tradition places the birth of Gui de Bourgogne (Pope Callixtus II) there around 1050 CE.
b_quingey.etymology_analysis: Derived from a Gallo-Roman personal name such as *Quintius or *Quinctius combined with the Gaulish-Latin possessive suffix *-iacum*, denoting an agricultural estate; local antiquarian tradition also linked it to Celtic roots meaning 'fine dwelling'.

b_lons_le_saunier.first_mention_attestation: First reliably attested in 1083 CE in connection with the priory and church of Saint-Désiré founded by Abbot Bernard I of Baume, though Roman-era salt exploitation is known archaeologically.
b_lons_le_saunier.etymology_analysis: Combines the pre-Roman/Gallo-Roman toponym *Ledo* (evolving through *Ledonis* to *Lons*) with the Old French occupational epithet *le saunier* ('the salt-maker'), referring to the town's medieval brine springs and saltworks.

b_salins.first_mention_attestation: Attested in a 523 CE charter of Burgundian King Sigismund donating salt pans *in villa quae Salinis*, reflecting the early medieval importance of its Jura brine springs.
b_salins.etymology_analysis: From Latin *salinae* ('saltworks'), referring to the natural saline springs exploited since antiquity; the suffix *-les-Bains* ('the baths') was added in 1926 to promote its thermal spa.

b_amaya.first_mention_attestation: Explicitly recorded by John of Biclaro in his *Chronicle* under the year 574 CE, when Visigothic King Leovigild entered Cantabria and captured the hillfort of Amaya.
b_amaya.etymology_analysis: A pre-Roman Cantabrian/Celtiberian or Vasconic toponym, commonly linked to an Indo-European or Vasconic root meaning 'summit', 'pastureland', or 'mother-height', referring to the fortified limestone plateau of Peña Amaya.

b_mirandadeebro.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the *Codex Vigilanus* (and *Chronicle of Alfonso III*) under the year 757 CE among the fortified places along the upper Ebro valley.
b_mirandadeebro.etymology_analysis: From Latin *miranda* (gerundive of *mirari*, 'to look at / watch over'), designating a strategic lookout above the river crossing, paired with the hydronym *Ebro* (from Latin *Hiberus*).

b_sedano.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented; the *alfoz de Sedano* first appears in 12th-century Castilian charters.
b_sedano.etymology_analysis: Likely a Roman-era fundus name formed from a Latin personal name such as *Setius* or *Sedius* with the possessive suffix *-anum*, or a pre-Roman substrate toponym of the northern Burgos highlands.

b_santiallana.first_mention_attestation: Originates around the monastery of Santa Juliana, first documented c. 870 CE when relics of Saint Juliana of Nicomedia were venerated at the site.
b_santiallana.etymology_analysis: Contracted from *Sancta Iuliana* (*Sant'Illana*), named for the early Christian martyr Saint Juliana of Nicomedia whose relics were housed in its abbey, with *del Mar* ('of the Sea') added later to distinguish the Cantabrian town.

b_santander.first_mention_attestation: The name Santander is first attested in a 1068 CE draft document of King Sancho II of Castile, deriving from the abbey of San Emeterio.
b_santander.etymology_analysis: Evolved from Latin *Sancti Emeterii* ('of Saint Emeterius') through *Sant Emter* and *Santander*, honoring the 3rd-century martyr whose relics were brought to the local monastery.

historical_names.name: Portus Victoriae Iuliobrigensium
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (c. 77 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman harbor on the Cantabrian coast traditionally identified with Santander Bay.

b_reinosa.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in documents from 1000 CE, when Count Sancho García of Castile divided the settlement into four *solares*.
b_reinosa.etymology_analysis: Derived from Latin *arenosa* ('sandy place', from *arena* + *-osa*) via apheresis of the initial vowel (*Arenosa* > *Reinosa*), referring to the sandy terrain near the upper Ebro.

b_medinadepomar.first_mention_attestation: First enters royal documentation in the late 12th century (c. 1181 CE) when King Alfonso VIII of Castile granted it a *fuero* modeled on that of Logroño.
b_medinadepomar.etymology_analysis: A hybrid Arabic-Romance toponym combining Arabic *madīna* ('town') with Romance *pomar* (from Latin *pomarium*, 'fruit orchard'), meaning 'town of the orchard'.

b_burgos.first_mention_attestation: Founded and first documented in 884 CE when Count Diego Rodríguez Porcelos fortified the hill on orders of King Alfonso III of Asturias.
b_burgos.etymology_analysis: From Late Latin *burgos* (plural of *burgus*, borrowed from Germanic *burgz*, 'fortress'), referring to the frontier castles and fortified hamlets established along the Arlanzón river.

b_atapuerca.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 963 CE in Castilian charters, prior to the famous 1054 Battle of Atapuerca.
b_atapuerca.etymology_analysis: Of debated etymology; most scholars derive it from a pre-Roman or Basque-Romance compound, or from Latin *alta porta* ('high pass') or *ad porcam*, referring to the ridge separating the Ebro and Duero basins.

b_lerma.first_mention_attestation: The territory of Lerma is first attested in late 10th-century Castilian charters (such as the 978 CE Covarrubias endowment), with its *carta puebla* granted in 1148 CE.
b_lerma.etymology_analysis: A pre-Roman toponym of Celtiberian or Vasconic origin, possibly connected to roots denoting a hilltop or uncultivated slope overlooking the Arlanza river.

b_palencia.first_mention_attestation: Recorded as *Pallantia* (Παλλαντία) by Strabo in his *Geography* (c. 20 CE) and later by Appian and Ptolemy as the chief Celtiberian city of the Vaccaei besieged by Rome in the 2nd century BCE.
b_palencia.etymology_analysis: Evolved from Celtiberian-Latin *Pallantia*, likely derived from an Indo-European root *pala* ('plain' or 'plateau') with the toponymic suffix *-antia*.

b_segovia.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned as *Segovia* by Livy (*Ab Urbe Condita*, c. 10 BCE, Book 91 fragment) in his account of the Sertorian War (79–72 BCE).
b_segovia.etymology_analysis: A Celtiberian name built on the Celtic root *sego-* ('victory, strength'), cognate with *Segobriga*, reflecting its status as a fortified hilltop oppidum.

b_cuellar.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 10th-century Castilian-Leonese repopulation records (c. 934 CE); its proposed identification with Roman *Colenda* remains unconfirmed.
b_cuellar.etymology_analysis: Derived from Latin *collis* ('hill') via *collar* ('ridge' or 'pass'), referring to the elevated ridge on which the walled town and castle stand; an alternative hypothesis links it to ancient *Colenda*.

b_uceda.first_mention_attestation: First documented in Christian sources upon its reconquest in 1085 CE, when King Alfonso VI donated the former Muslim fortress to the Cathedral of Toledo.
b_uceda.etymology_analysis: Likely derived from a Latin-Mozarabic collective plant name (*uliceta*, 'heather ground', or *oliceta*, 'olive grove') with the Spanish collective suffix *-eda*.

b_olmedo.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1085 CE among the towns captured by King Alfonso VI of León and Castile prior to its formal repopulation in 1093 CE.
b_olmedo.etymology_analysis: From Latin *ulmetum* ('elm grove', from *ulmus* + collective *-etum*), referring to the abundance of elm trees in the area.

b_coracera.first_mention_attestation: Built in the mid-15th century by Constable Álvaro de Luna at San Martín de Valdeiglesias (itself first documented in the 12th century).
b_coracera.etymology_analysis: Derived from Spanish *coraza* ('cuirass' or fortified curtain wall) with the suffix *-era*, or from an associated local estate name, denoting a strongly armored late-medieval castle.

b_soria.first_mention_attestation: Enters documented history during its repopulation between 1109 and 1114 CE under King Alfonso I of Aragon.
b_soria.etymology_analysis: Of uncertain pre-Roman origin; hypotheses link *Soria* to a Celtiberian or Vasconic root (compare Basque *zuri*, 'white', or *Oria*), or to a medieval castle *Oria*.

historical_names.name: Numantia
historical_names.source: Polybius, Histories (c. 150 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Celtiberian oppidum located ~7 km north of Soria at Garray.

b_osma.first_mention_attestation: Attested as the Visigothic episcopal see of *Oxoma*/*Osoma* from 597 CE in the acts of the Councils of Toledo, succeeding the Celtiberian-Roman city of *Uxama Argaela*.
b_osma.etymology_analysis: *Osma* descends from Celtiberian *Uxama* ('the highest', cognate with Gaulish *uxellos*), while *Burgo* ('borough') was added when Bishop Pedro de Bourges founded the cathedral quarter in 1101 CE.

b_sanesteban.first_mention_attestation: First prominently attested in 917 CE as the site of the Battle of San Esteban de Gormaz between Leonese and Umayyad forces.
b_sanesteban.etymology_analysis: Named after the Christian protomartyr Saint Stephen (*San Esteban*), with the qualifier *de Gormaz* linking it to the neighboring frontier fortress of Gormaz.

b_sanleonardodeyague.first_mention_attestation: Originally attested as San Leonardo in a 1173 CE privilege of Alfonso VIII, the village was renamed San Leonardo de Yagüe in 1952 CE following the death of Francoist general Juan Yagüe.

eponym.details: Named in part after Spanish general Juan Yagüe (1891–1952), whose surname was appended to San Leonardo in the mid-20th century; the base name honors the 6th-century Frankish saint Leonard of Noblac.

b_sanleonardodeyague.etymology_analysis: Originally named *San Leonardo* after the 6th-century Frankish hermit Saint Leonard of Noblac, with *de Yagüe* added in the 20th century in honor of Francoist general Juan Yagüe, who was born there.

b_valladolid.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1072 CE during the reign of Alfonso VI of León and Castile, shortly before Count Pedro Ansúrez led its repopulation.
b_valladolid.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived either from Arabic *Balad al-Walīd* ('town of al-Walīd') or from Latin-Romance *Vallis Olivetum* / *Valle de Olid* ('valley of olives' or 'valley of waters').

b_simancas.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Roman *Septimanca* in the *Antonine Itinerary* (c. 3rd century CE), before becoming the site of the 939 CE Battle of Simancas.
b_simancas.etymology_analysis: Evolved from Roman *Septimanca* (associated with Latin *septem*, 'seven', and a pre-Roman or road-station element), yielding medieval and modern *Simancas*.

b_arandadeduero.first_mention_attestation: First documented in the early 11th century (1008 CE); no settlement predating the 10th century is substantiated.
b_arandadeduero.etymology_analysis: Combines the pre-Roman toponym *Aranda* (possibly Celtiberian or Vasconic, related to valley or riverine terrain) with the hydronym *Duero* (Latin *Durius*).

b_freiburg.first_mention_attestation: Originated with the construction of *Castrum de Friburch* by the Dukes of Zähringen around 1091 CE, followed by the town's market charter in 1120 CE.
b_freiburg.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German *frī* ('free') + *burc* ('fortified town'), denoting a chartered free-market town, qualified by the regional choronym *Breisgau*.

b_sankt_blasien.first_mention_attestation: Predecessor monastic cell Cella Alba (Albzelle) is attested in 858 CE, whereas the monastery and settlement of Sankt Blasien date to the 983 CE foundation under Emperor Otto II after acquiring relics of Saint Blaise.
b_sankt_blasien.etymology_analysis: Named after the 4th-century Armenian martyr Saint Blaise (*Blasius*), whose relics were translated to the Black Forest monastery in the late 9th century, replacing the earlier name *Cella Alba* ('White/Alb Cell').

historical_names.name: Cella Alba
historical_names.source: Rheinau Abbey records (858 CE)
historical_names.notes: Early monastic cell on the Alb river prior to its rededication to Saint Blaise.

historical_names.name: Albzelle
historical_names.source: Rheinau Abbey records (858 CE)
historical_names.notes: Early monastic cell on the Alb river prior to its rededication to Saint Blaise.

b_offenburg.first_mention_attestation: First reliably attested in a 1148 CE Zähringen charter as *castrum Offinburc* (with some references citing c. 1100–1101).
b_offenburg.etymology_analysis: Compound of the Old High German personal name *Offo* (traditionally linked to a 7th-century Anglo-Saxon or Alamannic figure) and *Burg* ('fortress').

b_geroldseck.first_mention_attestation: The House of Geroldseck is first documented in a witness list from the 1080s CE, with their Black Forest castle of Hohengeroldseck attested from the 12th century.
b_geroldseck.etymology_analysis: Combines *hohen-* ('high') with the Germanic personal name *Gerold* and *Eck* ('mountain spur/ridge'), a standard medieval German castle-naming pattern.

b_colmar.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 823 CE in a donation charter of Emperor Louis the Pious as the royal fisc of *Columbarium*.
b_colmar.etymology_analysis: Descends from Latin *columbarium* ('dovecote', from *columba*, 'dove'), the name of the Carolingian royal estate (*fiscus*) attested in 823 CE, evolving into Alsatian/French *Colmar*.

b_selestat.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 727 CE as *Sclastat*, and again in 775 CE as *Scalistati* when Charlemagne celebrated Christmas at the royal villa.
b_selestat.etymology_analysis: From an Old High German compound in *-stat* ('place, stead'), with the first element *Scla-* / *Slecti-* (*Schlettstadt* in German) generally linked to reeds, marshland, or a wooden shelter.

b_strassburg.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 12 BCE as the Roman military camp *Argentoratum*; the Germanic name *Strateburgum* is recorded by Gregory of Tours in the late 6th century CE (c. 589 CE).
b_strassburg.etymology_analysis: From Old High German *Strāzburg* (Latinized *Strateburgum*), meaning 'fortified town at the crossing of roads', which replaced the Celtic-Roman name *Argentoratum*.

b_haguenau.first_mention_attestation: Founded around 1115 CE when Duke Frederick II of Swabia built a fortified hunting lodge on an island in the Moder river.
b_haguenau.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German *Hagenouwe*, combining *hagen* ('enclosed grove/hedge') and *ouwe* ('river island or water-meadow'), referring to the Hohenstaufen hunting island in the Moder.

b_lichtberg.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1206 CE as *Lichtemberc*, seat of the Lords of Lichtenberg in northern Alsace.
b_lichtberg.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German *lieht* ('bright, cleared of trees') + *berc* ('hill, mountain'), referring to the prominent cleared Vosges hilltops crowned by the castle.

b_montbelliard.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing in 985 CE as *Montem Billiardae* in the *Vita sancti Waldeberti*.
b_montbelliard.etymology_analysis: From Latin *Montem Billiardae* ('Mount of Billiarda'), combining *mons* ('hill') with an early medieval Germanic personal name (compare German *Mömpelgard*).
