b_mulhouse.first_mention_attestation: First attested in an 803 CE document in the Latinized form *Mulinhusen*.
b_mulhouse.etymology_analysis: From Old High German *Mulinhūsun* ('mill-houses'), referring to watermills along the Ill river (German *Mülhausen*, French *Mulhouse*).

b_ferrette.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1105 CE in connection with the castle and Counts of Ferrette (German *Pfirt*).
b_ferrette.etymology_analysis: Of uncertain origin; the Romance form *Ferrette* and German *Pfirt* (*Phirret* in 12th-century charters) have been variously linked to Latin *feretrum*, *pirum* ('pear'), or a pre-Roman Jura root.

b_porrentruy.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing in 1136 CE under the forms *Purrentru* and *Punrentrut*.
b_porrentruy.etymology_analysis: From Latin *Pons Ragentrudis* ('Bridge of Ragentrud'), referring to a crossing over the Allaine river; the German name *Pruntrut* may reflect a parallel folk-etymological adaptation.

b_bremen.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 782 CE in Frankish sources during Charlemagne's Saxon Wars, and established as a bishopric in 787 CE.
b_bremen.etymology_analysis: From Old Saxon *bremo* ('edge, brim, riverbank', cognate with English *brim*), referring to the settlement's position on a sandy dune edge along the Weser river.

b_verden.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the *Royal Frankish Annals* under October 782 CE as the site of the Massacre of Verden during Charlemagne's Saxon Wars.
b_verden.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Saxon roots meaning 'ford' or 'ferry' (cognate with German *Furt* and *Fähre*), referring to the strategic crossing over the Aller river.

b_zeven.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a 986 CE document in connection with the relocation of the Heeslingen convent to Zeven.
b_zeven.etymology_analysis: Attested early as *Scivena* / *Kivena*; while popular etymology connects it to Low German *seven* ('seven'), linguists link it to an Old Saxon hydronymic or marsh-plant root.

b_hannover.first_mention_attestation: First documented around 1150 CE (and securely in 1163 CE) as *Honovere* / *Hanovere*.
b_hannover.etymology_analysis: Generally derived from Middle Low German *(am) hohen Overe* ('at the high riverbank'), referring to the elevated bank of the Leine river.

b_wunsdorf.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned on 14 October 871 CE as *Vuonherestorp* in a royal charter of King Louis the German for the local collegiate church.
b_wunsdorf.etymology_analysis: From Old Saxon *Vuonherestorp*, combining the personal name *Wunheri* with *-thorp* ('village, hamlet'), yielding modern *Wunstorf*.

b_woldenberg.first_mention_attestation: Constructed and first attested between 1153 and 1160 CE by the Counts of Wöltingerode, who thereafter styled themselves Counts of Woldenberg.
b_woldenberg.etymology_analysis: From Middle Low German *wold* ('forest') + *berg* ('hill, mountain'), referring to the wooded ridge above Sillium where the castle stands.

b_hildesheim.first_mention_attestation: Established and first documented in 815 CE when Emperor Louis the Pious founded the Diocese of Hildesheim.
b_hildesheim.etymology_analysis: From early medieval *Hildeneshem* ('home/settlement of Hildini'), combining an Old Saxon personal name with *-hēm* ('homestead, settlement').

b_homburg.first_mention_attestation: First attested around 1129 CE in an allodial register of Count Siegfried IV of Boyneburg (Northeim) as *de Hoinburch*, built on the Großer Homburg near Stadtoldendorf.
b_homburg.etymology_analysis: From Middle Low German *Hoinburch* ('high castle'), referring to the hilltop fortress crowning the 403-meter Großer Homburg ridge in Lower Saxony.

b_dassel.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 860 CE in a deed of the Imperial Abbey of Corvey, long before the Counts of Dassel appeared in 1113 CE.
b_dassel.etymology_analysis: An Old Saxon settlement name (attested in Corvey records as *Dasle* / *Dassila*), generally interpreted as a compound of a terrain or animal root with *-lōh* ('clearing') or *-sal* ('hall/valley').

b_lippe.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1184/1185 CE by Bernard II of Lippe as *Lippe* (later *Lippstadt*), the first planned town in Westphalia.
b_lippe.etymology_analysis: Takes its name from the Lippe River (Roman *Lupia* / *Lippia*), with *-stadt* ('town') appended to distinguish the urban foundation from the noble House of Lippe.

historical_names.name: Karlsburg
historical_names.source: Annales Laureshamenses / Royal Frankish Annals (776–777 CE)
historical_names.notes: Charlemagne's 776 CE Karlsburg palace at Paderborn near the Lippe headwaters.

historical_names.name: Patresbrunn
historical_names.source: Annales Laureshamenses / Royal Frankish Annals (776–777 CE)
historical_names.notes: Charlemagne's 776 CE Karlsburg palace at Paderborn near the Lippe headwaters.

b_schwalenberg.first_mention_attestation: The County of Schwalenberg is first mentioned in 1127 CE with Count Widekind I, while Schwalenberg Castle was built between 1228 and 1231 CE.
b_schwalenberg.etymology_analysis: From Middle Low German *swale* ('swallow', depicted on the municipal arms) + *berg* ('hill, mountain'), paired since 1970 with neighboring *Schieder*.

historical_names.name: Schieder
historical_names.source: Carolingian records (822 CE)
historical_names.notes: Alt-Schieder, now part of Schieder-Schwalenberg, is first recorded in 822 CE.

b_everstein.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1116 CE through Conrad of Everstein, the earliest known bearer of the comital title named after the ancestral castle near Holzminden; Burg Everstein on the Burgberg ridge itself is explicitly documented in 1226 CE.
b_everstein.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Low German ever ('wild boar') and stein ('stone, rock, castle'), referring to the rocky hilltop stronghold on the Burgberg ridge in the Weser Uplands.

b_diepholz.first_mention_attestation: First attested around 1080–1088 CE through Gottschalk of Diepholz (de Thefholte) and his sister Gysela, who exchanged estates around Drebber and Diepholz with the Bishop of Osnabrück around 1085 CE.
b_diepholz.etymology_analysis: From Old Saxon *thef ('deep, low-lying') and holt ('wood, forest'), attested in medieval Latinized forms such as Thefholte, denoting a settlement or moated stronghold in a low-lying woodland along the Hunte river.

b_minden.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 798 CE in the Royal Frankish Annals (Annales regni Francorum) when Charlemagne marched north from Herstelle to Minden to cross the Weser during the Saxon Wars; shortly thereafter it became an episcopal see.
b_minden.etymology_analysis: Attested early as Mimthun and Mindon, the name likely derives from an Old Saxon or Germanic root related to 'mouth' or 'passage/crossing' (referring to the strategic ford across the Weser where the Bastau joins it) combined with a locative suffix.

b_bruchhausen.first_mention_attestation: Bruchhausen is first attested in written records in 1189 CE, while the neighbouring parish of Vilsen is first documented in 1227 CE alongside St. Cyriakus Church; the two were united in 1929 CE.
b_bruchhausen.etymology_analysis: A compound of two medieval settlement names: Bruchhausen combines Low German brok/bruch ('marsh, bog') with hausen ('houses, settlement'), while Vilsen derives from an older hydronymic or marshland root.

b_hoya.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written historical records in 1150 CE as a merchant settlement (wik) on the Weser; the Counts of Hoya are documented from 1202 CE.
b_hoya.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Saxon *hōh ('high') and *ō/*ouwe ('island, floodplain, water meadow'), describing a raised island or dry riverbank terrace in the Weser floodplain.

b_oldenburg.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a 1108 CE document as Aldenburg (apud Aldenburch), recording a pension of eels for Count Egilmar I at the ford of the navigable Hunte river.
b_oldenburg.etymology_analysis: From Old Saxon ald ('old') and burg ('fortress, stronghold'), originally attested as Aldenburg/Aldenburch and meaning 'the old fortress' at the Hunte river crossing.

b_leer.first_mention_attestation: Saint Ludger built the first chapel in East Frisia at the settlement then called Hleri in 791 CE; this chapel and settlement are first attested in a written document (Vita Liudgeri) in 850 CE.
b_leer.etymology_analysis: Attested in the 9th century as Hleri, deriving from an Old Frisian or Old Saxon root meaning 'pasture, clearing, or willow-grove' along the Leda river.

b_twistringen.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a written document in 1250 CE under the name Thuisteringe, although local parish traditions date back to the early 9th century.
b_twistringen.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1250 CE as Thuisteringe, combining a root related to Low German twistern ('to branch, fork')—referring to the branching headwaters of the Delme—or a personal name with the Germanic collective settlement suffix -ingen.

b_wolpe.first_mention_attestation: Burg Wölpe, the motte-and-bailey seat of the Counts of Wölpe on the Wölpe stream near Nienburg, is first attested in written records in 1151 CE.
b_wolpe.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Wölpe stream, a hydronym combining an Old Saxon or older European root with the widespread northwestern Germanic stream suffix -apa/-pe ('water, stream').

b_schauenburg.first_mention_attestation: Schaumburg (originally Schauenburg) Castle near Rinteln on the Weser is first attested around 1106–1110 CE when Adolf I became the first Lord of Schauenburg.
b_schauenburg.etymology_analysis: From Middle Low German scouwen ('to look, watch') and burg ('castle'), meaning 'lookout castle' in reference to its commanding hilltop position overlooking the Weser valley.

b_depenau.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a 1383 CE Hoya document as 'dat nige Slot, geheten de Depenauwe' ('the new castle called Diepenau'), built in 1382 CE by Count Erich I of Hoya and destroyed by the Bishop of Minden the following year.
b_depenau.etymology_analysis: From Middle Low German dep ('deep') and auwe ('water meadow, stream'), describing a lowland border fortress built in the marshy meadows near the border with Minden.

b_blankenburg.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in 1123 CE when Duke Lothair of Supplinburg installed Poppo I as count at Blankenburg Castle on the bare limestone ridge in the northern Harz foothills.
b_blankenburg.etymology_analysis: Derived from Middle Low German blank ('bright, white, bare') and burg ('castle'), referring to the white, bare limestone rock outcrop on which the castle was constructed.

b_hohenstein.first_mention_attestation: Although traditionally thought to have been built around 1120 CE, Hohnstein Castle in the southern Harz is first explicitly documented in a charter in 1202 CE.
b_hohenstein.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German hōh ('high') and stein ('stone, rock'), denoting a hilltop fortress perched on a steep porphyry crag above Neustadt im Harz.

b_dessau.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written records in 1213 CE on the left bank of the Mulde river near its confluence with the Elbe.
b_dessau.etymology_analysis: Of Polabian Slavic origin, commonly derived from *tis ('yew tree') or a related Slavic root with the possessive/locative suffix -ov (Germanized to -au).

b_zerbst.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 949 CE as the Gau Ciervisti, and explicitly as a fortified town (Zirwisti urbs) in 1018 CE in the chronicle of Thietmar of Merseburg.

morphemes.translation: worm / kermes red dye (or tribal name Ciervisti)

b_zerbst.etymology_analysis: Derived from Polabian Slavic *Čьrvišče (recorded as Ciervisti and Zirwisti), linked to the Slavic tribal name or the root *čьrvь ('worm, kermes dye') with the locative suffix -išče.

b_halberstadt.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 814 CE when Emperor Louis the Pious established the episcopal see of the Diocese of Halberstadt (moving the Carolingian mission from Osterwieck).
b_halberstadt.etymology_analysis: A compound of an Old Saxon personal name (such as *Halaberaht or *Albero) and stat ('place, settlement'), meaning 'Halaberaht's homestead'.

b_werningerode.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written records in 1121 CE in a deed mentioning Count Adalbert of Haimar as Count of Wernigerode.
b_werningerode.etymology_analysis: Combines the Germanic personal name Werniko/Warin with the Middle Low German suffix -rode ('forest clearing'), reflecting medieval deforestation and settlement in the northern Harz.

b_arnstein.first_mention_attestation: Burg Arnstein near Harkerode in the eastern Harz is first documented in 1156 CE as the ancestral seat of the Lords of Arnstein.

morphemes.language: Middle High German / Middle Low German
Middle High German / Middle Low German

b_arnstein.etymology_analysis: From Middle High/Low German arn ('eagle') and stein ('rock, castle'), meaning 'Eagle's Crag' in reference to the hilltop castle above the Eine valley.

b_magdeburg.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 805 CE as Magadoburg in Charlemagne's Capitulary of Diedenhofen (Thionville), designating it as a regulated frontier trading post with the Slavs.
b_magdeburg.etymology_analysis: Recorded in 805 CE as Magadoburg, combining Old Saxon burg ('fortress') with magad/magath, interpreted either as 'maiden' (later associated with the Virgin Mary or a pagan maiden deity) or 'great, mighty' (*magath-).

b_mockern.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 948 CE as Mokrianici in a tithe charter issued by King Otto I.
b_mockern.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Polabian Slavic name Mokrianici, from *mokry ('wet, swampy') and the suffix -anici, denoting 'people living in a marshy area'.

b_gommern.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 948 CE as Guntmiri in the founding charter of the Diocese of Brandenburg.
b_gommern.etymology_analysis: Attested in 948 CE as Guntmiri, deriving from a Polabian Slavic personal name or topographic root that evolved through Middle Low German into Gommern.

b_mansfeld.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 973 CE as Mannesfeld in an exchange charter of Emperor Otto II; the Counts of Mansfeld are documented from 1060 CE.
b_mansfeld.etymology_analysis: Attested in 973 CE as Mannesfeld, combining the Germanic personal name Manno (in the genitive) with Old Saxon feld ('field, open land').

b_sangerhausen.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a Fulda Abbey document dated 780–802 CE, and subsequently recorded as Sangerhus in the Hersfeld Tithe Register (881–899 CE).
b_sangerhausen.etymology_analysis: From Old High German/Old Saxon *sang ('burnt clearing, slash-and-burn site') and husen ('houses'), denoting a settlement established on land cleared by burning.

b_mersenburg.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written records in 850 CE, before becoming a major royal palace and episcopal seat under the Ottonians in the 10th century.
b_mersenburg.etymology_analysis: Combines Old Saxon mersc/meri ('marsh, wetland' or 'boundary') with burg ('fortress'), referring to the fortified site above the Saale floodplain.

b_leipzig.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1015 CE as Urbs Lipzi in the chronicle of Prince-Bishop Thietmar of Merseburg.
b_leipzig.etymology_analysis: From West Slavic (Sorbian) *Lipsk, derived from lipa ('linden tree') and the locative suffix -sk, meaning 'settlement among the linden trees'.

b_halle.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 806 CE in the Chronicon Moissiacense as Halla, where Charlemagne's son Charles the Younger built a fortified base on the Saale.
b_halle.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived from a Germanic or Celtic root *hall- associated with salt production and brine springs (or, in modern onomastics, an Indo-European root meaning 'slope'), reflecting the town's Bronze Age and medieval saltworks.

b_chur.first_mention_attestation: Known in Roman times as Curia Raetorum, Chur is first attested in written Christian records as the seat of a bishopric in 451–452 CE.
b_chur.etymology_analysis: From Roman Latin Curia (Raetorum), meaning 'court' or 'assembly hall' (possibly adapting a pre-Roman Celtic or Raetian *kora 'clan, tribe'), which developed into German Chur and Romansh Cuira.

b_farduzes.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 12th-century manuscripts (c. 1150–1175 CE) under the Romansh/Latinized name Faduzes (de Faduzes).
b_farduzes.etymology_analysis: Attested in the 12th century as Faduzes, derived from Old Romansh—either from Latin vallis dulcis ('sweet valley') or aquae ductus ('water conduit'), reflecting the Alpine Rhine valley's Romance-speaking heritage.

b_vares.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 765 CE as Senegaune in the testament of Bishop Tello of Chur.
b_vares.etymology_analysis: Attested in 765 CE as Senegaune, of obscure pre-Germanic (Romansh or Raetian) origin; the folk etymology connecting it to 'goose' (Gans) is reflected in its 15th-century canting coat of arms.

b_werdenburg.first_mention_attestation: Although Werdenberg Castle was built around 1228–1230 CE by Count Rudolf I of Montfort, the fortified market town of Werdenberg is first explicitly mentioned in written documents in 1289 CE.

morphemes.translation: river island, peninsula, or elevated dry ground

b_werdenburg.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German wert ('island, raised ground near water') and berg ('hill, mountain'), referring to the castle hill overlooking the Rhine plain.

b_konstanz.first_mention_attestation: Built over the late Roman fortress of Constantia, Konstanz is attested in written historical records from around 585 CE when the first bishop took up residence there.

morphemes.translation: named after Emperor Constantius Chlorus (or Constantius II)

b_konstanz.etymology_analysis: Derived from the late Roman fortress name Constantia, honoring the Roman emperor Constantius Chlorus (or his grandson Constantius II), which evolved into German Konstanz.

b_sankt_gallen.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a hermitage by Saint Gall around 612 CE, the Abbey of St. Gall was formally established in 719 CE by Saint Otmar and is richly documented in 8th-century abbey charters.
b_sankt_gallen.etymology_analysis: Named after Saint Gall (Latin Gallus, c. 550–645 CE), an Irish missionary companion of Columbanus whose 7th-century hermitage grew into the Abbey of St. Gall.

b_zurich.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Roman Turicum (statio Turicensis) on a 2nd-century CE Roman funerary inscription discovered on the Lindenhof hill.
b_zurich.etymology_analysis: From Roman Latin Turicum, adapted from a Gaulish place name *Turikon ('estate/settlement of Turos'), which underwent the High German consonant shift to become Zürich.

b_schwyz.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written records in 972 CE under the Old High German name Suittes.

morphemes.translation: to burn, forest clearing by fire

b_schwyz.etymology_analysis: Attested in 972 CE as Suittes, generally connected to Old High German *swedan ('to burn'), referring to an area of forest cleared by burning for settlement.

b_engelberg.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1120 CE with the foundation of Engelberg Abbey (Mons Angelorum, 'Mountain of Angels') by Conrad of Sellenbüren.
b_engelberg.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German engel ('angel') and berg ('mountain'), translating the monastic Latin name Mons Angelorum given to the Benedictine abbey founded in 1120 CE.

b_basel.first_mention_attestation: First recorded as Basilia in 237–238 CE, and later named by the Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus in 374 CE as a Roman fortification on the Rhine.
b_basel.etymology_analysis: From Latin (villa) Basilia, meaning 'estate of Basilius' (or less likely from basilica), recorded in the 3rd and 4th centuries CE and preserved in German Basel and French Bâle.

b_ansbach.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 748 CE in connection with the foundation of a Benedictine monastery; the settlement name appears as Onoltesbach around 790 CE and Onoltespah in 837 CE.
b_ansbach.etymology_analysis: Originally attested as Onoltesbach, combining the Old High German personal name Onold (with genitive -es) and pah/bach ('brook'), which contracted over centuries to Ansbach.

b_uffenheim.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written records in 1103 CE as Offenheim in a document of Hirsau Abbey.
b_uffenheim.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1103 CE as Offenheim, a classic Frankish -heim compound combining the Germanic personal name Uffo/Offo with heim ('homestead').

b_trubending.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written records in 1129 CE in an Eichstätt charter naming the free noble (edelfreie) Lords of Truhendingen.
b_trubending.etymology_analysis: Combines Middle High German hōh ('high', distinguishing the hilltop castle from Altentrüdingen) with Trüdingen, from Old High German Truhtmuntinga ('settlement of Truhtmunt's people').

b_bamberg.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 902 CE as Babenburg Castle in connection with the Babenberg Feud between the Popponids and Conradines.

eponym.details: Likely named Babenburg after Poppo II, Margrave of Thuringia (fl. c. 880–906 CE), whose name was also rendered as Babo.

b_bamberg.etymology_analysis: Originally Babenburg ('Babo's castle'), likely named after Poppo II of Thuringia (Babo); later shifted from -burg ('castle') to -berg ('hill') to give modern Bamberg.

b_greiffenst.first_mention_attestation: Greifenstein Castle near Heiligenstadt in Franconian Switzerland is first attested in written records in 1172 CE as Grifenstin.
b_greiffenst.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1172 CE as Grifenstin, from Middle High German grīf ('griffin') and stein ('rock, castle'), a typical High Medieval heraldic/symbolic castle name meaning 'Griffin's Crag'.

b_casel.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1286 CE (receiving market and town rights in 1328 CE) in Upper Franconia near Bamberg.
b_casel.etymology_analysis: Kasendorf (historically attested as Katzendorf and Katzenstadt, reflected in its canting coat of arms) combines Middle High German katze ('cat') with -dorf ('village').

b_iphofen.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 741–742 CE as one of the twenty-five royal churches and estates gifted by Carloman to the newly established Diocese of Würzburg.
b_iphofen.etymology_analysis: Combines Old High German hofen ('at the farmsteads/courts') with a personal name (Ippo/Iffo) or topographic root.

b_coburg.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a monastic donation document dated 1056 CE by Richeza of Lotharingia transferring the property to Archbishop Anno II of Cologne.
b_coburg.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old High German kuo ('cow', i.e. 'cow hill/fortress') or a topographic/personal root combined with burg ('fortress').

b_lichtenfels.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written records in 1142 CE; later chartered in 1231 CE by Duke Otto III of Merania.
b_lichtenfels.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German lieht ('bright, light, cleared') and fels ('rock, crag'), referring to a bright or cleared rocky eminence above the Upper Main valley.

b_mergentheim.first_mention_attestation: First attested in chronicles in 1058 CE as Mergintaim, the seat of the Counts of Mergentheim in the Taubergau.
b_mergentheim.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1058 CE as Mergintaim, combining an Old High German personal name with heim ('homestead'); the prefix Bad ('spa') was added in 1926 CE.

b_weinsberg.first_mention_attestation: The town of Weinsberg is first attested in a Hohenstaufen tax/income list in 1241 CE (though the hilltop castle above it was besieged in 1140 CE).
b_weinsberg.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German wīn ('wine, vineyard') or the personal name Wino combined with berg ('hill'), referring to the vineyard-covered Burgberg.

b_hall.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a written document in 1037 CE as Hall, although Celtic salt production on the site dates back to the 5th century BCE.
b_hall.etymology_analysis: Named after its ancient salt springs (Hall, traditionally linked to Celtic/Germanic terms for saltworks), with the regional qualifier Schwäbisch ('Swabian') added later to distinguish it from other salt towns.

b_nordlingen.first_mention_attestation: First attested in recorded history in 898 CE as a royal court (Nordilinga) in the Ries crater.
b_nordlingen.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old High German Nordilinga, combining the personal name Nordilo (or directional nord 'north') with the Alemannic settlement suffix -ingen.

b_dillingen.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing in 973 CE in the Vita of Saint Ulrich of Augsburg, in connection with the Hupaldinger Counts of Dillingen.
b_dillingen.etymology_analysis: Combines the Alemannic personal name Dillo/Tillo with the settlement suffix -ingen ('people of Dillo'), with the modern riverine qualifier 'an der Donau' ('on the Danube').

b_crailsheim.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1136 CE as Cröwelsheim in a medieval charter; it received town rights in 1338 CE.
b_crailsheim.etymology_analysis: Crailsheim (attested 1136 CE as Cröwelsheim) combines an Old High German personal name (or topographic term for a bend/hook) with the settlement suffix -heim ('homestead, village').

b_nurnberg.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1050 CE in the Sigena charter issued by Emperor Henry III as Norenberc, referring to the imperial castle site.
b_nurnberg.etymology_analysis: Nuremberg (1050 CE Norenberc) derives from Old High German nuor ('rock, crag') and berg ('hill, mountain'), referring to the sandstone rock ridge on which Nuremberg Castle stands.

b_riedfeld.first_mention_attestation: Documented in 741/742 CE as the Frankish royal estate (Königshof) of Reotfeld/Riedfeld when its tithe was granted to the newly founded Diocese of Würzburg.
b_riedfeld.etymology_analysis: Riedfeld (741/742 CE Reotfeld) combines Old High German hriot ('reed, marshy ground') with feld ('open field, plain'), describing the marshy floodplain along the Aisch river where the royal estate was established before Neustadt an der Aisch was founded nearby in the 13th century.

b_abenberg.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned between 1057 and 1075 CE as Abinberch; the modern spelling Abenberg is first attested in 1152 CE.
b_abenberg.etymology_analysis: Abenberg (1057–1075 CE Abinberch) is a compound of the Old High German personal name Abbo and berg ('hill, mountain', later 'castle'), meaning 'hill or castle of Abbo'.

b_wiltberg.first_mention_attestation: Burg Wildberg in the Haßberge/Grabfeld region of Lower Franconia is first attested in 1123 CE through its noble family (Herren von Wildberg); no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_wiltberg.etymology_analysis: Wiltberg/Wildberg (attested 1123 CE) combines Old High German wildi ('wild, untamed, forested') with berg ('hill, fortified height'), referring to the hilltop castle in the Haßberge hills of Lower Franconia.

b_schweinfurt.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 791 CE as Suinuurt (or Suinfurde) in early medieval Fulda Abbey charters.
b_schweinfurt.etymology_analysis: Schweinfurt (791 CE Suinuurt) combines Old High German swīn ('pig, wild boar') with furt ('ford'), denoting a shallow crossing over the Main river used by swine or wild boars.

b_henneberg.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1096 CE as the ancestral seat and adopted name of the Counts of Henneberg; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_henneberg.etymology_analysis: Henneberg (attested 1096 CE) combines Old High German henna ('hen, wild fowl') with berg ('hill, castle'), referring to the hillfort near Meiningen that gave its name to the House of Henneberg.

b_wurzburg.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 704 CE as castellum Virteburch in a charter of Duke Hedan II, and made the seat of a diocese by Saint Boniface in 742 CE.

morphemes.translation: herb, root, or Celtic personal/place element

b_wurzburg.etymology_analysis: Würzburg (704 CE Virteburch) combines an early element Virte-/Wurz- (often linked to Old High German wurz 'herb, spice' or a pre-Germanic Celtic root) with -burg ('fortress'), designating the stronghold on the Main river.

b_hochberg.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 748 CE as Hugbur (huegbur) when Bishop Burkard of Würzburg granted the parish to St. Andrew's Monastery.
b_hochberg.etymology_analysis: Höchberg (748 CE Hugbur, later reshaped by folk etymology to Höchberg) derives from Old High German hōh ('high') or hugu/bur ('hill/dwelling') with -berg ('hill'), describing its elevated position immediately west of Würzburg.

b_hammelburg.first_mention_attestation: First documented on 18 April 716 CE as Hamulo Castellum in a charter donating the estate to Saint Willibrord.
b_hammelburg.etymology_analysis: Hammelburg (716 CE Hamulo Castellum) combines the early Frankish personal name Hamulo (or a topographic root hamal 'steep slope') with -burg ('fortress').

b_fulda.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 744 CE when Sturmius, a disciple of Saint Boniface, founded Fulda Abbey on the banks of the Fulda river.
b_fulda.etymology_analysis: Fulda takes its name from the Fulda river (attested as Fuldaha), combining a pre-Germanic or Germanic root *fuldō ('flat land, field') with Old High German aha ('water, stream').

b_hersfeld.first_mention_attestation: Documented by 769 CE when Archbishop Lullus of Mainz founded Hersfeld Abbey (after an earlier hermitage established by Sturmius around 736 CE) at Hairulfisfeld.
b_hersfeld.etymology_analysis: Hersfeld (early medieval Hairulfisfeld / Herolfesfelt) combines the Old High German personal name Hariulf (later reinterpreted via hiruz 'hart, stag') with -feld ('field, plain').

b_lauterbach.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 812 CE in a document of the church in Schlitz.
b_lauterbach.etymology_analysis: Lauterbach (attested 812 CE) takes its name from the Lauterbach stream, combining Old High German lūtar ('clear, pure') with bah ('brook, stream').

b_kassel.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 913 CE as Chassalla in two royal deeds signed by King Conrad I; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_kassel.etymology_analysis: Kassel (913 CE Chassalla) derives from Latin castellum ('fortress, fortified post'), reflecting an early medieval fortification along the Fulda river.

b_ziegenhain.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1144 CE through Counts Gottfried and Boppo de Cigenhagen; it received town rights in 1274 CE. No written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_ziegenhain.etymology_analysis: Ziegenhain (1144 CE Cigenhagen) combines Middle/Old High German ziga ('goat') with hagen/hain ('hedged enclosure, grove'), referring to a fenced pasture or woodland.

b_hofgeismar.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1082 CE; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_hofgeismar.etymology_analysis: Hofgeismar (attested 1082 CE) pairs Hof ('manor, court') with Geismar, from Old High German geis- ('bubbling, gushing') and -mar ('spring, marsh'), referring to local mineral springs.

b_munden.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 802 CE as Gimundi in deeds of donation to Fulda Abbey.
b_munden.etymology_analysis: Münden (802 CE Gimundi) derives from Old High German gimundi ('river mouth, confluence'), referring to the junction of the Fulda and Werra rivers where they form the Weser.

b_marburg.first_mention_attestation: Contemporarily attested from 1138–1140 CE (with coins minted from 1140 CE); a later 14th-century compilation (the Reinhardsbrunner Chronik) anachronistically projects a reference back to 822 CE.
b_marburg.etymology_analysis: Marburg combines Old High German marca ('border, march') with -burg ('fortress'), denoting the border castle overlooking the Lahn river valley.

b_nidda.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 951 CE; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists for the town of Nidda itself.
b_nidda.etymology_analysis: Nidda (attested 951 CE) takes its name from the Nidda river, an ancient Old European/Celtic hydronym meaning 'flowing water' or 'shining river'.

b_budingen.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1131 CE through the Lords of Büdingen (Herren von Büdingen), with the settlement (villa) explicitly documented in 1206 CE; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_budingen.etymology_analysis: Büdingen (attested 1131 CE) is an -ingen settlement name formed from an Old High German personal name Budo and the collective suffix -ingen ('at the people of Budo').

b_wetzlar.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 832 CE as Weftifa (Wetzlar) in the Upper Lahngau, prior to the consecration of its Church of the Saviour in 897 CE.
b_wetzlar.etymology_analysis: Wetzlar combines an early hydronymic or personal element with the archaic suffix -lar ('meadow, clearing, settlement site'), characteristic of early medieval or pre-Frankish settlements along the Lahn.

b_siegen.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1079 CE in a charter mentioning Rupert of Laurenburg as Vogt at Siegen; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_siegen.etymology_analysis: Siegen (attested 1079 CE) derives from the Celtic or Old European river name Sieg (Sigina), referring to the river flowing through the town.

b_solms.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 788 CE as Sulmese in a donation charter of Lorsch Abbey.
b_solms.etymology_analysis: Solms (788 CE Sulmese) takes its name from the Solmsbach stream, an Old European hydronym meaning 'swelling or muddy water', at whose confluence with the Lahn the settlement lies.

b_diez.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 790 CE as Theodissa in the Lower Lahngau, long before the Counts of Diez were first mentioned in 1073 CE.
b_diez.etymology_analysis: Diez (790 CE Theodissa) derives from an early hydronym combining a Germanic/Old European root for 'rushing, roaring water' with the river suffix -issa.

b_ditmarschen.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written sources around 1075–1076 CE by Adam of Bremen as Tedmarsgoi (earlier forms Thiatmaresgaho); no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_ditmarschen.etymology_analysis: Dithmarschen (1076 CE Tedmarsgoi, from Thiatmaresgaho) derives from Old Saxon Thiatmar (either a personal name or 'great people') combined with -gō ('district') and later reshaped by -marsch ('marshland').

b_neumunster.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1127 CE when Vicelinus founded the Augustinian monastery Novum Monasterium ('New Minster') at Wippendorf; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_neumunster.etymology_analysis: Neumünster translates Latin Novum Monasterium ('New Minster'), named after the Augustinian monastery founded there by Vicelinus in 1127 CE.

b_itzehoe.first_mention_attestation: Itzehoe Castle was first mentioned in 1168 CE as Echeho, and the town (Opidium Ekeho) was first mentioned by Saxo Grammaticus in 1196 CE.
b_itzehoe.etymology_analysis: Itzehoe (1168 CE Echeho) combines a disputed first element (associated with pasture or Old Saxon ek 'oak') with -hoe ('elevation, raised river bend').

historical_names.name: Esesfeld
historical_names.source: Annales regni Francorum (809 CE)
historical_names.notes: Carolingian fortress built in 809 CE on the Stör river approximately 2 km from the later town of Itzehoe.

b_lubeck.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1143 CE by Adolf II, Count of Schauenburg and Holstein, on the river island of Bucu; the older Slavic settlement of Liubice is first recorded in 1072 CE (no written attestation <= 867 CE).

morphemes.translation: lovely, dear, or personal name Lub/Lubomir

b_lubeck.etymology_analysis: Lübeck derives from Polabian Slavic Liubice ('place of Lub/Lubomir' or 'lovely place'), transferred to the new 1143 CE German trading city from the nearby destroyed Obotrite center of Old Lübeck.

b_femera.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written sources around 1075 CE in Adam of Bremen's Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum as Fembre; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_femera.etymology_analysis: Fehmarn (1075 CE Fembre, medieval Femera) derives from Polabian Slavic *Vemorje ('in the sea'), referring to the Baltic island off the coast of Wagria.

b_kiel.first_mention_attestation: Founded between 1233 and 1242 CE by Adolf IV of Schauenburg and Holstein (first documented as tom Kyle and granted Lübeck town rights in 1242 CE); no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_kiel.etymology_analysis: Kiel (13th-century tom Kyle) derives from Middle Low German kīl ('wedge'), referring to the wedge-shaped Kiel Fjord (Kieler Förde) on which the town was founded.

b_stade.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in writing in 994 CE as Stethu when Vikings raided the settlement; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_stade.etymology_analysis: Stade (994 CE Stethu) derives from Old Saxon steth/stado ('riverbank, landing place'), describing its harbor on the Schwinge river near the Elbe.

b_bederkesa.first_mention_attestation: First documented in the 12th century (1159 CE) through the Knights of Bederkesa; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_bederkesa.etymology_analysis: Bederkesa (Low German Beers) combines an Old Saxon personal or topographic element with a water/stream suffix, referring to the settlement beside Lake Bederkesa.

b_cuxhaven.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1570 CE as Kuckshafen (later Kukeshaven in 1577 CE); it received city rights in 1907 CE.
b_cuxhaven.etymology_analysis: Cuxhaven (1570 CE Kuckshafen) derives from Low German kōg ('polder, diked land') and haven ('harbor'), referring to the port established at the mouth of the Elbe.

b_brunswick.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1031 CE as Brunesguik in documents of St. Magni Church; tradition attributes its founding to Saxon count Brun(o) (d. 880 CE).

eponym.details: Traditionally derived from the Saxon count Brun(o) (legendarily dated to 861/880 CE or Bruno II, d. before 1017 CE), combined with Low German -wik ('trading settlement'); an alternative etymology derives the first element from Brand ('clearing by burning').

b_brunswick.etymology_analysis: Braunschweig (1031 CE Brunesguik) combines the personal name Brun(o) (or alternatively brand 'clearing by burning') with Low German wik ('merchant resting place, trading settlement') at a ford on the Oker river.

b_wolfenbuttel.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1118 CE as Wulferisbuttle when Saxon count Widekind of Wolfenbüttel built a water castle there; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_wolfenbuttel.etymology_analysis: Wolfenbüttel (1118 CE Wulferisbuttle) combines the Old Saxon personal name Wulferi with the northern German settlement suffix -büttel ('homestead, settlement').

b_dannenberg.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1153 CE with the construction of Dannenberg Castle under Count Volrad I of Dannenberg; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_dannenberg.etymology_analysis: Dannenberg (attested 1153 CE) combines Low German dannen ('fir/pine') with berg ('hill, castle'), referring to a fortified hill in a conifer forest.

b_luchow.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1158 CE; it received city rights in 1293 CE. No written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_luchow.etymology_analysis: Lüchow (attested 1158 CE) derives from Polabian Slavic *Lugov ('place in the marshy meadow'), reflecting the Wendland wetlands along the Jeetzel river.

b_gifhorn.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1196 CE; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists (an 896 CE well excavated in 2014 is also post-867 and non-documentary).
b_gifhorn.etymology_analysis: Gifhorn (attested 1196 CE) combines a Low German root meaning 'fork' with horn ('spit of land, angle'), describing its position in the wedge between the Aller and Ise rivers.

b_hamburg.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Hammaburg by 831–834 CE when Emperor Louis the Pious established a Christian diocese and mission base there under Ansgar.

morphemes.translation: river bend, marshy tongue of land

b_hamburg.etymology_analysis: Hamburg (831–834 CE Hammaburg) combines Old Saxon hamma ('river bend, marshy projection') with -burg ('fortress'), referring to the early Carolingian stronghold between the Alster and Elbe rivers.

b_buxtehude.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in 959 CE as the manor of Buochstadon when it was donated to the Abbey of Magdeburg; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_buxtehude.etymology_analysis: Buxtehude (959 CE Buochstadon) combines Old Saxon buoch ('beech') with stadon/hude ('riverbank, landing place'), denoting a landing site among beech woods on the Este river.

b_ahrensburg.first_mention_attestation: The medieval castle Arx Arnsburga (Arnesvelde) is first documented through reeves in 1295 CE, and the precursor village Woldenhorn in 1314 CE; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_ahrensburg.etymology_analysis: Ahrensburg (1295 CE Arnsburga) derives from Middle Low German arn ('eagle') and burg ('castle'), named after the nearby medieval Arnesvelde castle.

b_luneburg.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in medieval records on 13 August 956 CE in a deed of Emperor Otto I granting the salt tax from Lüneburg (Hliuni); no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_luneburg.etymology_analysis: Lüneburg (956 CE Hliuni / Luniburg) combines Old Saxon hliuni ('refuge, shelter') with -burg ('fortress'), referring to the stronghold atop the Kalkberg hill.

b_uelzen.first_mention_attestation: Founded around 1250 CE by settlers moving from nearby Oldenstadt (itself first attested in 973 CE) and granted town rights in 1270 CE; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

morphemes.translation: personal name Ulli or marshy stream

b_uelzen.etymology_analysis: Uelzen (earlier Ullishusun, transferred from Oldenstadt) derives from an Old Saxon personal or stream name combined with -husen ('houses, settlement'), shortened to -en.

b_walsrode.first_mention_attestation: First recorded on 7 May 986 CE in an imperial deed of Emperor Otto III confirming the foundation of Walsrode Abbey by Count Walo; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

eponym.details: Named after Count Walo (fl. 986 CE), a Saxon nobleman who founded Walsrode Abbey in 986 CE, combined with -rode ('clearing').

b_walsrode.etymology_analysis: Walsrode (986 CE) combines the personal name of its 10th-century founder, Count Walo, with -rode ('cleared land, forest clearing').

b_celle.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 985 CE as Kiellu (and in 986 CE as Kellu at Altencelle); no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_celle.etymology_analysis: Celle (985 CE Kiellu) derives from Old Saxon kiellu/kellu ('fishing bay, settlement by a river bend') along the Aller river.

b_stendal.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a deed dated 1022 CE under Emperor Henry II, and granted market rights by Albert the Bear around 1160 CE; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_stendal.etymology_analysis: Stendal (attested 1022 CE) combines Old Saxon stēn ('stone') with dal ('valley'), meaning 'stone valley'.

b_gardelegen.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1186 CE through Count Henry of Gardelegen (Heinricus comes de Gardelege); no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

morphemes.translation: personal name Gardo or marshy ground

b_gardelegen.etymology_analysis: Gardelegen (1186 CE Gardelege) combines an Old Saxon personal or marsh-related root with -lege/-leben ('inherited estate, settlement').

b_werben.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1005 CE as Wiribeni iuxta Albim when King Henry II negotiated there; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_werben.etymology_analysis: Werben (1005 CE Wiribeni) derives either from Slavic vrba ('willow') or Old Saxon hwerban ('bend, turn'), referring to its strategic crossing on a bend of the Elbe.

b_baden.first_mention_attestation: First attested under the medieval German name Baden in 987 CE (later seat of the Margraves of Baden by 1112 CE); the Roman thermal settlement on the same site was known as Aquae.

morphemes.translation: at the baths (dative plural of bad 'bath')

b_baden.etymology_analysis: Baden (attested 987 CE) is the Old High German dative plural of bad ('bath'), translating the Roman name Aquae ('the Waters') for its thermal springs; the doubled form Baden-Baden arose to distinguish the town within the Margraviate of Baden-Baden.

historical_names.name: Aquae
historical_names.source: Roman stone inscription of Emperor Caracalla (213 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman thermal settlement established around 80 CE and attested by a 213 CE inscription under Caracalla.

historical_names.name: Aurelia Aquensis
historical_names.source: Roman stone inscription of Emperor Caracalla (213 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman thermal settlement established around 80 CE and attested by a 213 CE inscription under Caracalla.

b_sulz.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 790 CE as villa publica Sulza; a Roman military camp (Fort Sulz) had earlier stood on the hill around 74 CE.
b_sulz.etymology_analysis: Sulz (790 CE Sulza) derives from Old High German sulza ('salt water, brine spring'), named after the local salt springs along the upper Neckar river.

b_calw.first_mention_attestation: Calw is first attested in written records in 1037 CE in connection with the Counts of Calw, around whose earlier hilltop castle the town developed in the Nagold valley.
b_calw.etymology_analysis: The name Calw (early Latinized/Germanic forms such as Calwa) derives from Old High German 'kal' ('bald, bare, treeless') combined with a topographic suffix or 'awa' ('watery meadow'), referring to a bare hillside or clearing above the Nagold River.

b_nellenburg.first_mention_attestation: Nellenburg Castle is first attested in a 1056 CE charter of Count Eberhard VI of Nellenburg as 'castellum meum Nellenburc', though the Nellenburg comital line appears slightly earlier in 10th–11th century sources.
b_nellenburg.etymology_analysis: Nellenburg combines the Old High German personal name Nello (or Nella, later romanticized in local legend as Countess Nella) with 'burg' ('castle, stronghold'), denoting the fortified hill seat above Stockach.

b_furstenberg.first_mention_attestation: Fürstenberg Castle near Hüfingen is first mentioned in a 1175 CE deed as a possession of the House of Zähringen before becoming the residence of the Counts of Fürstenberg around 1250 CE.
b_furstenberg.etymology_analysis: Fürstenberg literally means 'Prince's Hill' (Middle High German 'vurste' + 'berc'), referring to the prominent conical hill in the Baar region on which the Zähringen and later Fürstenberg castle stood.

b_lupfen.first_mention_attestation: Hohenlupfen Castle in Talheim, the ancestral seat of the Counts of Lupfen, is first mentioned in written records in 1065 CE.
b_lupfen.etymology_analysis: Hohenlupfen combines the adjective 'hohen' ('high') with 'Lupfen', the name of the prominent hill spur above Talheim, likely related to Alemannic 'lupfen' ('to lift, rise up') describing the steep elevation.

b_clettgau.first_mention_attestation: The Klettgau region is first attested in 876 CE in a Rheinau Abbey cartulary as 'in pago Chleggouve' (alongside the village of Erzingen, 'villa Arcingen').
b_clettgau.etymology_analysis: Klettgau (attested as 'Chleggouve' in 876 CE) pairs Old High German 'gouwi' ('district, region') with an initial element 'Chlegg-' / 'Klett-', interpreted either as referring to burdock/clayey soil or a personal/tribal name.

b_grunningen.first_mention_attestation: Markgröningen is first mentioned in 779 CE as 'Gruoninga' in a deed of gift to the Monastery of Fulda.
b_grunningen.etymology_analysis: Originally attested as 'Gruoninga' in 779 CE, the name combines the Alamannic settlement suffix '-ingen' with either Old High German 'gruoni' ('green', referring to fertile meadows) or a personal name Grōno; 'Mark-' was added later to reflect its status as a border/market town.

b_sigmaringen.first_mention_attestation: Sigmaringen Castle is first mentioned in 1077 CE in accounts of Rudolf of Rheinfelden's unsuccessful siege of the fortress during his conflict with King Henry IV.
b_sigmaringen.etymology_analysis: Sigmaringen is a classic Alamannic '-ingen' patronymic settlement name meaning 'among the people of Sigimār', derived from the Germanic personal name Sigimār ('victory-famous').

b_berge.first_mention_attestation: Berg near Ehingen, the ancestral seat of the Swabian Counts of Berg-Schelklingen, is first attested around 1100 CE in regional Upper Swabian charters.
b_berge.etymology_analysis: Berg derives from Old High German 'berg' ('hill, mountain'), referring to the elevated spur south of Ehingen above the Danube valley where the Counts of Berg-Schelklingen held their castle.

b_heiligenberg.first_mention_attestation: Heiligenberg is first mentioned in written records in 1083 CE under the Latinized name 'Mons Sanctus' ('Holy Mountain').
b_heiligenberg.etymology_analysis: Heiligenberg (attested in Latin as 'Mons Sanctus' in 1083 CE) literally means 'Holy Mountain', likely referring either to early Christianization around Lake Constance or a pre-Christian sacred hill.

b_hohenberg.first_mention_attestation: Hohenberg (Oberhohenberg) Castle in the Swabian Alb is first documented in 1170 CE with the appearance of Count Burkhard I of Hohenberg (and explicitly as a castle in 1179 CE).
b_hohenberg.etymology_analysis: Hohenberg means 'High Mountain' (from Old High German 'hōh' + 'berg'), named for the 1,011-meter peak in the Swabian Alb; 'Ober-' ('upper') later distinguished it from Niederhohenberg.

b_rottweil.first_mention_attestation: The early medieval settlement of Rotuvilla (whence Rottweil) is first attested in 771 CE, succeeding the Roman municipium Arae Flaviae founded in 73–74 CE.
b_rottweil.etymology_analysis: Rottweil (attested in 771 CE as 'Rotuvilla') combines Old High German 'rōt' ('red') with 'wīl' (from Latin 'villa'), likely referring to the red-tiled roofs or red brick ruins of the Roman municipium Arae Flaviae.

historical_names.name: Arae Flaviae
historical_names.source: Roman foundation (73–74 CE) and Tabula Peutingeriana; royal court 'rotuvilla' (771 CE)
historical_names.notes: Founded as the Roman municipium Arae Flaviae in 73–74 CE and later known as the royal court Rotuvilla by 771 CE.

b_ulm.first_mention_attestation: The earliest written mention of Ulm dates to 22 July 854 CE, when King Louis the German signed a document at the royal palace of 'Hulma' in the Duchy of Swabia.
b_ulm.etymology_analysis: Attested as 'Hulma' in 854 CE, the name Ulm is generally derived from a Germanic or pre-Germanic hydronymic root meaning 'marshy, damp ground' (compare Old High German 'ulmig', decayed/damp) at the confluence of the Blau, Iller, and Danube.

b_hellenenstein.first_mention_attestation: Hellenstein Castle above Heidenheim an der Brenz is first mentioned in 1096 CE through Gozbert of Hellenstein, with the castle itself built during the 12th century.
b_hellenenstein.etymology_analysis: Hellenstein combines the Middle High German element 'Hellen-' (either from a personal name Hello or 'helle', bright/exposed) with 'stein' ('stone, crag'), a standard designation for a hilltop stone castle.

b_helfenstein.first_mention_attestation: Helfenstein Castle above Geislingen an der Steige was built around 1100 CE as the ancestral seat of the Counts of Helfenstein.
b_helfenstein.etymology_analysis: Helfenstein derives from a Germanic personal name (such as Helpo or Helfrich) or 'helfan' ('to help') combined with 'stein' ('rock, castle'); later folk etymology linked its sound to 'Elefant' ('elephant'), which the counts adopted as canting arms.

b_schelklingen.first_mention_attestation: The castle and village of Schelklingen ('castro et villae Schälkalingen') are first mentioned in an 1127 CE deed of the Lords of Schelklingen.
b_schelklingen.etymology_analysis: Schelklingen (attested as 'Schälkalingen' in 1127 CE) is an Alamannic '-ingen' settlement name formed from a personal name derived from Old High German 'scalk' ('servant, retainer') with diminutive '-il-'.

b_wurttemberg.first_mention_attestation: Wirtemberg Castle near Stuttgart had its castle chapel consecrated in 1083 CE under Conrad I of Württemberg, who is attested as 'Konrad de Wirtinisberg' in 1092 CE.
b_wurttemberg.etymology_analysis: Early forms 'Wirtenberg' and 'Wirtinisberg' combine 'berg' ('hill') with 'Wirtin-', either from a Germanic personal name Wirto/Wirtin or adapted from a Celtic hillfort name such as *Virodunum.

b_tubingen.first_mention_attestation: Hohentübingen Castle is first recorded in 1078 CE as 'castrum Twingia' when besieged by King Henry IV, while the town of Tübingen itself is first mentioned in official records in 1191 CE.
b_tubingen.etymology_analysis: Tübingen (early 'Twingia' / 'Tuwingen') is an Alamannic '-ingen' name either derived from a personal name Tuwo or from Old High German 'twingan' ('to press, narrow'), referring to the narrow Neckar valley.

b_teck.first_mention_attestation: Teck Castle above Kirchheim unter Teck is first mentioned in written records in 1152 CE, and Adalbert I styled himself 'Dux de Tecke' in 1189 CE.
b_teck.etymology_analysis: Teck (medieval 'Tecke') is the name of the prominent Swabian Alb spur (Teckberg), likely from an Old High German or pre-Germanic topographic root denoting a ridge or rocky projection.

b_zollern.first_mention_attestation: The House of Hohenzollern is first mentioned in 1061 CE in the annals of Berthold of Reichenau ('Buchardus de Zolorin'), while the castle itself is explicitly named 'Castro Zolre' in 1267 CE.
b_zollern.etymology_analysis: Hohenzollern combines 'hohen' ('high') with 'Zolorin' / 'Zolre', referring to the isolated conical hill in the Swabian Alb; scholars link 'Zolre' either to a pre-Germanic hill name or to Old High German 'zol' (customs/toll station).

b_vehringen.first_mention_attestation: Veringen (modern Veringenstadt) is first mentioned around 786 CE as 'Faringa' in early medieval Swabian records.
b_vehringen.etymology_analysis: Attested as 'Faringa' around 786 CE and 'Veringin' by 1130 CE, the name derives from an Alamannic personal name Faro (or 'fara', kin group/crossing) plus '-ingen'; 'stadt' ('town') was added after the urban foundation around 1250 CE.

b_reutlingen.first_mention_attestation: Reutlingen is first mentioned in writing in the Bempflingen Treaty ('Bempflinger Vertrag'), dated to approximately 1089–1090 CE.
b_reutlingen.etymology_analysis: Reutlingen is an Alamannic '-ingen' settlement name meaning 'among the people of Reutilo', formed from the Germanic personal name Reutilo.

b_gleichenstein.first_mention_attestation: Gleichenstein Castle in the Eichsfeld is first mentioned by name in 1246 CE when Count Heinrich I styled himself 'Graf von Gleichenstein', after rebuilding it on the site of the earlier Velsecke Castle (attested 1180 CE).
b_gleichenstein.etymology_analysis: Gleichenstein combines 'Gleichen' (transferred from the Counts of Tonna/Gleichen's ancestral seat) with 'stein' ('rock, castle'), replacing the earlier castle name Velsecke ('rock-corner').

b_ebeleben.first_mention_attestation: Ebeleben is first mentioned in a 1198 CE document naming Friedrich von Ebeleben, a ministerial of Landgrave Hermann of Thuringia.
b_ebeleben.etymology_analysis: Ebeleben belongs to the characteristic Thuringian '-leben' toponymic group (Old High German 'leiba', 'inheritance, left-behind estate'), combined with the personal name Ebo or Ebilo.

b_muhlhausen.first_mention_attestation: Mühlhausen in Thuringia is first mentioned in written records in 967 CE as a royal court on the Unstrut River.
b_muhlhausen.etymology_analysis: Mühlhausen derives from Old High German 'muli' ('mill') and 'hūsun' (dative plural of 'hūs', 'house'), meaning 'at the mill-houses' along the Unstrut and Schwemmnotte.

b_goslar.first_mention_attestation: Goslar is first mentioned in a 979 CE deed issued by Emperor Otto II as a settlement on the Gose creek.
b_goslar.etymology_analysis: Goslar combines the hydronym 'Gose' (the local stream) with the Old Saxon/Germanic toponymic element '-lār' ('clearing, open pasture, settlement site').

b_gottingen.first_mention_attestation: Göttingen is first mentioned as the village of 'Gutingi' in a 953 CE charter of Emperor Otto I granting possessions there to the Moritz monastery in Magdeburg.
b_gottingen.etymology_analysis: Attested as 'Gutingi' in 953 CE, Göttingen derives from the name of the local stream 'Gote' combined with the suffix '-ingi' ('those living along the Gote').

b_lobdaburg.first_mention_attestation: Lobdeburg near Jena is first attested in 1166 CE when the noble family of Auhausen began styling themselves Lords of Lobdeburg (with the castle itself documented in 1186 CE).
b_lobdaburg.etymology_analysis: Lobdeburg pairs 'burg' ('castle') with 'Lobda-' (connected to the nearby settlement Lobeda), either from Old High German 'louba' ('leafy/forested mountain') or transferred from Ladenburg on the Neckar.

b_hof.first_mention_attestation: Hof (originally Regnitzhof) was founded around 1080 CE when farmers settled and built a chapel on Klausenberg along the Saale.
b_hof.etymology_analysis: Hof derives from Old High German 'hof' ('enclosed courtyard, manor, court'), reflecting its early medieval Latin name 'Curia Variscorum' ('Court of the Varisci') and earlier name Regnitzhof.

b_orlamunde.first_mention_attestation: Orlamünde on the Saale at the mouth of the Orla is first mentioned in a 1039 CE deed.
b_orlamunde.etymology_analysis: Orlamünde literally means 'mouth of the Orla' (Old High German 'münde', 'river mouth' + the river name Orla), describing its position where the Orla empties into the Saale.

b_schwarzburg.first_mention_attestation: Schwarzburg Castle is first mentioned in a 1071 CE deed as 'Swartzinburg'.

morphemes.translation: black, dark (referring to the Schwarza river)

b_schwarzburg.etymology_analysis: Attested as 'Swartzinburg' in 1071 CE, the name combines 'burg' ('castle') with 'swarz' ('black, dark'), referring to the dark-slate Schwarza River valley below the castle.

b_kafernburg.first_mention_attestation: The Counts of Kevernburg (Käfernburg) near Arnstadt are first attested in 1103 CE through Count Sizzo III, while the castle itself is explicitly documented in 1141 CE.
b_kafernburg.etymology_analysis: Early forms 'Kevernburg' / 'Kevernberc' pair 'burg' ('castle') with 'kever-' (related to Middle High German 'kever', 'beetle', or a personal/hill name).

b_schmalkalden.first_mention_attestation: Schmalkalden is first mentioned in an 874 CE deed as 'Smalcalta' in the Frankish Duchy of Thuringia.
b_schmalkalden.etymology_analysis: Attested as 'Smalcalta' in 874 CE, Schmalkalden derives from Old High German 'smal' ('narrow') and 'kalt' ('cold'), originally naming the narrow, cold Schmalkalde stream.

b_eisenach.first_mention_attestation: Eisenach is first mentioned in a 1150 CE document as 'Isinacha', following the 1080 CE mention of nearby Wartburg Castle.
b_eisenach.etymology_analysis: Attested as 'Isinacha' in 1150 CE, Eisenach combines Old High German 'īsan' ('iron') with 'aha' ('water, stream'), meaning 'iron-bearing stream' or 'iron-water'.

b_gleichen.first_mention_attestation: Gleichen Castle (Burg Gleichen) is first mentioned as 'Gliche' in 1034 CE in the annals of Reinhardsbrunn Monastery, and was famously besieged by Emperor Henry IV in 1088–1089 CE.
b_gleichen.etymology_analysis: The name 'Gliche' / 'Gleichen' derives from Old High German 'glīh' ('like, similar'), referring to the striking resemblance of the three neighboring hill castles (Burg Gleichen, Mühlburg, and Wachsenburg) known collectively as Drei Gleichen.

b_beichtinen.first_mention_attestation: Beichlingen is first officially documented in 1014 CE as the seat of the comital family of Beichlingen.
b_beichtinen.etymology_analysis: Beichlingen is a Germanic '-ingen' settlement name meaning 'among the people of Bichilo', formed from an Old High German personal name with the collective suffix '-ingen'.

b_durne.first_mention_attestation: Walldürn is first mentioned in written records in 795 CE (as 'Durne' / 'Turna' in the Lorsch Codex), with 'Wall-' added from 1408 CE after its pilgrimage.
b_durne.etymology_analysis: Originally attested as 'Durne' in 795 CE (likely from Old High German 'durri', 'dry, arid', or 'dorn', 'thorn'), the prefix 'Wall-' ('pilgrimage') was added in the 15th century due to the Holy Blood pilgrimage.

b_mosbach.first_mention_attestation: Mosbach is first mentioned around 825 CE as 'Mosabach' in the records of Reichenau Abbey, and its Benedictine abbey is next recorded in 976 CE under Emperor Otto II.
b_mosbach.etymology_analysis: Attested as 'Mosabach' in 825 CE, Mosbach combines Old High German 'mos' ('moss, bog') and 'bah' ('brook'), meaning 'mossy/boggy stream'.

b_wertheim.first_mention_attestation: Wertheim (initially 'Werdheim') is first mentioned in 779 CE as an outlying holding of Fulda Abbey, with the castle suburbium attested in 1192 CE.
b_wertheim.etymology_analysis: Attested as 'Werdheim' in 779 CE, Wertheim combines Old High German 'werid' ('river island, raised dry bank') with 'heim' ('homestead'), describing the settlement at the confluence of the Tauber and Main.

b_erbach.first_mention_attestation: Erbach im Odenwald is first mentioned in written records in 1095 CE as a settlement in the Odenwald.
b_erbach.etymology_analysis: Erbach derives from Old High German 'bah' ('brook') combined with 'erda' ('earth', referring to a stream that disappears underground in karst terrain) or 'erila' ('alder').

b_seligenstadt.first_mention_attestation: Seligenstadt had its first documentary mention on 11 January 815 CE in a donation charter under its earlier name 'Obermühlheim', before being renamed Seligenstadt after Einhard transferred the relics of Saints Marcellinus and Peter around 828 CE.

morphemes.translation: blessed, holy (referring to the saints' relics)

b_seligenstadt.etymology_analysis: Seligenstadt literally means 'place/town of the blessed ones' (Old High German 'sālig' + 'stat'), coined after Charlemagne's biographer Einhard brought the relics of Saints Marcellinus and Peter from Rome to Obermühlheim in 828 CE.

historical_names.name: Obermühlheim
historical_names.source: Donation charter (11 January 815 CE)
historical_names.notes: Original name of the settlement prior to the 828 CE relic translation.

b_weinheim.first_mention_attestation: Weinheim is first mentioned in 755 CE as 'Winenheim' in the Lorsch Codex (Codex Laureshamensis).
b_weinheim.etymology_analysis: Attested as 'Winenheim' in 755 CE, Weinheim combines the Frankish personal name Wino with Old High German 'heim' ('homestead'); the modern spelling reflects later folk association with 'Wein' ('wine').

b_frankfurt.first_mention_attestation: Frankfurt is first mentioned in 794 CE as 'Franconofurd' in connection with the imperial assembly and church synod presided over by Charlemagne.
b_frankfurt.etymology_analysis: Attested as 'Franconofurd' in 794 CE, Frankfurt means 'ford of the Franks', referring to a shallow crossing of the Main River used by the Franks.

b_limburg.first_mention_attestation: Limburg an der Lahn is first mentioned in 910 CE as 'Lintpurc' in connection with the founding of the St. George collegiate church.
b_limburg.etymology_analysis: Attested as 'Lintpurc' in 910 CE, Limburg combines 'purc' ('castle') with 'Lint-', most plausibly derived from the nearby Linterer Bach stream (possibly linked to Gaulish 'linda', 'water') rather than the later dragon ('Lindworm') legend.

b_russelsheim.first_mention_attestation: Rüsselsheim's first written mention as 'Rucilesheim' occurs in an inventory of royal hunting rights dated around 840 CE (with earlier Lorsch forms listed from 764/5 CE).
b_russelsheim.etymology_analysis: Attested as 'Rucilesheim' around 840 CE, Rüsselsheim means 'the homestead of Rucile', combining a Frankish personal name with Old High German 'heim'.

b_hanau.first_mention_attestation: Hanau is first mentioned in 1143 CE in a Mainz deed naming Dammo von Hagenowe, referring to the moated castle surrounded by arms of the Kinzig River.
b_hanau.etymology_analysis: Early forms 'Hagenowe' (1143 CE) combine Old High German 'hagan' ('fenced woodland, enclosure') with 'ouwa' ('water-meadow, island'), describing the fortified island in the Kinzig bend.

b_kronberg.first_mention_attestation: Kronberg im Taunus is first mentioned in a 1230 CE document naming Otto von Kronberg ('von Cronberg' / 'Cronenburg'), after the castle was built around 1220–1230 CE.

morphemes.translation: crown (referring to the castle's hilltop silhouette)

b_kronberg.etymology_analysis: Kronberg (medieval 'Cronenberg' / 'Cronenburg') combines Middle High German 'krōne' ('crown') and 'berg' ('hill'), referring to the crown-like appearance of the castle perched on the Taunus foothills.

b_kaiserslautern.first_mention_attestation: The settlement is first documented around 830 CE as Carolingian 'villa Luthra' in the Lorsch Reichsurbar, whereas the prefix 'Kaisers-' honors Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa (r. 1152–1190) and is first attested as 'Keyserslûtern' in 1322 CE.

eponym.details: The 'Kaisers-' prefix ('Emperor's') honors Holy Roman Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa (r. 1152–1190), who built an imperial palace (Kaiserpfalz) at Lautern.

b_kaiserslautern.etymology_analysis: Originally attested as 'villa Luthra' (830 CE), from Old High German 'lūttar' ('clear') + 'aha' ('stream', the Lauter), the town later received the prefix 'Kaisers-' ('Emperor's') in reference to Frederick Barbarossa's 12th-century imperial palace.

historical_names.name: villa Luthra
historical_names.source: Lorsch Reichsurbar (c. 830 CE)
historical_names.notes: Carolingian name of the settlement prior to Frederick Barbarossa's 12th-century Kaiserpfalz.

historical_names.name: Lutra
historical_names.source: Lorsch Reichsurbar (c. 830 CE)
historical_names.notes: Carolingian name of the settlement prior to Frederick Barbarossa's 12th-century Kaiserpfalz.

b_letningen.first_mention_attestation: Altleiningen (originally Leiningen) had its first documentary mention in 780 CE in the Lorsch Codex, which lists woodland 'in linunga marca'.
b_letningen.etymology_analysis: Attested as 'linunga marca' in 780 CE, Leiningen refers to the 'Leinbaum' (Norway maple or linden) growing along the Eckbach (formerly Leinbach); 'Alt-' ('old') was added in 1242 CE to distinguish it from Neuleiningen.

b_kreusnach.first_mention_attestation: Crossed by a major Roman road, Kreuznach was a Roman vicus and auxiliary castrum built in 370 CE under Emperor Valentinian I, later attested as the Carolingian palace 'Cruciniacum' by 820 CE.
b_kreusnach.etymology_analysis: Kreuznach (early 'Cruciniacum') is a Gallo-Roman '-acum' estate name meaning 'estate of Cruciniac', which was later Germanized into '-ach' and folk-etymologically associated with 'Kreuz' ('cross').

b_rockenhausen.first_mention_attestation: Rockenhausen is first mentioned in written records in 897 CE as 'Rogkenhuson'.
b_rockenhausen.etymology_analysis: Attested as 'Rogkenhuson' in 897 CE, Rockenhausen combines the Germanic personal name Roggo/Rocko with Old High German 'hūsun' ('at the houses of'), meaning 'settlement of Roggo'.

b_veldenz.first_mention_attestation: Schloss Veldenz and the lordship of Veldenz are first securely attested in 1156 CE in a charter of Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa confirming the Bishop of Verdun's rights over the castle and surrounding territory.
b_veldenz.etymology_analysis: The toponym Veldenz likely derives from a Gallo-Roman or pre-Germanic root such as *Valentia or a hydronymic/topographic base adapted into Old High German with the suffix -enza, reflecting early medieval Romance-Germanic contact in the Moselle valley.

b_klingenberg.first_mention_attestation: Klingenberg am Main is first attested in 1100 CE when a nobleman named Heinrich styled himself after the old Clingenburg castle overlooking the Main river.

morphemes.translation: narrow mountain gorge or babbling brook

b_klingenberg.etymology_analysis: Klingenberg combines Middle High German klinge (referring to a steep valley, gorge, or rushing stream) with berg ('hill, mountain'), denoting the fortified spur of the Clingenburg above the Main.

b_gelnhausen.first_mention_attestation: Gelnhausen is first documented in 1133 CE as 'de Geilenhusen', prior to Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa's foundation of the imperial palace and chartered town in 1169–1170 CE.

morphemes.translation: at the houses, settlement (dative plural of hūs)

b_gelnhausen.etymology_analysis: Recorded as Geilenhusen in 1133 CE and Gelenhusen in 1158 CE, the name is a classic Old High German -hausen compound meaning 'at the houses/homestead of Geilo', formed from an early medieval personal name and the dative plural of hūs.

b_rieneck.first_mention_attestation: Rieneck receives its first documentary mention in 790 CE in the early Carolingian period, long before the 12th-century expansion of Rieneck Castle.
b_rieneck.etymology_analysis: The name Rieneck pairs an Old High German topographic element (related to rein 'ridge, border strip' or a local stream name) with eck ('corner, spur'), describing the prominent spur above the Sinn valley.

b_mainz.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the Roman legionary camp Castrum Mogontiacum by Nero Claudius Drusus around 13–12 BCE and attested in classical Roman sources such as Tacitus and Ptolemy.
b_mainz.etymology_analysis: Mainz developed continuously from Roman Mogontiacum (later Maguntia), a Gallo-Roman settlement name derived from the Celtic deity Mogons and the possessive/locative suffix -iacum.

b_wiesbaden.first_mention_attestation: The Roman thermal settlement at Wiesbaden is first attested in 121 CE as Aquae Mattiacorum ('Waters of the Mattiaci'); the Germanic name Wisibada appears by 828–830 CE in Einhard's writings.

morphemes.translation: at the baths (dative plural of bad)

b_wiesbaden.etymology_analysis: Wiesbaden derives from Old High German Wisibada ('meadow baths'), referencing the hot mineral springs already famous in Roman times as Aquae Mattiacorum.

b_katzenelnbogen.first_mention_attestation: Katzenelnbogen is first attested around 1094–1095 CE when Diether I and his son Henry I began building Katzenelnbogen Castle and took the name of the County of Katzenelnbogen.
b_katzenelnbogen.etymology_analysis: Attested as Cazenelenboge around 1100 CE, the name literally means 'cat's elbow' in Middle High German, likely describing a sharp bend in the ridge or stream valley where the castle was built (with older folk-etymologies linking it to the Germanic Chatti).

b_boppard.first_mention_attestation: Boppard is attested in Late Roman times as the castrum Baudobriga (also Bodobriga) in the 4th century CE, and later as a Frankish royal estate in a charter of 643 CE.
b_boppard.etymology_analysis: Boppard evolved from the Celtic-Roman fort name Baudobriga / Bodobriga, combining a Celtic root with -briga ('hillfort, stronghold'), which underwent Germanic sound shifts into medieval Bopard.

b_speyer.first_mention_attestation: Following a Roman camp founded around 10 BCE (Noviomagus / Civitas Nemetum), Speyer is attested as a bishopric in 346 CE, and the name Spira first appears in 614 CE.

morphemes.translation: to spew, spurt, or rush (cognate with German speien)

b_speyer.etymology_analysis: First recorded as Spira in 614 CE, the name originally designated the Speyerbach stream (from a Germanic root meaning 'rushing/spurting water') before transferring to the city on its banks, replacing the Roman-Celtic name Noviomagus Nemetum.

historical_names.name: Noviomagus
historical_names.source: Synod of Cologne acts (346 CE) and Council of Paris (614 CE for Spira)
historical_names.notes: Celtic Noviomagus ('new field') and Roman Civitas Nemetum preceded the 7th-century Germanic name Spira.

historical_names.name: Civitas Nemetum
historical_names.source: Synod of Cologne acts (346 CE) and Council of Paris (614 CE for Spira)
historical_names.notes: Celtic Noviomagus ('new field') and Roman Civitas Nemetum preceded the 7th-century Germanic name Spira.

b_hockenheim.first_mention_attestation: Hockenheim is first attested in 769 CE as 'Ochinheim' in a donation charter recorded in the Lorsch Codex (Codex Laureshamensis).
b_hockenheim.etymology_analysis: First recorded as Ochinheim in 769 CE, Hockenheim is an Old High German -heim settlement name meaning 'homestead of Ocho/Hoccho', with an inorganic initial H- emerging by the 13th century.

b_heidelberg.first_mention_attestation: The name 'Heidelberch' is first documented in 1196 CE in a charter of Schönau Abbey; no written attestation of Heidelberg exists prior to 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: heath, bilberry (Heidelbeere) or personal name Heidilo

b_heidelberg.etymology_analysis: First attested as Heidelberch in 1196 CE, the name combines Middle High German berc ('mountain, hill') with either heide ('heathland') / heidelbeere ('bilberry') or an early personal name Heidilo.

historical_names.name: Bergheim
historical_names.source: Lorsch Codex (769 CE) for Bergheim, now a central district of Heidelberg
historical_names.notes: Bergheim on the Neckar is attested in 769 CE and was later absorbed into Heidelberg.

historical_names.name: Heiligenberg
historical_names.source: Lorsch Codex (769 CE) for Bergheim, now a central district of Heidelberg
historical_names.notes: Bergheim on the Neckar is attested in 769 CE and was later absorbed into Heidelberg.

b_weissenburg.first_mention_attestation: Weissenburg (modern French Wissembourg) grew around the Benedictine Weissenburg Abbey, founded in 661 CE by Bishop Dragobodo of Speyer and attested in early Merovingian charters.
b_weissenburg.etymology_analysis: German Weißenburg (French Wissembourg) derives from Old High German wīz ('white') + burg ('fortress, walled settlement'), referring either to the whitewashed walls of the abbey or pale local sandstone.

b_pirmasens.first_mention_attestation: Pirmasens is first mentioned in 860 CE as 'Pirminiseusna', a woodland colony belonging to Hornbach Abbey.

morphemes.translation: Saint Pirmin (founder of Hornbach Abbey, d. 753)

b_pirmasens.etymology_analysis: Attested as Pirminiseusna in 860 CE, the name commemorates Saint Pirmin (c. 670–753 CE), founder of nearby Hornbach Abbey, combined with a Germanic element denoting a settlement or forest clearing.

b_vaihingen.first_mention_attestation: Vaihingen is first mentioned in 779 CE in the Lorsch Codex (as Fehinga) as a settlement in the Enzgau, prior to the 1096 CE attestation of its castle.
b_vaihingen.etymology_analysis: Vaihingen follows the Alemannic-Frankish -ingen patronymic pattern, meaning 'place of the people/kin of Feho'.

b_heilbronn.first_mention_attestation: Heilbronn is first mentioned in 741 CE as 'villa Helibrunna' in an official charter of the Diocese of Würzburg.

morphemes.translation: healing, holy, or personal name Heilo

b_heilbronn.etymology_analysis: Recorded as Helibrunna in 741 CE, the name combines Old High German brunna ('spring, well') with heil ('healing, holy'), referring to a sacred or medicinal spring near the early Michaelsbasilica.

b_lowenstein.first_mention_attestation: Löwenstein is first attested in writing in 1123 CE, following the late 11th-century construction of Löwenstein Castle by the Counts of Calw; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: lion (from the heraldic lion of the Counts of Calw-Löwenstein)

b_lowenstein.etymology_analysis: Löwenstein combines Middle High German lewe/löwe ('lion') with stein ('rock, stone fortress'), a classic high medieval aristocratic castle name.

b_worms.first_mention_attestation: Originally the Celtic oppidum Borbetomagus, Worms became a Roman garrison and Civitas Vangionum by 14 BCE–1st century CE, with a bishopric attested by 614 CE and Frankish royal assemblies from 764 CE as Wormatia.

morphemes.translation: warm spring, bubbling water, or river name

b_worms.etymology_analysis: Worms evolved from Celtic Borbetomagus ('water meadow / field on the Bormo'), which was Latinized as Wormatia in Late Antiquity and the Early Middle Ages before contracting to Worms.

historical_names.name: Borbetomagus
historical_names.source: Roman imperial sources (1st century CE) and Council of Paris (614 CE)
historical_names.notes: Celtic-Roman urban center on the Rhine; Wormatia is the direct medieval Latin precursor of Worms.

historical_names.name: Civitas Vangionum
historical_names.source: Roman imperial sources (1st century CE) and Council of Paris (614 CE)
historical_names.notes: Celtic-Roman urban center on the Rhine; Wormatia is the direct medieval Latin precursor of Worms.

b_besensheim.first_mention_attestation: Bensheim is first documented in 765 CE as 'Basinsheim' in the Codex Laureshamensis of Lorsch Abbey, later evolving through Besensheim to Bensheim.
b_besensheim.etymology_analysis: Attested as Basinsheim in 765 CE and later Besensheim, the name means 'homestead of Basinus', combining an early Frankish personal name with -heim.

b_munster.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 793 CE by Saint Ludger as Mimigernaford (a bishopric from 805 CE), the city first appears under the new name Monasterium (whence Münster) in 1068 CE.

morphemes.translation: monastery, minster (borrowed into Old Saxon/German as Münster)

b_munster.etymology_analysis: The modern name Münster derives from Latin monasterium ('monastery'), referring to the cathedral monastery founded by Saint Ludger at the earlier Saxon ford of Mimigernaford.

historical_names.name: Mimigernaford
historical_names.source: Vita Liudgeri and Carolingian ecclesiastical records (793–805 CE)
historical_names.notes: Original Old Saxon name of the settlement on the Aa river before Monasterium/Münster replaced it.

historical_names.name: Mimigardeford
historical_names.source: Vita Liudgeri and Carolingian ecclesiastical records (793–805 CE)
historical_names.notes: Original Old Saxon name of the settlement on the Aa river before Monasterium/Münster replaced it.

b_warendorf.first_mention_attestation: Warendorf is first securely attested as a municipal community (civitas) in 1224 CE; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.
b_warendorf.etymology_analysis: Warendorf (Low German Warendorp) combines a personal name (Waro) or topographic element with -dorp/-dorf ('village'), situated at a crossing on the Ems.

b_ahlen.first_mention_attestation: Ahlen is first mentioned around 850 CE (as 'villa Alna') in the Vita Liudgeri II, written by Altfrid.
b_ahlen.etymology_analysis: Attested around 850 CE as Alna, the name's precise etymology is debated among linguists, though it is generally linked to an Old Saxon hydronymic or topographic root near the Werse crossing (not to eels, despite folk-etymological canting arms).

b_soest.first_mention_attestation: Soest is first mentioned in writing in 836 CE in the Dagobertsche Schenkung (and translation records of Saint Patroclus/Vitus) along the Westphalian Hellweg.
b_soest.etymology_analysis: Recorded in medieval sources as Susat / Sosat, Soest derives from a pre-urban Saxon toponym of uncertain origin, possibly connected to the local salt springs that made it an early Hellweg center.

b_osnabruck.first_mention_attestation: Osnabrück developed around the missionary bishopric founded by Charlemagne in 780 CE (and securely established prior to 803 CE).
