b_osnabruck.etymology_analysis: Osnabrück (Old Saxon Osnabrugga) combines a disputed first element (often linked to the Hase river, the Osning hills, or 'oxen') with Old Saxon brugga ('bridge'), marking a key river crossing.

b_ravensberg.first_mention_attestation: Ravensberg Castle and the Counts of Ravensberg are first attested in the 12th century (around 1140–1141 CE, when Otto I of Calvelage moved his seat to Ravensberg); no attestation exists <= 867 CE.
b_ravensberg.etymology_analysis: Ravensberg means 'raven's hill' (or 'hill of Hraban'), a characteristic 12th-century hilltop castle name in the Teutoburg Forest.

b_vechta.first_mention_attestation: Vechta is first attested in the late 11th to 12th century (c. 1080–1188 CE) in regional charters of the Lordship of Vechta and Ravensberg; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.
b_vechta.etymology_analysis: Vechta (Low Saxon Vechte) derives from a Low German hydronymic or wetland root (cognate with the Vechte river) referring to the boggy moorland crossing of the Vechtaer Moorbach.

b_cloppenburg.first_mention_attestation: Cloppenburg Castle was founded in 1297 CE by the Counts of Tecklenburg; the name Cloppenburg has no attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: uncertain (possibly personal name Kloppe or 'to knock/clap')

b_cloppenburg.etymology_analysis: Cloppenburg (Low German Cloppenborg) is a late-13th-century castle name ending in -borg ('fortress'), whose first element is variously linked to a personal name or a Low German verb/noun.

historical_names.name: Krapendorf
historical_names.source: Early parish foundation records of Krapendorf (before 819 CE)
historical_names.notes: Krapendorf is the oldest parish and settlement nucleus of modern Cloppenburg, predating the 1297 castle.

b_paderborn.first_mention_attestation: Paderborn is first mentioned in 777 CE in Frankish royal annals when Charlemagne held an Imperial Diet and missionary synod at the Pader springs.
b_paderborn.etymology_analysis: Paderborn combines the hydronym Pader with Old Saxon born ('spring, source'), directly describing the more than 200 karst springs in the city center that feed the River Pader.

b_brakel.first_mention_attestation: Brakel is first attested in 836 CE as 'villa brechal' in the account of the translation of Saint Vitus's relics from Saint-Denis to Corvey Abbey.

morphemes.translation: broken ground, clearing, or newly plowed land

b_brakel.etymology_analysis: Attested as villa brechal in 836 CE, Brakel derives from an Old Saxon topographic root related to 'breaking' (clearing or plowing) land.

b_wiedenbruck.first_mention_attestation: Wiedenbrück is first documented in 952 CE when Emperor Otto I granted market, mint, and customs rights to the Bishop of Osnabrück; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.
b_wiedenbruck.etymology_analysis: Wiedenbrück combines Old Saxon wīda ('willow') with brügge ('bridge'), referring to a bridge crossing the Ems river.

b_lippstadt.first_mention_attestation: Lippstadt was founded in 1185 CE as a planned city by Bernhard II of Lippe; no written attestation of Lippstadt exists <= 867 CE.
b_lippstadt.etymology_analysis: Lippstadt means 'town on the Lippe', combining the ancient hydronym Lippe (Roman Lupia) with Middle Low German stadt ('town').

b_tecklenburg.first_mention_attestation: Tecklenburg Castle is first attested in writing in a charter of 1184 CE; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.
b_tecklenburg.etymology_analysis: Tecklenburg is a 12th-century hilltop castle name ending in -burg ('fortress'), overlooking the northern edge of the Teutoburg Forest.

b_papenburg.first_mention_attestation: Papenburg is first verifiably documented in 1458 CE in a feudal contract of Hayo von Haren ('von der Papenburch'), with the fen colony later founded in 1631 CE.
b_papenburg.etymology_analysis: Papenburg (Low Saxon Papenbörg) derives from Middle Low German papen ('priests, clerics') + borg ('castle'), referring to the medieval moated manor held by clerical or ecclesiastical lords.

b_meppen.first_mention_attestation: Meppen is first documented in 834 CE in a deed of donation by Emperor Louis the Pious transferring Meppen to Corvey Abbey.
b_meppen.etymology_analysis: Meppen derives from an Old Saxon root (mappe) denoting a river delta or confluence, accurately describing its site where the Hase meets the Ems.

b_bentheim.first_mention_attestation: Bad Bentheim is first attested around 1050 CE under the name 'Binithem'; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.
b_bentheim.etymology_analysis: Attested as Binithem c. 1050 CE, Bentheim combines Old Saxon binit ('rushes, reeds') with -hem ('homestead'), denoting a settlement near reedy lowlands.

b_waldeck.first_mention_attestation: Waldeck Castle, overlooking the Eder river, is first attested in 1120 CE; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.
b_waldeck.etymology_analysis: Waldeck literally means 'forest corner/spur', a high medieval castle name combining Wald ('forest') and Eck ('promontory, spur').

b_wittenstein.first_mention_attestation: Burg Wittgenstein (Schloss Wittgenstein) above Bad Laasphe is first mentioned in 1187 CE as 'Widegensteyne'; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

eponym.details: Named after Count Widekind I of Battenberg and Wittgenstein (fl. late 12th century, post-867 CE).

b_wittenstein.etymology_analysis: First attested as Widegensteyne in 1187 CE, Wittgenstein means 'Widekind's rock/castle', combining the personal name Widekind with -stein.

b_buren.first_mention_attestation: Büren in Westphalia is first mentioned in 1095 CE as 'Buranon', prior to the formal foundation of the town and castle in 1195 CE; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: dwelling, cottage, or storehouse (dative plural būron)

b_buren.etymology_analysis: Attested as Buranon in 1095 CE, Büren derives from the dative plural of Old Saxon būr ('dwelling, cottage'), meaning 'at the dwellings'.

b_bedford.first_mention_attestation: Bedford is securely attested in the Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum (c. 886 CE) and in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 915 CE (the 571 CE 'Bedcanford' entry is disputed by modern historians); thus it lacks a secure attestation <= 867 CE.
b_bedford.etymology_analysis: Bedford (Old English Bedanford) means 'Beda's ford', referring to an early Anglo-Saxon crossing of the River Great Ouse.

b_ampthill.first_mention_attestation: Ampthill is first recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as 'Ammetelle'; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.
b_ampthill.etymology_analysis: Recorded as Ammetelle in 1086 CE, Ampthill derives from Old English ǣmethyll ('ant-hill, hill infested with ants').

b_luton.first_mention_attestation: Luton first appears in written records in the late 8th century (792 CE) as 'Lygetun', meaning 'settlement on the River Lea'.
b_luton.etymology_analysis: Attested as Lygetun in the 8th century, Luton combines the Brittonic river name Lea (Old English Lyge) with Old English tūn ('enclosure, settlement').

b_buckingham.first_mention_attestation: Buckingham is first documented in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle in 914 CE when King Edward the Elder fortified it against the Danes; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.
b_buckingham.etymology_analysis: Buckingham (Old English Buccingahamm) means 'river-meadow of Bucca's people', referring to the loop of the River Great Ouse enclosing the town.

b_aylesbury.first_mention_attestation: Aylesbury is recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle under the year 571 CE as 'Ægelesburh', one of four settlements taken by Cuthwulf from the Britons.
b_aylesbury.etymology_analysis: Attested as Ægelesburh in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (s.a. 571 CE), Aylesbury means 'Ægel's stronghold', combining an Old English personal name with burh ('fortress').

b_newport.first_mention_attestation: Newport Pagnell (in Buckinghamshire) is first mentioned in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as 'Neuport'; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

eponym.details: The manorial affix 'Pagnell' derives from the Anglo-Norman Paynel family (Ralph Paynel and his descendants), who held the manor after the Norman Conquest of 1066 CE.

morphemes.translation: surname of the post-1066 feudal lords

b_newport.etymology_analysis: Recorded as Neuport in the 1086 Domesday Book, the name means 'new market town' (Old English nīwe + port), with 'Pagnell' added later from the Anglo-Norman Paynel lords of the manor.

b_wycombe.first_mention_attestation: High Wycombe is first documented as 'Wicumun' in 970 CE and appears in the 1086 Domesday Book as 'Wicumbe'; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.
b_wycombe.etymology_analysis: Attested as Wicumun in 970 CE, Wycombe combines Old English wīc ('dwellings, settlement') with cumb ('valley', a Brittonic loanword), referring to the Wye valley.

b_colchester.first_mention_attestation: The Old English name 'Colneceaster' (modern Colchester) is first attested in the 10th century (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 917 CE, when Edward the Elder recaptured it from the Danes), succeeding Roman Camulodunum and 9th-century British Cair Colun.
b_colchester.etymology_analysis: Colchester (Old English Colneceaster) means 'Roman fort/walled town on the River Colne', combining the pre-English river name Colne with Old English ceaster (from Latin castra).

historical_names.name: Camulodunum
historical_names.source: Roman imperial sources (1st century CE) for Camulodunum; Historia Brittonum (c. 828 CE) for Cair Colun
historical_names.notes: First capital of Roman Britain (Camulodunum), built on the Iron Age Trinovantian oppidum.

historical_names.name: Cair Colun
historical_names.source: Roman imperial sources (1st century CE) for Camulodunum; Historia Brittonum (c. 828 CE) for Cair Colun
historical_names.notes: First capital of Roman Britain (Camulodunum), built on the Iron Age Trinovantian oppidum.

b_maldon.first_mention_attestation: Maldon is first attested in 913 CE in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle as 'Maeldun'; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.
b_maldon.etymology_analysis: Attested as Maeldun in 913 CE, Maldon derives from Old English mǣl ('cross, monument') + dūn ('hill'), meaning 'monument on the hill'.

b_chelmsford.first_mention_attestation: Chelmsford is first recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as 'Celmeresfort'; no written attestation of the English name exists <= 867 CE.
b_chelmsford.etymology_analysis: Recorded as Celmeresfort in 1086 CE, Chelmsford derives from Old English Cēolmǣresford ('Ceolmaer's ford'), which also gave its name to the River Chelmer by back-formation.

historical_names.name: Caesaromagus
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary and Roman Britain geographical records (2nd–3rd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman mansio and settlement ('Caesar's field/market') on the road from Londinium to Camulodunum.

b_dunmow.first_mention_attestation: Great Dunmow is first recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE (with ten entries for estates in the vill); no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.
b_dunmow.etymology_analysis: Dunmow derives from Old English dūn ('hill') + mǣwe ('meadow'), meaning 'meadow on the hill', situated along Roman Stane Street.

b_berkhamsted.first_mention_attestation: Berkhamsted is first mentioned in writing in 970 CE; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.
b_berkhamsted.etymology_analysis: Berkhamsted derives from Old English beorc-hāmstede ('homestead among the birches'), referring to a settlement in the Chilterns.

b_saint_albans.first_mention_attestation: King Offa of Mercia founded St Albans Abbey around 793 CE at the shrine of Saint Alban (already mentioned by Bede c. 720–731 CE), succeeding the Roman city of Verulamium.
b_saint_albans.etymology_analysis: St Albans is named after Saint Alban, the first recorded British Christian martyr (3rd–4th century CE), whose shrine at Verulamium became the site of Offa's 793 CE abbey.

historical_names.name: Verlamion
historical_names.source: Tacitus's Annals (14.33, 60–61 CE) and earlier Catuvellaunian coinage
historical_names.notes: Major Roman municipium and pre-Roman Catuvellaunian oppidum immediately adjacent to the medieval abbey.

historical_names.name: Verulamium
historical_names.source: Tacitus's Annals (14.33, 60–61 CE) and earlier Catuvellaunian coinage
historical_names.notes: Major Roman municipium and pre-Roman Catuvellaunian oppidum immediately adjacent to the medieval abbey.

historical_names.name: Verlamacæstir
historical_names.source: Tacitus's Annals (14.33, 60–61 CE) and earlier Catuvellaunian coinage
historical_names.notes: Major Roman municipium and pre-Roman Catuvellaunian oppidum immediately adjacent to the medieval abbey.

b_hertford.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 673 CE in Bede's Ecclesiastical History of the English People (Latin: Herutford) as the site of the Synod of Hertford, the first national synod of the English Church.
b_hertford.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old English Heorotford (recorded by Bede as Herutford), meaning 'ford frequented by harts/stags', referring to a crossing over the River Lea.

b_london.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Londinium by the Roman historian Tacitus in his Annals (14.33, written c. 115 CE), describing the Roman commercial settlement sacked during Boudica's revolt in 60 CE.

morphemes.translation: possibly 'wild/bold place' or a personal name

b_london.etymology_analysis: From Romano-British Londinium, a Latinized adaptation of an earlier Brittonic toponym of uncertain root (variously linked to a personal name or a lost Celtic root meaning 'wild' or 'flooded'), later Old English Lunden.

b_southwark.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the early 10th-century Burghal Hidage (c. 914 CE) as Suthringa geweorc ('defensive work of the people of Surrey'), and in the 1086 Domesday Book as Sudweca.
b_southwark.etymology_analysis: From Old English Sūþgeweorc ('southern defensive work') or Sūþringa geweorc ('fortification of the men of Surrey'), referring to the burh guarding the southern approach to London Bridge across the Thames.

b_woxbrigge.first_mention_attestation: Omitted from the 1086 Domesday Book; first recorded in 1107 CE as Woxbrigge, a daughter settlement of Hillingdon at a crossing of the River Colne.
b_woxbrigge.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old English Wixan-brycg ('bridge of the Wixan'), referencing the 7th-century Anglo-Saxon Wixan tribe who settled in Middlesex, with later loss of the initial w- producing Uxbridge.

b_gore.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the 1086 Domesday Book as the Hundred of Gara (in the county of Middlesex).

morphemes.translation: triangular piece of land, gore, spit of land

b_gore.etymology_analysis: From Old English gāra ('triangular piece of land' or 'wedge-shaped strip'), referring to the shape of the moot-site or meeting place of the Middlesex hundred.

b_brentford.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in 705 CE in an Anglo-Saxon charter as Breguntford, referring to the crossing over the River Brent.
b_brentford.etymology_analysis: A hybrid Brittonic-Old English compound meaning 'ford over the River Brent', where the river name Brent derives from Brittonic *brigant- ('high' or 'holy', related to the goddess Brigantia) combined with Old English ford.

b_dover.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Roman Antonine Itinerary (c. late 2nd to 3rd century CE) as Portus Dubris (and Dubris), and later in Old English charters from 696 CE as Dofras.
b_dover.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Brittonic plural noun *dubrās ('waters'), referring to the estuary of the River Dour; Latinized by the Romans as Dubris (Portus Dubris) and borrowed into Old English as Dofras, yielding modern Dover.

b_canterbury.first_mention_attestation: Attested under its Old English name Cantwaraburh ('stronghold of the people of Kent') in 8th-century sources including Bede's Ecclesiastical History (731 CE, as Doruuernis / Cantuariorum civitas) and Kentish charters.
b_canterbury.etymology_analysis: From Old English Cantwaraburh, meaning 'stronghold of the Kentish people', combining the Brittonic-derived regional name Cantium/Cent with Old English -ware ('dwellers') and burh ('fortress').

historical_names.name: Durovernum Cantiacorum
historical_names.source: Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE) and the Antonine Itinerary
historical_names.notes: Romano-British civitas capital of the Cantiaci on the exact site of modern Canterbury.

historical_names.name: Durovernum
historical_names.source: Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE) and the Antonine Itinerary
historical_names.notes: Romano-British civitas capital of the Cantiaci on the exact site of modern Canterbury.

b_rochester.first_mention_attestation: First recorded under its Old English name Hrofæscæstre by Bede in his Ecclesiastical History of the English People (c. 731 CE), following the foundation of its bishopric in 604 CE.

morphemes.translation: swift-stream fort (reinterpreted as personal name Hrof)
Roman fort, walled town (from Latin castra)

b_rochester.etymology_analysis: Bede interpreted Old English Hrofæscæstre as 'Hrof's fortified camp', though modern scholarship derives Hrof- from a reduction of Romano-British Durobrivis ('fort by the bridge' or 'swift stream') combined with Old English ceaster.

historical_names.name: Durobrivae
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (Iter III, late 2nd–3rd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Romano-British walled town on the River Medway at the exact site of Rochester.

historical_names.name: Durobrivis
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (Iter III, late 2nd–3rd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Romano-British walled town on the River Medway at the exact site of Rochester.

b_tonbridge.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the 1086 Domesday Book as Tonebrige.
b_tonbridge.etymology_analysis: Recorded in Domesday Book (1086) as Tonebrige, from Old English tūn-brycg ('bridge belonging to the estate/manor') or Tunnan-brycg ('Tunna's bridge') across the River Medway.

b_chertsey.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing by Bede in his Ecclesiastical History (c. 731 CE) as Cerotaesei ('island of Cerotus'), referring to Chertsey Abbey founded in 666 CE.
b_chertsey.etymology_analysis: From Old English Ceortes-ēg (Bede's Cerotaesei), meaning 'Ceorot's island', combining a Brittonic or Old English personal name with Old English ēg ('island' or 'raised ground in marshland').

b_guildford.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the will of King Alfred the Great (c. 880–885 CE) as Gyldeforda, bequeathed to his nephew Æthelwold.

morphemes.translation: golden (referring to golden sand or marigolds)

b_guildford.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old English Gyldeford ('golden ford'), referring to the golden-coloured sand or yellow marigolds at the crossing of the River Wey.

b_kingston.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in 838 CE as Cyninges tun in a charter (Sawyer 1438) documenting a royal council presided over by King Egbert of Wessex and Archbishop Ceolnoth.
b_kingston.etymology_analysis: From Old English Cyninges tūn ('the king's manor/estate'), reflecting its status as a royal West Saxon estate on the River Thames.

b_tandbridge.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the 1086 Domesday Book as Tenrige, held by the wife of Salie from Richard Fitz Gilbert.

morphemes.translation: twig, branch, or boundary stake (or personal name)

b_tandbridge.etymology_analysis: Recorded as Tenrige in 1086, from Old English hrycg ('ridge', referring to the Greensand Ridge) prefixed by an Old English element (possibly tān 'twig/stake' or a personal name).

b_lewes.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the early 10th-century Burghal Hidage (c. 914 CE) as Læwes, one of the fortified burhs of Wessex.
b_lewes.etymology_analysis: Debated Old English origin, commonly derived from the plural of Old English hlǣw ('hill, mound, barrow') or lǣw ('gash, cut'), referring to the hills or gap in the South Downs through which the River Ouse passes.

b_chichester.first_mention_attestation: First recorded under its Old English name Cisseceaster in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle entry for 895 CE.

morphemes.translation: personal name (son of Ælle of Sussex)
Roman fort, walled town (from Latin castra)

b_chichester.etymology_analysis: From Old English Cisseceaster ('fortress of Cissa'), combining the personal name Cissa (traditionally a son of Ælle, first king of the South Saxons) with Old English ceaster.

historical_names.name: Noviomagus Reginorum
historical_names.source: Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE) and the Antonine Itinerary
historical_names.notes: Romano-British civitas capital of the Regni/Regini located directly beneath modern Chichester.

historical_names.name: Noviomagus Regnorum
historical_names.source: Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE) and the Antonine Itinerary
historical_names.notes: Romano-British civitas capital of the Regni/Regini located directly beneath modern Chichester.

b_arun.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the 1086 Domesday Book as Harundel, held by Earl Roger of Montgomery.
b_arun.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old English hārhūne-dell ('horehound dell/valley'), referring to the common horehound plant growing in the hollow; the River Arun was later back-formed from the town name.

b_hastings.first_mention_attestation: First attested in contemporary records in an Anglo-Saxon charter of 857 CE (Sawyer 318) referring to monks residing 'in Hastingas' (with later 12th-century chronicles also noting Offa's 771 CE conquest of the Hestingorum gens).
b_hastings.etymology_analysis: From Old English Hæstingas ('the people/followers of Hæsta'), originally designating the tribal territory in eastern Sussex before becoming the name of the principal coastal settlement.

b_launceston.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the 1086 Domesday Book as Lanstaveton (alongside Dunheved; coinage from a Cornish mint here begins under Æthelred II c. 976–1016 CE).
b_launceston.etymology_analysis: A hybrid Cornish-Old English name (Domesday Lanstaveton) meaning 'settlement of the church-enclosure of St Stephen', from Cornish lann ('enclosure/church') + Stefan + Old English tūn.

b_tintagel.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing c. 1136 CE in Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae as Tintagol, with the village historically known as Trevena.
b_tintagel.etymology_analysis: Generally derived from Cornish *din ('fort') and *tagell ('neck, narrow constriction'), referring to the fortified headland connected to the mainland by a narrow isthmus.

b_helston.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the 1086 Domesday Book as Henlistone, one of two urban places in Cornwall noted in the survey.
b_helston.etymology_analysis: A Cornish-Old English hybrid (Domesday Henlistone) combining Cornish hen ('old') and lis ('court') with Old English tūn ('manor/settlement'), meaning 'manor of the old court'.

b_exeter.first_mention_attestation: First recorded under its Old English name Escanceaster in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle entry for 876 CE, when Danish forces occupied the city.

morphemes.translation: Roman fort, walled town (from Latin castra)

b_exeter.etymology_analysis: From Old English Escanceaster ('Roman fort on the River Exe'), combining the Anglicized Brittonic river name Exe (*Iska) with Old English ceaster.

historical_names.name: Isca Dumnoniorum
historical_names.source: Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE) and the Antonine Itinerary
historical_names.notes: Roman legionary fortress and civitas capital of the Dumnonii at the exact site of Exeter.

historical_names.name: Isca
historical_names.source: Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE) and the Antonine Itinerary
historical_names.notes: Roman legionary fortress and civitas capital of the Dumnonii at the exact site of Exeter.

b_totnes.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the early 10th-century Burghal Hidage (or shortly thereafter on 10th-century Anglo-Saxon coins) as Totanæs / Totenais (traditional 907 CE charter date is unverified).
b_totnes.etymology_analysis: From Old English Tottan-næss ('Totta's headland' or 'lookout promontory'), referring to the ridge overlooking the River Dart.

b_okehampton.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the 1086 Domesday Book as Ochementone, a borough and market held by Baldwin the Sheriff.
b_okehampton.etymology_analysis: From Old English Ochementone ('settlement on the River Okement'), combining the Brittonic river name Okement with Old English tūn.

b_barnstaple.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in Version B of the Burghal Hidage (c. 914–919 CE) as Beardastapol, replacing the earlier nearby burh at Pilton.
b_barnstaple.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old English Beardastapol ('Bearda's pillar/post'), referring to a boundary marker or market post near the River Taw.

b_brecon.first_mention_attestation: Established as a Norman castle and borough c. 1093 CE by Bernard de Neufmarché; known in Welsh as Aberhonddu ('mouth of the Honddu').
b_brecon.etymology_analysis: Anglicized from Brycheiniog (the early medieval Welsh kingdom allegedly named after Brychan); the native Welsh town name Aberhonddu means 'mouth of the River Honddu'.

historical_names.name: Cicucium
historical_names.source: Ravenna Cosmography (c. 700 CE, as Cicutio)
historical_names.notes: Roman cavalry fort (Y Gaer / Brecon Gaer) located 3 miles west of Brecon, whose stone was reused to build Brecon.

historical_names.name: Cicutio
historical_names.source: Ravenna Cosmography (c. 700 CE, as Cicutio)
historical_names.notes: Roman cavalry fort (Y Gaer / Brecon Gaer) located 3 miles west of Brecon, whose stone was reused to build Brecon.

historical_names.name: Y Gaer
historical_names.source: Ravenna Cosmography (c. 700 CE, as Cicutio)
historical_names.notes: Roman cavalry fort (Y Gaer / Brecon Gaer) located 3 miles west of Brecon, whose stone was reused to build Brecon.

b_talgarth.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in 1121 CE as Talgart (and as Talgard after 1130 CE).
b_talgarth.etymology_analysis: From Welsh tâl ('brow, end') and garth ('ridge, hill promontory'), meaning 'end of the ridge'.

b_carmarthen.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE) as Maridunum and in the Antonine Itinerary (Iter XII) as Muridunum, civitas capital of the Demetae.
b_carmarthen.etymology_analysis: Anglicized from Welsh Caerfyrddin, which prefixes caer ('fort') to Myrddin (derived from Romano-British Moridunum, 'sea fort', rather than the later folk etymology linking it to Merlin).

b_llandovery.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the early 12th century with the construction of Llandovery Castle c. 1110–1116 CE (Welsh: Llanymddyfri).
b_llandovery.etymology_analysis: Anglicized from Welsh Llanymddyfri ('church amidst the waters'), referring to its position near the confluence of the rivers Tywi, Brân, and Bawddwr.

historical_names.name: Alabum
historical_names.source: Ravenna Cosmography (c. 700 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman auxiliary fort at Llanfair Hill just northeast of modern Llandovery.

b_cardiff.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the late 11th century (c. 1081–1093 CE) with the Norman fortification built within the Roman fort by William the Conqueror or Robert Fitzhamon (Welsh: Caerdyf / Caerdydd).
b_cardiff.etymology_analysis: Anglicized from Middle Welsh Caerdyf (modern Welsh Caerdydd), meaning 'fort on the River Taff', referring to the Roman fort beside the river.

b_swansea.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Welsh as Aper Tyui (c. 1150 CE) and on coins from the 1140s / in Gerald of Wales (1188 CE) as Sweynsei.

eponym.details: Named after an Old Norse personal name Sveinn (anglicized Sweyn), a Viking leader or settler (post-867 Viking activity on the Gower coast).

b_swansea.etymology_analysis: The English name Swansea derives from Old Norse Sveinsey ('Sveinn's island/sandbank'), while the Welsh name Abertawe means 'mouth of the River Tawe'.

b_caerphilly.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1268 CE when Gilbert de Clare, Lord of Glamorgan, began building Caerphilly Castle.
b_caerphilly.etymology_analysis: From Welsh Caerffili ('fort of Ffili'), combining caer ('fort', referring either to the Roman fort or medieval castle) with the personal name of the early Welsh saint Ffili.

b_casnewydd.first_mention_attestation: First recorded by the Normans in 1126 CE as novus burgus ('new borough'), and in Welsh as Castell Newydd ar Wysg (Casnewydd) in the Brut y Tywysogion c. 1172 CE.
b_casnewydd.etymology_analysis: Welsh Casnewydd is a contraction of Castell Newydd ar Wysg ('new castle on the Usk'), while English Newport ('new port') distinguishes the Norman-era harbour from the older Roman port upstream at Caerleon.

historical_names.name: Isca Augusta
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (Iter XII, late 2nd–3rd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman legionary fortress of Isca Augusta at Caerleon upstream on the Usk, which Newport superseded as the principal port.

historical_names.name: Caerleon
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (Iter XII, late 2nd–3rd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman legionary fortress of Isca Augusta at Caerleon upstream on the Usk, which Newport superseded as the principal port.

b_monmouth.first_mention_attestation: First recorded under its English/Norman name in the 1086 Domesday Book as Monemude, following the construction of Monmouth Castle c. 1067–1071 CE.
b_monmouth.etymology_analysis: From Old English Monemude ('mouth of the River Monnow'), corresponding to Welsh Trefynwy ('town on the Mynwy').

historical_names.name: Blestium
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (Iter XIII, late 2nd–3rd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman auxiliary fort at the exact site of modern Monmouth.

historical_names.name: Blestio
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (Iter XIII, late 2nd–3rd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman auxiliary fort at the exact site of modern Monmouth.

b_pembroke.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in 1093 CE when Arnulf de Montgomery built Pembroke Castle in the Welsh cantref of Penfro.
b_pembroke.etymology_analysis: Anglicized from Welsh Penfro ('headland' or 'land's end'), combining pen ('head/end') and bro ('land/region').

b_st_davids.first_mention_attestation: First attested in surviving contemporary writing in Asser's Life of King Alfred (893 CE) as Menevia (Welsh: Mynyw, later Tyddewi 'David's house').

morphemes.translation: Saint David (6th-century patron saint of Wales)

b_st_davids.etymology_analysis: English St Davids and Welsh Tyddewi ('David's house') commemorate the 6th-century Saint David (Dewi Sant), who founded the monastic community earlier known as Mynyw / Latin Menevia.

b_fishguard.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in ecclesiastical tax records (Taxatio Ecclesiastica) in 1291 CE (with medieval Welsh name Abergwaun).
b_fishguard.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Fiskigarðr ('fish-catching enclosure/weir'), reflecting Viking-age coastal activity; the Welsh name Abergwaun means 'mouth of the River Gwaun'.

b_reading.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle entry for 871 CE as Readingum, when the Danish army encamped there and fought the Battle of Reading.
b_reading.etymology_analysis: From Old English Readingas ('the people of Reada'), an early Anglo-Saxon tribal/kin-group name.

b_newbury.first_mention_attestation: Recorded in the 1086 Domesday Book under its earlier manor name Ulwardetone, and in late 11th-century Norman charters (c. 1080–1086) as Neuberie ('new borough').
b_newbury.etymology_analysis: From Old English/Anglo-Norman Neuberie (nīwe + burh), meaning 'new borough', founded after the Norman Conquest beside the earlier manor of Ulwardetone.

b_abingdon.first_mention_attestation: Although Abingdon Abbey is traditionally dated to c. 676 CE, earlier charters are later forgeries; the name Abbendun first appears in 10th-century charters (such as Sawyer 567, dated 955 CE).
b_abingdon.etymology_analysis: From Old English Æbbandūn ('Æbba's hill' or 'Æbbe's hill'), originally referring to nearby Boars Hill before being transferred to the abbey site on the Thames.

b_gloucester.first_mention_attestation: Attested under its Old English name Gleawanceaster in Bede's Ecclesiastical History (c. 731 CE) and in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (s.a. 577 CE).

morphemes.translation: Roman fort, walled town (from Latin castra)

b_gloucester.etymology_analysis: From Old English Glēawceaster, combining the Anglicized Romano-British name Glevum (from Brittonic *gloiu 'bright') with Old English ceaster.

b_bristol.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle entry for 1051/1052 CE as Brycgstow (with coins minted at Bristol under King Cnut c. 1020 CE).
b_bristol.etymology_analysis: From Old English Brycgstōw ('the place at the bridge'), referring to the early crossing over the River Avon.

b_winchcombe.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in a Mercian royal charter of King Coenwulf dated 811 CE (Sawyer 167) as Wincelcumbe, following the founding of Winchcombe Abbey c. 798 CE.
b_winchcombe.etymology_analysis: From Old English Wincelcumb ('valley with a bend/nook'), describing its sheltered Cotswold valley setting.

b_forest_of_dean.first_mention_attestation: First recorded as an administrative royal forest in the 1086 Domesday Book as Dene (and later Danubia by Gerald of Wales).
b_forest_of_dean.etymology_analysis: The origin of Dean is uncertain, variously linked to Old English denu ('valley') or a corruption of Welsh din ('hillfort'), prefixed by 'Forest of' to denote the royal hunting forest.

b_oxford.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle entry for 911 CE (also dated 912) as Oxnaford, when King Edward the Elder took possession of the burh.
b_oxford.etymology_analysis: From Old English Oxnaford ('ford of the oxen'), referring to a shallow crossing of the River Thames used by cattle drovers.

b_banbury.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the 1086 Domesday Book as Banesberie, an administrative centre of the Bishop of Lincoln.
b_banbury.etymology_analysis: From Old English Bannanbyrig ('Banna's stronghold/fortified enclosure'), combining the personal name Banna with burh.

b_witney.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in a Saxon charter of King Edgar dated 969 CE as Wyttannige.
b_witney.etymology_analysis: From Old English Wittan-ēg ('Witta's island/dry meadow'), referring to dry ground beside the River Windrush.

b_salisbury.first_mention_attestation: Modern Salisbury (New Sarum) was founded in 1220 CE with the laying of the new cathedral's foundation stone, receiving its city charter in 1227 CE, superseding Old Sarum.
b_salisbury.etymology_analysis: Derived via Middle English Sarisberie from Old English Searoburh (itself a partial calque of Romano-British Sorbiodunum, with burh translating Celtic -dunon 'fortress').

historical_names.name: Sorbiodunum
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (Iter XII/XV, late 2nd–3rd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Iron Age hillfort and Roman settlement (Old Sarum) 2 miles north of modern Salisbury, later known in Old English as Searoburh.

historical_names.name: Sorviodunum
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (Iter XII/XV, late 2nd–3rd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Iron Age hillfort and Roman settlement (Old Sarum) 2 miles north of modern Salisbury, later known in Old English as Searoburh.

historical_names.name: Searoburh
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (Iter XII/XV, late 2nd–3rd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Iron Age hillfort and Roman settlement (Old Sarum) 2 miles north of modern Salisbury, later known in Old English as Searoburh.

b_wilton.first_mention_attestation: First attested in contemporary charters on 22 April 854 CE (Sawyer 302 and 308), issued by King Æthelwulf of Wessex 'in palatio nostro quod dicitur Wiltun'.
b_wilton.etymology_analysis: From Old English Wiltūn ('settlement/estate on the River Wylye'), which also gave its name to Wiltshire (Wiltunscire).

b_ramsbury.first_mention_attestation: First attested in historical records in 909 CE with the creation of the Anglo-Saxon bishopric of Ramsbury (Old English: Hræfnesburh).
b_ramsbury.etymology_analysis: From Old English Hræfnesburh ('Raven's fort' or 'Hræfn's stronghold'), recorded as Ramesberie in the 1086 Domesday Book.

b_malmesbury.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Bede's Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum (731 CE, Book V, ch. 18) as Maildubi Urbem ('the city of Maildubh'), referring to the monastery founded in the 7th century by the Irish monk Máel Dub.
b_malmesbury.etymology_analysis: Malmesbury derives from the Old English compound *Maeldubesburh*, combining the Old Irish personal name *Máel Dub* (Latinized by Bede as *Maildubus*, meaning 'dark disciple') with Old English *burh* ('fortified place' or 'monastic enclosure'), referring to the 7th-century monastic foundation.

b_yns_mon.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Mona in Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia (c. 77 CE) and later in Tacitus's Agricola (c. 98 CE) and Annals (c. 116 CE) describing the Roman campaigns against the Druids.
b_yns_mon.etymology_analysis: The Welsh name Ynys Môn combines Welsh *ynys* ('island') with *Môn*, recorded by Roman writers as *Mona* and likely cognate with Proto-Celtic *moniyos* ('mountain' or 'island'). The English name Anglesey is a later Old Norse compound, *Ǫngullsey*, meaning 'Ǫngull's island' or 'island of the strait'.

b_holyhead.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Welsh name is first recorded in 1225 CE as Karkeby (and Castro Kyby in 1291), while the English name Holyhead appears from the 14th century as Haliheved.
b_holyhead.etymology_analysis: The English name Holyhead derives from Old English *hālig* ('holy') and *hēafod* ('headland'), referring to the sacred headland associated with the early Christian monastery. Its Welsh name, Caergybi, combines *caer* ('fort') with the 6th-century saint Cybi, whose community occupied the late Roman fort.

b_caernarfon.first_mention_attestation: The name Caernarfon is first attested in 1221 CE as Kaerinarfon in a charter of Llywelyn the Great to Penmon Priory, and in the Brut y Tywysogion as Kaerenarvon.
b_caernarfon.etymology_analysis: Caernarfon derives from Welsh *caer yn Arfon*, meaning 'the fortress in the land opposite Môn (Anglesey)'. *Arfon* itself is a contraction of *ar* ('facing, opposite') and *Môn* (Anglesey).

historical_names.name: Segontium
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (3rd century CE) as Seguntio; Historia Brittonum (c. 828 CE) as Cair Segeint
historical_names.notes: Roman auxiliary fort of Segontium on the outskirts of modern Caernarfon, later called Cair Segeint in early Welsh sources.

historical_names.name: Cair Segeint
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (3rd century CE) as Seguntio; Historia Brittonum (c. 828 CE) as Cair Segeint
historical_names.notes: Roman auxiliary fort of Segontium on the outskirts of modern Caernarfon, later called Cair Segeint in early Welsh sources.

b_llyn.first_mention_attestation: Attested c. 150 CE in Claudius Ptolemy's Geographia as Ganganorum Promontorium ('Promontory of the Gangani').
b_llyn.etymology_analysis: The Welsh regional name Llŷn is derived from Old Irish *Laigin* ('Leinstermen', the people of Leinster), reflecting late- and post-Roman Irish settlement in northwest Wales. Ptolemy earlier recorded the headland as *Ganganorum Promontorium*.

b_llandudno.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; named after the 6th-century Celtic monk St Tudno, with parish documentation emerging in the High to Late Middle Ages.
b_llandudno.etymology_analysis: Llandudno is a Welsh compound of *llan* ('sacred enclosure, church, parish') and the personal name *Tudno* (with soft consonant mutation to *Dudno*), referring to the 6th-century saint who established a hermitage on the Great Orme.

b_cardigan.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the town of Cardigan (Welsh Aberteifi) developed around the Norman castle founded c. 1093–1110 CE.
b_cardigan.etymology_analysis: Cardigan is an anglicization of *Ceredigion* ('Ceredig's land'), the surrounding territory named after Ceredig, son of Cunedda. Its Welsh name, *Aberteifi*, means 'mouth (*aber*) of the River Teifi'.

b_aberystwyth.first_mention_attestation: The fortified town was laid out by Edward I from 1277 CE as Llanbadarn Gaerog, with the name Aberystwyth first recorded around 1400 CE.
b_aberystwyth.etymology_analysis: Aberystwyth is a Welsh compound of *aber* ('mouth of a river') and the hydronym *Ystwyth* (meaning 'winding' or 'supple'), referring to the mouth of the River Ystwyth where the medieval castle and town were established.

b_denbigh.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Denbigh (Welsh Dinbych) first appears in medieval records in the mid-to-late 13th century (c. 1256–1282 CE).
b_denbigh.etymology_analysis: Denbigh is an anglicization of Welsh *Dinbych*, a compound of *din* ('fortress') and *bych* (mutated form of *bach*, 'little'), translating to 'little fortress'.

b_wrexham.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in 1161 CE as Wristlesham (referring to a castle there), with the form Wrexham appearing in 1186 and Wrechcessham in 1202.
b_wrexham.etymology_analysis: Wrexham is generally derived from the Old English personal name *Wryhtel* combined with *hamm* ('water meadow' or 'enclosure in a river bend'), referring to the meadows along the River Gwenfro.

b_ruthin.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Ruthin Castle was begun in 1277 CE by Reginald de Grey and the borough received its charter in 1282 CE.
b_ruthin.etymology_analysis: Ruthin derives from Welsh *Rhuthun* (earlier *Rhudd-ddin*), combining *rhudd* ('red') and *din* ('fortress'), referring to the red sandstone outcrop on which the castle was built.

b_dolgellau.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the 1253 Survey of Merioneth (and 1254 Norwich Taxation) as Dolkelew.
b_dolgellau.etymology_analysis: Dolgellau combines Welsh *dôl* ('meadow') with a plural or mutated form related to *gelli* ('grove, copse') or *cell* ('cell'), yielding 'meadow of the groves'.

b_corwen.first_mention_attestation: Earliest documented reference is in 1222 CE in the Shrewsbury Cartulary, which mentions sixteen clerics at Corwen.
b_corwen.etymology_analysis: Corwen is traditionally derived from Welsh *côr* ('choir, church') and *gwen* (feminine/mutated form of *gwyn*, 'white' or 'blessed'), meaning 'the white church', though an alternative derivation from *corfaen* ('boundary stone' or 'dwarf stone') has also been proposed.

b_hereford.first_mention_attestation: Hereford became the seat of Bishop Putta between 676 and 688 CE, and served as the Anglo-Saxon administrative centre of western Mercia by the early 8th century.
b_hereford.etymology_analysis: Hereford derives from Old English *here* ('army') and *ford* ('ford'), meaning 'army ford'—a crossing over the River Wye suitable for a military force. Its Welsh name, *Henffordd*, means 'old road'.

b_wigmore.first_mention_attestation: First reliably attested in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as Wigemore (earlier 19th-century identifications with Wigingamere in the 917/921 Anglo-Saxon Chronicle are now assigned to Newport, Essex).
b_wigmore.etymology_analysis: Wigmore (Domesday *Wigemore*) derives from Old English *wicga-mōr*, referring to a 'quaking marsh' or yielding moorland.

b_clifford.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as Cliford, recording the Norman castle built between 1069 and 1071 CE by William fitz Osbern.
b_clifford.etymology_analysis: Clifford is an Old English compound of *clif* ('cliff, steep bank') and *ford* ('ford'), describing the river crossing on the River Wye beneath a steep bank.

b_hurstingstone.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as one of the hundreds of Huntingdonshire, named from the meeting stone near Old Hurst.
b_hurstingstone.etymology_analysis: Hurstingstone derives from Old English *Hyrstingastān*, meaning 'the stone of the dwellers at Hurst' (Old Hurst), referring to the ancient stone where the hundred moot assembled.

b_norman_cross.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 963 CE in an Anglo-Saxon charter as Northmannescros, referring to the cross and hundred meeting place in Huntingdonshire.
b_norman_cross.etymology_analysis: Norman Cross derives from Old English *Norþmannescros* ('Northman's cross'), referring to a Scandinavian settler rather than a post-1066 Norman, marking the junction of Ermine Street and the Yaxley–Folksworth road.

b_leightonstone.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as a hundred of Huntingdonshire, named after the moot stone at Leighton Bromswold.
b_leightonstone.etymology_analysis: Leightonstone combines the settlement name *Leighton* (from Old English *lēac-tūn*, 'herb/kitchen garden') with Old English *stān* ('stone'), referring to the meeting stone at Leighton Bromswold.

b_leicester.first_mention_attestation: Attested c. 150 CE in Claudius Ptolemy's Geographia as Ratae (Roman civitas capital Ratae Corieltauvorum), and in the early 9th century in Latinized form as Legorensis civitatis (Old English Ligera ceastre in 924 CE).

morphemes.translation: Roman fort, walled town (from Latin castrum)

b_leicester.etymology_analysis: Leicester derives from Old English *Ligera ceaster* ('fortress of the Ligore'), where *Ligore* is a folk name from the Brittonic river name *Ligor* (now the River Soar) and *ceaster* comes from Latin *castrum*.

b_melton.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as Medeltone, with the manorial affix Mowbray added in the 12th century.

eponym.details: The affix 'Mowbray' derives from the Anglo-Norman de Mowbray family (such as Robert de Mowbray, fl. late 11th century), who became lords of the manor after the Norman Conquest of 1066.

b_melton.etymology_analysis: Melton (Domesday *Medeltone*) derives from Old English *middel-tūn* ('middle settlement', with Scandinavian influence *meðal*), indicating a central market town among surrounding hamlets. The affix *Mowbray* was added from the post-Conquest Anglo-Norman de Mowbray lords.

b_bosworth.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as Boseworde.
b_bosworth.etymology_analysis: Bosworth (Domesday *Boseworde*) derives from the Old English personal name *Bōsa* and *worþ* ('enclosure, homestead'), with 'Market' added later to distinguish it from Husbands Bosworth.

b_rutland.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1002 CE as Roteland when granted to Emma of Normandy on her marriage to King Æthelred the Unready, and later recorded in the Will of Edward the Confessor and the 1086 Domesday Book.
b_rutland.etymology_analysis: Rutland (recorded as *Roteland*) is most widely explained as Old English *Rōtan land* ('land belonging to Rōta'), though an alternative folk/antiquarian etymology connects it to Old English *rēad* ('red', referring to its ironstone soil).

b_northampton.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle entry for 914 CE as Ham tune.
b_northampton.etymology_analysis: Northampton derives from Old English *Hāmtūn* ('home farm / principal settlement'), with the directional prefix *norþ-* added by the time of the 1086 Domesday Book (*Northantone*) to distinguish it from Southampton.

b_peterborough.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 655 CE and attested in Bede (731 CE) as Medeshamstede, the abbey and town were refounded c. 970 CE by Bishop Æthelwold as a fortified 'Burh', soon called Burgh St Peter / Peterborough.
b_peterborough.etymology_analysis: Peterborough derives from Old English *Petres burh* ('fortified town/monastery of Saint Peter'), replacing the earlier Anglo-Saxon name *Medeshamstede* ('homestead in the meadows') after the abbey was fortified and dedicated to St Peter in the late 10th century.

historical_names.name: Medeshamstede
historical_names.source: Bede's Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum (731 CE) and 8th-century Anglo-Saxon charters
historical_names.notes: Original name of the 7th-century Mercian monastery at Peterborough prior to its late-10th-century renaming.

historical_names.name: Medyhæmstede
historical_names.source: Bede's Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum (731 CE) and 8th-century Anglo-Saxon charters
historical_names.notes: Original name of the 7th-century Mercian monastery at Peterborough prior to its late-10th-century renaming.

b_kettering.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a royal charter of King Eadwig in 956 CE granting ten cassati of land at Cytringan to his minister Ælfsige.
b_kettering.etymology_analysis: Kettering (attested as *Cytringan* and *Kyteringas* in the 10th century) combines an Old English personal or group name with the suffix *-ingas* ('people of'), meaning 'the place or territory of Cytra's/Ketter's people'.

b_nottingham.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle entry for 868 CE as Snotengaham, recording the Viking army wintering there.
b_nottingham.etymology_analysis: Nottingham derives from Old English *Snotingahām* ('homestead of Snot's people'), which later lost its initial *S-* under Norman-French orthographic and phonological influence.

b_newark.first_mention_attestation: First reliably attested in 1055 CE when Leofric, Earl of Mercia, and Godiva granted Newark to the monastery of Stow (a purported 664 CE charter is a later Peterborough forgery).
b_newark.etymology_analysis: Newark (recorded as *Newerca* and *Nouwerk*) derives from Old English *nīwe weorc* ('new fortification' or 'new work'), with '-on-Trent' added to specify its position on the River Trent.

b_retford.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as Redforde.
b_retford.etymology_analysis: Retford (Domesday *Redforde*) derives from Old English *rēad ford* ('red ford'), referring to a crossing over the River Idle stained by red clay or ferruginous soil.

b_shrewsbury.first_mention_attestation: First attested in English in a charter of 901 CE as Scrobbesburh (dative Scrobbesbyrig).
b_shrewsbury.etymology_analysis: Shrewsbury derives from Old English *Scrobbesburh* ('fortified place of the scrub/brushwood'), which evolved via dative *Scrobbesbyrig* into modern Shrewsbury (and via Anglo-Norman *Sloppesberie* into *Salop*). The Welsh name *Amwythig* ('fortified place') translates the same sense.

b_ludlow.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Lodelowe before 1138 CE, following the foundation of Ludlow Castle by the de Lacy family c. 1075–1094 CE.
b_ludlow.etymology_analysis: Ludlow derives from Old English *hlūd-hlǣw* ('hill/mound by the loud waters'), referring to the rapids on the River Teme below the hilltop where the castle and church were built.

b_bishops_castle.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the motte-and-bailey castle was built in 1087 CE by the Bishop of Hereford on lands earlier held in Lydbury North.
b_bishops_castle.etymology_analysis: Bishop's Castle is named for the motte-and-bailey fortress erected in 1087 CE by the Bishop of Hereford to defend his Shropshire borderlands against Welsh raids.

b_stafford.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle entry for 913 CE, when Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians, built a burh at Stafford.
b_stafford.etymology_analysis: Stafford derives from Old English *stæþ-ford* ('ford by a landing-place / river bank'), referring to the crossing over the River Sow.

b_wolverhampton.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a charter of King Æthelred II in 985 CE granting ten hides at Heantune to Lady Wulfrun (later Wulfrūnehēantūn from 1070 CE).

eponym.details: Named after Wulfrun (fl. 943–994 CE), an Anglo-Saxon noblewoman who received the estate of Heantune in 985 CE and endowed its collegiate church in 994 CE.

b_wolverhampton.etymology_analysis: Wolverhampton derives from Old English *Wulfrūnehēantūn* ('Wulfrun's high/principal enclosure'), prefixing the name of the 10th-century benefactress Wulfrun to *Hēantūn* ('high farm').

b_stoke_on_trent.first_mention_attestation: Stoke-upon-Trent (the parish after which the federated city is named) is first attested in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE.
b_stoke_on_trent.etymology_analysis: Stoke-on-Trent takes its name from Stoke-upon-Trent, from Old English *stoc* ('outlying farmstead or religious dependency') situated on the River Trent (from Brittonic *Trisanton*).

b_warwick.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Mercian Register of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 914 CE as Wæringwicum, when Æthelflæd built a fortress there.
b_warwick.etymology_analysis: Warwick (Old English *Wǣringwīc*) derives from *wering* ('weir, river dam') and *wīc* ('settlement, dwelling'), meaning 'dwellings by the weir' on the River Avon.

b_coventry.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1043 CE as Couaentree in connection with the Benedictine priory founded by Leofric, Earl of Mercia, and Godiva.
b_coventry.etymology_analysis: Coventry (1043 *Couaentree*, Domesday *Coventrev*) is most widely derived from Old English *Cofan trēo* ('Cofa's tree'), referring to a prominent boundary or assembly tree.

b_birmingham.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as the small manor of Bermingeham.
b_birmingham.etymology_analysis: Birmingham (Domesday *Bermingeham*) derives from Old English *Beormingahām*, meaning 'homestead of the people of Beorma'.

b_worcester.first_mention_attestation: Earliest definitive record is Weogorna civitas ('city of the Weogoran') in an ecclesiastical charter of c. 691 CE, following the establishment of the diocese of Worcester c. 680 CE.

morphemes.translation: winding river / people of the winding river
Roman fort, walled city (from Latin castrum)

b_worcester.etymology_analysis: Worcester derives from Old English *Weogornaceaster* ('fortress of the Weogoran'), combining a pre-English tribal or river name (*Weogora*) with Old English *ceaster* (from Latin *castrum*).

b_evesham.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 709 CE (as Eoveshomme / Eofesham) upon the consecration of Evesham Abbey founded by St Egwin, Bishop of Worcester.
b_evesham.etymology_analysis: Evesham derives from Old English *Eofeshamm*, meaning 'Eof's river-bend meadow', traditionally linked to the swineherd Eof whose vision led to the founding of Evesham Abbey in 709 CE.

b_kidderminster.first_mention_attestation: The monastic estate on the River Stour at Kidderminster is attested in the 736 CE Ismere Diploma of King Æthelbald of Mercia (granting land at Sture in Usmere to Ealdorman Cyneberht); the name Chideminstre appears in the 1086 Domesday Book.
b_kidderminster.etymology_analysis: Kidderminster derives from Old English *Cyddanmynster* ('Cydda's minster'), referring to the early Mercian monastic foundation on the River Stour.

historical_names.name: Sture in Usmere
historical_names.source: Ismere Diploma (736 CE) of King Æthelbald of Mercia
historical_names.notes: Territory along the River Stour encompassing the monastic foundation that later became Kidderminster.

b_chester.first_mention_attestation: Attested c. 150 CE in Claudius Ptolemy's Geographia as Deva (the Roman legionary fortress Deva Victrix), and in Bede (731 CE) as Legacaestir ('city of the legions').

morphemes.translation: Roman fort, walled city (from Latin castrum)

b_chester.etymology_analysis: Chester derives directly from Old English *ceaster* ('Roman fort, walled town', borrowed from Latin *castrum*), shortened from the earlier Old English *Legacaestir* ('city of the legions').

b_northwich.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 3rd-century Antonine Itinerary and 7th-century Ravenna Cosmography as Condate; the English name Norwich appears in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE.
b_northwich.etymology_analysis: Northwich derives from Old English *norþ-wīc* ('north salt-town'), distinguishing it as the northernmost of the Cheshire salt-producing *-wich* towns (alongside Middlewich and Nantwich).

historical_names.name: Condate
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (3rd century CE) and Ravenna Cosmography (7th century CE)
historical_names.notes: Latinized Brittonic name meaning 'confluence', referring to the junction of the Rivers Dane and Weaver.

b_macclesfield.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as Maclesfeld.
b_macclesfield.etymology_analysis: Macclesfield (Domesday *Maclesfeld*) derives from the Old English personal name *Maccel* and *feld* ('open land, clearing'), meaning 'Maccel's open country'.

b_derby.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle entry for 917 CE as Deoraby, when Lady Æthelflæd of Mercia captured it from the Danes (alongside the older English name Norþworþig).
b_derby.etymology_analysis: Derby derives from Old Norse *Djúra-bý* (recorded in Old English as *Deoraby*), meaning 'village of the deer', replacing or coexisting with the Anglo-Saxon *Norþworþig* ('north enclosure').

historical_names.name: Derventio
historical_names.source: Ravenna Cosmography (7th century CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman fort and settlement at Little Chester on the northern edge of modern Derby, named from the River Derwent ('valley thick with oaks').

b_chesterfield.first_mention_attestation: A charter of King Eadred in 955 CE mentions Cestrefeld (though possibly referring to Chesterfield in Staffordshire); the Derbyshire town is certainly attested in the 1086 Domesday Book as Cestrefeld.
b_chesterfield.etymology_analysis: Chesterfield derives from Old English *ceaster-feld* ('open land by the Roman fort'), referring to the Roman fort site underlying the medieval town.

b_castleton.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE in connection with William Peverel's castle at Pechesers.
b_castleton.etymology_analysis: Castleton derives from Middle English *castel-tūn* ('settlement by the castle'), referring to the village that grew beneath Peveril Castle after the Norman Conquest.

b_lancaster.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Lancaster in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE under the spelling Loncastre.
b_lancaster.etymology_analysis: Lancaster (Domesday *Loncastre*) combines the Brittonic river name *Lune* (*Lon*) with Old English *ceaster* ('Roman fort'), meaning 'Roman fort on the River Lune'.

b_salford.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as Salford, the head of a royal Anglo-Saxon manor and hundred.
b_salford.etymology_analysis: Salford derives from Old English *salh-ford* ('willow ford'), referring to a ford across the River Irwell bordered by willow trees.

b_west_derby.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as Derbei, the caput of the West Derby Hundred.
b_west_derby.etymology_analysis: West Derby (Domesday *Derbei*) derives from Old Norse *Djúra-bý* ('deer village' or 'deer park'), with 'West' added later to distinguish it from Derby in Derbyshire.

b_kendal.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE under Yorkshire as Cherchebi ('church-village'), later Kirkby Kendal; no written attestation of the settlement exists on or before 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: River Kent (ancient river name of uncertain Celtic origin)

b_kendal.etymology_analysis: Kendal derives from the Brittonic hydronym Kent combined with Old Norse dalr ('valley'), meaning 'valley of the River Kent'. In the 1086 Domesday Book it appears as Cherchebi (Old Norse kirkju-bý, 'church-village'), and for centuries it was known as Kirkby Kendal before shortening to Kendal.

historical_names.name: Alone
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (early 3rd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman fort at Watercrook two miles south of Kendal, built c. 90 CE and recorded as Alone in the Antonine Itinerary and Alunna in the Ravenna Cosmography.

historical_names.name: Alavana
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (early 3rd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman fort at Watercrook two miles south of Kendal, built c. 90 CE and recorded as Alone in the Antonine Itinerary and Alunna in the Ravenna Cosmography.

b_appleby.first_mention_attestation: First attested in early 12th-century Anglo-Norman records (c. 1130 Pipe Rolls / foundation of Appleby Castle by Ranulf le Meschin, followed by its 1179 royal charter); Westmorland was omitted as a separate county in the 1086 Domesday Book and no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_appleby.etymology_analysis: Appleby combines Old English æppel (or Old Norse apall, 'apple tree') with Old Norse býr ('farmstead, village'), denoting a settlement associated with apple orchards. The suffix '-in-Westmorland' was added in 1974 to preserve the link to the historic county.

b_cambridge.first_mention_attestation: The name Grantebrycge (whence Cambridge) is first attested in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle annal for 875 CE; the earlier Castle Hill site was recorded as Roman Duroliponte (c. 215 CE) and by Bede as Grantacaestir (731 CE).
b_cambridge.etymology_analysis: Originally named Grantacaestir ('fort on the Granta') and Grantebrycge ('Granta bridge') in Old English after the Brittonic river name Granta, the initial consonant shifted under Anglo-Norman influence (Cantebrigge) to Cambridge, from which the river name Cam was later back-formed.

historical_names.name: Duroliponte
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (early 3rd century CE); Bede, Historia ecclesiastica (731 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman town on Castle Hill recorded as Duroliponte in the Antonine Itinerary and later as Grantacaestir by Bede.

historical_names.name: Grantacaestir
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (early 3rd century CE); Bede, Historia ecclesiastica (731 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman town on Castle Hill recorded as Duroliponte in the Antonine Itinerary and later as Grantacaestir by Bede.

b_radfield.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as Radefelle (and in the contemporary Inquisitio Comitatus Cantabrigiensis as Radefelde), naming a rural hundred of Cambridgeshire; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_radfield.etymology_analysis: Radfield derives from Old English rād ('riding, road') and feld ('open land, field'), referring to open country beside an ancient riding road or trackway in eastern Cambridgeshire.

b_papworth.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as Papeworde; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.

eponym.details: The affix 'Everard' commemorates Everard de Beche, a Norman knight who was granted the manor of Papworth after the 1066 Norman Conquest.

b_papworth.etymology_analysis: Papworth comes from the Old English personal name Pappa and weorþ ('enclosure, homestead'). After the Norman Conquest of 1066, the manor was held by the knight Everard de Beche, whose given name was appended to distinguish the village from neighbouring Papworth St Agnes.

b_ely.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Bede's Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum (731 CE) as Elge, referring to the fenland district and monastery founded by Æthelthryth in 673 CE.
b_ely.etymology_analysis: Ely is recorded by Bede as Elge and is conventionally interpreted as Old English ǣl ('eel') plus *ġē ('district', cognate with German Gau), meaning 'eel district', though an alternative Brythonic derivation from helig ('willows') or heli ('salt water') has also been proposed.

b_norwich.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing as Norvic on silver pennies minted during the reign of King Æthelstan (924–939 CE); although Middle Saxon settlement existed earlier, no written attestation survives on or before 867 CE.
b_norwich.etymology_analysis: Norwich derives from Old English norþ ('north') and wīc ('trading settlement, port'), denoting the northern Anglo-Saxon trading settlement on the River Wensum relative to nearby Venta Icenorum and Westwic.

historical_names.name: Venta Icenorum
historical_names.source: Ptolemy, Geographia (c. 150 CE); Antonine Itinerary
historical_names.notes: Roman civitas capital of the Iceni at Caistor St Edmund, five miles south of Norwich, abandoned c. 450 CE.

historical_names.name: Venta
historical_names.source: Ptolemy, Geographia (c. 150 CE); Antonine Itinerary
historical_names.notes: Roman civitas capital of the Iceni at Caistor St Edmund, five miles south of Norwich, abandoned c. 450 CE.

b_thetford.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle entry for 870 CE (compiled c. 890 CE) as Theodford, where the Great Heathen Army took winter quarters; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_thetford.etymology_analysis: Thetford derives from Old English þēod ('people, public') and ford ('ford'), meaning 'the people's ford' or 'chief ford' across the Little Ouse and Thet rivers.

b_walsingham.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as Walsingaham (alongside a 1061 CE foundation tradition for the Marian shrine); no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_walsingham.etymology_analysis: Walsingham derives from Old English Wælsinga-hām, meaning 'homestead of the followers of Wæls', combining an early Anglo-Saxon personal name with the group-forming suffix -ingas and hām.

b_lynn.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 1086 CE Domesday Book as Lena (later Bishop's Lynn), the town was renamed King's Lynn in 1537 CE when Henry VIII took possession of it from the Bishops of Norwich.

eponym.details: Originally called Lenn and later Bishop's Lynn (after the Bishops of Norwich), it was renamed King's Lynn in 1537 CE under King Henry VIII after the Dissolution of the Monasteries.

morphemes.translation: lake, pool / tenure in fee, farm

b_lynn.etymology_analysis: Lynn (Domesday Lun, Lenn) is either from Brythonic *lindo- (cf. Welsh llyn, 'lake, pool') referring to tidal waters near the Wash, or Old English lēan ('farm, tenure in fee'). The prefix 'King's' replaced 'Bishop's' in 1537 under Henry VIII.

b_ipswich.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle entry for 993 CE as Gipeswic (plundered by Vikings); although archaeological evidence shows a 7th-century wic emporium, no written attestation survives on or before 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: personal name Gip (or gīp 'gap, estuary mouth')

b_ipswich.etymology_analysis: Ipswich (Old English Gipeswīc) combines either an Old English personal name Gip or a topographic element meaning 'gap/opening' with wīc ('trading settlement, port') on the River Orwell estuary.

b_sudbury.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle entry for 799 CE as Suðbyrig, recording the death there of Ælfhun, Bishop of Dunwich.
b_sudbury.etymology_analysis: Sudbury derives from Old English Sūþburh ('southern stronghold'), distinguishing it from a northern burh in East Anglia such as Bury St Edmunds or Norwich.

b_blything.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as Blidinga (centred on the royal estate of Blythburgh); no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_blything.etymology_analysis: Blything derives from Old English Blīðingas, meaning 'the people of the River Blyth' (from Old English blīðe, 'gentle, pleasant'), naming the Suffolk hundred drained by the River Blyth.

b_beodericsworth.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a 945 CE charter of King Edmund I (S 507) as Beodricesworth (following the translation of St Edmund's relics there under Æthelstan c. 925 CE); no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.

eponym.details: Named after Edmund the Martyr, King of East Anglia, who was killed by the Great Heathen Army in 869 CE and whose shrine at Beodericsworth gave rise to the name Bury St Edmunds (Burgum Sancti Edmundi).

b_beodericsworth.etymology_analysis: Originally named Beodericsworth (Old English Beodrices-weorþ, 'Beodric's enclosure'), the town was renamed Bury St Edmunds (Latin Burgum Sancti Edmundi) in the 11th century from Old English burh ('fortified/abbey town') and the shrine of King Edmund the Martyr (d. 869 CE).

b_carlisle.first_mention_attestation: Attested c. 100 CE in the Vindolanda writing tablets as Luguvalium (and later in the Antonine Itinerary, Bede's Historia ecclesiastica of 731 CE as Lugubalia, and Historia Brittonum as Caer Ligualid).
b_carlisle.etymology_analysis: Carlisle derives from Cumbric Caer Ligualid ('fort of Luguvalos'), combining Brittonic *cair ('fort') with the Romanized name Luguvalium, meaning the settlement or stronghold of a Brittonic leader named Luguvalos ('strong as the god Lugus').

b_whitehaven.first_mention_attestation: First attested c. 1135–1140 CE in charters of St Bees Priory as Qwithofhavene and Withofhavene; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_whitehaven.etymology_analysis: Whitehaven (earliest forms Qwithofhavene, Withofhavene) means 'harbour by the white headland', combining Old Norse/Old English elements for 'white', 'headland', and 'harbour', referring to the pale sandstone cliffs flanking the bay.

b_furness.first_mention_attestation: First recorded as Fudernesio in the 1127 CE foundation charter of Furness Abbey (while parts of the peninsula appear under the Manor of Hougun in the 1086 Domesday Book); no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_furness.etymology_analysis: Furness (recorded as Fudernesio in 1127) combines Old Norse nes ('headland, promontory') with Old Norse fuð ('rump, hindquarters', or possibly a personal name), describing the shape of the southern Cumbrian peninsula.

b_wigton.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 12th-century records (c. 1163 and Testa de Nevill 1212 as Wiggeton); no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_wigton.etymology_analysis: Wigton derives from the Old English personal name Wicga and tūn ('enclosure, farmstead, hamlet'), meaning 'Wicga's farmstead'.

b_durham.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 995 CE as Dunholm when the Community of St Cuthbert translated the saint's relics there, as recorded by Symeon of Durham; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: island, peninsula in a river bend

b_durham.etymology_analysis: Durham derives from Old English dūn ('hill') and Old Norse holmr ('island'), referring to the steep rocky peninsula formed by a tight meander of the River Wear, later Normanized from Dunholm to Duresme/Durham.

b_hartlepool.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Bede's Historia ecclesiastica (731 CE) as Heruteu ('hart island'), referring to the monastery founded c. 640 CE on the Hartlepool headland; the full compound Hartlepool appears in the 12th century.
b_hartlepool.etymology_analysis: Hartlepool combines Old English heorot ('stag, hart') and ēg ('island, peninsula', preserved in Bede's Heruteu) with Old English pōl ('pool, harbour'), meaning 'pool by the stag headland'.

b_darlington.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Dearthington in a record of 1003 CE (preserved in Historia de Sancto Cuthberto) when Styr son of Ulf granted the estate to St Cuthbert; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_darlington.etymology_analysis: Darlington derives from Old English Deornōþingtūn (recorded as Dearthington in 1003), meaning 'the estate or settlement of Deornōþ's people'.

b_bamburgh.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Bede's Historia ecclesiastica (731 CE) as Bebbanburh (and in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle under 547 CE and Historia Brittonum as Din Guarie), serving as the royal fortress of Bernicia and Northumbria.

morphemes.translation: personal name of Queen Bebba (c. 600 CE)

b_bamburgh.etymology_analysis: Bamburgh derives from Old English Bebbanburh ('Bebba's fortress'), named by King Æthelfrith of Northumbria after his wife Queen Bebba around 600 CE, replacing the earlier Brittonic fort name Din Guarie.

b_rothbury.first_mention_attestation: First attested in early 12th-century records (c. 1107 CE; Latinized as Rodeberia, 1165 Roebiri); despite a 9th-century Anglo-Saxon cross fragment found in the church, no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_rothbury.etymology_analysis: Rothbury combines Old English burh ('stronghold, fortified enclosure') with either the Old English personal name Hrōþa or a word related to rōþ ('clearing'), denoting a fortified settlement beside the River Coquet.

b_lindisfarne.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Bede's Historia ecclesiastica (731 CE) as Lindisfarnensis (and in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle under 793 CE and Historia Brittonum as Medcaut), following the foundation of the monastery by St Aidan in 634 CE.
b_lindisfarne.etymology_analysis: Lindisfarne is generally explained as Old English Lindis-farena ('island of travellers from Lindsey'), though an alternative Brittonic origin has also been proposed; in Welsh/Brittonic tradition it was called Ynys Metcaut (Medcaut).

historical_names.name: Medcaut
historical_names.source: Bede, Historia ecclesiastica (731 CE); Historia Brittonum (c. 828 CE)
historical_names.notes: Recorded by Bede in 731 CE and as Medcaut in Historia Brittonum.

b_hexham.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Stephen of Ripon's Vita Wilfridi (c. 710–720 CE) and Bede's Historia ecclesiastica (731 CE) as Hagustaldesham / Hagustaldensis, referring to the abbey founded by St Wilfrid in 674 CE.
b_hexham.etymology_analysis: Hexham derives from Old English Hagustaldeshām ('estate of the hagustald', a young noble warrior or landless retainer), which contracted over time through Hagustaldesham to Hextoldesham and Hexham.

b_welshpool.first_mention_attestation: First attested in medieval Welsh and Anglo-Norman sources around 1196–1212 CE as Y Trallwng (English Pool, later Welshpool) when Gwenwynwyn ab Owain moved the capital of Powys Wenwynwyn there from Mathrafal; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: Welsh (distinguishing prefix added against Poole, Dorset)

b_welshpool.etymology_analysis: Welshpool translates its Welsh name Y Trallwng ('the marshy hollow or pool'), referring to a nearby pond in Powis Castle park; 'Welsh' was prefixed in English to distinguish it from Poole in Dorset.

b_newtown.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1279 CE when Roger Mortimer received a market charter for Nova Villa ('Newtown', originally Llanfair-yng-Nghedewain); no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_newtown.etymology_analysis: Newtown (Latin Nova Villa, modern Welsh Y Drenewydd) was founded in 1279 by Roger Mortimer as a planned market town to replace Dolforwyn Castle; its earlier Welsh parish name was Llanfair-yng-Nghedewain ('St Mary's church in Cedewain').

b_llandrindod.first_mention_attestation: First attested in late 13th-century ecclesiastical records (c. 1291 CE, Taxatio Ecclesiastica, associated with the 13th/14th-century parish church of the Holy Trinity); no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_llandrindod.etymology_analysis: Llandrindod Wells combines Welsh llan ('church, parish') and Trindod ('Trinity', with soft mutation to Drindod), meaning 'parish of the Holy Trinity'; 'Wells' was added in the 18th/19th century when it developed as a spa town.

b_rhayader.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1177 CE in Welsh chronicles (Brut y Tywysogion) as Rhaeadr Gwy when Rhys ap Gruffydd built Rhayader Castle; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_rhayader.etymology_analysis: Rhayader is an anglicization of Welsh Rhaeadr Gwy, meaning 'waterfall on the River Wye', referring to a cataract on the Wye that was demolished in 1780 to build a bridge.

b_wareham.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (annals for 784/786 CE and 876 CE) as Werham, a royal West Saxon settlement and later fortified burh on the River Frome.
b_wareham.etymology_analysis: Wareham derives from Old English wer ('weir, dam') and hām ('homestead') or hamm ('water-meadow'), referring to a settlement beside a river weir between the Frome and Piddle rivers.

b_poole.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the late 12th century (c. 1196 CE) as the port of La Pole / Poole began emerging from the manor of Canford; omitted from the 1086 Domesday Book, with no written attestation on or before 867 CE.
b_poole.etymology_analysis: Poole derives directly from Old English pōl ('pool, tidal inlet'), referring to the vast natural harbour of Poole Harbour.

b_shaftesbury.first_mention_attestation: First attested in connection with King Alfred's foundation of Shaftesbury Abbey and fortified burh in 880 CE (recorded in Asser's Life of King Alfred, 893 CE, and the Burghal Hidage as Sceaftesburg); no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_shaftesbury.etymology_analysis: Shaftesbury derives from Old English Sceaftesburh, combining burh ('fortified town') with sceaft (either 'shaft/pole' or a personal name Sceaft, possibly referring to the prominent hilltop spur).

b_lyme.first_mention_attestation: Attested in a 774 CE charter of King Cynewulf of Wessex (S 263), granting land at Lim (on the River Lym) to Sherborne Abbey for salt-panning.

morphemes.translation: of the King (added under Edward I in 1284)

b_lyme.etymology_analysis: Lyme Regis takes its base name from the River Lym (attested as Lim in 774 CE, a pre-English hydronym), with Latin Regis ('of the King') appended after Edward I granted a royal charter in 1284.

b_winchester.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Ptolemy's Geographia (c. 150 CE) as Οὐέντα (Venta) and in the Antonine Itinerary as Venta Belgarum, later Old English Wintanceaster.
b_winchester.etymology_analysis: Winchester derives from Brittonic Venta ('market, tribal centre', in Roman Venta Belgarum) combined with Old English ceaster ('walled Roman town', from Latin castra), yielding Wintanceaster.

b_southampton.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Hamwic in the Vita Willibaldi (c. 778 CE) and as Hamtun in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (837 CE), succeeding nearby Roman Clausentum (attested in the Antonine Itinerary, c. 215 CE).
b_southampton.etymology_analysis: Southampton derives from Old English Hamwic/Hamtun ('home-settlement' or 'water-meadow town'), with Sūþ- ('south') later prefixed to distinguish it from Northampton.

historical_names.name: Clausentum
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (c. 215 CE, Clausentum); Vita Willibaldi (c. 778 CE, Hamwic)
historical_names.notes: Roman port Clausentum at Bitterne Manor preceded the Middle Saxon emporium of Hamwic (Hamtun).

b_portsmouth.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 1180 CE by Anglo-Norman merchant Jean de Gisors (first named Portsmouth in charters shortly after 1181, and absent from the 1086 Domesday Book); the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (compiled c. 890 CE) has a retrospective 501 CE entry for Portesmuða generally linked to Portchester, and no contemporary written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_portsmouth.etymology_analysis: Portsmouth derives from Old English Portesmūða, meaning 'mouth of the harbour (Portus)', though an Anglo-Saxon folk etymology attributed it to a legendary Jutish leader named Port.

historical_names.name: Portus Adurni
historical_names.source: Notitia Dignitatum (c. 400 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman Saxon Shore fort at Portchester on the north side of Portsmouth Harbour.
