b_basingstoke.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a 990 CE charter as Embasinga stocæ and in the 1086 Domesday Book as Basingestoches; no written attestation of Basingstoke exists on or before 867 CE (neighbouring Basing is first recorded in the 871 CE Anglo-Saxon Chronicle).
b_basingstoke.etymology_analysis: Basingstoke derives from Old English Basinga-stoc, meaning 'the outlying settlement of Basa's people (the Basingas)', originally dependent on Old Basing two miles to the east.

b_christchurch.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle entry for 901 CE as Tweoxneam (Twynham), later renamed Christchurch after Christchurch Priory was founded in 1094 CE; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_christchurch.etymology_analysis: Originally called Tweoxneam (Twynham, Old English betweoxn ēam 'between the rivers' Avon and Stour), the town was renamed Christchurch in the 12th century after the Norman priory church dedicated to Christ.

b_carisbrooke.first_mention_attestation: First attested by name as Caresbroc in 12th-century charters (c. 1158 CE; omitted by name in the 1086 Domesday Book, which records the castle under Alvington/Bowcombe); the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (compiled c. 890 CE) mentions Wihtgarabyrig under 530/544 CE, post-867 in compilation.
b_carisbrooke.etymology_analysis: Carisbrooke (12th-century Caresbroc) combines a lost Brittonic stream name Cary with Old English brōc ('brook'), meaning 'the brook called Cary' (likely an earlier name for Lukely Brook).

b_bath.first_mention_attestation: The Old English name Hat Bathu (æt Baðum, whence Bath) first appears in a charter of 675 CE, succeeding the Roman spa town of Aquae Calidae / Aquae Sulis (c. 150 CE).
b_bath.etymology_analysis: Bath derives from Old English (æt þǣm hātum) bæðum, meaning '(at the hot) baths', translating the Roman thermal spa name Aquae Sulis ('waters of the goddess Sulis').

historical_names.name: Aquae Calidae
historical_names.source: Ptolemy, Geographia (c. 150 CE); Antonine Itinerary
historical_names.notes: Roman spa town centred on the thermal springs dedicated to Sulis Minerva.

historical_names.name: Aquae Sulis
historical_names.source: Ptolemy, Geographia (c. 150 CE); Antonine Itinerary
historical_names.notes: Roman spa town centred on the thermal springs dedicated to Sulis Minerva.

b_winterstoke.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as a hundred of Somerset (named after a lost village of Winterstoke); no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_winterstoke.etymology_analysis: Winterstoke derives from Old English winter and stoc ('outlying settlement, cattle farm'), denoting a seasonal winter farmstead that gave its name to the Somerset hundred.

b_ilchester.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Lindinis in the 7th-century Ravenna Cosmography (c. 700 CE) and as Lendiniae on Roman inscriptions from Hadrian's Wall, later Old English Gifelceaster.
b_ilchester.etymology_analysis: Ilchester derives from Old English Gifelceaster ('Roman fort on the River Gifle/Ivel', now the River Yeo), succeeding the Romano-British town of Lindinis.

historical_names.name: Lindinis
historical_names.source: Ravenna Cosmography (c. 700 CE); Hadrian's Wall inscriptions
historical_names.notes: Romano-British town of the Durotriges at the Fosse Way crossing of the River Yeo.

historical_names.name: Lendiniae
historical_names.source: Ravenna Cosmography (c. 700 CE); Hadrian's Wall inscriptions
historical_names.notes: Romano-British town of the Durotriges at the Fosse Way crossing of the River Yeo.

b_taunton.first_mention_attestation: Attested in an 854 CE charter of King Æthelwulf of Wessex (S 311, granting land at Tantun to Winchester), as well as the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle entry for 722 CE recording Queen Æthelburh's destruction of the fort built by King Ine.
b_taunton.etymology_analysis: Taunton (Old English Tantūn) means 'settlement on the River Tone', combining the pre-English river name Tone with Old English tūn.

b_pockington.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in writing in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as Poclinton (the second-largest settlement in Yorkshire); no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_pockington.etymology_analysis: Pocklington derives from Old English Pocelingtūn, meaning 'farmstead or estate of Pocela's people'.

b_cottingham.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as Cotingeham; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_cottingham.etymology_analysis: Cottingham derives from Old English Cottingahām, meaning 'homestead or village of Cotta's people'.

b_bridlington.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in writing in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as Bretlinton; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE (Ptolemy's Gabrantovicum bay refers broadly to the coastal bay).

morphemes.translation: personal name Bretel, Bridla, or Berhtel

b_bridlington.etymology_analysis: Bridlington (Domesday Bretlinton) combines an Old English personal name (Bretel, Bridla, or Berhtel) with -ingtūn, meaning 'farmstead of Bretel's people'.

b_lincoln.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Ptolemy's Geographia (c. 150 CE) as Λίνδον (Lindon) and in the Antonine Itinerary as Lindo (Lindum Colonia).
b_lincoln.etymology_analysis: Lincoln is a contraction of Roman Lindum Colonia, combining a Latinized Brittonic name *lindon ('pool, lake', referring to Brayford Pool on the River Witham) with Latin colonia ('Roman colony').

b_stamford.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle entry for 922 CE as Steanford (and 942 CE as Stanford); no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_stamford.etymology_analysis: Stamford derives from Old English Stānford ('stony ford'), referring to a paved or rocky crossing of the River Welland where Ermine Street passed.

b_boston.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the early 12th century (c. 1130 CE, as St Botolph's / Botulfston; omitted by name from the 1086 Domesday Book, where it fell under Skirbeck/Drayton). Modern historians reject the older identification with St Botolph's 654 CE monastery at Icanho (now placed at Iken, Suffolk); no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: Saint Botolph (7th-century abbot, died c. 680 CE)

b_boston.etymology_analysis: Boston is a contraction of Botolph's town (or Botolph's stone), named after the 7th-century Anglo-Saxon abbot Saint Botolph (d. c. 680 CE), patron saint of travellers to whom the medieval parish church was dedicated.

b_bolingsbroke.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086 CE as Bulingbroc; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_bolingsbroke.etymology_analysis: Bolingbroke (Domesday Bulingbroc) derives from Old English Bulingbrōc, meaning 'the brook of Bula's (or Bulla's) people'.

b_grimsby.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written records in the 1086 Domesday Book as Grimesbi, though Danish settlement on the Haven dates to the 9th century CE.

morphemes.translation: personal name Grímr (masked one / Odinic byname)

b_grimsby.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Norse Grímsbýr, meaning 'Grímr's farmstead or settlement'. While local folklore and the medieval Lay of Havelock the Dane attribute the name to a Danish fisherman named Grim, toponymists identify the first element as the common Scandinavian personal name Grímr combined with the Old Norse settlement suffix býr.

b_york.first_mention_attestation: First recorded by name as the Roman legionary fortress Eboracum in writing tablets and classical sources dating to c. 95–104 CE.
b_york.etymology_analysis: Roman Eboracum Latinized the Brittonic *Eburākon ('place of yew trees' or 'estate of Eburos'). Under Anglo-Saxon rule it was reanalyzed by folk etymology as Old English Eoforwīc ('boar settlement'), which Old Norse speakers subsequently adapted as Jórvík, yielding modern York.

b_scarborough.first_mention_attestation: According to Icelandic saga tradition (Kormáks saga), founded c. 966 CE as Skarðaborg by the Viking raider Thorgils Skarthi; a 4th-century Roman signal station previously stood on the headland.

eponym.details: Thorgils Skarthi (10th-century Viking raider nicknamed Skarthi, 'hare-lip')

b_scarborough.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Skarðaborg, meaning 'Skarthi's stronghold', later Anglicized with Old English burh to Scarborough. Saga tradition identifies the eponymous founder as the 10th-century Norse raider Thorgils Skarthi.

b_whitby.first_mention_attestation: The Scandinavian name Witebi (Whitby) is first attested in the 1086 Domesday Book, superseding the earlier Anglo-Saxon monastic settlement of Streoneshalh.
b_whitby.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Hvítabýr, meaning 'Hvíti's farmstead' (or less likely 'white settlement'). The Norse name replaced the pre-Viking Old English name Streoneshalh ('Streon's nook of land') after Scandinavian settlement in Northumbria.

historical_names.name: Streoneshalh
historical_names.source: Bede's Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum (731 CE), recording the 657 CE founding of Streoneshalh Abbey by King Oswiu and the 664 CE Synod of Whitby
historical_names.notes: Streoneshalh was the Anglo-Saxon monastery and settlement on the exact site of modern Whitby from 657 CE until Viking raids in the late 9th century.

b_richmond.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1071 CE by the Breton nobleman Alan Rufus on lands granted by William the Conqueror, with Richmond Castle completed by 1086.
b_richmond.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old French Richemont ('strong hill'), transferred by Alan Rufus from Richemont in Normandy to his newly built castle overlooking the River Swale.

historical_names.name: Ingetlingum
historical_names.source: Bede's Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum (731 CE), recording the 651 CE killing of King Oswine of Deira at Ingetlingum (Gilling West) and the founding of a monastery there
historical_names.notes: Gilling West (Ingetlingum), 3.5 miles north of Richmond, served as the pre-Conquest royal and administrative center of the Gilling Wapentake before Alan Rufus shifted the caput to Richmond in 1071.

historical_names.name: Gilling
historical_names.source: Bede's Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum (731 CE), recording the 651 CE killing of King Oswine of Deira at Ingetlingum (Gilling West) and the founding of a monastery there
historical_names.notes: Gilling West (Ingetlingum), 3.5 miles north of Richmond, served as the pre-Conquest royal and administrative center of the Gilling Wapentake before Alan Rufus shifted the caput to Richmond in 1071.

b_yarlestre.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the 1086 Domesday Book as Yarlestre (also rendered Gerlestre), the name of a wapentake in the North Riding of Yorkshire encompassing Thirsk.
b_yarlestre.etymology_analysis: A Scandinavian-Anglo-Saxon hybrid toponym meaning 'the earl's tree' (Old Norse jarl + Old English trēow / Old Norse tré), designating the open-air assembly tree where the wapentake court met before it relocated to Birdforth in the 12th century.

b_leeds.first_mention_attestation: First attested around 731 CE in Bede's Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum (Book II, Chapter 14) as regio quae vocatur Loidis.

morphemes.translation: violent, fast-flowing (referring to the River Aire)

b_leeds.etymology_analysis: Derived from Brittonic *Lātēnses (via Late Brittonic *Lādēses), combining Celtic *lāt- ('violent, boiling', referring to the River Aire) with the borrowed Latin plural suffix -ēnses, meaning 'people of the fast-flowing river'. This regional name Loidis later narrowed to the town of Leeds.

b_doncaster.first_mention_attestation: First attested as the Roman fort Danum in the 2nd-century CE Antonine Itinerary (and later in the Notitia Dignitatum and as Cair Daun in the c. 800 Historia Brittonum).

morphemes.translation: Roman fort, walled town (from Latin castra)

b_doncaster.etymology_analysis: Combines the Brittonic river name Danum (modern River Don, from Celtic *dānu- 'river/water') with Old English ceaster (borrowed from Latin castra 'military camp'), yielding 'Roman fort on the River Don'.

b_halifax.first_mention_attestation: First recorded around 1091 CE as Halyfax; it is not mentioned in the 1086 Domesday Book.
b_halifax.etymology_analysis: Most likely derived from Old English halh-gefeaxe, meaning 'area of coarse grass in a nook of land'. Later 16th-century antiquarians reinterpreted the elements as Old English hālig feax ('holy hair'), giving rise to local legends.

b_sheffield.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the 1086 Domesday Book, appearing twice as Escafeld and Scafeld.
b_sheffield.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old English scēað-feld, meaning 'open countryside by the River Sheaf', where scēað ('sheath, boundary') referred to the river serving as a border between Mercia and Northumbria.

b_bolton.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the 1086 Domesday Book as Bodelton, a manor in the Staincliffe wapentake of the West Riding of Yorkshire.
b_bolton.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old English bōþl-tūn, meaning 'settlement with a hall or manor house', a common northern English toponymic compound that regularly evolved into Bolton.

b_ripon.first_mention_attestation: First attested in accounts of c. 658–660 CE (recorded by Bede and Eddius Stephanus) as Inhrypum, when King Alhfrith of Deira granted land there to Eata of Hexham to found a monastery.
b_ripon.etymology_analysis: From Old English Inhrypum, a dative plural tribal name meaning '(in the territory of) the Hrype', an Anglian folk group settled along the River Ure.

b_dokkum.first_mention_attestation: First attested in connection with the martyrdom of Saint Boniface in 754 CE, recorded as Dockynchirica ('church of Dokkum') in Willibald's Vita Bonifatii.
b_dokkum.etymology_analysis: Usually explained as a compound of the Old Frisian personal name Docko and hēm ('homestead, settlement'), though an alternative derivation links it to Tockingen ('settlement on a tidal stream').

b_appingedam.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a historical document dated 1224 CE, having developed as a trade settlement along the Delf around 1200.
b_appingedam.etymology_analysis: A compound meaning 'the dam built in the Appe (or Apt)', referring to a dam constructed across the confluence of the local stream Appe and the Delf canal (now Damsterdiep).

b_delfzijl.first_mention_attestation: First established and attested around 1317 CE when a sluice was built in the Delf canal (with a nearby monastery mentioned in 1319).
b_delfzijl.etymology_analysis: Derived from Middle Dutch Delf ('dug canal', from delven 'to delve/dig') and zijl ('sluice, water outlet'), meaning 'sluice of the Delf' where the canal met the Ems estuary.

b_leeuwarden.first_mention_attestation: First attested c. 825 CE as Villa Lintarwrde, formed from the merger of three terp villages (Nijehove, Oldehove, and Hoek) along the Middelzee.
b_leeuwarden.etymology_analysis: Composed of an uncertain first element (often linked to *lēwe 'lee, sheltered', or the early form Lintar-) and Old Frisian werth/wurd ('dwelling mound, terp'). Over 200 historical spelling variants exist, yielding Dutch Leeuwarden and West Frisian Ljouwert.

b_staveren.first_mention_attestation: First reliably attested around 1000 CE as Stavron (and on 11th-century coins as STAVERUN / STAVERON), though later chronicles retroject it as the burial place of 8th-century Frisian kings.
b_staveren.etymology_analysis: From the dative plural of Old Frisian staver ('pole, stake'), meaning '(settlement) at the boundary poles', likely referring to stakes marking a protected market peace.

b_harlingen.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1228 CE as Herlinge, a non-agricultural settlement west of Almenum and Ludingakerke Abbey (with city rights traditionally dated to 1234).
b_harlingen.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Old Frisian patronymic/estate name Harlinga (from a personal name Harilo + associative suffix -inga), meaning 'settlement of the people of Harilo'.

historical_names.name: Almenum
historical_names.source: Ecclesiastical tradition recording that Saint Boniface established the first Christian church in Friesland on the terp of Almenum in 754 CE
historical_names.notes: Almenum was the older terp settlement immediately east of Harlingen; it was absorbed within Harlingen's city walls in 1579–1580.

b_wadeilannen.first_mention_attestation: First described in antiquity by Pliny the Elder in his Naturalis Historia (c. 77 CE), which recounts the Frisian coastal peoples living on artificial mounds (terpen) amid the tidal flats.
b_wadeilannen.etymology_analysis: Dutch Waddeneilanden (West Frisian Waadeilannen) means 'islands of the tidal mudflats', combining wad ('mudflat, shallow', cognate with wade/ford) with eilanden ('islands').

b_emden.first_mention_attestation: Existed from at least the late 8th or early 9th century (c. 800 CE) as a Frisian trading settlement on a terp at the mouth of the Ems, recorded under early forms such as Amuthon.
b_emden.etymology_analysis: Developed from Old Frisian Amuthon ('at the river mouth'), combining a river/water root with mūtha ('mouth'), which underwent syncope through Embda and Emda to modern Emden.

b_wilhelmshaven.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1869 CE as a Prussian naval port by King William I of Prussia on territory ceded by the Grand Duchy of Oldenburg under the 1853 Jade Treaty.

eponym.details: King William I of Prussia (Wilhelm I, 1797–1888), who founded the naval port in 1869

morphemes.translation: personal name William (King Wilhelm I of Prussia)

b_wilhelmshaven.etymology_analysis: German Wilhelmshaven literally means 'William's Harbor', named in 1869 after King Wilhelm I of Prussia. The medieval Frisian fortress of Sibetsburg had earlier stood on the site from before 1383 until its destruction in 1433.

b_varel.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1123 CE as the manor farm Farle in a letter from Pope Callixtus II to the Benedictine monastery of Rastede.
b_varel.etymology_analysis: Attested as Farle in 1123; the second element reflects Germanic *lōh ('grove, clearing'), while the first element is debated between a botanical term ('fern'), a sacred grove, or a Germanic hundred assembly site.

b_arnhem.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned by name in 893 CE as Arneym or Arentheym in the land register (Urbar) of Prüm Abbey.
b_arnhem.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Dutch Arneym / Arentheym, combining Germanic *arnu- ('eagle', or a personal name derived from it) with heim ('homestead, settlement'), meaning 'home of the eagles' or 'Arn's homestead'.

historical_names.name: Meginhardeswich
historical_names.source: Carolingian charter c. 814 CE mentioning Meginhardeswich (modern Meinerswijk in southern Arnhem)
historical_names.notes: Meginhardeswich (modern Meinerswijk on the south bank of the Nederrijn within Arnhem) is attested in 814 CE, predating the 893 CE first mention of Arneym.

b_apeldoorn.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 792/793 CE in a donation charter as villa ut marca Appoldro.
b_apeldoorn.etymology_analysis: Attested as Appoldro in the late 8th century, meaning 'apple tree' (Old Dutch *apul-tra, cognate with English apple-tree), with the second element later reshaped by folk etymology to Dutch doorn ('thorn').

b_harderwijk.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1231 CE as Harderewich and Herderewich, when Count Otto II of Guelders granted it city rights.
b_harderwijk.etymology_analysis: Combines Middle Dutch herdere/hardere ('shepherd' or 'dweller on the hard/sandy ridge') with wijk ('settlement, trading post', from Latin vicus), denoting a herdsmen's or ridge settlement on the edge of the Veluwe.

b_geldern.first_mention_attestation: First documented around 900 CE under early forms such as Gelre, Gielra, and Gellero (folk legend places its founding around 878 CE).
b_geldern.etymology_analysis: First recorded c. 900 as Gelre / Gellero; its exact etymology is uncertain, likely deriving from a pre-medieval or Old Low Franconian hydronymic or marshland root at the confluence of the Niers and Fleuth, rather than the folkloric dragon's cry 'Gelre!'.

b_nijmegen.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the 1st century BCE (c. 15 BCE), when the Romans established a military camp on the Hunerberg overlooking the Waal, near which Oppidum Batavorum and later Ulpia Noviomagus Batavorum grew.
b_nijmegen.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Latinized Celtic name Noviomagus (Gaulish *Nowiomagos, 'new field' or 'new market'), part of the Roman imperial title Ulpia Noviomagus Batavorum, which evolved into Old Dutch Numegen and modern Nijmegen.

b_tiel.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 896 CE, when the Frankish king Zwentibold granted Tiel the right to levy tolls as a riverine trading port.

morphemes.translation: narrow channel, goal, or cultivated strip (uncertain)

b_tiel.etymology_analysis: Attested from 896 CE as Tiele; the name is of Old Dutch or Germanic origin, likely referring to a water channel, landing place, or boundary point between the Waal and Linge rivers.

b_zutphen.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the 11th century (c. 1059 CE, with early forms such as Sutphem in 1101), though archaeological evidence shows Germanic settlement from c. 300 CE and a circular fortress after the 882 Norman raid.

morphemes.translation: peat bog, fen, or marshy pasture

b_zutphen.etymology_analysis: From Middle Dutch Sutfen (Old Dutch *sūth-fene), meaning 'south fen' or 'southern marshland', referring to its position relative to the low-lying fenlands at the confluence of the IJssel and Berkel.

b_borculo.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written sources in 1151 CE in connection with the Lords of Borculo and Hof van Borculo castle along the Berkel and Groenlose Slinge.
b_borculo.etymology_analysis: Derived from early forms such as Burclo and Borkelo, combining Middle Dutch/Old Saxon burch ('stronghold', or less likely 'birch') with lō ('woodland clearing, grove'), referring to a fortified manor in a wooded clearing.

b_bredevoort.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1188 CE as castrum Breidervort in a property list of the Archbishop of Cologne.
b_bredevoort.etymology_analysis: From Middle Dutch / Low Saxon brede ('broad') and voort ('ford'), meaning 'broad ford' (cognate with English Bradford).

b_amsterdam.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1275 CE in a toll-exemption charter granted by Count Floris V of Holland to the inhabitants near the Amestelledamme.
b_amsterdam.etymology_analysis: Derived from Amestelledamme ('dam in the Amstel'), combining the river/district name Amestelle (from Aa 'water/river' + stelle 'shoreline, higher bank') with Middle Dutch dam.

b_delft.first_mention_attestation: First established and attested around 1075 CE as a comital manor beside the Delf canal by Godfrey III, Duke of Lower Lorraine.
b_delft.etymology_analysis: Named after the Delf, an artificial drainage canal dug across the silted Gantel creek wall; the noun derives from Old Dutch delven ('to dig, delve').

b_rotterdam.first_mention_attestation: Originates around 1270 CE when a dam was constructed across the Rotte stream, though a smaller settlement at the mouth of the Rotte existed from c. 950 CE.
b_rotterdam.etymology_analysis: Means 'dam on the Rotte', combining the river name Rotte (Old Dutch *rot-ā, 'muddy water') with Middle Dutch dam.

b_dort.first_mention_attestation: First attested around 1120 CE in the Annales Egmundani, which refer to Count Dirk IV of Holland being killed in 1049 near Thuredrech.
b_dort.etymology_analysis: From early forms Thuredriht (c. 1120) and Thuredrecht (c. 1200), meaning 'towing channel or thoroughfare along the Thure' (where boats were hauled between the Dubbel and Merwede rivers); modern scholarship rejects an earlier derivation from Latin traiectum.

b_haarlem.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the 10th century (918–948 CE) as Haralem.
b_haarlem.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Dutch *Haarlo-heim, combining haar ('elevated sandy ridge'), lō ('forest'), and heim ('homestead, settlement'), meaning 'settlement on a forested sand dune'.

b_edam.first_mention_attestation: Founded around 1230 CE when the tidal channel of the E or IJe was dammed (with the earliest surviving spelling Aedamme attested in 1342–1343).
b_edam.etymology_analysis: Derived from IJedam / Aedamme, meaning 'dam on the river E (or IJe)', a tidal stream that emptied into the Zuiderzee.

b_medemblik.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a royal charter of 985 CE as villa Medemelacha, named after the nearby watercourse.
b_medemblik.etymology_analysis: Derived from the early medieval stream name Medemelacha (Germanic *miduma- 'middle' + *laku- 'marshy watercourse'), which was transferred to the settlement.

b_aalkmar.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a 10th-century document (c. 939 CE) as Allecmere, with later 11th–12th century forms Alcmere and Alcmare.
b_aalkmar.etymology_analysis: From Old Dutch Allecmere / Alcmere; the second element mere means 'lake, marsh', while the first element alk/allec is generally interpreted as an archaic word for 'swamp' or 'marshland' (though 'temple' has also been proposed).

b_middelburg.first_mention_attestation: Dates to the late 8th or early 9th century as one of three circular ringforts (borgs) on Walcheren against Viking raids, with a monastery built on the site in 844 CE.
b_middelburg.etymology_analysis: From Old Dutch *Middelburg, meaning 'middle fortress', referring to its central position on Walcheren between the ringforts of Domburg (Duinburcht) and Souburg (Zuidburcht).

b_bergen_op_zoom.first_mention_attestation: First attested around 1198–1212 CE when it received city status, emerging on the sandy ridge of the Brabantse Wal.
b_bergen_op_zoom.etymology_analysis: Means 'hills on the edge/border', referring to the sandy ridge (Brabantse Wal) rising above the marine clay marshes; unrelated to the later De Zoom canal.

b_brielle.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1257 CE as Briel (with fire beacons recorded from 1280 and town rights granted in 1330).

morphemes.translation: enclosed woodland, hunting park, marshy thicket

b_brielle.etymology_analysis: Derived via Middle Dutch briel from Celtic/Gaulish *brogilo- ('enclosed area, woodland, or hunting grounds'). Early records distinguish the current town from an earlier Den ouden Briel on Voorne-Putten.

b_groningen.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing in 1040 CE as villa Cruoninga in a donation charter of Holy Roman Emperor Henry III to the Bishop of Utrecht.
b_groningen.etymology_analysis: From 1040 Cruoninga / Groninga, combining either Old Saxon grōni ('green', referring to the green fields at the tip of the Hondsrug) or a personal name Grōno with the collective suffix -inga.

b_assen.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1258 CE, when Mariënkamp Abbey was relocated to the site from near Coevorden.
b_assen.etymology_analysis: Derived from the dative plural of aske/asse ('ash tree'), meaning '(settlement) at the ash trees', around which Mariënkamp Abbey was built in 1258.

b_emmen.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1139 CE as a curtis (manor) at Emne / Empne.
b_emmen.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1139 as Emne / Empne; likely derived from an Old Saxon root meaning 'flat, even terrain' (cognate with Dutch effen) on the sandy Hondsrug ridge.

b_steenwijk.first_mention_attestation: First attested with certainty in 1206 CE as Stenwic (receiving city rights in 1327).
b_steenwijk.etymology_analysis: Compound of Old Dutch steen ('stone', referring to the abundant glacial erratic boulders in the local moraine soil) and wijk ('settlement, village', from Latin vicus).

b_utrecth.first_mention_attestation: Founded around 50 CE as the Roman border fortress (castellum) of Traiectum along the Limes Germanicus.
b_utrecth.etymology_analysis: Combines Latin Traiectum ('crossing, ford' over the Rhine) with Old Dutch ūt ('downstream, outer') — yielding Ultraiectum / Ûtrecht — to distinguish it from upstream Maastricht (Mosae Traiectum).

b_amersfoort.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1028 CE as Amersfoirde, referring to a ford across the Amer River (modern Eem).
b_amersfoort.etymology_analysis: Compound of the hydronym Amer (the medieval name of the River Eem) and Old Dutch voort ('ford'), meaning 'ford across the Amer'.

b_zwolle.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing in 1040 CE as Suolle, though the settlement was established around 800 CE by Frisian merchants and Carolingian troops on a sand ridge.

morphemes.translation: swelling, raised sand hill (cognate with swell)

b_zwolle.etymology_analysis: From Old Dutch/Old Saxon Suolle ('swelling, elevation', cognate with English swell), referring to the dry sand ridge rising above the surrounding marshy rivers (IJssel, Vecht, Aa, and Zwarte Water).

b_kampen.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written records in 1227 CE as Kampen (receiving city rights in 1236, with wooden structures attested archaeologically from c. 1150).
b_kampen.etymology_analysis: Derived from Middle Dutch kamp ('enclosed piece of land or field', borrowed from Latin campus 'field'), in the plural/locative form Kampen ('at the enclosed fields').

b_ommen.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written records in 1133 CE as 'de vmme', and granted city rights in 1248 CE by the Bishop of Utrecht.

morphemes.translation: uncertain root, possibly derived from a prehistoric hydronym

b_ommen.etymology_analysis: First recorded as 'de vmme' in 1133 CE, the toponym Ommen has an obscure origin. Linguistic scholarship suggests it may derive from a prehistoric hydronym associated with the Vecht river valley rather than a personal name.

b_almelo.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written sources in 1157 CE under the form 'almelo'.
b_almelo.etymology_analysis: Attested as 'almelo' in 1157 CE, the name is a Germanic compound combining a reflex of Proto-Germanic *alma- ('elm tree') with Old Dutch 'lo' ('open woodland' or 'glade'), referring to a clearing in an elm forest.

b_coevorden.first_mention_attestation: The place name first appears in 1036 CE in the personal designation 'Fredericus van Coevorden', and is attested as 'koiforde' in 1148 CE.
b_coevorden.etymology_analysis: Coevorden is a Germanic topographic compound meaning 'cow ford' or 'cattle crossing' (comparable to English Oxford and German Kuhfurt), combining Dutch 'koe' ('cow') and 'voorde' ('ford').

b_bacs.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 535 CE in a letter written by Eastern Roman Emperor Justinian I, and later noted as an Avar fortress in 873 CE.

morphemes.translation: uncertain origin; possibly from Old Turkic 'baya' (title) or a Slavic/Vlach pastoral term

b_bacs.etymology_analysis: The origin of the name Bač (Hungarian: Bács) is debated: Hungarian linguists derive it from an Old Turkic dignity title 'baya' via the personal name Bácsa, while other scholars connect it to a widespread Balkan Slavic or Vlach pastoral root.

b_titel.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in medieval written records in 1077 CE under the form 'Tytul', though the site had earlier been a Roman military camp.

morphemes.translation: Roman military camp name of uncertain pre-Roman or Illyrian-Celtic origin

b_titel.etymology_analysis: The modern Serbian and Hungarian name Titel continues the Roman military camp name Titulium, attested in antiquity at the confluence of the Tisza and Danube rivers.

historical_names.name: Titulium
historical_names.source: Roman military camp records in Pannonia Inferior (1st–2nd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Titel occupies the site of the Roman military camp Titulium at the confluence of the Tisza and Danube.

b_bodrog.first_mention_attestation: Bodrog fortress and its associated 11th-century Hungarian county are attested in late 11th-century charters (c. 1093 CE) before the fortress was destroyed in the Mongol invasion of 1241 CE.

morphemes.translation: possibly derived from the Slavic tribal name Obodriti (Bodrići) or a personal name

b_bodrog.etymology_analysis: Named after the medieval fortress of Bodrog near modern Sombor, the toponym is widely linked by historians to the South Slavic Obodrites (Praedenecenti) who inhabited the Middle Danube region in the 9th century.

b_zenta.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in historical records in 1216 CE under the Hungarian name 'Szintarev' (Senta).

morphemes.translation: uncertain root, possibly from a personal name or Latin 'sancta' (holy)

b_zenta.etymology_analysis: First recorded as 'Szintarev' in 1216 CE (with Hungarian 'rév' meaning 'ferry'), the town's name Senta (Hungarian: Zenta) is of uncertain origin, possibly deriving from an early medieval personal name or ecclesiastical designation.

b_csongrad.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written documents in the 1075 CE founding charter of Garamszentbenedek Abbey as 'Castrum Csongrad' (and later in the Gesta Hungarorum).
b_csongrad.etymology_analysis: Csongrád is a Hungarian adaptation of the South Slavic compound *Čьrnъ gradъ, meaning 'black castle' or 'black fortress', referring to the dark-timbered or earthen stronghold on the Tisza River.

b_kiskunhalas.first_mention_attestation: The earliest surviving written documents mentioning the settlement as 'Halas' date to 1347 CE, following the arrival of Cuman settlers in the 13th century.
b_kiskunhalas.etymology_analysis: The name Kiskunhalas combines 'Kiskun' ('Little Cumania', referring to the Cuman peoples settled there in the 13th century) with 'halas' ('abounding in fish', from 'hal' + '-as'), referencing the fish-rich lakes that once surrounded the town.

b_bekes.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written charters in 1220 CE under the form 'Bekues'.

eponym.details: Possibly named after its first medieval castle steward (ispán), Békés, in the 11th century.

b_bekes.etymology_analysis: Békés derives from the Hungarian adjective 'békés' ('peaceful', from 'béke' + '-s'), which was originally the name of the medieval castle—likely named after its first steward—that gave its name to Békés County.

b_svarvas.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in medieval Hungarian charters in the early 15th century (c. 1406 CE) as 'Szarvashalom' ('stag hill'), though an Avar-era cemetery with a runiform bone needlecase was excavated nearby.
b_svarvas.etymology_analysis: Szarvas is the standard Hungarian word for 'stag' or 'deer' (from 'szarv', meaning 'horn' or 'antler', plus the adjectival suffix '-as'), originally attested in the medieval settlement name Szarvashalom ('stag hill').

b_oroshaza.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written records in 1466 CE as 'Orosháza', before being destroyed during the Ottoman wars and resettled in 1744 CE.

eponym.details: Named after a medieval Hungarian landowner named Oros (a diminutive personal name derived from 'úr', meaning 'lord').

b_oroshaza.etymology_analysis: Orosháza is a Hungarian possessive compound meaning 'Oros's house', combining the medieval personal name Oros with 'háza' ('house of').

b_nagyvarad.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1113 CE under the Latin name 'Varadinum' in a diploma of the Benedictine Abbey of Zobor, while the Citadel of Oradea is first documented in 1241 CE.
b_nagyvarad.etymology_analysis: The Hungarian name Nagyvárad combines 'nagy' ('great') with 'Várad' (from 'vár', meaning 'fortress' or 'citadel', plus the suffix '-ad'), which was borrowed into Romanian as 'Oradea' and Latinized as 'Varadinum'.

b_gyozeg.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written records in 1291 CE under the form 'Gyozeg' (modern Hungarian: Bihardiószeg).
b_gyozeg.etymology_analysis: The Romanian name Diosig derives from Hungarian Diószeg (Bihardiószeg), a compound of 'dió' ('walnut') and 'szeg' ('corner' or 'river bend'), referring to a walnut-grove settlement at a bend.

b_debrecen.first_mention_attestation: First documented in written records in 1235 CE under the form 'Debrezun'.
b_debrecen.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1235 CE as 'Debrezun', Debrecen has three main proposed etymologies: from a Slavic compound meaning 'good land' (dobre zliem), from Proto-Slavic *dьbrь ('gorge' or 'valley'), or from the Turkic verb 'debresin' ('to live/move').

b_belenyes.first_mention_attestation: Earliest mention in recorded history dates to 1263 CE, when it was documented as having been burned down during the 1241 CE Mongol invasion, and later appeared as 'Benenus' in 1291 CE.

morphemes.translation: likely from a personal name or Slavic *bělъ ('white') with Hungarian suffix -es

b_belenyes.etymology_analysis: The Romanian name Beiuș is adapted from Hungarian Belényes (attested as Benenus in 1291 CE and Belinis in 1300 CE), whose root is generally traced to a medieval personal name or a Slavic stem.

b_zolonta.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1214 CE under the name 'Zolonta' and later recorded in a 1332 CE papal document as 'Zalanta'.

morphemes.translation: uncertain root, possibly from a Slavic *slatina ('salt marsh/spring') or personal name

b_zolonta.etymology_analysis: Attested as 'Zolonta' in 1214 CE and 'Zalanta' in 1332 CE before adopting the Hungarian spelling Szalonta in 1587 CE, the name was later adapted into Romanian as Salonta; its ultimate root is likely Slavic or an early medieval personal name.

b_elesd.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written records between 1291 and 1294 CE (Hungarian: Élesd).
b_elesd.etymology_analysis: The Romanian name Aleșd is adapted from Hungarian Élesd, formed from the Hungarian adjective 'éles' ('sharp', possibly referring to a pointed ridge or a personal name) with the old Hungarian toponymic suffix '-d'.

b_szabolcs.first_mention_attestation: The area first appears in written documents around 1067 CE, and in 1092 CE King Ladislaus I convened a famous synod at the fortress ('in civitate Zabolch').

eponym.details: Named after Szabolcs, a 10th-century Hungarian tribal chieftain recorded in the Gesta Hungarorum as the builder of the earthen fortress by the Tisza River.

b_szabolcs.etymology_analysis: Szabolcs takes its name directly from the 10th-century Magyar chieftain Szabolcs, who according to the Gesta Hungarorum constructed the earthen fortification overlooking the Tisza River.

b_nyir.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a royal charter in 1209 CE under the name 'Nyír', while a 1326 CE source records the compound 'Nyíregyháza' indicating the presence of a church.
b_nyir.etymology_analysis: Nyíregyháza combines 'nyír' ('birch', originally the settlement's 1209 CE name) with 'egyháza' ('church of', from Old Hungarian 'egyház' meaning 'holy house/church'), referring to a church settlement in the birch-forested Nyírség region.

b_nagyboszormeny.first_mention_attestation: First attested in historical charters in 1248 CE as 'Bezermen' / 'Nagyböszörmény', prior to the 17th-century settlement of Hajdú soldiers.

morphemes.translation: Muslim / Ismaelite inhabitant in medieval Hungary

b_nagyboszormeny.etymology_analysis: Hajdúböszörmény combines 'böszörmény'—the medieval Hungarian ethnonym for Muslim settlers (borrowed via Turkic from Arabic 'muslim') who inhabited the area in the Árpádian era—with the prefix 'Hajdú-', added after Prince István Bocskai settled Hajdú soldiers there in the early 17th century.

b_szobszlo.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in writing in 1075 CE when King Géza I donated half of Szoboszló's royal duty taxes to Garamszentbenedek Abbey.

eponym.details: The base name Szoboszló derives from the Slavic personal name Soběslav, later prefixed with 'Hajdú-' after 1606 CE.

b_szobszlo.etymology_analysis: Originally recorded as Szoboszló in 1075 CE from the Slavic personal name Soběslav, the town received the prefix 'Hajdú-' after István Bocskai granted landholdings there to 700 Hajdú cavalrymen in 1606 CE.

b_szatmar.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Gesta Hungarorum (c. 1200 CE) as 'castrum Zotmar', referring to a 10th-century fortified settlement; Szatmár and Németi were united in 1715 CE.

eponym.details: The historical Hungarian name Szatmár derives from 'castrum Zotmar' ('Zotmar's fort'), named after a 10th-century knight or chieftain Zotmar.

b_szatmar.etymology_analysis: The medieval Hungarian name Szatmár derives from the personal name Zotmar ('castrum Zotmar' in the Gesta Hungarorum). In Romanian, the earlier form Sătmar was replaced in the 19th–20th centuries by Satu Mare ('great village'), a folk-etymological reinterpretation.

b_nagybanya.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written documents issued by King Charles I of Hungary in 1328 CE under the Latin name 'Rivulus Dominarum' ('Ladies' River').
b_nagybanya.etymology_analysis: Both Romanian Baia Mare and Hungarian Nagybánya mean 'Great Mine', reflecting the town's medieval gold and silver mining industry after its initial 1328 CE Latin attestation as Rivulus Dominarum.

b_szilagy.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written documents in 1258 CE as 'Wathasomlyowa' ('Wata's mountain'), though 5th-century Gepid gold hoards and a Dacian fortress were found nearby.
b_szilagy.etymology_analysis: The Hungarian name Szilágysomlyó combines the regional name Szilágy (meaning 'elm grove/stream', later Latinized in Romanian as Silvaniei) with 'somlyó', an archaic Hungarian word for a mountain or rounded hill.

b_kraszna.first_mention_attestation: The village was first mentioned in written records in 1213 CE as 'Karasna', while the historical Kraszna County is first mentioned in 1164 CE.
b_kraszna.etymology_analysis: Situated on the Crasna (Hungarian: Kraszna) River, the settlement takes its name from the Slavic adjective 'krasna' meaning 'beautiful' or 'pleasant'.

b_tasnad.first_mention_attestation: First reliably attested in written documents in 1246 CE under the name 'Tusnad' (Hungarian: Tasnád; an unverified 1021 CE reference is also sometimes cited locally).

morphemes.translation: likely from a medieval personal name or Slavic root with Hungarian suffix -d

b_tasnad.etymology_analysis: First attested as 'Tusnad' in 1246 CE, the Romanian name Tășnad derives from Hungarian Tasnád, which is generally traced to an early medieval personal name or Slavic toponymic base with the Hungarian suffix '-d'.

b_nagykaroly.first_mention_attestation: Existed as an estate center by 1264 CE and is recorded in medieval charters as 'Karul' in 1320 CE and 'Karol' in 1385 CE.

eponym.details: Named after the Károlyi noble family (branch of the Kaplon clan), whose ancestral estate center was Károly (Nagykároly).

b_nagykaroly.etymology_analysis: The Hungarian name Nagykároly ('Great Károly') combines 'nagy' ('great') with the name of the Károlyi family (attested as 'Karul' in 1320 CE), from which the Romanian name Carei was adapted.

b_zarand.first_mention_attestation: The first documentary record of the locality Zărand (Hungarian: Zaránd) dates to 1318 CE, though the broader Zaránd County is mentioned in 1203 CE.

morphemes.translation: uncertain origin, possibly from a medieval personal name or Slavic root

b_zarand.etymology_analysis: The Romanian name Zărand derives from Hungarian Zaránd, the name of the medieval castle and county seat, whose etymology is uncertain and likely reflects an early medieval personal name.

b_nagyhalmagy.first_mention_attestation: The first documentary record of Hălmagiu (Hungarian: Nagyhalmágy) dates to 1390 CE.
b_nagyhalmagy.etymology_analysis: The Romanian name Hălmagiu is of Hungarian origin (from Nagyhalmágy), combining 'alma' ('apple') and 'ágy' ('riverbed'), referring to an apple-growing valley along the Crișul Alb and Hălmăgel rivers.

b_pankota.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written documents in 1202–1203 CE under the Latinized name 'villa Pankota'.

morphemes.translation: uncertain origin, likely from a medieval personal name or Slavic root

b_pankota.etymology_analysis: Attested as 'villa Pankota' in 1202–1203 CE, the Romanian name Pâncota continues the Hungarian toponym Pankota, whose root is likely an early medieval personal name.

b_gyor.first_mention_attestation: Győr was established as an episcopal and county seat by King Stephen I around 1009 CE (and recorded as 'Geuru' in the Gesta Hungarorum), built on the ruins of Roman Arrabona.

morphemes.translation: personal or clan name (Geur), or possibly from a Slavic/Turkic root

b_gyor.etymology_analysis: Recorded as 'Geuru' in medieval chronicles, the Hungarian name Győr is associated with an early Hungarian personal or clan name (the Győr kindred), replacing the ancient Celtic-Roman name Arrabona.

historical_names.name: Arrabona
historical_names.source: Roman Pannonian sources (1st–2nd century CE, e.g., Tabula Peutingeriana and Roman inscriptions)
historical_names.notes: Győr stands directly on the site of the Celtic settlement and Roman fort and town of Arrabona, occupied by Hungarians around 900 CE.

b_moson.first_mention_attestation: Moson was first attested in written sources in 1137 CE as 'Mussun', while Magyaróvár was attested in 1271 CE as 'Altenburch' on the site of the Roman fortress Ad Flexum.

morphemes.translation: mossy, marshy (elided from 'castle in the marsh')

b_moson.etymology_analysis: Mosonmagyaróvár unites two medieval towns: Moson (attested 1137 CE as 'Mussun'), from Slavic *mъšьnъ ('mossy/marshy [castle]'), and Magyaróvár ('ancient Hungarian castle'), referring to the ruins of the Roman fort Ad Flexum.

historical_names.name: Ad Flexum
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (Itinerarium Antonini, c. 300 CE)
historical_names.notes: The Magyaróvár quarter of Mosonmagyaróvár stands on the site of the Roman military camp Ad Flexum.

b_sopron.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned as an important city in 1153 CE, having developed as Sopronvár in the 11th century on the ruins of the Roman city Scarbantia.

eponym.details: Named in Hungarian after an 11th-century castle steward (ispán) named Suprun.

b_sopron.etymology_analysis: Sopron takes its Hungarian name from an 11th-century castle steward named Suprun, who oversaw the fortress built atop the abandoned Roman walls of Scarbantia (German: Ödenburg, 'deserted castle').

historical_names.name: Scarbantia
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (c. 77 CE)
historical_names.notes: Sopron's main square and medieval core occupy the exact site of the Roman municipium Scarbantia.

b_kapuvar.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a royal charter of King Stephen III of Hungary in 1162 CE as 'Copu' ('gate').
b_kapuvar.etymology_analysis: Kapuvár literally means 'Gate Castle' in Hungarian ('kapu' + 'vár'), referring to its strategic role guarding the western frontier march (gyepű) of the Kingdom of Hungary.

b_koszeg.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a charter of 1248 CE as 'castrum Kuszug' (German: Güns, named after the Gyöngyös stream).
b_koszeg.etymology_analysis: Kőszeg combines Hungarian 'kő' ('stone') and 'szeg' ('corner' or 'spur'), referring to the rocky hill spur on which the medieval border fortress was built.

b_vasvar.first_mention_attestation: First attested in surviving charters in the early 13th century (1217 and 1226 CE), though it served as the seat of Vas County from the 11th century.
b_vasvar.etymology_analysis: Vasvár means 'Iron Castle' in Hungarian ('vas' + 'vár'; Latinized as Castrum Ferreum and German Eisenburg), reflecting its medieval iron-working and iron-trading importance.

b_kormend.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written records in 1238 CE as 'Villa Curmend terra regis', and granted town privileges by King Béla IV in 1244 CE.

morphemes.translation: uncertain root, possibly from an Old Hungarian personal name or topographic term with suffix -d

b_kormend.etymology_analysis: Attested as 'Curmend' in 1238 CE, the name Körmend is of uncertain Old Hungarian or pre-Hungarian origin, likely deriving from a personal name or river-crossing term.

b_szentgotthard.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1183 CE when King Béla III of Hungary established a Cistercian abbey at the confluence of the Rába and Lapincs rivers in honor of Saint Gotthard.

eponym.details: Named after Saint Gotthard of Hildesheim (960–1038 CE, canonized 1131 CE), to whom the Cistercian abbey founded in 1183 CE was dedicated.

b_szentgotthard.etymology_analysis: Szentgotthárd literally means 'Saint Gotthard' in Hungarian, taking its name from the Cistercian monastery dedicated to Saint Gotthard of Hildesheim in 1183 CE.

b_veszprem.first_mention_attestation: First attested as 'Besprem' prior to 1002 CE in early royal charters of Stephen I, and established as Hungary's first episcopal seat by 1009 CE.

eponym.details: Derived from the West Slavic personal name Bezprym (compare the Polish prince Bezprym, c. 986–1032 CE, or an earlier 10th-century Slavic ruler).

b_veszprem.etymology_analysis: Attested as 'Besprem' before 1002 CE, Veszprém derives from the West Slavic personal name Bezprym (rendered in Hungarian with prothetic/assimilated consonants).

b_zirc.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1182 CE when King Béla III founded the Cistercian Abbey of Zirc on royal woodland in the Bakony hills.

morphemes.translation: uncertain root, possibly from a personal name or Slavic woodland term

b_zirc.etymology_analysis: Recorded from 1182 CE in connection with the Cistercian abbey founded by Béla III, the name Zirc is of uncertain origin, possibly reflecting an early medieval personal name or Slavic root.

b_vasarhely.first_mention_attestation: The name 'Vásárhely' ('market place') is attested from 1363 CE after King Charles Robert granted weekly market rights in 1325 CE; an earlier church site named 'Durnava' was first mentioned in 890 CE.
b_vasarhely.etymology_analysis: Somlóvásárhely combines the name of nearby Somló Hill with 'vásárhely' ('market place', from 'vásár' + 'hely'), reflecting the medieval market town that grew around its Benedictine nunnery.

b_baranyavar.first_mention_attestation: Baranyavár is attested in 12th–13th century chronicles and charters (c. 1150 CE in the Gesta Hungarorum as 'castrum Borona' and 1232–1235 CE as 'Baranawar').

eponym.details: Likely named after its first 11th-century Hungarian castle steward (ispán), Brangna/Baranya, or derived from Slavic 'bara' (marsh).

b_baranyavar.etymology_analysis: The historical Hungarian name Baranyavár ('Baranya's castle', adapted into Croatian as Branjin Vrh) gave its name to Baranya County and is derived either from an early castle steward named Brangna or from Slavic 'bara' ('marsh').

b_siklos.first_mention_attestation: Siklós Castle and settlement are first mentioned in a royal charter of 1294 CE as the property of the Soklyosi family.
b_siklos.etymology_analysis: Recorded as Soklyos/Siklós in medieval charters, the name is traditionally linked to Hungarian 'sikló' ('grass snake') + '-s' ('abounding in') or a related personal/clan name.

b_pecs.first_mention_attestation: The medieval city is first mentioned in 871 CE under the Latin name 'Quinque Basilicae' ('Five Cathedrals'), while the Hungarian name 'Pécs' first appears in documents in 1235 CE as 'Pechyut'.

morphemes.translation: five (referring to five early Christian chapels/churches)

b_pecs.etymology_analysis: The modern name Pécs (first attested in 1235 CE) derives from Proto-Slavic *pęčь or Illyrian *penče meaning 'five', paralleling its 871 CE Latin name Quinque Basilicae ('Five Cathedrals') and German Fünfkirchen.

historical_names.name: Sopianae
historical_names.source: Roman Pannonian inscriptions and itineraries (2nd–4th century CE, e.g., Antonine Itinerary)
historical_names.notes: Pécs occupies the exact site of the Roman provincial city of Sopianae (from Celtic 'sop', marsh), famous for its 4th-century Christian necropolis.

b_mohacs.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in official documents in 1093 CE as 'Mohach' when King Ladislaus I granted the settlement to the Bishopric of Pécs.
b_mohacs.etymology_analysis: Attested as 'Mohach' in 1093 CE, Mohács derives from Slavic *Mъchačь ('mossy place'), combining *mъchъ ('moss', cf. Hungarian 'moha') with the Slavic suffix -ačь.

b_kolon.first_mention_attestation: The nearby Carolingian stronghold of Mosapurc (Moosburg) is attested in the Conversio Bagoariorum et Carantanorum (written c. 870 CE, post-867), while Zalavár takes its name from the Benedictine abbey of Zalavár consecrated in 1019 CE.
b_kolon.etymology_analysis: Zalavár means 'Zala Castle' in Hungarian, named after the Zala River on which it stands. In the 9th century it was known in Frankish sources as Mosapurc ('marsh fortress') and in Slavic as Blatnograd.

b_egerszeg.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written sources in 1247 CE as 'Egurscug' and in 1293 CE as 'Egerszeg'.
b_egerszeg.etymology_analysis: Zalaegerszeg combines the river name Zala with 'éger' ('alder') and 'szeg' ('corner' or 'river bend'), meaning 'alder-tree bend on the Zala'.

b_letenye.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written records in 1341 CE under the form 'Letyne' (also cited as 1314 CE 'Letnye' in some local summaries).
b_letenye.etymology_analysis: Attested as 'Letyne' in 1341 CE, Letenye is of Slavic origin, derived from *lěto ('summer') or a Slavic personal name formed from that root.

b_somogyvar.first_mention_attestation: Documented from 1091 CE when King Ladislaus I founded the Benedictine Abbey of Saint Giles at Somogyvár (also associated with Koppány's late 10th-century stronghold in 997 CE tradition).
b_somogyvar.etymology_analysis: Somogyvár ('Somogy Castle') combines the regional/clan name Somogy (traditionally linked to 'som', cornelian cherry, or an early Hungarian personal name) with 'vár' ('castle').

b_kaposvar.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in 1009 CE as Kapos in King Stephen I's founding charter establishing the borders of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Pécs.

morphemes.translation: adjectival suffix (having gates / river name Kapos)

b_kaposvar.etymology_analysis: Kaposvár is a Hungarian compound meaning 'castle on the Kapos'. The river name Kapos derives from Hungarian kapu ('gate') with the suffix -s, combined with vár ('castle', 'fortress').

b_csurgo.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1019 CE in the establishing charter of the Benedictine Abbey of Zalavár, when King Stephen I donated the village and its estates.
b_csurgo.etymology_analysis: Csurgó derives from the Hungarian verb csurog / csurg- ('to trickle, gush') with the participial suffix -ó, referring to a trickling spring or stream at the site.

b_szigetvar.first_mention_attestation: First attested as a settlement named Zygeth in 1391 CE when the Anthemi family settled in the area; the brick fortress was begun in 1420 CE.
b_szigetvar.etymology_analysis: Szigetvár is a transparent Hungarian compound of sziget ('island', referring to the elevated island-like ground in the Almás marshland) and vár ('castle, fortress').

b_tolna.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written records in 1055 CE as 'in Thelena' in King Andrew I's founding charter of Tihany Abbey.
b_tolna.etymology_analysis: The medieval name Thelena (later Tolna) is most commonly derived from Medieval Latin teloneum ('tollhouse, customs post'), reflecting its role as a Danube crossing and toll station, though an alternative Slavic derivation from *tъlъ ('back, bank') has also been proposed.

historical_names.name: Alta Ripa
historical_names.source: Itinerarium Antonini (c. 300 CE) and Notitia Dignitatum (c. 400 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman auxiliary fort on the Pannonian limes at or near Tolna, later eroded by shifts in the Danube riverbed.

b_simontornya.first_mention_attestation: Simon, son of Salamon of the Döröcske kindred, is first attested in 1264 CE in a charter of King Béla IV, and built the residential tower that gave Simontornya its name around 1272 CE.

eponym.details: Named after Simon, son of Salamon of the Döröcske kindred (attested 1264–1277 CE), who built the residential tower (tornya) here around 1272 CE.

b_simontornya.etymology_analysis: Simontornya literally means 'Simon's tower' in Hungarian, combining the personal name Simon (referring to 13th-century nobleman Simon, son of Salamon) with torony ('tower') and the possessive suffix -a.

b_dombovar.first_mention_attestation: First attested in medieval written records in 1313 CE as Dumbov (with its parish church recorded in 1332 CE).
b_dombovar.etymology_analysis: The first element Dombó- is derived from a Slavic root *dǫbovъ ('oak', referring to oak woods, or via a medieval personal/landowner name Dombó), combined with the Hungarian noun vár ('castle, fortress').

historical_names.name: Pons Sociorum Mansuetina
historical_names.source: Itinerarium Antonini (c. 300 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman road station and bridge crossing over the Kapos river located in the Újdombóvár area, near the late Roman fortification at Alsóhetény (Iovia).

b_arad.first_mention_attestation: First officially mentioned as the town of Orod between 1078 and 1081 CE (with the surrounding area first noted in 1028 CE).

eponym.details: Named after its first medieval ispán (count), Arad (11th century CE).

morphemes.translation: personal name (derived from úr, 'lord', or an early Hungarian clan/personal name)

b_arad.etymology_analysis: Arad (earlier Orod) takes its name from its 11th-century Hungarian ispán (count) Arad, whose name is linked in Hungarian tradition to úr ('lord') or an Old Hungarian personal name.

b_lippa.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in written documents in 1315 CE under the name Lipwa, and mentioned in 1324 CE as castellanus de Lypua.
b_lippa.etymology_analysis: Lipova (Hungarian Lippa) derives from the Slavic noun lipa ('linden tree') combined with the Slavic toponymic suffix -ova, indicating a place characterized by linden trees.

b_csanad.first_mention_attestation: First attested in early 11th-century Hungarian ecclesiastical and chronicle tradition (c. 1030 CE, when St. Gerard became bishop of Marosvár/Csanád; recorded as Chonadiensis in 1111 CE).

eponym.details: Named after Csanád (Chanadinus), the 11th-century Hungarian commander under King Stephen I who defeated Ajtony around 1028 CE and became the first ispán of Csanád County.

b_csanad.etymology_analysis: Cenad (Hungarian Csanád, medieval Latin Chanadinum) is named after Csanád, the 11th-century royal commander who defeated the local ruler Ajtony at Marosvár (Urbs Morisena) and gave his name to the castle, county, and diocese.

b_szeged.first_mention_attestation: The name Szeged was first mentioned in 1183 CE in a charter of King Béla III of Hungary.
b_szeged.etymology_analysis: Szeged is commonly derived from Old Hungarian szeg ('corner, bend'), referring to the sharp bend of the Tisza River, with the toponymic suffix -ed; alternative hypotheses link it to sziget ('island') or a truncated survival of the Roman name Partiscum.

historical_names.name: Partiscum
historical_names.source: Claudius Ptolemy, Geographia (c. 150 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman trading post and settlement on an island in the Tisza River at or near modern Szeged, attested as Partiskon by Ptolemy.

b_nagylak.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in historical documents in 1313 CE under the name Noglog.
b_nagylak.etymology_analysis: Nădlac (Hungarian Nagylak, 1313 Noglog) is a Hungarian compound of nagy ('large, great') and lak ('dwelling, residence', related to lakni 'to dwell'), meaning 'large dwelling place'.

b_kevevar.first_mention_attestation: The earliest medieval mention of the settlement dates to 1071 CE under the name Keuee.

morphemes.translation: Keve (personal/tribal name or stone/pebble root köv-)

b_kevevar.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Kevevára ('castle of Keve', attested 1071 Keuee) combines an early Hungarian personal or toponymic element Keve with vár ('castle') and possessive -a; the Serbian name Kovin is a Slavic adaptation of the same root.

historical_names.name: Contra Margum
historical_names.source: Notitia Dignitatum (c. 400 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman fort located on the Danube bank at Kovin, directly opposite Margum on the southern bank.

b_pancsova.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written sources in 1153 CE (and described in 1154 CE by the Arab geographer Muhammad al-Idrisi as a mercantile town).

morphemes.translation: swamp, marshy lowland (cf. Slavic *pętь / Hungarian pányva)

b_pancsova.etymology_analysis: Pančevo (Hungarian Pancsova) is a medieval Banat toponym adapted into South Slavic with the suffix -čevo and into Hungarian as Pancsova, reflecting a local Slavic or pre-Slavic root associated with the marshy confluence of the Tamiš and Danube.

b_becse.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned during the Kingdom of Hungary in 1091 CE under the Latinized name Bechey, and later in 1238 CE as Becse.

eponym.details: Named after the medieval Bechey (Becse) noble family/clan that held possessions in the area.

b_becse.etymology_analysis: Bečej (Hungarian Óbecse, 1091 Bechey) derives from the medieval Hungarian personal and clan name Becse (Bechey), who held estates along the Tisza.

b_krasso.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written records in 1323 CE under the name Kraso, referring to the medieval castle of Krassó (Krassóvár).
b_krasso.etymology_analysis: Carașova (Hungarian Krassóvár, 1323 Kraso) takes its name from the Caraș (Krassó) River on whose upper course it sits, combined with the Slavic toponymic suffix -ova (or Hungarian vár 'castle').

b_ersomlyo.first_mention_attestation: The earliest historical sources referring to the site (under the Hungarian name Érdsomlyó / Érsomlyó) date from 1227 CE, while the town of Vršac is first mentioned in 1427 CE in a charter of King Sigismund.
b_ersomlyo.etymology_analysis: The Serbian name Vršac derives from Proto-Slavic *vьrxъ ('summit, peak') with the suffix -ac, referring to the hill above the town; the medieval Hungarian name Érdsomlyó / Érsomlyó combines ér ('stream') with somlyó ('cornel-tree hill' or 'marshy hill').

b_fehertemplom.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in medieval Hungarian documents in 1355 CE under the name Fehéregyház (later Fehértemplom), before the modern town was refounded in 1717 CE.
b_fehertemplom.etymology_analysis: Fehértemplom (earlier Fejéregyház, Serbian Bela Crkva, German Weißkirchen, Romanian Biserica Albă) is a descriptive compound meaning 'white church' in Hungarian (fehér 'white' + templom 'church'), calqued across the region's languages.

b_temesvar.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a medieval document in 1177 CE as Castrensis de Thymes, with the fortress Temeswar recorded in 1212 CE (and a possible earlier mention in al-Idrisi in 1154 CE).
b_temesvar.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Temesvár (adapted into Romanian as Timișoara) means 'castle on the Timiș River', combining the hydronym Temes (ultimately from an Indo-European root *thib- 'swamp') with Hungarian vár ('castle').

b_lugos.first_mention_attestation: First appears in written history in 1334 CE when a papal tithe register mentions a priest Martin of Lucas, followed by posesio Lugas in 1369 CE.
b_lugos.etymology_analysis: Lugoj (Hungarian Lugos) is most widely derived from the Slavic root lug- / luh- ('swamp forest, water meadow') with the Hungarian adjectival suffix -os, referring to the marshy terrain along the Timiș River (though Latin lucus 'grove' and Banat dialectal logos 'sedge' have also been proposed).

b_boksanbanya.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a written document in 1331 CE.
b_boksanbanya.etymology_analysis: Bocșa (Hungarian Boksánbánya, adding bánya 'mine') is derived from the Slavic word bok ('side, hill slope'), reflecting the settlement's location on the slopes beside the Bârzava River.

b_beregszasz.first_mention_attestation: Founded as Villa Lamperti (attested 1063 CE) and later known as Lampertszásza, the town is first consistently attested under the name Beregszász in 1504 CE (officially renamed Berehove in 1946 CE).
b_beregszasz.etymology_analysis: Berehove derives from Slavic *bergъ / Ukrainian berih ('river bank'), while the historical Hungarian name Beregszász combines Bereg (the county/settlement name) with szász ('Saxon'), referring to the German colonists who rebuilt it after 1241 CE.

b_nagyszolos.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1262 CE under the name Zceuleus.
b_nagyszolos.etymology_analysis: The historical Hungarian name Nagyszőlős (1262 Zceuleus) means 'great vineyard' (nagy 'great' + szőlős 'vineyard'), reflecting its role as a royal winemaking center; Ukrainian Vynohradiv is a modern translation of the same meaning.

b_munkacz.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing in the Gesta Hungarorum (c. 1200 CE) as Muncas, which anachronistically projects the name back to the late 9th-century Hungarian Conquest.
b_munkacz.etymology_analysis: Mukachevo (Hungarian Munkács) most likely derives from a Hungarian personal/surname Muncas (from munkás 'worker', or munka 'work, toil' as folk-etymologized in the Gesta Hungarorum), though a Proto-Slavic derivation from *muka ('flour') has also been suggested.

b_alsoverecke.first_mention_attestation: First reliably attested in Hungarian state records in 1263 CE (with earlier 12th-century references to Werezka in the pass).
b_alsoverecke.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Alsóverecke means 'Lower Verecke' (alsó 'lower' + Verecke, the name of the mountain pass), while Ukrainian Nyzhni Vorota ('Lower Gates') translates the same topographic sense of the Carpathian pass.

b_borsova.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written documents in 1213 CE under the name Borsoha.
b_borsova.etymology_analysis: Borzhava (Hungarian Nagyborzsova, 1213 Borsoha) takes its name directly from the Borzhava (Borzsa) River on whose right bank the village and medieval earthwork fortress stood.

b_maramarossziget.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned as a town in 1326 CE (with earlier 11th-century mentions of a settlement in the area).
b_maramarossziget.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Máramarossziget (adapted into Romanian as Sighetu Marmației) means 'island in Máramaros', combining the regional name Máramaros with Hungarian sziget ('island', referring to the confluence of the Tisa and Iza).

b_tecso.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written records in 1211 CE under the name Tecu (and later in 1333 CE as Thecho).

morphemes.translation: medieval settlement name (possibly from a personal name or Slavic *teč- 'flow')

b_tecso.etymology_analysis: Tiachiv (Hungarian Técső, 1211 Tecu) is a medieval Upper Tisza settlement name attested from the early 13th century, adapted across Hungarian, Rusyn/Ukrainian (Tiachovo/Tiachiv), and Romanian (Teceu).

b_borsa.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1353 CE as part of the Cuhea domain of the Bogdănești (and in a royal charter of 1365 CE under the name Bors).
b_borsa.etymology_analysis: Borșa (1365 Bors) is commonly linked either to the Hungarian personal name Bors (or the Borsa kindred) or to a local topographic/botanical term in Maramureș.

b_huszt.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written records in 1324 CE as terra Huzth (with the castle first documented in 1353 CE).

morphemes.translation: from the Khustets/Husztica stream (or Romanian husti)

b_huszt.etymology_analysis: Khust (Hungarian Huszt, 1324 Huzth) is most likely named after the Khustets (Husztica) stream, though a connection to the Romanian culinary term husti has also been proposed.

b_okormezo.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written records in 1415 CE as a possession of Hungarian feudal lords under the name Ökörmező.
b_okormezo.etymology_analysis: The historical Hungarian name Ökörmező means 'ox meadow' (ökör 'ox' + mező 'field, meadow'); it was renamed Mizhhiria ('between the mountains' in Ukrainian) in 1953 CE.

b_abauj.first_mention_attestation: The first known written record pertaining to Abaújvár dates to 1046 CE (as Novum Castrum / Újvár, built by King Samuel Aba).

eponym.details: Named after the Aba kindred (genus Aba) and King Samuel Aba (r. 1041–1044 CE), who built the stone castle (Újvár, 'New Castle') here.

b_abauj.etymology_analysis: Abaújvár means 'Aba's New Castle' in Hungarian, combining the clan name Aba (after King Samuel Aba) with új ('new') and vár ('castle'), distinguishing it from the nearby older earthwork hillfort Óvár ('old castle').

b_kassa.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in writing in 1230 CE under the Latinized name Villa Cassa.
b_kassa.etymology_analysis: Košice (Hungarian Kassa, 1230 Villa Cassa) most likely derives from the Slavic personal name Koš or Koša with the patronymic suffix -ici > -ice ('Koš's people').

b_torna.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in historical records in 1198 CE.

morphemes.translation: thorny place (Slavic *tьrnъ) or stream name Torna

b_torna.etymology_analysis: Turňa (Hungarian Torna) derives from the local hydronym/toponym Torna, generally linked to Slavic *tьrnъ ('thorn, bramble') or Hungarian torony ('tower'); 'nad Bodvou' specifies its location on the Bodva River.

b_borsod.first_mention_attestation: The medieval village and castle of Borsod (later incorporated into Edelény) are first attested in written records in 1108 CE.

eponym.details: Named after Bors, an early medieval Hungarian magnate (10th–11th century CE) who held the castle.

morphemes.translation: Bors (personal name, possibly from Turkic or Hungarian bors 'pepper', or Slavic Boriš)

b_borsod.etymology_analysis: Borsod derives from the personal name Bors (an early medieval magnate, of debated Turkic, Hungarian, or Slavic origin) combined with the Old Hungarian place-name suffix -d.

b_miskolc.first_mention_attestation: First attested around 1200 CE as 'que nunc vocatur Miscoucy' (and in 1225 CE as de Myschouch).

eponym.details: Associated with the medieval Miskolc kindred (de genere Myscouch), derived from the Slavic personal name Miško (a diminutive of Michael).

b_miskolc.etymology_analysis: Miskolc derives from Miško, a Slavic diminutive of Michael, via the Slavic form Miškovec > Hungarian Miskolc, associated with the medieval Miskolc kindred.

b_szendro.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written records in 1317 CE.

eponym.details: Named after its medieval Hungarian owner, Szend (post-867 CE).

b_szendro.etymology_analysis: Szendrő is named after its medieval Hungarian owner Szend, with an archaic Hungarian toponymic suffix.

b_saris.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written records in 1217 CE under the name Sarus.

morphemes.translation: mud, marsh (Hungarian sár) or pre-Hungarian Slavic root

b_saris.etymology_analysis: The etymology of Šariš (Hungarian Sáros, 1217 Sarus) is debated: Hungarian linguists derive it from sár ('mud') + -os ('muddy'), whereas Slovak scholars propose a pre-Hungarian Slavic or older origin.

b_barfta.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in writing in 1241 CE as Bardujef (when monks from Bártfa complained of border disputes).
b_barfta.etymology_analysis: Bardejov (1241 Bardujef) most likely derives from the Christian personal name Barděj/Barduj (short for Bartholomew) with the Slavic possessive suffix -ov; an alternative Hungarian folk/scholarly theory links Bártfa to bárd ('hatchet') + fa ('tree').

b_spis.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Latin charters in 1198 CE (and 1209 CE) as silva Zepus / terra Scepus.
b_spis.etymology_analysis: Spiš (Latin Scepus/Zepus, Hungarian Szepes, German Zips) is widely derived from Old Slavic *sъ-pich-jь ('cut forest / forest clearing'), matching early Latin references to silva Zepus, though an alternative Hungarian derivation from szép ('beautiful') has been proposed.

b_kesmark.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in writing in 1251 CE under the Latin name Villa (Saxonum apud Ecclesiam) Sancte Elisabeth, receiving its town charter in 1269 CE.
b_kesmark.etymology_analysis: Kežmarok (Hungarian Késmárk) is a Slovak adaptation of the German name Kesmark / Käsemarkt ('cheese market'), reflecting the medieval town's royal privilege to hold a cheese market.

b_ungvar.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in writing in 1154 CE by the Arab geographer Muhammad al-Idrisi as Gunkbar / Unkbar, and around 1200 CE in the Gesta Hungarorum as Hung.
b_ungvar.etymology_analysis: The historical name Ungvár combines the river name Ung (Uzh) with Hungarian vár ('castle, fortress'). The modern Slavic name Uzhhorod (coined in the 19th century) is a literal calque of Ungvár (Uzh + horod 'town/fortress').

b_nagyberezna.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written records in 1409 CE in connection with a judicial proceeding held by headman Boncha.
b_nagyberezna.etymology_analysis: Velykyi Bereznyi (Hungarian Nagyberezna) means 'Great Birch-place', combining a size qualifier (Hungarian nagy / Ukrainian velykyi 'great') with Slavic bereza ('birch tree').

b_zemplen.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in historical records in 1214 CE.
b_zemplen.etymology_analysis: Zemplín (Hungarian Zemplén) derives from Slavic *zemlьnъ ('earthen', from zemľa 'earth'), referring to the early medieval earthen ramparts of Zemplín Castle.

b_szerencs.first_mention_attestation: First attested in authentic written records in the 13th century, with the Abbey of St. Peter and St. Paul documented in 1241 CE.
b_szerencs.etymology_analysis: Szerencs is traditionally linked to Hungarian szerencse ('luck, fortune', itself a Slavic loanword from *sъręťa 'meeting, good fortune') or an Old Hungarian personal name.

b_zynna.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in historical records in 1249 CE under the name Schena, when King Béla IV settled German colonists from Košice there.

morphemes.translation: Seňa (Slavic personal name or hay-meadow root *sěno)

b_zynna.etymology_analysis: Seňa (Hungarian Abaújszina, 1249 Schena, 1251 Zyna) is of Slavic origin, derived either from the Slavic personal name Seňa or from a Slavic toponymic root related to *sěno ('hay').

b_toporo.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a charter of the Buda chapter in 1248 CE as Tapoly (when Peter, son of Sobeslav, gave it to his wife as a dowry).
b_toporo.etymology_analysis: Topoľany (Hungarian Topolyán, 1248 Tapoly) derives from Slovak topoľ ('poplar tree') with the plural inhabitant suffix -any, referring to people living among poplar trees.

b_varanno.first_mention_attestation: First written mention of Vranov itself dates to 1332–1337 CE (while constituent localities now part of the town are attested from 1229 CE).
b_varanno.etymology_analysis: Vranov (Hungarized as Varannó) derives from Slovak vrana ('crow') with the possessive suffix -ov; 'nad Topľou' denotes its position on the Topľa River.

b_esztergom.first_mention_attestation: The earliest medieval written mention of the name is 'strigonensis comes' in 1079–1080 CE (though the royal and archiepiscopal seat was established here under King Stephen I around 1000 CE).
b_esztergom.etymology_analysis: Esztergom (medieval Latin Strigonium) is most widely derived from the Slavic stem strěg- ('guard, watch'), referring to a fortified lookout over the Danube, adapted into Hungarian with a prothetic vowel e- (comparable to strecha > esztercha).

historical_names.name: Solva
historical_names.source: Claudius Ptolemy, Geographia (c. 150 CE), Itinerarium Antonini, and Notitia Dignitatum
historical_names.notes: Roman mansio and auxiliary fort on the Danube limes located on the Castle Hill and water-town area of Esztergom.

b_beny.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in historical records in 1135 CE written as Byn.

eponym.details: Named after Bény, son of Hont (11th century CE), to whom King Stephen I granted the estate.

b_beny.etymology_analysis: Bíňa (Hungarian Bény, 1135 Byn) is named after Bény, son of Hont (count of Hont), who received the estate from King Stephen I in the early 11th century.

b_hewes.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a charter in 1203 CE under the name Hewes.
b_hewes.etymology_analysis: Heves (1203 Hewes) derives from the Hungarian noun hő / hév ('heat, warmth') with the adjectival suffix -es, referring either to warm thermal springs or to the rapidly warming sandy soil of the area.

b_tur.first_mention_attestation: First documented in the Váradi Regestrum during the reign of King Andrew II of Hungary (1205–1235) as villa Tur.

morphemes.translation: river/settlement name (possibly from Turkic *tur 'settlement, fortress' or aurochs)

b_tur.etymology_analysis: Mezőtúr combines Hungarian mező ('field' or 'plain') with the medieval settlement name Túr (attested as villa Tur in the early 13th century), distinguishing the market town on the Great Hungarian Plain from other settlements named Túr.

b_szolnok.first_mention_attestation: First officially recorded in 1075 CE under the name Zounok in a royal charter of the Kingdom of Hungary.

eponym.details: Named after Szolnok (Zounok), an 11th-century Hungarian nobleman who served as the first ispán (royal count) of Szolnok County.

morphemes.translation: personal name Zounok / Szaunik (or title linked to só 'salt')

b_szolnok.etymology_analysis: Attested as Zounok in 1075, the toponym is traditionally derived from the personal name of Szolnok (Szaunik/Zounok), the first ispán of the castle and county in the early 11th century; an alternative hypothesis links it to an official title associated with the Tisza salt trade (Hungarian só, 'salt').

b_gyongospata.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written Hungarian records in 1010 CE.

morphemes.translation: settlement name (associated with the Aba/Pata clan)

b_gyongospata.etymology_analysis: Gyöngyöspata pairs the regional qualifier Gyöngyös (derived from Hungarian gyöngy 'pearl' + adjectival suffix -s) with Pata, the medieval settlement and castle name recorded from the 11th century.

b_eger.first_mention_attestation: First attested in early 11th-century Kingdom of Hungary ecclesiastical records upon King Stephen I's establishment of the Diocese of Eger around 1009 CE.
b_eger.etymology_analysis: The Hungarian toponym Eger derives from the common noun éger ('alder tree'), referring to the alder groves along the Eger stream; in medieval Latin it was rendered as Agria.

b_komarom.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in a disputed 1075 CE charter as Camarum, and securely attested in 1218 CE as Kamarn.
b_komarom.etymology_analysis: Komárom (Slovak Komárno) is generally derived from Slavic komár ('mosquito') with a locative suffix, referring to the marshy Danube confluence, though an alternative theory links it to Latin commercium ('trading post').

historical_names.name: Brigetio
historical_names.source: Roman military inscriptions and Ptolemy's Geography (2nd century CE)
historical_names.notes: The Roman legionary fortress and municipium of Brigetio stood at Szőny on the southern bank of the Danube, now part of modern Komárom.

b_batorkeszi.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in 1156 CE under its Hungarian name as villa Kesceu.

morphemes.translation: Keszi (one of the seven Magyar tribes)

b_batorkeszi.etymology_analysis: Originally attested as villa Kesceu (1156) after the Magyar tribe Keszi, the settlement later acquired the prefix Bátor- (Hungarian Bátorkeszi, Slovak Bátorove Kosihy) in the 16th century when it became an estate of the Báthory family.
