b_szekesfehervar.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1009 CE in a charter of the Bishopric of Veszprém under its Latin name Alba Civitas.
b_szekesfehervar.etymology_analysis: Székesfehérvár literally means 'White Castle with the Royal Seat' (Latin Alba Regia), combining székes ('with a throne/seat', referring to its role as the royal coronation and burial city) with fehér ('white') and vár ('castle').

historical_names.name: Gorsium
historical_names.source: Roman inscriptions and the Itinerarium Antonini (2nd–3rd century CE)
historical_names.notes: The Roman provincial center of Gorsium (renamed Herculia under Diocletian) lay 12 km south at modern Tác and served as the ancient urban predecessor in the region.

historical_names.name: Herculia
historical_names.source: Roman inscriptions and the Itinerarium Antonini (2nd–3rd century CE)
historical_names.notes: The Roman provincial center of Gorsium (renamed Herculia under Diocletian) lay 12 km south at modern Tác and served as the ancient urban predecessor in the region.

b_csakvar.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE for Csákvár; the medieval settlement is first documented in 13th-century Hungarian royal charters as an ancestral estate of the Csák kindred.

eponym.details: Named after the Csák kindred (gens Csák), whose eponymous 10th–11th century ancestor held the estate and castle.

b_csakvar.etymology_analysis: Csákvár is a compound of the Hungarian clan name Csák and vár ('castle, fortress'), denoting the medieval stronghold of the Csák kindred in Fejér County.

historical_names.name: Floriana
historical_names.source: Itinerarium Antonini (late 3rd–early 4th century CE)
historical_names.notes: The Roman town and late-Roman inner fortress of Floriana stood directly on the site of modern Csákvár.

b_kalocsa.first_mention_attestation: First attested around 1000–1001 CE upon King Stephen I's foundation of the Bishopric (later Archdiocese) of Kalocsa (Latin Colocia).

morphemes.translation: uncertain toponym (possibly from Slavic *kaluža 'muddy marsh' or an early personal name)

b_kalocsa.etymology_analysis: Attested in medieval Latin as Colocia, the name Kalocsa has multiple proposed origins, most commonly linked either to a Slavic root meaning 'muddy/marshy place' (reflecting its Danube floodplain setting) or to an early Hungarian personal name.

b_visegrad_hun.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1009 CE as a county town and the chief seat of an archdeaconry in the Kingdom of Hungary.
b_visegrad_hun.etymology_analysis: Visegrád is of South/West Slavic origin (cognate with Vyšehrad), composed of elements meaning 'upper' and 'castle/fortress', referring to the hilltop citadel overlooking the Danube Bend.

historical_names.name: Pone Navata
historical_names.source: Notitia Dignitatum (4th–5th century CE)
historical_names.notes: The late Roman military camp of Pone Navata stood on Sibrik-domb just above Visegrád.

b_pest.first_mention_attestation: First attested as an independent medieval town in written Hungarian records in 1148 CE.
b_pest.etymology_analysis: The name Pest is most widely derived from Slavic pešť ('oven' or 'cave'), likely referring to lime kilns or to the thermal caves in Gellért Hill across the Danube (echoed in the German name Ofen), though some link it to Ptolemy's Pession.

historical_names.name: Pession
historical_names.source: Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE) and Roman military records (c. 294 CE)
historical_names.notes: Ptolemy recorded Pession in antiquity, and the Romans built the fortified Danube bridgehead of Contra-Aquincum on the Pest bank.

historical_names.name: Contra-Aquincum
historical_names.source: Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE) and Roman military records (c. 294 CE)
historical_names.notes: Ptolemy recorded Pession in antiquity, and the Romans built the fortified Danube bridgehead of Contra-Aquincum on the Pest bank.

b_cegled.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a written Hungarian document in 1290 CE.
b_cegled.etymology_analysis: The name Cegléd is most likely derived from Old Hungarian cigle or cegle ('riverbank willow') with a toponymic suffix, though alternative theories connect it to szeglet ('corner', as a crossroads) or a personal name.

b_kecskemet.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written records in 1368 CE.
b_kecskemet.etymology_analysis: Kecskemét stems from the Hungarian word kecske ('goat'), reflecting the town's historic role in livestock herding on the Great Plain, combined with an obscure second element.

b_mantua.first_mention_attestation: Attested in classical Latin literature by the 1st century BCE, notably in Virgil's Eclogues and Georgics (c. 37–30 BCE) and later in Livy and Pliny.
b_mantua.etymology_analysis: Classical Mantua (Italian Mantova) derives from the Etruscan city name Manthva, associated with the Etruscan underworld god Mantus (and linked in Roman tradition to the prophetess Manto).

b_guastalla.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 864 CE as Uuardestalla (Wardistalla) in a charter of King Louis II of Italy granting the place to his wife Engelberga.
b_guastalla.etymology_analysis: Guastalla derives from Lombardic *warda-stall ('guard post' or 'watch station'), attested as Uuardestalla in 864 CE, reflecting its early medieval role as a fortified river post near the Po.

b_brescello.first_mention_attestation: Attested in classical Roman historiography as Brixellum (notably in Tacitus's Histories and Pliny's Naturalis Historia, 1st century CE, in connection with Emperor Otho's death in 69 CE).
b_brescello.etymology_analysis: Brescello descends from Latin Brixellum (or Brixillum), a diminutive formation on the Celtic root *briga- ('height, hillfort'), cognate with Brixia (Brescia).

b_modena.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Roman historiography for 218 BCE during the Second Punic War (Polybius and Livy), and refounded as the Roman colony of Mutina in 183 BCE.
b_modena.etymology_analysis: Modena evolves from Latin Mutina, a pre-Roman (Etruscan or Celtic) toponym attested from the late 3rd century BCE, variously interpreted as meaning 'elevation/mound' or 'foggy settlement'.

b_canossa.first_mention_attestation: First documented in the mid-10th century CE (c. 940–950) when Adalbert Atto of Canossa built the fortress on the Apennine cliff; earlier, the village below was known as Ciano d'Enza.

morphemes.translation: white, grey-white (referring to the white limestone cliff)

b_canossa.etymology_analysis: Canossa is commonly linked to Latin cana ('white/hoary', referring to the pale Apennine limestone crag on which the castle stands) or to a pre-Roman substrate root with the suffix -ossa.

b_reggio_emilia.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the Roman castrum of Regium Lepidi in 187 BCE by consul Marcus Aemilius Lepidus along the Via Aemilia, and attested in classical Roman sources.
b_reggio_emilia.etymology_analysis: Reggio Emilia derives from Roman Regium Lepidi ('royal town of Lepidus'), named after its 187 BCE founder Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, with the modern regional qualifier Emilia added after Italian unification.

b_cento.first_mention_attestation: First formally constituted and documented as an organized community in 1185 CE under the Bishop of Bologna and the Abbot of Nonantola.
b_cento.etymology_analysis: Cento derives from Latin centum ('hundred'), referring to the Roman centuriation (land-grid division into hundred-lot centuries) of the Po Valley.

b_aquileia.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a Latin military colony in 181 BCE by a Roman triumvirate (Livy, Ab Urbe Condita), rapidly becoming a major Roman city.
b_aquileia.etymology_analysis: Aquileia was traditionally associated in Roman lore with aquila ('eagle', an omen at its 181 BCE founding), though modern linguistics often links it to a pre-Roman/Venetic root *akw- ('water') or the nearby Aquilis river.

b_trieste.first_mention_attestation: First attested in classical literature in the 1st century BCE as Tergeste (in Julius Caesar's Commentarii de Bello Gallico and later Strabo and Pliny).
b_trieste.etymology_analysis: Trieste descends from pre-Roman Tergeste, formed from the Venetic/Illyrian root terg- ('market, trading place') and the Venetic toponymic suffix -este.

b_udine.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 983 CE as Udene (Utinum) in a donation charter by Holy Roman Emperor Otto II to the Patriarchate of Aquileia.

morphemes.translation: uncertain pre-Roman or Latinate hill-settlement name

b_udine.etymology_analysis: Attested as Udene in 983 CE and Latinized as Utinum, the name's origin is uncertain, likely deriving from a pre-Roman or late Latin root.

b_grado.first_mention_attestation: Attested in late antiquity from the 5th century CE (island tribunes met at Grado in 466 CE), and famously recorded in 568 CE when the Patriarch of Aquileia fled to the island of Gradus.
b_grado.etymology_analysis: Grado derives from Latin gradus ('step' or 'landing stage'), referring to its role as the coastal port and landing point (Aquae Gradatae) serving Aquileia.

b_caorle.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Caprulae from the 6th century CE (c. 568 CE) when refugees from Concordia Sagittaria settled on the lagoon island, becoming a bishopric in the 7th century.
b_caorle.etymology_analysis: Caorle descends from Latin Caprulae (related to capra, 'goat', i.e. 'little goat island' or Insula Capriae), evolving through Venetian into Caorle.

b_pordenone.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 897 CE in a diploma of King Berengar I of Italy as Curtis Naonis, and later recorded as Portus Naonis ('port on the Noncello') in 1192–1194.
b_pordenone.etymology_analysis: Pordenone derives from Medieval Latin Portus Naonis ('port on the Naon/Noncello river'), reflecting its origin as an early medieval river port.

b_portogruaro.first_mention_attestation: Officially founded and first documented on 10 January 1140 CE when Bishop Gervinus of Concordia granted land on the Lemene river to fishermen to build a port.
b_portogruaro.etymology_analysis: Portogruaro combines Italian porto ('port') with Gruaro (the nearby settlement/estate, from Latin gruarius, 'place of cranes'), denoting the 1140 river port serving Concordia.

b_gorizia.first_mention_attestation: First recorded on 28 April 1001 CE in a charter of Holy Roman Emperor Otto III donating the castle and village of Gorizia (Gorica).
b_gorizia.etymology_analysis: Gorizia (Slovene Gorica, German Görz) derives from Slavic/Slovene gorica ('little hill', diminutive of gora 'mountain/hill'), referring to the castle hill overlooking the Soča/Isonzo plain.

b_triglavski.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written sources in 1065 CE, with Tolmin Castle on Kozlov Rob first attested in 1188 CE.
b_triglavski.etymology_analysis: Tolmin (Italian Tolmino, German Tolmein) is a pre-Slavic/Romanized Alpine toponym adapted into Slovene, attested from the 11th century in the upper Soča valley.

b_genoa.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Roman historiography from the Second Punic War (218–205 BCE, e.g. Livy's Ab Urbe Condita recording Mago Barca's landing at Genua in 205 BCE).
b_genoa.etymology_analysis: Genoa (Italian Genova, Latin Genua) is a pre-Roman Ligurian toponym generally derived from Indo-European *ĝenu- ('knee, bend', cognate with Celtic *genu- 'mouth/bend'), referring to the curving gulf or coastal bend.

b_monaco.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned around 500 BCE by the Greek geographer Hecataeus of Miletus as Monoikos, a Ligurian port.
b_monaco.etymology_analysis: Monaco derives from Ancient Greek Mónoikos ('single house' or 'single temple', Latinized as Portus Herculis Monoeci), referring to the Phocaean Greek sanctuary of Heracles on the headland.

b_savona.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Livy (Ab Urbe Condita, 28.46) as the Ligurian Alpine town of Savo, where Mago Barca deposited his booty in 205 BCE.
b_savona.etymology_analysis: Savona descends from the pre-Roman Ligurian toponym Savo (later Latinized as Savona / Sagona), recorded by Livy in the context of the Second Punic War.

b_luni.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned by the Roman poet Ennius for the year 215 BCE as a harbour used by Roman fleets, and formally founded as the Roman colony of Luna in 177 BCE.
b_luni.etymology_analysis: Luni derives from Latin Luna, named after the Roman moon goddess Luna, to whom a major temple was dedicated in the 177 BCE colony.

b_chiavari.first_mention_attestation: First documented in medieval Genoese records in 1147 CE when a castle was constructed there by the Republic of Genoa (medieval Latin Clavaria).
b_chiavari.etymology_analysis: Chiavari (medieval Latin Clavaria) is traditionally derived from Latin clavis ('key'), referring to its strategic position controlling the coastal and Apennine passes east of Genoa.

b_pula.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Hellenistic Greek poetry by Callimachus (3rd century BCE) as Polai, and later by Strabo and Pliny as the Roman colony of Pola (Pietas Julia).

morphemes.translation: ancient Histrian coastal settlement name (linked in Greek myth to 'city of refuge')

b_pula.etymology_analysis: Pula (Italian Pola) descends from classical Pola / Polai, an ancient Histrian toponym adapted into Greek and Latin.

b_piran.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in the early Middle Ages in the Ravenna Cosmography (c. 700 CE) in Latin as Pyrrhanum.
b_piran.etymology_analysis: Piran (Italian Pirano, Latin Pyrrhanum) is commonly linked to Greek pyr ('fire'), referring to a coastal lighthouse or signal beacon on the Istrian peninsula, or alternatively to a Celtic/Roman personal name.

b_pazin.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned as Castrum Pisinum on 7 June 983 CE in a donation deed by Holy Roman Emperor Otto II to the Diocese of Poreč.
b_pazin.etymology_analysis: Pazin (Italian Pisino) derives from Medieval Latin Pisinum (attested in 983 CE as Castrum Pisinum), of pre-Slavic/Romance origin.

b_labin.first_mention_attestation: Attested in classical antiquity as Albona in Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia (1st century CE, c. 77 CE).
b_labin.etymology_analysis: Labin descends via Slavic metathesis from the ancient Roman and Liburnian/Histrian toponym Albona, built on the pre-Roman root *alb- ('hill' or 'white') with the suffix -ona.

b_brescia.first_mention_attestation: Attested in classical historiography (Polybius and Livy) as Brixia, the chief town of the Celtic Cenomani in the late 3rd century BCE.
b_brescia.etymology_analysis: Brescia derives from Latin Brixia, a Latinization of a Gaulish/Celtic toponym from *briga- ('height, hillfort'), referring to the Cidneo hill overlooking the plain.

b_bergamo.first_mention_attestation: Attested in classical Roman sources as Bergomum (quoted from Cato the Elder by Pliny the Elder, and granted Roman municipium status in 49 BCE).
b_bergamo.etymology_analysis: Bergamo descends from classical Latin Bergomum, derived from a Celtic/pre-Celtic root *berg- ('height, hill, fortification') associated with the mountain god Bergimus and the hilltop Città Alta.

b_chiari.first_mention_attestation: First documented as a fortified settlement in 1125 CE under the Latin name Clarium.
b_chiari.etymology_analysis: Chiari derives from Medieval Latin Clarium (from clarus, 'clear/bright'), likely denoting a cleared area or bright open plain in western Brescia.

b_como.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in Livy's account of the Roman campaign of 196 BCE, when consul Marcus Claudius Marcellus captured Comum from the Comenses and Insubres.
b_como.etymology_analysis: Como descends from Latin Comum (refounded as Novum Comum in 59 BCE), a pre-Roman Celtic/Orobian toponym attested from 196 BCE.

b_pombia.first_mention_attestation: Attested in late antiquity and the Lombard period (7th–8th century CE) as Flavia Plumbia, serving as a Lombard administrative and mint center.
b_pombia.etymology_analysis: Pombia derives from Roman/Lombard-era Plumbia (Flavia Plumbia), linked to Latin plumbum ('lead'), evolving phonetically in Piedmontese/Italian to Pombia.

b_bellinzona.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 590 CE by Gregory of Tours in Latin as Belitio / Bilitio (accusative Bilitionem) in his account of a Frankish invasion.
b_bellinzona.etymology_analysis: Attested as Bilitio in 590 CE and Berinzona in 721 CE, Bellinzona is of Lepontic (Cisalpine Celtic) origin, possibly from belitio ('juniper bushes').

b_cremona.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a Roman colonia in 218 BCE north of the Po River (attested in Polybius and Livy), retaining the earlier Cenomani/pre-Roman name.
b_cremona.etymology_analysis: Cremona is a pre-Roman toponym adopted by the Romans in 218 BCE; its exact meaning is uncertain, though it is often linked to a pre-Latin/Celtic root *cram-/*carra ('rock, stony ridge').

b_roncaglia.first_mention_attestation: First prominently attested in 1154 CE as the plain near Piacenza where Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa convened the first Diet of Roncaglia.
b_roncaglia.etymology_analysis: Roncaglia derives from Medieval Latin *runcalia (from runcare, 'to clear/cultivate land'), denoting cleared agricultural fields on the Po plain near Piacenza.

b_crema.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1074 CE in a charter citing Rozo da Crema (and in 1098 when Matilda of Canossa granted the Insula Fulcheria to Cremona); the 570 CE foundation story is a 16th-century legend.
b_crema.etymology_analysis: Crema is most widely derived from a pre-Latin/Celtic root *cram-/*crem- ('rock' or 'elevated ridge', rising above the surrounding marshes of Lake Gerundo), cognate with Cremona.

b_milano.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in Polybius's Histories for 222 BCE, when the Romans captured Mediolanum, the chief oppidum of the Insubres.
b_milano.etymology_analysis: Milan (Italian Milano, Latin Mediolanum) derives from Gaulish *Mediolānon ('[settlement] in the middle of the plain'), reflecting its central position in the western Po Valley.

b_monza.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Roman epigraphic evidence (the Ara dei Modiciates, c. 2nd–3rd century CE) as Modicia, and later in early medieval Lombard sources under Queen Theodelinda (c. 595 CE) as Modoetia.

morphemes.translation: pre-Latin settlement name (later folk-etymologized as Modoetia)

b_monza.etymology_analysis: Monza evolves through Lombard vernacular from Roman Modicia (likely of pre-Latin/Celtic Insubrian origin), later reinterpreted in medieval legend as Modoetia (from Latin modo 'here' + etiam 'yes').

b_gallarate.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 974 CE in a medieval parchment referring to the settlement as loco et fundo Galerate.
b_gallarate.etymology_analysis: Gallarate (attested as Galerate in 974 CE) combines a Roman or pre-Roman base with the characteristic northwestern Italian toponymic suffix -ate (shared with nearby Casorate and Samarate).

b_varese.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a surviving parchment dated 922 CE as Varesium; no written attestation <= 867 CE is documented.
b_varese.etymology_analysis: Derived from Medieval Latin Varesium (also Baretium, Varetium), generally traced to a Celtic or pre-Roman hydronymic root *var- ('water', 'stream'), referring to the marshy and lacustrine terrain near Lake Varese, combined with a Latinized locative suffix.

b_parma.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a Roman colonia in 183 BCE and attested in Livy's Ab Urbe Condita (Book 39, written late 1st century BCE) as Parma.
b_parma.etymology_analysis: From Latin Parma, either borrowed from an Etruscan personal or clan name (Parma / Parmni) or linked to the Latin word parma ('round shield'), perhaps referring to the circular shape of the Roman camp or the nearby Parma torrent.

b_florentiola.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a Lombard royal diploma of King Hildeprand dated 31 March 744 CE, confirming properties along the Via Emilia.
b_florentiola.etymology_analysis: Derived from Latin Florentiola, a diminutive of Florentia ('flourishing' or 'blooming'), referring to a Roman station along the Via Emilia, with the modern qualifier d'Arda added from the Arda river.

b_piacenza.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the Roman military colony of Placentia in 218 BCE, attested in Polybius's Histories and Livy's Ab Urbe Condita.
b_piacenza.etymology_analysis: From Latin Placentia, an auspicious Roman colonial name derived from the present participle placens ('pleasing, agreeable', from placere, 'to please'), which evolved regularly into Italian Piacenza.

b_pavia.first_mention_attestation: Known in Roman antiquity as Ticinum (43 BCE), the city became the Lombard capital and took the name Papia (whence Pavia) in the late 6th to 7th centuries CE (c. 650 CE).
b_pavia.etymology_analysis: The modern name Pavia derives from Late Latin/Lombard Papia (attested by the 7th century CE, perhaps from the Roman gens Papia or a Germanic adaptation), which replaced the earlier Roman name Ticinum (named after the Ticino river).

historical_names.name: Ticinum
historical_names.source: Classical Roman sources (1st century BCE, e.g., Strabo, Pliny the Elder, Tacitus)
historical_names.notes: Ticinum was the Roman municipium on the Ticino river before the name Papia (modern Pavia) became standard under the Lombards.

b_lodi.first_mention_attestation: Modern Lodi (Lodi Nuovo) was founded on 3 August 1158 CE by Emperor Frederick Barbarossa after the destruction of Laus Pompeia; no written attestation of the new site <= 867 CE exists.
b_lodi.etymology_analysis: Italian Lodi derives from Latin Laus (genitive Laudis), part of the Roman name Laus Pompeia (named in honor of Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo in 89 BCE, likely adapting an earlier Celtic toponym), transferred from ancient Lodi Vecchio to the 1158 CE foundation.

historical_names.name: Laus Pompeia
historical_names.source: Roman civic records and Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia (1st century CE)
historical_names.notes: Laus Pompeia (modern Lodi Vecchio, 7 km west of Lodi) was a Roman municipium and 4th-century bishopric destroyed by Milan in 1111 and 1158, prompting Frederick Barbarossa to refound Lodi on a new site.

historical_names.name: Lodi Vecchio
historical_names.source: Roman civic records and Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia (1st century CE)
historical_names.notes: Laus Pompeia (modern Lodi Vecchio, 7 km west of Lodi) was a Roman municipium and 4th-century bishopric destroyed by Milan in 1111 and 1158, prompting Frederick Barbarossa to refound Lodi on a new site.

b_vigevano.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 963 CE in documents mentioning the castle of Vigevano; no written attestation <= 867 CE is documented.
b_vigevano.etymology_analysis: From Medieval Latin Vigebanum / Vigevanum, traditionally analyzed as a compound of Latin vicus ('village') and a personal name (such as Lombard Gebuin) or a pre-Roman substrate element, evolving into Western Lombard Avgevan and Italian Vigevano.

b_tortona.first_mention_attestation: Attested in classical Roman sources as Dertona (a Roman colonia founded c. 120–100 BCE, recorded by Strabo, Pliny the Elder, and Velleius Paterculus).
b_tortona.etymology_analysis: Derived from Latin Dertona (later Tortona via vowel assimilation), a Ligurian or pre-Roman toponym attested as a Roman colony on the Via Postumia.

b_voghera.first_mention_attestation: After the ancient Roman town of Iria was destroyed by the Rugii in the 5th century CE, the medieval settlement is first attested as Viqueria in the 10th century (c. 950 CE); no written attestation of Viqueria/Voghera <= 867 CE exists.
b_voghera.etymology_analysis: From Medieval Latin Viqueria, a contraction of vicus Iriae ('village of Iria'), preserving the name of the ancient Roman colony Forum Iulium Iriensium on the Staffora (formerly Iria) river.

historical_names.name: Iria
historical_names.source: Augustan colonial records and Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia
historical_names.notes: Ancient Iria (made colonia Forum Iulium Iriensium under Augustus) occupied the same site before its destruction in late antiquity and medieval re-emergence as Viqueria.

historical_names.name: Forum Iulium Iriensium
historical_names.source: Augustan colonial records and Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia
historical_names.notes: Ancient Iria (made colonia Forum Iulium Iriensium under Augustus) occupied the same site before its destruction in late antiquity and medieval re-emergence as Viqueria.

b_trento.first_mention_attestation: Attested in classical Roman sources as Tridentum from the late 1st century BCE (following the Roman conquest of the Alps around 15 BCE, recorded by Strabo, Pliny the Elder, and Ptolemy).
b_trento.etymology_analysis: From Latin Tridentum, traditionally interpreted as 'three teeth/peaks' (tri- + dens) referring to the three hills surrounding the city (Doss Trento, Sant'Agata, San Rocco), though possibly a Latinization of a pre-Roman Raetian or Celtic toponym.

b_bolzano.first_mention_attestation: First attested under Bavarian rule in 679 CE as Bauzanum / Bauzana, and in 769 CE when Duke Tassilo III of Bavaria issued the foundation charter of Innichen Abbey in Bolzano.
b_bolzano.etymology_analysis: From Medieval Latin Bauzanum (yielding Italian Bolzano and German Bozen), formed from a personal name (such as Bautius) with the Roman estate suffix -anum, succeeding the nearby Roman military station Pons Drusi.

historical_names.name: Pons Drusi
historical_names.source: Roman military itinerary / Tabula Peutingeriana (Pons Drusi); 679 CE Bavarian records (Bauzanum)
historical_names.notes: Pons Drusi ('Bridge of Drusus') was the Roman military settlement founded after 15 BCE before the early medieval form Bauzanum appeared.

b_val_camonica.first_mention_attestation: Attested via the Camunni people in classical Roman sources from the late 1st century BCE (conquered in 16 BCE under Augustus; recorded by Strabo, Cassius Dio, and Pliny the Elder, and in Latin inscriptions as Vallis Camunnorum).
b_val_camonica.etymology_analysis: Derived from Latin Vallis Camunnorum ('Valley of the Camunni'), naming the Alpine valley of the Oglio river after the ancient Camunni tribe.

b_tirano.first_mention_attestation: The settlement developed along the Adda river below Dosso Castle, first mentioned in 1073 CE; no written attestation <= 867 CE is documented.
b_tirano.etymology_analysis: Likely derived from a Romanized estate name (*Tiranum, from a personal name such as Tirus or Tirius) or a pre-Roman Alpine root with the Latin suffix -anum.

b_pisa.first_mention_attestation: Attested in classical Roman sources as Pisae (became a Roman colony in 180 BCE, recorded by Livy, Polybius, Strabo, and Virgil).
b_pisa.etymology_analysis: From Latin Pisae (singular Pisa), probably of Etruscan or Ligurian origin meaning 'mouth' or 'estuary', referring to its position at the confluence of the Arno and Serchio rivers near the sea.

b_livorno.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written records in 1017 CE as Livorna, a small fishing village belonging to Pisa; no written attestation of Livorno/Livorna <= 867 CE exists.

morphemes.translation: Illyrian/Roman light galley (or Etruscan personal name)

b_livorno.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived from Latin Liburna (a light Roman warship, lending its name to the natural cove, later Livorna and Livorno), or from an Etruscan personal name via Latin Labrone.

historical_names.name: Labrone
historical_names.source: Cicero (letter to his brother Quintus, 1st century BCE)
historical_names.notes: Cicero mentions Labrone as an anchorage on the Tuscan coast near the later site of Livorno.

historical_names.name: Portus Herculis Labronis
historical_names.source: Cicero (letter to his brother Quintus, 1st century BCE)
historical_names.notes: Cicero mentions Labrone as an anchorage on the Tuscan coast near the later site of Livorno.

b_piombino.first_mention_attestation: First reliably attested in 1022 CE with the foundation of the Monastery of San Giustiniano; no written attestation of Piombino <= 867 CE is documented.
b_piombino.etymology_analysis: Derived from Populino ('Little Populonia'), the name given to the coastal refuge settled by inhabitants fleeing ancient Populonia after 9th-century raids, which evolved into Piombino.

historical_names.name: Populonia
historical_names.source: Livy (205 BCE supply contribution) and Strabo
historical_names.notes: Ancient Etruscan and Roman Populonia (Etruscan Pupluna) was the major port and episcopal center immediately north of Piombino before its 9th-century decline.

historical_names.name: Pupluna
historical_names.source: Livy (205 BCE supply contribution) and Strabo
historical_names.notes: Ancient Etruscan and Roman Populonia (Etruscan Pupluna) was the major port and episcopal center immediately north of Piombino before its 9th-century decline.

b_arezzo.first_mention_attestation: Attested as the Etruscan city of Arretium in Roman historical accounts from 311 BCE onward (Livy, Book 9; later Strabo and Pliny the Elder).
b_arezzo.etymology_analysis: From Latin Arretium, an adaptation of an earlier Etruscan city name of uncertain root, which evolved regularly into Italian Arezzo.

b_vallombrosa.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a Benedictine abbey by Saint John Gualbert in 1036 CE; no written attestation <= 867 CE is documented.
b_vallombrosa.etymology_analysis: From Latin vallis umbrosa ('shady valley'), describing the densely forested Apennine valley where the abbey was established in 1036 CE (previously known locally as Acquabella).

b_cortona.first_mention_attestation: Attested in classical sources as the Etruscan city of Curtun / Roman Cortona from the late 4th century BCE onward (Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, and Polybius).
b_cortona.etymology_analysis: From Etruscan Curtun, Latinized as Cortona, an ancient member of the Etruscan League whose root is of pre-Indo-European or Etruscan origin.

b_firenze.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the Roman colonia of Florentia in 59 BCE and attested in classical Roman sources including Florus, Tacitus, and Pliny the Elder.
b_firenze.etymology_analysis: From Latin Florentia ('the flourishing one', from florere, 'to bloom'), which evolved through Fiorenza into Italian Firenze and English Florence.

b_impruneta.first_mention_attestation: The parish church of Santa Maria in Impruneta is first attested in written records in 1032 CE; no written attestation <= 867 CE is documented.
b_impruneta.etymology_analysis: From Medieval Latin in pruneta or in pineta ('among the plum groves' or 'among the pine woods'), combining the Latin preposition in with a botanical collective noun in -eta.

b_empoli.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 4th-century CE Tabula Peutingeriana as In Portu, and consolidated as a town around its castle (Emporium / Empolis) from the 8th century CE.
b_empoli.etymology_analysis: Derived from Latin Emporium (from Greek emporion, 'market' or 'river port'), reflecting its early role as a commercial river port on the Arno, evolving into Italian Empoli.

historical_names.name: In Portu
historical_names.source: Tabula Peutingeriana (4th century CE)
historical_names.notes: In Portu ('At the Port') appears on the 4th-century Roman road map before the medieval form Emporium / Empolis.

b_volterra.first_mention_attestation: Attested as the Etruscan city of Velathri (Latinized as Volaterrae) in Roman accounts from the early 3rd century BCE (including Livy, Strabo, and Cicero).
b_volterra.etymology_analysis: From Etruscan Velathri, adapted into Latin as Volaterrae and evolving into Italian Volterra.

b_lucca.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the Roman colonia of Luca in 180 BCE and attested in Livy, Cicero, Strabo, and Pliny the Elder.
b_lucca.etymology_analysis: From Latin Luca, likely derived from a Ligurian or Celtic root *luk- meaning 'marsh' or 'wooded clearing' in the Serchio plain.

b_pistorja.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Sallust's Bellum Catilinae (c. 42 BCE) as Pistoria, site of the Battle of Pistoria in 62 BCE, and later in Pliny the Elder and Ptolemy.
b_pistorja.etymology_analysis: From Latin Pistoria (later Pistorium), traditionally linked to pistores ('bakers') who provisioned Roman troops during the Ligurian campaigns, though a pre-Roman substrate origin has also been proposed.

b_prato.first_mention_attestation: The history of Prato begins in the 10th century CE with the two settlements Borgo al Cornio and Castrum Prati; no written attestation <= 867 CE is documented.
b_prato.etymology_analysis: From Latin pratum ('meadow'), referring to the open pastureland around Castrum Prati in the Bisenzio plain.

b_orbetello.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 805 CE when Charlemagne and Pope Leo III donated the territory of Orbetello to the Abbey of Tre Fontane.
b_orbetello.etymology_analysis: From Medieval Latin Orbetellum / Orbitellus, generally derived from a diminutive of Latin herbetum ('grassy place'), or alternatively from urbs ('city') + diminutive suffix.

historical_names.name: Cosa
historical_names.source: Velleius Paterculus and Livy (Roman colony founded 273 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Roman Cosa (on the nearby promontory of Ansedonia) was the major classical settlement overlooking the Orbetello lagoon prior to its decline.

b_soana.first_mention_attestation: Attested in classical Roman sources as Suana (Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia, c. 77 CE, and Ptolemy), and as an episcopal see from the 5th century CE (medieval Soana).
b_soana.etymology_analysis: From Etruscan/Latin Suana, which became Soana in the Middle Ages and Sovana in modern Italian.

b_grosseto.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a document of 803 CE as a locus held by the Counts Aldobrandeschi.
b_grosseto.etymology_analysis: From Medieval Latin Grossetum, probably derived from Late Latin grossus ('thick, dense') with the collective suffix -etum, referring to dense vegetation or marshy thickets along the Ombrone river.

historical_names.name: Rusellae
historical_names.source: Livy (Roman conquest in 294 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Etruscan and Roman Rusellae (a few kilometers north of Grosseto) was the regional capital and bishopric until its decline and transfer to Grosseto in 1138 CE.

historical_names.name: Roselle
historical_names.source: Livy (Roman conquest in 294 BCE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Etruscan and Roman Rusellae (a few kilometers north of Grosseto) was the regional capital and bishopric until its decline and transfer to Grosseto in 1138 CE.

b_siena.first_mention_attestation: Attested in classical Roman sources as Sena Julia (founded as a Roman colony under Augustus; recorded by Pliny the Elder, c. 77 CE, and Tacitus, c. 70 CE).

morphemes.translation: Siena (possibly from Etruscan Saina or Gaulish Senones)

b_siena.etymology_analysis: From Latin Sena (Sena Julia), variously linked to the Etruscan family name Saina, the Gaulish Senones tribe, or Latin senex ('old'), evolving into Italian Siena.

b_montalcino.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a historical document dated 29 December 814 CE, indicating a church and settlement on the hill.
b_montalcino.etymology_analysis: From Medieval Latin Mons Ilcinus ('Mount of the Holm Oaks', from mons + ilcinus, adjective from ilex), which became Italian Montalcino.

b_chiusi.first_mention_attestation: Attested as the Etruscan city of Clevsin (Roman Clusium) in classical accounts of Lars Porsena's campaign against Rome (c. 508 BCE; Livy, Polybius, and Pliny the Elder).

morphemes.translation: enclosed place (associated with Latin claudere, 'to close')

b_chiusi.etymology_analysis: From Etruscan Clevsin, adapted into Latin as Clusium (folk-etymologized via claudere/clusum, 'closed') and evolving into Italian Chiusi.

b_asciano.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 714 CE in Lombard-era records concerning a dispute over the pieve (parish church) between the bishops of Siena and Arezzo.
b_asciano.etymology_analysis: Derived from Latin praedium Axianum or Ascianum ('estate of Axius/Ascius'), combining a Roman gentilicium with the possessive estate suffix -anum.

b_oviedo.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the charter of 25 November 781 CE (recording the 761 CE monastic foundation by Máximo and Fromestano in locum quod dicunt Oveto) and in royal charters of the Kingdom of Asturias.
b_oviedo.etymology_analysis: From Medieval Latin Oveto / Ovetum, of disputed pre-Roman or Celtic origin (variously linked to a personal name or a topographic root for a sheepfold/highland), evolving via Asturian Uviéu into Spanish Oviedo.

b_riano.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Leonese royal records from 1181–1183 CE as a tenencia held by Count Alfonso Ramírez; no written attestation <= 867 CE is documented.
b_riano.etymology_analysis: Typically derived from Latin rivus angulus ('river bend') or a Latinized personal/topographic form *Rivianus, referring to its mountain valley position on the Esla river.

b_villaviciosa.first_mention_attestation: Founded by royal charter (carta puebla) of King Alfonso X of Castile on 17 October 1270 CE as Puebla de Maliayo, later renamed Villaviciosa; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_villaviciosa.etymology_analysis: From Spanish villa ('town') + viciosa (from Latin vitiosa in the medieval sense of 'fertile, lush, abundant'), referring to the fertile valley of the ria.

b_gijon.first_mention_attestation: Attested in classical Roman and early medieval sources as Gigia (also Gegionem, referring to the Roman wall at Cimavilla; preceded by the Asturian oppidum of Noega at Campa Torres).
b_gijon.etymology_analysis: Derived from Roman Gegionem / Gigia (or a hypothetical Roman *Sessio evolving into Asturian Xixón), Castilianized as Gijón.

b_pravia.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Flavionavia in Ptolemy's Geographia (c. 150 CE, located at Santianes de Pravia), and Pravia served as capital of the Kingdom of Asturias under King Silo (774–783 CE).
b_pravia.etymology_analysis: Of uncertain pre-Roman or Latin origin (sometimes linked to a Celtic root or Roman personal/topographic name), attested in Asturian royal history from the 8th century CE.

b_luarca.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Medieval Latin as uillam Luarcam in a document dated 912 CE (later receiving a royal fuero in 1270 CE); no written attestation <= 867 CE is documented.
b_luarca.etymology_analysis: Attested in 912 CE as Luarcam; linguists such as Xosé Lluis García Arias propose a derivation from Latin lorica ('breastplate, defensive enclosure') or a compound of a pre-Roman hydronymic element with arca ('chest, enclosure').

b_gangasdelnarcea.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a document dated 20 January 905 CE (as Cangas, later Cangas de Tineo until 1927 CE); no written attestation <= 867 CE is documented.
b_gangasdelnarcea.etymology_analysis: From Asturian canga ('narrow valley, gorge', of pre-Roman origin) with the modern river qualifier del Narcea (replacing the older Cangas de Tineo in 1927 CE).

b_carballido.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE is documented for Carballido.
b_carballido.etymology_analysis: From Asturian/Galician carballo ('oak tree', of pre-Roman origin) combined with the collective suffix -ido (from Latin -etum), meaning 'oak grove'.

b_avila.first_mention_attestation: Attested in classical sources as Obila (Vettonian fortress) and Abula / Abila (recorded in Ptolemy's Geographia, c. 150 CE, and Roman civic remains).
b_avila.etymology_analysis: From pre-Roman Vettonian Obila ('High Mountain') and Romanized Abila / Abela, evolving into Spanish Ávila.

b_medinadelcampo.first_mention_attestation: Founded on La Mota hill in the 11th century CE (attested from 1077 CE onward); no written attestation <= 867 CE is documented.
b_medinadelcampo.etymology_analysis: A hybrid Arabic-Spanish toponym combining Arabic madīnah ('city, town') with Spanish del Campo ('of the plain/field').

b_laadrada.first_mention_attestation: Granted town privileges by King Henry III of Castile on 14 October 1393 CE (with its castle built in the 14th century); no written attestation <= 867 CE is documented.

morphemes.translation: turn-taking, irrigation or guard shift (from adra)

b_laadrada.etymology_analysis: From Spanish la ('the') + adrada (related to medieval Spanish adra, 'turn' or 'shared shift' for irrigation or watch duty, possibly via Arabic dawr).

b_sierradegredos.first_mention_attestation: Mountains and passes of the Sierra de Gredos are first systematically documented in the 14th-century Libro de la Montería of Alfonso XI (c. 1340–1350 CE); no written attestation <= 867 CE is documented.

morphemes.translation: Gredos (possibly from creta, 'chalk/clay', or pre-Roman root)

b_sierradegredos.etymology_analysis: From Spanish sierra ('mountain range', literally 'saw') + de Gredos, where Gredos is of uncertain origin (sometimes linked to Latin creta, 'chalk/clay', or a pre-Roman oronymic root).

b_benavente.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Benavente by King Ferdinand II of León during his repopulation campaign of 1164 CE (receiving its fuero in 1167 CE), replacing the earlier medieval name Malgrat; no written attestation <= 867 CE is documented.
b_benavente.etymology_analysis: An auspicious 12th-century renaming (modeled on Italian Benevento, from Latin Beneventum, 'good wind' or 'welcome arrival') bestowed by Ferdinand II of León to replace the ominous earlier name Malgrat.

b_alba.first_mention_attestation: First attested in medieval records from 1140 CE (recording its medieval Jewish community and Leonese repopulation); no written attestation <= 867 CE is documented.
b_alba.etymology_analysis: From Latin alba ('white') or a pre-Roman root *alb- ('hill, height'), qualified by the Tormes river on which the town stands.

b_leon.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the Roman legionary camp of Legio VI Victrix around 29 BCE and permanently established by Legio VII Gemina in 74 CE, attested in Roman inscriptions, Ptolemy's Geographia, and the Antonine Itinerary.
b_leon.etymology_analysis: From Latin Legio ('legion', specifically the camp of Legio VII Gemina), which underwent regular Romance phonetic evolution (Legione > Leione > León).

b_sarria.first_mention_attestation: Founded as Vilanova de Sarria by King Alfonso IX of León in the late 12th century (c. 1196 CE); no written attestation <= 867 CE is documented.
b_sarria.etymology_analysis: Named after the Sarria river, from a pre-Roman or Indo-European hydronymic root *sar- ('to flow, stream').

b_villablino.first_mention_attestation: Granted its royal carta puebla by King Alfonso X of Castile on 24 March 1270 CE; no written attestation <= 867 CE is documented.
b_villablino.etymology_analysis: From Spanish villa ('estate, town') + a Latinized personal name (such as Ablinus or Flabinus) in the Laciana valley.

b_guardo.first_mention_attestation: Cea is first attested in written records in the 10th-century Leonese inventory Nodicia de kesos (dated c. 974–980 CE), which records cheeses sent to Cea.
b_guardo.etymology_analysis: The settlement takes its name from the Cea River (earlier attested as Ceia), an ancient pre-Roman hydronym of uncertain Indo-European or Celtiberian origin.

b_valenciadecampos.first_mention_attestation: The Esla bluff settlement is attested in late antiquity as Castrum Coviacense (later Coyanza) in 457 CE, before being renamed Valencia de Campos in the 13th century and Valencia de Don Juan in 1387 CE after Infante John of Portugal.

eponym.details: The modern modifier 'de Don Juan' honors Infante John of Portugal (1349–1397), who was created Duke of Valencia de Campos in 1387 CE.

b_valenciadecampos.etymology_analysis: Originally known as Comeniaca and Castrum Coviacense (medieval Coyanza), the town was renamed Valencia de Campos in the 13th century from Latin valentia ('strength') and later Valencia de Don Juan after Infante John of Portugal became its duke in 1387 CE.

historical_names.name: Castrum Coviacense
historical_names.source: Late antique chronicles of the Visigothic-Suevic war (457 CE)
historical_names.notes: Continuous settlement on the Esla bluff known in antiquity and the early Middle Ages as Castrum Coviacense and Coyanza prior to its 13th- and 14th-century renamings.

historical_names.name: Comeniaca
historical_names.source: Late antique chronicles of the Visigothic-Suevic war (457 CE)
historical_names.notes: Continuous settlement on the Esla bluff known in antiquity and the early Middle Ages as Castrum Coviacense and Coyanza prior to its 13th- and 14th-century renamings.

historical_names.name: Coyanza
historical_names.source: Late antique chronicles of the Visigothic-Suevic war (457 CE)
historical_names.notes: Continuous settlement on the Esla bluff known in antiquity and the early Middle Ages as Castrum Coviacense and Coyanza prior to its 13th- and 14th-century renamings.

b_bejar.first_mention_attestation: Béjar was founded and chartered by King Alfonso VIII of Castile in October–November 1208 CE; earlier mentions of Biclara or Biclaro are not securely identified with this site.

morphemes.translation: highland settlement name of pre-Roman origin

b_bejar.etymology_analysis: The toponym Béjar is considered to be of pre-Roman Iberian or Celtiberian origin, later Latinized in medieval sources as Biclara or Biclaro, though its exact root meaning remains uncertain.

b_salamanca.first_mention_attestation: Salamanca is first attested in written history by Polybius (Histories, c. 150 BCE) as Helmantica/Salmantica in his account of Hannibal's siege of the Vettonian city in 220 BCE.
b_salamanca.etymology_analysis: Attested in classical sources as Helmantica, Salmantica, and Hermandica, the name combines a pre-Roman root *sala- (often linked to river fords or settlements along the Tormes) with a Celtic/pre-Roman suffix -mantica.

b_ciduadrodrigo.first_mention_attestation: Ciudad Rodrigo was repopulated and fortified in 1161 CE under King Ferdinand II of León, taking its name from Count Rodrigo González Girón who had earlier rebuilt the settlement.

eponym.details: Named after Count Rodrigo González Girón (fl. 12th century), who led the 12th-century repopulation of the town.

b_ciduadrodrigo.etymology_analysis: The medieval name literally means 'City of Rodrigo', from Spanish ciudad ('city') and the personal name of Count Rodrigo González Girón, who repopulated the former Roman site of Mirobriga in the 12th century.

historical_names.name: Mirobriga
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (c. 77 CE) and Ptolemy, Geography
historical_names.notes: Ancient Vettonian oppidum Mirobriga (renamed Augustobriga under Roman rule) located at the same site.

historical_names.name: Augustobriga
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (c. 77 CE) and Ptolemy, Geography
historical_names.notes: Ancient Vettonian oppidum Mirobriga (renamed Augustobriga under Roman rule) located at the same site.

b_zamora.first_mention_attestation: The settlement on the Duero is first attested in the Roman Antonine Itinerary (c. 280 CE) as Ocellum Duri (Ocellodurum), and on Visigothic coins of King Sisebut (612–621 CE) as Semure.

morphemes.translation: fortified rock or wild olive place

b_zamora.etymology_analysis: The modern name Zamora derives from Visigothic Semure (via Andalusi Arabic Semurah/Azemur, sometimes linked to 'wild olive' or a pre-Roman root), which superseded the Roman name Ocellum Duri ('Eye of the Duero').

historical_names.name: Ocellum Duri
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (c. 280 CE); Visigothic coins of Sisebut (612–621 CE)
historical_names.notes: Ocellum Duri was the Roman station on the Emerita–Asturica road, followed by Visigothic Semure.

historical_names.name: Ocellodurum
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (c. 280 CE); Visigothic coins of Sisebut (612–621 CE)
historical_names.notes: Ocellum Duri was the Roman station on the Emerita–Asturica road, followed by Visigothic Semure.

b_toro.first_mention_attestation: The medieval town of Toro is attested from its repopulation under Alfonso III and Infante García around 899–910 CE, with city walls dating to 910 CE.

morphemes.translation: bull (after a Celtiberian granite bull sculpture)

b_toro.etymology_analysis: According to local historical tradition, the name Toro ('bull', from Latin taurus) derives from an ancient Celtiberian granite bull sculpture (verraco) discovered by the Christian settlers who repopulated the town in 899–910 CE.

historical_names.name: Arbocala
historical_names.source: Polybius, Histories (c. 150 BCE) and Livy for Arbocala; Antonine Itinerary for Albucella
historical_names.notes: Toro is widely identified with the ancient Vaccaean city of Arbocala besieged by Hannibal in 220 BCE and the Roman station Albucella.

historical_names.name: Albucella
historical_names.source: Polybius, Histories (c. 150 BCE) and Livy for Arbocala; Antonine Itinerary for Albucella
historical_names.notes: Toro is widely identified with the ancient Vaccaean city of Arbocala besieged by Hannibal in 220 BCE and the Roman station Albucella.

b_villafafila.first_mention_attestation: Villafáfila is first attested in writing in a 936 CE charter of the Monastery of Sahagún recording a sale of salt pans in Lampreana bordering 'Villa Fafila'.
b_villafafila.etymology_analysis: The name combines Medieval Latin villa ('rural estate, village') with the Visigothic/Germanic personal name Fáfila (Favila), referring to an early medieval landowner or settler.

b_bar.first_mention_attestation: Bar-le-Duc (originally Bar / Barrum) was founded around 951 CE when Count Frederick I of Upper Lorraine built a fortress overlooking the Ornain valley.
b_bar.etymology_analysis: Bar derives from the Gaulish root *barro- ('height, summit'), referring to the promontory above the Ornain; 'le-Duc' was added later to reflect its status as seat of the Dukes of Bar.

historical_names.name: Caturrigis
historical_names.source: Roman itineraries and Caturiges tribal records (3rd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Gallo-Roman settlement of Caturrigis lay in the immediate Barrois valley before the 10th-century fortress of Bar was built.

b_verdun.first_mention_attestation: Verdun is first attested in Roman sources as Verodunum in the Antonine Itinerary (c. 280 CE), and later famously as the site of the 843 CE Treaty of Verdun.
b_verdun.etymology_analysis: Verdun derives from the Gallo-Roman toponym Verodunum, combining Gaulish *vero- ('great' or 'upper') with *dūnon ('fortress, fortified hill').

b_argonne.first_mention_attestation: Saint-Mihiel originated with the Benedictine abbey of Saint-Mihiel, founded in 708 or 709 CE by Count Wulfoalde and his wife Adalsinde.
b_argonne.etymology_analysis: The town is named after Saint-Mihiel Abbey, dedicated to the Archangel Michael (regional Lorraine form Mihiel) upon its foundation in 708–709 CE.

b_briey.first_mention_attestation: Briey is first attested in 1072 CE when a castle held by the Counts of Bar is recorded there, followed by the form potestas Briacensis in 1096 CE.

morphemes.translation: hill/fortress or Gaulish personal name Brigos

b_briey.etymology_analysis: Briey derives either from Gaulish briga ('fortress, hill') or the Gaulish personal name Brigos/Brigius combined with the Gallo-Roman estate suffix -acum (attested as Briacensis in 1096).

b_hayange.first_mention_attestation: Hayange is first mentioned in an official Carolingian record in 821 CE during the reign of Emperor Louis the Pious, and later appears as Hainges and Haingas in 875 CE.

morphemes.translation: personal name Haius or forest clearing (heie)

b_hayange.etymology_analysis: Attested in early medieval forms as Heiyingen Villa and Hainges (875), Hayange combines a Germanic personal name (such as Haius) or woodland root with the Frankish patronymic suffix -ingen, Frenchified to -ange.

b_vaucouleurs.first_mention_attestation: Vaucouleurs is attested in medieval charters from the 13th century (e.g., Vauquelour in 1266 CE, Valcolor in 1310 CE); earlier Carolingian records (859–865 CE) mention the neighboring royal palace of Tusey.

morphemes.translation: colors (Valley of Colors, Latinized Vallis Coloris)

b_vaucouleurs.etymology_analysis: Vaucouleurs derives from Old French val ('valley') and couleurs ('colors'), rendered in medieval Latin as Vallis Coloris, referring to the colorful meadows of the Meuse valley.

historical_names.name: Tusiacum
historical_names.source: Carolingian charters and synod of Tusey (859–865 CE)
historical_names.notes: The Carolingian royal palace of Tusey (Tusiacum super Mosam), site of the 860 church council, lay immediately adjacent to Vaucouleurs.

b_toul.first_mention_attestation: Toul is first attested in classical geography by Ptolemy (c. 150 CE) as Tullum, the capital of the Gallic Leuci tribe (Tullum Leucorum), and became a bishopric around 365 CE.
b_toul.etymology_analysis: Toul derives from Gallo-Roman Tullum (Tullum Leucorum), from a pre-Roman/Gaulish root *tull- meaning 'elevation' or 'swelling', referring to the strategic site on the Moselle.

b_aachen.first_mention_attestation: Aachen was developed by the Romans as the thermal spa settlement Aquae Granni in the 1st–2nd centuries CE, and is attested in Carolingian annals from 765 CE when Pepin the Short erected a royal palace there.

morphemes.translation: waters, streams (dative plural, translating Latin Aquae)

b_aachen.etymology_analysis: The German name Aachen comes from Old High German ahha ('water, stream', dative plural), directly translating the Latin Aquae in the Roman name Aquae Granni ('Waters of Grannus', the Celtic healing god).

b_limbourg.first_mention_attestation: Limbourg is first attested in 1064 CE as Lemburc (comes Udo de Lemburc) after Count Frederick of Luxembourg built a fortified residence on the Vesdre promontory around 1030 CE.

morphemes.translation: lime tree or dragon/snake (borrowed from Salian Limburg)

b_limbourg.etymology_analysis: Named after the 11th-century castle of Lemburc/Limburg, whose name was likely transferred from the Salian fortress of Limburg in the Palatinate (from Old High German linta 'lime tree' or lint 'dragon' + burg 'fortress').

b_duren.first_mention_attestation: Düren is first attested under its own name in the Royal Frankish Annals for 747 CE as 'villa quae dicitur Duria', while nearby Roman Marcodurum is attested by Tacitus (Histories, c. 105 CE) for events of 69–70 CE.
b_duren.etymology_analysis: Villa Duria (modern Düren) preserves the Celtic root *duro- ('gate, fortified enclosure'), likely shortened from or related to the nearby Gallo-Roman settlement of Marcodurum.

historical_names.name: Marcodurum
historical_names.source: Tacitus, Histories (c. 105 CE) for Marcodurum; Royal Frankish Annals (747 CE) for Villa Duria
historical_names.notes: Roman Marcodurum lay 4 km north of downtown Düren, which appears as Villa Duria by 747 CE.

b_eschweiler.first_mention_attestation: Eschweiler is first mentioned in 828 CE by Einhard, the biographer of Charlemagne, as a Carolingian royal estate.
b_eschweiler.etymology_analysis: Eschweiler combines Old High German asc ('ash tree') with -weiler (from Latin villare, 'homestead, hamlet'), meaning 'ash-tree hamlet'.

b_prum.first_mention_attestation: Prüm is first attested in 721 CE in the foundation charter of Prüm Abbey (Monasterium Prumia) by Bertrada the Elder and her son Charibert, Count of Laon.
b_prum.etymology_analysis: The town and abbey take their name from the Prüm River (Latinized as Prumia), an ancient pre-Germanic hydronym of the Eifel region.

b_kleve.first_mention_attestation: Kleve is first documented in 1092 CE when Count Dietrich of Cleves took his title from the castle of Cleve.
b_kleve.etymology_analysis: Kleve derives from Old Saxon/Middle Low German klif ('cliff, steep slope'), referring to the prominent moraine ridge on which Schwanenburg Castle was built.

b_gladbach.first_mention_attestation: Mönchengladbach began with the founding of Gladbach Abbey in 974 CE by Archbishop Gero of Cologne and the monk Sandrad of Trier.
b_gladbach.etymology_analysis: Originally named Gladbach after the local brook ('smooth/bright stream'), the prefix München-/Mönchen- ('monks'') was added in 1888 to distinguish it from Bergisch Gladbach, referring to its 974 CE abbey.

b_wezel.first_mention_attestation: Wesel originated as a Franconian manor first recorded as 'Wesele' in an 8th-century charter copy from Echternach Abbey (c. 750 CE).
b_wezel.etymology_analysis: The name Wesel (early medieval Wesele) derives from an Old Frankish/Germanic root related to *wisa ('meadow, floodplain'), describing its position at the confluence of the Lippe and Rhine.

b_moers.first_mention_attestation: Moers is first securely documented in 1186 CE as the seat of the Counts of Moers, while the Roman fort of Asciburgium stood at nearby Moers-Asberg from the late 1st century BCE.
b_moers.etymology_analysis: Moers (older Dutch Murse, Meurs) derives from a Germanic root related to moor/marsh (*mōraz), referring to the marshy Lower Rhine lowland.

historical_names.name: Asciburgium
historical_names.source: Tacitus, Germania and Histories (c. 98–105 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman legionary/auxiliary camp Asciburgium was located at Moers-Asberg within the modern city.

b_maastricht.first_mention_attestation: Maastricht is first attested in written documents around 575 CE by Gregory of Tours as '[ad] Treiectinsem [urbem]', and in 634 CE as 'Treiectensis'.
b_maastricht.etymology_analysis: Maastricht is an Old Dutch compound of Masa- (the Meuse River) and *treiekt (borrowed from Latin traiectus, 'crossing, ford'), meaning 'crossing on the Meuse'.

b_eindhoven.first_mention_attestation: Eindhoven is first attested in 1232 CE when Duke Henry I of Brabant granted town and market rights to the settlement at the confluence of the Dommel and Gender.
b_eindhoven.etymology_analysis: Eindhoven derives from Middle Dutch ende ('end, border') and hoven ('farmsteads, manors'), meaning 'farmsteads at the end' (of the Woensel territory).

b_tilburg.first_mention_attestation: Tilburg is first attested as 'Tilliburg' in documents dating to 709 CE.

morphemes.translation: tilth, cultivated land or personal name Tillo

b_tilburg.etymology_analysis: Attested in 709 CE as Tilliburg, the name combines an Old Frankish element (either a personal name Tillo or a root meaning 'cultivated land/hill') with -burg ('fortified place').

b_arnsberg.first_mention_attestation: Arnsberg is first mentioned in 789 CE in the Carolingian records (Urbar) of Werden Abbey, long before the Counts of Werl-Arnsberg moved their seat there around 1070 CE.
b_arnsberg.etymology_analysis: Arnsberg derives from Old Saxon arn ('eagle') and berg ('mountain, hill'), meaning 'eagle's hill', referring to the Schlossberg overlooking the Ruhr.

b_bilstein.first_mention_attestation: Bilstein Castle in Lennestadt was built between 1202 and 1225 CE by Dietrich I of Bilstein, with the castle's 750th anniversary commemorated from 1225 CE.
b_bilstein.etymology_analysis: Bilstein (related to Beilstein/Bielstein) means 'steeply prominent rock', transferred from the volcanic keratophyre spur on which the castle was built.

b_bergh.first_mention_attestation: The Counts of Berg first emerged in written records in 1101 CE (at Burg Berge in Odenthal, before relocating to Schloss Burg an der Wupper in 1133 CE).
b_bergh.etymology_analysis: The County of Berg (and its ancestral seats Burg Berge and Burg an der Wupper) takes its name from German Berg ('mountain, hill'), referring to the hilly Bergisches Land.

b_siegburg.first_mention_attestation: Siegburg originated with the foundation of Michaelsberg Abbey on the hill above the Sieg River in 1064 CE by Archbishop Anno II of Cologne; the resulting settlement was first mentioned as a city in 1182 CE.
b_siegburg.etymology_analysis: Siegburg literally means 'fortress on the Sieg', combining the river name Sieg (an ancient pre-Germanic hydronym) with German -burg ('castle, fortress').

b_cologne.first_mention_attestation: Cologne was elevated to a Roman colonia in 50 CE as Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium, succeeding the earlier Ubii settlement Oppidum Ubiorum founded in the late 1st century BCE.
b_cologne.etymology_analysis: The modern name Cologne (German Köln) derives directly from Latin Colonia in Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium, the Roman colony established in 50 CE.

historical_names.name: Oppidum Ubiorum
historical_names.source: Tacitus, Annals and Roman inscriptions (50 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman colony name from 50 CE, preceded by Oppidum Ubiorum.

b_bonn.first_mention_attestation: Bonn is attested in Roman historiography by Tacitus (Histories, c. 105 CE) as Castra Bonnensia / Bonna, established as a Roman military camp during Drusus's Germanic campaigns around 12–11 BCE.
b_bonn.etymology_analysis: Bonn derives from the Latinized Celtic name Bonna, from Gaulish *bona meaning 'foundation' or 'settlement', originally referring to an Eburones/Ubii settlement near the Roman camp.

b_neuss.first_mention_attestation: Neuss is attested in Roman sources by Tacitus (Histories, c. 105 CE) as Novaesium, originating from Roman military camps built along the Rhine from 16 BCE onward.
b_neuss.etymology_analysis: Neuss derives from Latin Novaesium (attested later as Nivisium castellum by Gregory of Tours), a Gallo-Roman adaptation of an earlier Celtic toponym.

b_nauenahr.first_mention_attestation: Ahrweiler is first mentioned in 893 CE as Arwilre/Arewilre in the Prüm Urbar (estate register of Prüm Abbey), while Neuenahr Castle was founded between 1204 and 1225 CE.
b_nauenahr.etymology_analysis: Formed in 1969 by merging Bad Neuenahr ('New Ahr' spa, named for 13th-century Neuenahr Castle) and Ahrweiler (893 CE Arwilre, 'hamlet on the Ahr River').

b_dortmund.first_mention_attestation: Dortmund is first mentioned in official documents around 882 CE (880–884 CE) in the Werden Abbey Urbar as 'Throtmanni', while the nearby hillfort of Sigiburg (Hohensyburg) was recorded in 772 CE.

morphemes.translation: throat, narrow passage, or bubbling stream

b_dortmund.etymology_analysis: Dortmund evolved from Old Saxon Throtmanni (later Dorpmunde), whose first element relates to a narrow passage or watercourse and whose second element means 'mouth' or 'protection'.

historical_names.name: Sigiburg
historical_names.source: Royal Frankish Annals (772–775 CE)
historical_names.notes: The Saxon hillfort Sigiburg (modern Hohensyburg in southern Dortmund) was captured by Charlemagne in 772 CE.

b_essen.first_mention_attestation: Although Essen Abbey was founded around 845 CE, the first documented written mention of Essen dates to 898 CE under King Zwentibold, with early forms such as Astnide.

morphemes.translation: place of ash trees or eastern region

b_essen.etymology_analysis: Essen developed from Old Saxon Astnide (through Astnidum, Assinde, and Esnede), most likely meaning 'place where ash trees grow' or 'region in the east', unrelated to the German verb essen ('to eat').

b_recklinghausen.first_mention_attestation: Recklinghausen is first mentioned in written records in 1017 CE as 'Ricoldinchuson'.
b_recklinghausen.etymology_analysis: From 1017 CE Ricoldinchuson, Recklinghausen means 'at the houses of the kin of Ricold', combining an Old Saxon personal name with the patronymic suffix -ing and dative plural -huson ('houses').

b_koblenz.first_mention_attestation: Koblenz was established around 9–8 BCE by Drusus as the Roman military post Castellum apud Confluentes at the confluence of the Rhine and Moselle.

morphemes.translation: flowing together, confluence (of the Rhine and Moselle)

b_koblenz.etymology_analysis: Koblenz derives from Latin (ad) Confluentes ('at the confluence'), referring to the meeting of the Moselle and Rhine rivers.

b_adenau.first_mention_attestation: Adenau is mentioned for the first time in written records in 992 CE under the name 'Adenova'.

morphemes.translation: personal name Ado or stream name

b_adenau.etymology_analysis: Attested in 992 CE as Adenova, the name combines a personal or stream root with Old High German ouwa ('meadow, watery plain').

b_cochem.first_mention_attestation: Cochem is first mentioned in written records in 886 CE as 'Villa cuchema'.

morphemes.translation: curved bend or hill settlement on the Moselle

b_cochem.etymology_analysis: First attested as Villa cuchema in 886 CE, the name Cochem is of pre-Germanic (likely Celtic or Gallo-Roman) origin, referring to the bend or hill spur along the Moselle.

b_sponhem.first_mention_attestation: Sponheim is first documented in 1044 CE with Siegfried I, Count of Sponheim, and the early 11th-century comital seat and church at Sponheim.

morphemes.translation: wood-chip, cleared woodland, or personal name

b_sponhem.etymology_analysis: Earlier attested as Spanheim, the name combines a Germanic root (linked to woodland clearing or a personal name) with -heim ('homestead, settlement').

b_mark.first_mention_attestation: Burg Mark (near Hamm) is first documented by 1198 CE when it was acquired by the Counts of Berg-Altena, who subsequently styled themselves Counts of the Mark.
b_mark.etymology_analysis: Burg Mark means 'Castle of the March', from German Burg ('castle') and Mark ('borderland, march'), reflecting its frontier position on the Ahse.

b_hagen.first_mention_attestation: Hagen is first mentioned in written records around 1200 CE as a small settlement near the confluence of the Volme and Ennepe rivers.
b_hagen.etymology_analysis: Hagen derives from German/Old Saxon hag/hagen meaning 'hedged enclosure' or 'enclosed woodland clearing'.

b_hukeswag.first_mention_attestation: Hückeswagen is first mentioned in 1085 CE as a Franconian Salhof in an imperial confirmation of a donation by Abbess Svanhild of Essen.

morphemes.translation: deep water, pool, bend in the Wupper

b_hukeswag.etymology_analysis: Attested as Hukensuuage and Huckengeswage, the name signifies the settlement by a river pool or bend associated with a man named Hugobert or Hugibald.

b_sayn.first_mention_attestation: The County of Sayn and its ancestral castle first emerged in written records in 1139 CE.
b_sayn.etymology_analysis: Sayn takes its name from the Saynbach stream, an ancient regional hydronym in the Westerwald foothills.

b_wied.first_mention_attestation: Altwied Castle (originally Burg Wied) is first attested in 1129 CE when Count Metfried is named 'Meffridus de Widhe'.

morphemes.translation: old (added after Neuwied was founded in 1652)

b_wied.etymology_analysis: Originally called Wied after the Wied River, the prefix Alt- ('old') was added after the Counts of Wied founded Neuwied on the Rhine in 1652 CE.

b_isenburg.first_mention_attestation: Isenburg is first documented in 1103 CE (Rembold II of Isenburg), following the construction of Isenburg Castle around 1100 CE above the Saynbach and Iserbach.
b_isenburg.etymology_analysis: Isenburg combines Old High German īsan ('iron', also reflected in the nearby Iserbach) with -burg ('castle'), literally 'iron castle'.

b_bouillon.first_mention_attestation: The castle of Bouillon is first mentioned in 988 CE in a letter to Godfrey the Captive from his brother, Archbishop Adalberon of Reims.

morphemes.translation: personal name Bullo or bubbling water

b_bouillon.etymology_analysis: Attested in medieval Latin as Bullionis / Castrum Bullionis (988 CE), Bouillon derives from a Gallo-Roman or Germanic root (often linked to a personal name or a bend/eddy of the Semois).

b_chiny.first_mention_attestation: Chiny is first attested around 971 CE in connection with Otto, ancestor of the Counts of Chiny, who established a comital stronghold in the Ardennes.
b_chiny.etymology_analysis: Chiny (Walloon Tchini) derives from a Gallo-Roman estate name in -iacum formed from a personal name such as *Canius or *Chinius.

b_saint_hubert.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 825 CE when the relics of Saint Hubert of Liège (d. 727 CE) were translated on 30 September 825 to the Benedictine Abbey of Andage, which thereafter became known as Saint-Hubert.

morphemes.translation: bright mind/spirit (referring to Saint Hubert of Liège, d. 727 CE)

b_saint_hubert.etymology_analysis: Named in commemoration of Saint Hubert, Bishop of Liège (d. 727 CE), whose body was translated in 825 CE to the Benedictine monastery previously called Andage. The personal name Hubert derives from Germanic *Huguberht ('bright in mind/heart').

historical_names.name: Andage
historical_names.source: Acts of the Council of Aachen (817 CE), recording the Benedictine Abbey of Andage (originally founded c. 687 CE).
historical_names.notes: Before the 825 CE translation of Saint Hubert's relics, the monastic settlement was known as Andage (Latinized Andagium).

historical_names.name: Andagium
historical_names.source: Acts of the Council of Aachen (817 CE), recording the Benedictine Abbey of Andage (originally founded c. 687 CE).
historical_names.notes: Before the 825 CE translation of Saint Hubert's relics, the monastic settlement was known as Andage (Latinized Andagium).

b_virton.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing in 1183 CE as Vertunum in a papal bull of Pope Lucius III confirming it as a fiefdom of the House of Chiny.
b_virton.etymology_analysis: Attested as Vertunum (1183 CE), Vertun (1187 CE), and Verton (1240 CE). Modern toponymists generally derive it from a Gaulish compound of viro- ('true' or 'man') and -dunon ('fortress, hill-fort'), rather than a popular folk etymology linking it to the Vire and Ton rivers.

b_liege.first_mention_attestation: First referenced in 558 CE as Vicus Leudicus; the settlement gained major ecclesiastical prominence around 705 CE following the martyrdom of Saint Lambert.
b_liege.etymology_analysis: Derived from a Germanic root *liudik-, formed from *liudiz ('people', cognate with German Leute and Dutch lieden), Latinized as Leodicum or Leodium and reflected in Walloon Lîdje, Dutch Luik, and German Lüttich.

b_la_roche.first_mention_attestation: First attested in charters between 1046 and 1065 CE as Rupe Seremani, and later as Rupes in Arduennam (1139 CE) and La Roiche en Ardenne (1275 CE).
b_la_roche.etymology_analysis: Named for the steep rocky promontory overlooking a bend of the River Ourthe on which the medieval castle stands, combined with the regional choronym Ardenne (from Gaulish *Arduenna, 'highland').

b_huy.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a 7th-century testament (634 CE) as Hoius vicus, referring to the settlement at the mouth of the Hoyoux river on the Meuse.
b_huy.etymology_analysis: Takes its name from the small River Hoyoux (Latinized as Hoius), which flows into the Meuse at the site of the Roman castrum and early medieval vicus.

b_luxembourg.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 963 CE as castellum Lucilinburhuc in an exchange charter between Count Siegfried I of the Ardennes and the Abbey of Saint Maximin in Trier.
b_luxembourg.etymology_analysis: Recorded as Lucilinburhuc in 963 CE, traditionally interpreted as Old High German 'little castle' (luzzil + burg), though some modern historians also connect the first element with Letze ('fortification, barrier').

b_bastogne.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 634 CE in the testament of Adalgisel Grimo, when the local Frankish lord ceded territories at Bastogne to Saint Maximin's Abbey near Trier.
b_bastogne.etymology_analysis: The early medieval toponym (reflected in French Bastogne, Dutch Bastenaken, and German Bastenach) derives from a Gallo-Roman estate formation meaning the domain of a landowner named Basto.

b_clervaux.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation exists by 867 CE; the settlement developed around Clervaux Castle, whose oldest surviving parts were built in the 12th century by Gerard, Count of Sponheim.
b_clervaux.etymology_analysis: French Clervaux means 'clear valley' (Latin clara vallis), while the Luxembourgish Klierf and German Clerf reflect the local hydronym of the Clerve river.

b_vianden.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 698 CE in a charter recording the gift of a vineyard in Monte Viennense by Saint Irmina to the Abbey of Echternach.
b_vianden.etymology_analysis: Attested in 698 CE as Monte Viennense (and earlier as Viennensis), a Gallo-Roman toponym of pre-Roman origin that evolved into German/Luxembourgish Vianden.

b_diekirch.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing in 938 CE under the form Theochirica, and later as Diecirke (1182 CE) and Diekirke (1221 CE).
b_diekirch.etymology_analysis: From Old High German *Diot-kiricha (attested as Theochirica in 938 CE), meaning 'people's church' or 'church of the people'.

b_namur.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing around 700 CE as Namuco in the Ravenna Cosmography, and later in 962 CE as Namucho.
b_namur.etymology_analysis: Linguists derive Namur (early forms Namuco, Namucho) from a Gaulish personal name Namo combined with the Celtic suffix -uco, denoting the estate or settlement of Namo at the Sambre–Meuse confluence.

b_charleroi.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned as a settlement in the 7th century (and as Deonant in the Ravenna Cosmography, c. 700 CE), when Bishop Perpète of Maastricht moved his residence to Dinant and founded the church of Saint Vincent.
b_charleroi.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Celtic compound *Divo-Nanto, meaning 'sacred valley' or 'divine gorge', referring to the narrow Meuse valley at Dinant.

b_couvin.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing in 872 CE under the form Cubinium in the pagus Laumanensis.
b_couvin.etymology_analysis: Attested as Cubinium in 872 CE, generally derived from a Gallo-Roman personal name (Cupius or Covius) with the Latin possessive suffix -inius denoting an estate, though a Gaulish derivation from co-bo ('victory') has also been proposed.

b_metz.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Tacitus's Histories (c. 109 CE) as Divodurum, the chief Gallo-Roman town of the Mediomatrici; the name evolved to Mettis by the 5th century CE.

morphemes.translation: the Mediomatrici tribe (who lived in the region)

b_metz.etymology_analysis: Originally called Divodurum Mediomatricorum ('sacred fortress of the Mediomatrici'), the city's name was shortened in Late Antiquity to Mediomatrix and by the 5th century CE contracted to Mettis, yielding modern Metz.

historical_names.name: Divodurum
historical_names.source: Tacitus, Histories I.63 (c. 109 CE).
historical_names.notes: Celtic oppidum and Gallo-Roman civitas capital before the ethnic name Mediomatrici/Mettis replaced Divodurum in Late Antiquity.

historical_names.name: Divodurum Mediomatricorum
historical_names.source: Tacitus, Histories I.63 (c. 109 CE).
historical_names.notes: Celtic oppidum and Gallo-Roman civitas capital before the ethnic name Mediomatrici/Mettis replaced Divodurum in Late Antiquity.

b_saarburg.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a contract dated 17 September 964 CE for the construction of a hilltop castle (Saarburg) on the Churbelum hill by Count Siegfried I of Luxembourg.
b_saarburg.etymology_analysis: Compound of the river name Saar (Roman Saravus) and German Burg ('castle, fortress'), referring to the 10th-century castle built above the Saar river.

b_forbach.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation exists by 867 CE; Forbach is first mentioned in the 10th century under the form Furpac, and its castle on the Schlossberg was built at the end of the 12th century.
b_forbach.etymology_analysis: Attested in the 10th century as Furpac, a Germanic hydronymic compound combining an element meaning 'fir/pine' (or 'furrow') with -bach ('brook, stream').

b_faulquemont.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Latin as Falconis montem between 1120 and 1162 CE under Bishop Stephen of Bar of Metz, and later as Falconis mons (1210 CE) and Falquemont (1319 CE).

eponym.details: Named after a post-867 nobleman, Falco (or Folco) of Malberg, who held the motte-and-bailey castle ('mount of Falco', Falconis mons) after 1115 CE.

b_faulquemont.etymology_analysis: From Latin Falconis mons ('mount of Falco'), named after Falco (Folco) of Malberg in the early 12th century, corresponding to German Falkenberg.

b_nancy.first_mention_attestation: First attested around 1050 CE as Nanciaco / Nanciacum when Gerard, Duke of Lorraine, built a small fortified town at the site.
b_nancy.etymology_analysis: Attested as Nanciaco and Nanciacum in the 11th century, formed with the Gallo-Roman estate suffix -iacum attached either to a Gaulish personal name or to a Celtic root related to *nanto ('valley').

b_epinal.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 983 CE as Spinal (and c. 1000 CE as Castrum de Aspinaul) in connection with the foundation of the town and monastery by Bishop Thierry I of Metz.
b_epinal.etymology_analysis: Attested as Spinal in 983 CE (Latinized Spinalium), derived from Latin spina ('thorn') with a collective suffix, referring to a thorny or scrub-covered site along the Moselle.

b_blankenberg.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1034 CE as Lienatis villa (or Lineatis villa), and later as Lunaris villa (1135 CE) and Lunivilla (1154–1157 CE).

morphemes.language: Pre-Roman or Germanic root (later folk-etymologized to Latin luna)

b_blankenberg.etymology_analysis: First recorded as Lienatis villa in 1034 CE; clerical Latinization as Lunaris villa (1135 CE) and folk etymology linked the obscure first element to Latin luna ('moon'), yielding French Lunéville and German Lünstadt.

b_salm.first_mention_attestation: Construction of Château de Salm in the Vosges (Alsace/Lorraine) began in 1205 CE under Henry III, Count of Salm, on territory of the Senones Abbey.

morphemes.translation: dark/black (originally the Salm river in the Ardennes)

b_salm.etymology_analysis: Named after the Counts of Salm (who originated in the Ardennes along the River Salm, from Celtic *salwa 'dark, blurred', later folk-etymologized to German Salm 'salmon'), who built this Vosges stronghold between 1205 and 1225 CE.

b_neufchateau.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Novum Castrum in 1094 CE when Thierry, son of Duke Gerard I of Lorraine, constructed a new castle at the site.
b_neufchateau.etymology_analysis: From Old French Neufchâteau (Latin Novum Castrum, 'new castle'), named for the fortress built by Thierry of Lorraine in 1094 CE.

historical_names.name: Noviomagus
historical_names.source: Roman Antonine Itinerary and Tabula Peutingeriana (3rd–4th century CE).
historical_names.notes: Gallo-Roman market town along the road from Lyon to Trier, known as Noviomagus ('new field/market') before the 1094 CE castle gave rise to Novum Castrum.

b_vaudemont.first_mention_attestation: First attested when the County of Vaudémont was granted to Gerard I in 1070 CE, and in 12th-century charters as Wadonimons (1127–1168 CE) and Gademonte (1135 CE).
b_vaudemont.etymology_analysis: Early forms such as Wadonimons and Wedani mons combine a Germanic personal name (Wado) or the theonym Wodan with Romance mont ('hill, mount'), referring to the fortified hilltop.

b_lure.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing in 817 CE in a document of the Council of Aachen under the form Luterhaa, and subsequently cited in the Treaties of Verdun (843 CE) and Meerssen (870 CE).
b_lure.etymology_analysis: Toponymists (Dauzat, Rostaing, Delamarre) derive Lure from Gaulish lautron ('bath'), referring to the abundant springs, ponds, and marshes surrounding the abbey founded by Saint Desle in the 7th century.
