b_puttlingen.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation exists by 867 CE; Püttlingen is first documented during the Investiture Controversy (1075–1122 CE) when the Bishops of Metz enfeoffed the area to the Lords of Forbach.
b_puttlingen.etymology_analysis: Follows the characteristic Lorraine-Saarland -ingen settlement pattern, combining a Germanic personal name (such as *Puttilo) with the collective suffix -ingen ('settlement of the followers of Puttilo').

b_finstigen.first_mention_attestation: Officially attested on 18 September 1070 CE as Filistenges and Vinstringen in a charter authorizing the abbesses of Remiremont to mint coins there, following an undated 10th-century form Filestengas.
b_finstigen.etymology_analysis: Attested as Filestengas (10th century) and Filistenges / Vinstringen (1070 CE), derived from a Germanic personal name (Filisteus or Filista) with the -ing suffix, Germanized as Finstingen and Frenchified as Fénétrange.

b_saarbrucken.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 999 CE as castellum Sarabrucca in an imperial deed of Emperor Otto III.
b_saarbrucken.etymology_analysis: Recorded as Sarabrucca in 999 CE, combining the river name Saar with either Old High German brucka ('bridge') or Celtic *briga ('hill, rock', reflected in High German Brocken) for the rocky outcrop of the castle.

historical_names.name: Vicus Saravus
historical_names.source: Roman archaeological and epigraphic records of the Gallo-Roman settlement near Halberg hill (1st–5th century CE).
historical_names.notes: A Gallo-Roman vicus named Vicus Saravus existed just west of Halberg hill along the Metz–Worms road from the 1st to 5th centuries CE.

b_zweibrucken.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the late 12th century (c. 1170 CE) as Middle High German Zweinbrücken (Latinized Geminus Pons / Bipontum) as the seat of the County of Zweibrücken.
b_zweibrucken.etymology_analysis: Literally 'two bridges' in German (Latinized as Geminus Pons and Bipontum, and translated into French as Deux-Ponts), referring to two bridges crossing the Schwarzbach river.

b_bitsch.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1172 CE as Bytis Castrum, referring to the stronghold standing on a sandstone rock above the valley; the modern town formed from Rohr and Kaltenhausen in the 17th century.

morphemes.language: Germanic / Gallo-Roman root (possibly personal name Bito)
morphemes.translation: fortress of Bito or wet/marshy place

b_bitsch.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1172 CE as Bytis Castrum, giving its name to the County of Bitsch (French Bitche), likely from an early medieval personal name or local topographic root.

b_trier.first_mention_attestation: Founded by the Romans c. 16 BCE as Augusta Treverorum and attested in writing by Pomponius Mela (De situ orbis, c. 44 CE) and Tacitus (Histories); later shortened to Treveris / Trier.
b_trier.etymology_analysis: Founded as Augusta Treverorum ('city of Augustus among the Treveri'), the name Trier derives from the Late Latin locative form in Treveris, referring to the Celtic Treveri tribe.

b_beda.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Roman itineraries (c. 300 CE) as Vicus Beda, expanded into a road fortress under Constantine I around 330 CE, and documented c. 715 CE as castrum bedense.
b_beda.etymology_analysis: Combines the Celtic toponym Beda (attested in Roman Vicus Beda and Frankish castrum bedense) with German -burg ('fortress'), yielding modern Bitburg.

b_konz.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 371 CE as Contionacum in several imperial edicts of Emperor Valentinian I preserved in the Codex Theodosianus, and mentioned by the Roman poet Ausonius.
b_konz.etymology_analysis: From Latin Contionacum (the Late Roman imperial summer residence at the confluence of the Saar and Moselle), formed with the Gallo-Roman estate suffix -acum and contracted to Konz.

b_wadern.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 950 CE in records connected with Mettlach Abbey.

morphemes.language: Old High German / Moselle Franconian root
morphemes.translation: settlement or personal root (from early medieval Waderella / Wadern)

b_wadern.etymology_analysis: First attested in 950 CE in Mettlach Abbey charters; the name belongs to the early medieval Moselle Franconian toponymic layer of the Hochwald region.

b_najera.first_mention_attestation: First attested in early 10th-century chronicles recounting the 923 CE conquest of the Muslim fortress of Náxara by Ordoño II of León and Sancho Garcés I of Pamplona.

morphemes.translation: place between the rocks / southern place

b_najera.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Arabic name Náxara, traditionally interpreted as 'town between the rocks' (referring to the crags overlooking the Najerilla river).

historical_names.name: Tritium
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (c. 77 CE).
historical_names.notes: Roman town of Tritium Magallum (modern Tricio), whose territory spanned part of modern Nájera and neighboring Tricio.

historical_names.name: Tritium Magallum
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (c. 77 CE).
historical_names.notes: Roman town of Tritium Magallum (modern Tricio), whose territory spanned part of modern Nájera and neighboring Tricio.

b_logrono.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a 965 CE donation charter as Lucronio, when King García Sánchez I of Pamplona granted the site to the Monastery of San Millán.
b_logrono.etymology_analysis: Attested as Lucronio (965 CE) and illo Gronio (1095 CE Fuero of Logroño); most scholars interpret it as the Late Latin article illo prefixed to a Celtic word Gronio/Gronno meaning 'the ford' or 'the crossing' over the Ebro.

b_arnedo.first_mention_attestation: First attested in medieval chronicles for 908–909 CE, when the Muslim town (rendered as Arneto in 10th-century Latin sources) was conquered by Sancho I of Pamplona.
b_arnedo.etymology_analysis: Derived from Latin Arenetum ('place of sand'), referring to the sandy terrace beside the Cidacos river on which the town sits.

b_pamplona.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing in Strabo's Geographica (c. 20 CE) as Pompaelo, founded by the Roman general Pompey during the Sertorian Wars around 75–74 BCE.
b_pamplona.etymology_analysis: Derived from Latin Pompaelo (Strabo's 'Pompeiopolis'), named after Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus who wintered there in 75–74 BCE, combined with a Vasconic element meaning 'city' (parallel to the Basque name Iruña).

b_tafalla.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing in the 10th-century Chronicle of Arib ibn Sa'id, which recounts a raid on Tafalla by Abd al-Rahman III during his 924 CE campaign against Pamplona.

morphemes.translation: medieval Arabicized form of an uncertain local root

b_tafalla.etymology_analysis: Recorded in 10th-century Arabic and Navarrese sources as Tafalla; its ultimate pre-Roman or Arabic etymology remains uncertain, though a Roman predecessor Curnonion has been speculatively proposed for the area.

b_lizarra.first_mention_attestation: Founded and first chartered in 1090 CE by King Sancho Ramírez of Pamplona beside the fortified settlement of Lizarra along the Way of St. James.

morphemes.translation: star (associated with the Milky Way / Compostela pilgrimage)

b_lizarra.etymology_analysis: Combines Romance Estella ('star', linked to the pilgrimage to Santiago) with Basque Lizarra (from lizar 'ash tree' + definite article -a), the name of the adjacent Navarrese settlement.

b_tudela.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing in Martial's Epigrams (Book IV, 55, c. 88–89 CE) as Tutela, and later fortified by the Umayyads in 802 CE under Amrus ibn Yusuf as Tuṭīla.
b_tudela.etymology_analysis: Derived from Latin Tutela ('guardianship' or 'protection'), referring to a Roman defensive post or tutelary settlement in the Ebro valley, later Arabicized as Tuṭīla and Basque Tutera.

b_tarazona.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Isidore of Seville's Historia de regibus Gothorum (c. 624 CE), which records that the Visigothic king Swinthila (621–631 CE) founded the fortified town of Oligicus to control the Vascones.

morphemes.translation: possibly from Latin *olivetum ('olive grove') or a Vasconic root

b_tarazona.etymology_analysis: Recorded as Oligicus in Isidore of Seville's 7th-century chronicle; the name evolved into Spanish Olite (while its official Basque name is Erriberri, meaning 'new town/land').

b_irun.first_mention_attestation: The medieval town of Irun is first documented in 1203 CE in the charter of Fuenterrabía (Hondarribia), standing on the site of the Roman-Vasconic port of Oiasso.
b_irun.etymology_analysis: Derived from Basque *Iri-on (hiri 'town' + on 'good', or a contraction of Iruña 'the city'), replacing the classical name Oiasso.

historical_names.name: Oiasso
historical_names.source: Strabo, Geographica, and Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (1st century CE).
historical_names.notes: Roman-Vasconic port and mining town whose foundations lie directly beneath modern Irun.

b_izurum.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing in 1014 CE, when the monastery of Saint Sebastian (within the boundaries of Hernani) was donated to the Abbey of Leire by King Sancho III of Pamplona.
b_izurum.etymology_analysis: Both Spanish San Sebastián and Basque Donostia (from Done + Sebastian) derive from the monastery of Saint Sebastian (3rd-century martyr) attested in 1014 CE.

b_bilibio.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing in the late 9th century (c. 883 CE) in the Chronicle of Alfonso III under the forms Bizkai and Bizcai.
b_bilibio.etymology_analysis: Linguists (including Koldo Mitxelena) connect Basque Bizkaia (Spanish Vizcaya, English Biscay) with bizkar ('low ridge' or 'prominence'), referring to the hilly coastal terrain.

b_alava.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Arabic chronicles for the year 792 CE under the toponym Al-ba (ألبة), and subsequently in 9th-century Asturian and Muslim accounts.

morphemes.translation: historical Basque territory (possibly linked to Roman mansio Alba or a pre-Roman root)

b_alava.etymology_analysis: Attested as Arabic Al-ba in 792 CE and in 9th-century Asturian chronicles; scholars have debated a connection to the Roman road station Alba (near Albéniz) or a native Basque/pre-Roman root Araba.

b_wismar.first_mention_attestation: Founded around 1226 CE under Henry Borwin I, Lord of Mecklenburg, and granted Lübeck town rights shortly thereafter.

morphemes.translation: high, great (from a Slavic personal name *Vyšemir)

b_wismar.etymology_analysis: Derived from a Polabian Slavic personal name *Vyšemir (or a nearby Slavic settlement/harbor name *Vyšemirja), Germanized as Wismar.

b_ratzeburg.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 11th century as Racisburg, first attested in historical records around 1044 CE when Christian missionaries led by Ansverus established a monastery there.

eponym.details: Named after the 11th-century Polabian Slavic prince Ratibor (nicknamed Ratse), ruler of the Polabians.

b_ratzeburg.etymology_analysis: Attested as Racisburg in the 11th century, combining the shortened name of the Polabian prince Ratibor (Ratse) with German -burg ('castle, stronghold').

b_schwerin.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in writing in 1018 CE by Thietmar of Merseburg as Zuarina (an Obotrite Slavic fortress), and granted city rights in 1160 CE by Henry the Lion.
b_schwerin.etymology_analysis: Attested as Zuarina in 1018 CE, from Polabian Slavic *Zvěrin ('place of wild beasts/game'), later Germanized as Schwerin.

b_parchim.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing in 1170 CE as Parchim (and 1202 CE as Parchem); the German town was founded around 1210 CE.

morphemes.translation: scab, barren/rough ground (or personal name Parchom)

b_parchim.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Polabian *Parchom, either from a Slavic personal name or from *parch ('barren/rough field'), attested from 1170 CE as Parchim.

b_rostock.first_mention_attestation: First attested in historical accounts for 1161 CE when King Valdemar I of Denmark burned the Slavic settlement recorded as Roztoc.
b_rostock.etymology_analysis: From Polabian Slavic Roztoc (*ras-tokŭ, 'fork or widening of a river'), referring to the broadening of the Warnow estuary into the Baltic Sea.

b_gustrow.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1228 in the deed confirming the city rights of Schwerin (with the collegiate church founded in 1226 and a Wendish castle documented at the site from 1219); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_gustrow.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Polabian Slavic form Guščerov, meaning 'place of lizards' (from Proto-Slavic *jaščerъ / Polabian *guščer 'lizard' with the toponymic suffix -ov), adapted into Middle Low German and Modern German as Güstrow.

b_rugen.first_mention_attestation: The island of Rügen is first unambiguously attested as Runa in Adam of Bremen's Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum (c. 1075 CE), while its Slavic inhabitants (the Rani/Rujani) are recorded from 955 CE; earlier classical and early medieval mentions of the Rugii (Tacitus, 98 CE) and Rugini (Bede, c. 731 CE) are tribal ethnonyms rather than a confirmed attestation of the island settlement itself.

morphemes.translation: Rugian / Rani (tribal root, possibly connected to Germanic Rugii)

b_rugen.etymology_analysis: The island's name derives from the medieval West Slavic tribe of the Rani (Rujani / Rugiani), whose ethnonym is frequently linked to the earlier East Germanic Rugii recorded in the Baltic region by Tacitus; the Slavic form was adapted into German as Rügen.

b_stralsund.first_mention_attestation: Founded and granted town privileges in 1234 by Prince Wizlaw I of Rügen (with the form Stralesund recorded in 1240); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_stralsund.etymology_analysis: A hybrid Slavic-Germanic compound combining the Polabian name of the adjacent island/fishing village Strale or Stralow ('arrow', cognate with Polish strzała) with the Middle Low German sund ('strait, sound'), referring to the Strelasund strait separating Rügen from the mainland.

b_werle.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1160 in Helmold of Bosau's Chronica Slavorum as the Obotrite stronghold Burg Werle, where Prince Niklot was killed during Henry the Lion's campaign; no written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: bend, curve, or elevated bank (or personal name)

b_werle.etymology_analysis: The name of the Obotrite stronghold Werle (near modern Kassow on the Warnow river) derives from a Polabian Slavic toponymic root adapted into Low German as Werle, later giving its name to the Lordship of Werle.

b_neubrandenburg.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1248 by Margrave John I of Brandenburg on the shore of Lake Tollense; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_neubrandenburg.etymology_analysis: Literally 'New Brandenburg', named in 1248 by the Ascanian Margrave John I of Brandenburg after the older seat of Brandenburg an der Havel (itself from Polabian Branibor + German Burg 'castle').

b_neustrelitz.first_mention_attestation: Laid out as a new ducal residence in 1733 (becoming capital of Mecklenburg-Strelitz in 1736) near the older town of Strelitz after the latter burned in 1712; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_neustrelitz.etymology_analysis: Literally 'New Strelitz', combining German neu ('new') with Strelitz, which derives from the Polabian word Strelci ('archers' or 'shooters', cognate with Russian streltsy).

b_wolgast.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1128 during Bishop Otto of Bamberg's second missionary journey to Pomerania (recorded in the biographies by Ebo and Herbord); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_wolgast.etymology_analysis: Derived from a West Slavic (Polabian/Pomeranian) personal or tribal name *Voligost (from *vol-/*vel- 'great/will' + *gostь 'guest/host'), Germanized as Wolgast.

b_griefswald.first_mention_attestation: Originates with the foundation of Eldena (Hilda) Abbey by Cistercian monks in 1199, with market rights granted to Greifswald in 1241 and Lübeck town law in 1250; no written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: griffin (heraldic emblem of the Dukes of Pomerania)

b_griefswald.etymology_analysis: Literally 'Griffin's Forest' (Middle Low German Gripeswolt), referring to the griffin emblem of the House of Griffins (Dukes of Pomerania) and the wooded clearing around Eldena Abbey.

b_berlin.first_mention_attestation: Berlin is first mentioned in a written document in 1244 (with its sister settlement Cölln first attested in 1237); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_berlin.etymology_analysis: Of West Slavic (Polabian) origin, formed from a root *berl-/*bьrl- ('swamp, bog') with the Slavic toponymic suffix -in; the association with German Bär ('bear') is a later folk etymology.

b_botzow.first_mention_attestation: Originally attested in 1216 CE as Bötzow, the town was renamed Oranienburg in 1653 CE after Princess Louise Henriette of Orange-Nassau (Oranien-Nassau).

eponym.details: Named Oranienburg in 1653 after Princess Louise Henriette of Orange-Nassau (Oranien-Nassau, 1627–1667), wife of Elector Frederick William of Brandenburg, who built a Dutch-style palace there.

b_botzow.etymology_analysis: Originally a Slavic settlement named Bötzow (attested 1216), it was renamed Oranienburg ('Orange Castle') in 1653 after Princess Louise Henriette of Orange-Nassau, who commissioned Schloss Oranienburg.

b_rosenfelde.first_mention_attestation: Originally attested in 1265 CE as Rosenfelde, the village and estate were renamed Friedrichsfelde in 1699 CE after Frederick III, Elector of Brandenburg.

eponym.details: Renamed Friedrichsfelde in 1699 after Frederick III, Elector of Brandenburg (1657–1713, later King Frederick I in Prussia).

b_rosenfelde.etymology_analysis: Originally attested in 1265 as Rosenfelde ('rose field'), the settlement was renamed Friedrichsfelde ('Frederick's field') in 1699 in honor of Elector Frederick III of Brandenburg.

b_brandenburg.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 928/929 CE in Widukind of Corvey's Res gestae Saxonicae as the Hevelli stronghold Brennaburg (conquered by King Henry I), and in 948 CE when Otto I founded the Bishopric of Brandenburg; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_brandenburg.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Polabian name Branibor (variously interpreted as 'marshy forest' or 'defensive pine forest', or linked to a personal name), adapted into German as Brennaburg and Brandenburg.

b_potsdam.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned as Poztupimi in a 993 CE deed of Emperor Otto III gifting the place to Quedlinburg Abbey; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_potsdam.etymology_analysis: Attested in 993 CE as Poztupimi, generally explained as deriving from an Old West Slavic (Polabian) phrase *pod dubimi ('beneath the oaks') or a personal name *Postąpim, later Germanized as Potsdam.

b_lehnin.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1180 when Margrave Otto I of Brandenburg founded the Cistercian Lehnin Abbey (Kloster Lehnin); no written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: hind, deer, or lazy/sluggish water (with -in suffix)

b_lehnin.etymology_analysis: Kloster ('monastery') refers to the Cistercian abbey founded in 1180; Lehnin is of Polabian Slavic origin (either from *lenь 'hind/deer' or a personal/topographic root with the Slavic -in suffix).

b_tangermunde.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1009 CE in the chronicle of Thietmar of Merseburg (with the town itself documented in a 1275 deed); no written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: the Tanger river (tributary of the Elbe)

b_tangermunde.etymology_analysis: Named for its location at the mouth (German Mündung) of the Tanger river where it flows into the Elbe.

b_havelberg.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 948 CE when Emperor Otto I founded the Bishopric of Havelberg; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_havelberg.etymology_analysis: A German compound combining the river name Havel (recorded in classical/early sources as Habola/Havela) with -berg ('hill, mountain'), referring to the ridge overlooking the Havel near its confluence with the Elbe.

b_klenow.first_mention_attestation: Originally attested in 1333 CE as Klenow, the ducal residence was renamed Ludwigslust ('Ludwig's pleasure') in 1754 CE after Duke Christian Ludwig II of Mecklenburg-Schwerin.

eponym.details: Named Ludwigslust ('Ludwig's pleasure') in 1754 after Duke Christian Ludwig II of Mecklenburg-Schwerin (1683–1756), who built a hunting lodge on the site of Klenow in 1724.

b_klenow.etymology_analysis: The original Slavic village name Klenow (attested 1333 as villa Clonow, from Polabian *klen 'maple tree' + -ow) was replaced in 1754 by Ludwigslust ('Ludwig's pleasure'), after Duke Christian Ludwig II of Mecklenburg-Schwerin.

b_prenzlau.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a written document in 1187 (and described in 1188 as a castle with market and tavern, castrum cum foro et taberna); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_prenzlau.etymology_analysis: Derived from a West Slavic personal name (such as Premyslav or Pręmysł) with the possessive suffix -ov, Germanized as Prenzlau.

b_templin.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned as Templyn in a deed dated 2 October 1270 issued by Bishop Henry of Ostheeren of Brandenburg; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_templin.etymology_analysis: Recorded in 1270 as Templyn; scholars derive it either from a Slavic toponymic root meaning 'stump' (with suffix -in) or from a Germanic root meaning 'pointed hill'.

b_schwedt.first_mention_attestation: First documented in August 1265 under the form Scwet; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_schwedt.etymology_analysis: First attested as Scwet in 1265, the name derives from a West Lechitic descendant of Proto-Slavic *světъ ('light, bright'), referring to a bright or cleared place by the Oder.

b_eberswalde.first_mention_attestation: Established as Everswolde in 1254 by the Ascanian Margrave John I of Brandenburg and first mentioned in a written document on 23 April 1276; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_eberswalde.etymology_analysis: Derived from Middle Low German Everswolde, meaning 'forest of the boars' (Eber 'boar' + Wald 'forest').

b_ruppin.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1238 as Ruppin (founded by the Counts of Lindow-Ruppin beside the older settlement of Alt Ruppin); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_ruppin.etymology_analysis: Combines German neu ('new', distinguishing it from Alt Ruppin) with the Slavic toponym Ruppin, marked by the Slavic suffix -in.

b_lindow.first_mention_attestation: Town history begins around 1230 with the foundation of the Cistercian nunnery (Kloster Lindow) by the Counts of Arnstein (who also styled themselves Counts of Lindau); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_lindow.etymology_analysis: Named by its founders, the Counts of Arnstein, after their possession Lindau in Anhalt (ultimately from 'linden tree' or a Slavicized -ow form).

b_nowen.first_mention_attestation: The settlement of Nowen is first mentioned in an 1186 deed issued by the Bishop of Brandenburg; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_nowen.etymology_analysis: First attested as Nowen in 1186, likely from a Polabian Slavic root *nov- ('new') or a transferred Low German settlement name, evolving into Modern German Nauen.

b_schwetz.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a written document in 1198; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_schwetz.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Polish verb świecić ('to shine'), referring to a bright or sunlit clearing/site by the Vistula; Germanized as Schwetz.

b_berent.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a 1284 document of Duke Mestwin II of Pomerelia under the name Costerina; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_berent.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1284 as Costerina, the Polish/Kashubian name derives from Slavic *kostьrь ('thickets, shrubs') with the suffix -ina; the later German name Berent (earlier Bern) arose as a separate Germanized/settlement form.

b_tuchowna.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1287 when the local church was consecrated by Archbishop Jakub Świnka of Gniezno (with archaeological settlement from c. 980 CE); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_tuchowna.etymology_analysis: Represented in CK3 by the key b_tuchowna (corresponding to Tuchola, German Tuchel, in Pomerelia), the name derives from the Old Polish personal name Tuchoł or the Slavic root *tuch-, adapted into German as Tuchel.

b_konitz.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 1205 in Piast Poland (and documented under Pomerelian and Teutonic rule in the 13th–14th centuries); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_konitz.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Polish/Pomeranian word chojna ('pine tree, pine forest') with the plural toponymic suffix -ice, Germanized as Konitz.

b_gdansk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 997 CE (as Gyddanyzc in the Vita sancti Adalberti, written c. 1000 CE) during Saint Adalbert of Prague's mission; no written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: wet, moist (or Gdania, former name of the Motława river)

b_gdansk.etymology_analysis: Derived either from Gdania (an older name for the Motława river) or directly from the Proto-Slavic root *gъd- ('wet, moist') with the suffix -ńsk; Germanized as Danzig.

b_sopot.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in a written document as Sopoth in 1283 (and Sopot in 1291); no written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: stream, spring (onomatopoeic for murmuring running water)

b_sopot.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Old Lechitic word sopot meaning 'stream' or 'spring', an onomatopoeic formation imitating the sound of running water; Germanized as Zoppot.

b_wladyslawowo.first_mention_attestation: First officially recorded in 1635 as the fort Władysławowo on the Hel Peninsula (designed in 1634 by Fryderyk Getkant), while the modern fishing port was built in 1936–1938 on the site of Wielka Wieś (Großendorf); no written attestation <= 867 CE.

eponym.details: Named after King Władysław IV Vasa of Poland (1595–1648), who initiated the construction of the Polish Navy and commissioned the nearby fort Władysławowo in 1634–1635.

b_wladyslawowo.etymology_analysis: Formed from the royal given name Władysław (King Władysław IV Vasa) and the Polish possessive toponymic suffix -owo.

b_trsow.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1198 as Trsow in a charter of Duke Grimislav granting lands to the Knights Hospitaller (and later recorded as Dersowe/Dirschau in 1252); no written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: weaver or reed/bush root (or personal name Dersław for Dirschau)

b_trsow.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1198 as Trsow (evolving into modern Polish Tczew, associated with 'weaver's town'), while the parallel form Dersowe / German Dirschau derives from the personal name Dersław.

b_hammerstein.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1388–1389 as Hammerstein, a site of negotiations between the Teutonic Order and the Dukes of Pomerania (receiving Kulm town rights in 1395); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_hammerstein.etymology_analysis: The modern Polish name Czarne ('black [place/river]') was introduced after 1945, replacing the medieval German name Hammerstein ('hammer stone', referring to an iron hammer mill at the Teutonic castle).

b_miastko.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a 1478 feudal document as the village of Rummelsburg (with a Massow family reference as lords of Rummelsburg after 1335, and town status by 1506/1617); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_miastko.etymology_analysis: Miastko literally means 'little town' in Polish (diminutive of miasto, calquing its historical description as a Städtchen), replacing the earlier German name Rummelsburg in Pommern.

b_slupsk.first_mention_attestation: First historically referenced around 1015 CE in connection with Bolesław I the Brave (and unambiguously documented in charters of Świętopełk II in 1236 as castellanus de Slupcz); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_slupsk.etymology_analysis: Derived from Pomeranian/Polish słup ('pole, pile', referring to pile-built structures on marshy ground) or stołp ('tower, keep') on the Słupia river, with the toponymic suffix -sk; Germanized as Stolp.

b_koszalin.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1214 in a donation to the Premonstratensian monastery at Belbuck (receiving Lübeck law in 1266); no written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: personal name Koszala (from kosz 'basket' or koszaly)

b_koszalin.etymology_analysis: Derived from a Pomeranian Slavic personal name (such as Koszala) with the possessive suffix -in, Germanized as Köslin.

b_lebno.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1320 as a settlement by the Łeba river (locus prope fluvium Lebam, originally Łebno), and chartered as Lewinburg (later Lauenburg) in 1341 by the Teutonic Knights; no written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: from the Łeba river / Łebno (folk-etymologized as Low German Lau 'lion')

b_lebno.etymology_analysis: The earlier Slavic settlement name Łebno (derived from the Łeba river) was adapted by the Teutonic Order into Lewinburg and Low German Lauenburg ('lion castle'), which was subsequently Polonized as Lembork and Lębork.

b_bytow.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in a 1321 donation charter of Duke Wartislaw IV of Pomerania (passing to the Teutonic Order in 1329 and receiving Kulm law in 1346); no written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: personal name Byt (from Slavic *byti 'to be, dwelling')

b_bytow.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Slavic personal name Byt (or *byt 'dwelling') with the possessive suffix -ów; Germanized as Bütow.

b_cammin.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written documents in 1124 (in connection with Otto of Bamberg's Pomeranian mission, becoming the seat of the Bishopric of Cammin in 1176); no written attestation <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: stone, rock (referring to a large glacial boulder in the Dziwna)

b_cammin.etymology_analysis: Named Kamień ('stone, rock') after a massive glacial boulder in the Dziwna riverbed (Germanized as Cammin/Kammin), with the post-1945 Polish qualifier Pomorski ('Pomeranian').

b_dramberg.first_mention_attestation: Founded and granted town charter in 1297 as Dramburg under the Margraves of Brandenburg; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_dramberg.etymology_analysis: Both the Polish name Drawsko (from the Drawa river + -sko) and the historical German name Dramburg (from the river Drage/Drawa + -burg 'fortress') derive from the hydronym Drawa.

b_belgard.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the early 12th-century chronicle of Gallus Anonymous (Gesta principum Polonorum) in connection with Bolesław III Wrymouth's 1102–1107 campaigns in Pomerania; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_belgard.etymology_analysis: Derived from Pomeranian Slavic *Bělogard ('white stronghold/town', from *bělъ 'white' + *gardъ 'stronghold'), Germanized as Belgard.

b_swinoujscie.first_mention_attestation: Swinemünde was founded in 1748 on the site of the village of Westswine (with 12th-century predecessors along the Świna strait) and received town privileges in 1765; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_swinoujscie.etymology_analysis: Polish Świnoujście is a calque of the German name Swinemünde, meaning 'mouth of the Świna' (the central outlet of the Szczecin Lagoon into the Baltic Sea).

b_kolobrzeg.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1000 CE by Thietmar of Merseburg as Salsa Cholbergiensis when the Bishopric of Kołobrzeg was established during the Congress of Gniezno; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_kolobrzeg.etymology_analysis: Derived from Slavic *Kolobreg ('by the shore', from koło 'by/near' + brzeg 'shore'), recorded in Latinized form as Cholberg in 1000 CE and Germanized as Kolberg.

b_stargad.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written sources in 1124 (when part of Poland under Bolesław III Wrymouth, receiving Magdeburg rights in 1243); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_stargad.etymology_analysis: Of Pomeranian Slavic origin meaning 'old stronghold/town' (from stari 'old' + gard 'town/stronghold').

b_lobez.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a 1271 document referring to the knight Borco as dominus de Lobis (Lord of Łobez); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_lobez.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1271 as Lobis (German Labes), the name derives from an Old Slavic/Pomeranian word denoting riverside thickets/bushes (or, in older hypotheses, 'swan').

b_landsberg.first_mention_attestation: Founded and granted city rights in 1257 by Margrave John I of Brandenburg as Landsberg an der Warthe; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_landsberg.etymology_analysis: Founded in 1257 as German Landsberg an der Warthe ('land castle/hill on the Warta'), it was renamed Gorzów Wielkopolski after 1945 (from a 19th-century Polish name form linked to gorzenie/góra plus the regional qualifier Wielkopolski).

b_driesen.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1092 CE in the chronicle of Gallus Anonymous as the Polish stronghold of Drzeń; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_driesen.etymology_analysis: Derived from the older Polish stronghold name Drzeń (attested 1092, related to Old Slavic *drězga 'forest'), which was adapted into German as Driesen and re-Polonized in diminutive form as Drezdenko.

b_arnswalde.first_mention_attestation: First unambiguously attested as a town in 1284 (the surrounding area was donated to Kołbacz Abbey in 1233/1237, though the supposed 1233/1234 mention of Hoscno is refuted); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_arnswalde.etymology_analysis: The Polish name Choszczno derives from Old Polish chwoszcz ('horsetail/brushwood') with the suffix -no; the medieval German name Arnswalde means 'eagle's forest'.

b_kreuz.first_mention_attestation: Developed as a railway junction settlement (Kreuz) upon the opening of the Poznań–Szczecin railway in 1848 and Berlin–Königsberg railway in 1851 (adjacent to the 18th-century village of Łokacz, receiving town rights in 1936); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_kreuz.etymology_analysis: Polish Krzyż ('cross', calquing German Kreuz) refers to the crossing of two major 19th-century railway lines (Poznań–Szczecin and Berlin–Bydgoszcz), with Wielkopolski added to denote Greater Poland.

b_walcz.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1303 when it was granted city rights by the Margraves of Brandenburg; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_walcz.etymology_analysis: The Polish name Wałcz derives from an Old Polish personal name (Wałek) or topographic root with a possessive suffix, while its historical German name Deutsch Krone ('German Crown') was used during Brandenburg-Prussian rule.

b_pila.first_mention_attestation: First reliably attested in 1449 parish church records as Piła-Snydemole, with a 1456 letter of Elector Frederick II of Brandenburg also citing burghers of Snydemole and Piła; an earlier 1380s foundation charter is attributed to Queen Jadwiga.
b_pila.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Polish common noun piła ('saw'), referring to a water-powered sawmill on the Gwda river that formed the economic core of the medieval settlement, mirrored in its former German name Schneidemühl ('sawmill').

b_szczecinek.first_mention_attestation: Founded and first attested in 1310 CE when Duke Wartislaw IV of Pomerania-Wolgast granted town rights to the new settlement under the name Neustettin.
b_szczecinek.etymology_analysis: The modern Polish name Szczecinek is a diminutive of Szczecin ('Little Szczecin'), calquing the original 14th-century German name Neustettin ('New Stettin') bestowed in reference to the Pomeranian ducal capital.

b_soldin.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written records as Soldin in a 1270 CE deed, shortly before a Dominican monastery was founded there in 1275 CE.
b_soldin.etymology_analysis: The modern Polish name Myślibórz (adopted after 1945) is a possessive toponym from the Old Polish personal name Myślibor; the historical medieval name Soldin derives from an earlier West Slavic (Pomeranian/Polabian) root.

b_kostschin.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1232 CE in a Polish charter issued by Duke Władysław Odonic granting the settlement to the Knights Templar.

morphemes.translation: brome grass, reed, or marshy thicket

b_kostschin.etymology_analysis: Kostrzyn derives from the Old Polish root kostra/kostrzewa (referring to marsh grasses or reeds typical of the Oder-Warta confluence) with the toponymic suffix -in; nad Odrą ('upon the Oder') distinguishes it from Kostrzyn in Greater Poland.

b_szczecin.first_mention_attestation: First potentially attested in writing around 991 CE as Schinesghe in the Dagome iudex (though debated with Gniezno), and unambiguously attested in the early 12th century during Bolesław III Wrymouth's and Otto of Bamberg's Pomeranian campaigns.
b_szczecin.etymology_analysis: Linguists generally derive Szczecin from a Proto-Slavic root *ščet- ('bristle' or 'crest/ridge', referring either to stiff marsh vegetation or a personal name *Ščeta) combined with the possessive toponymic suffix *-inъ.

b_ucramund.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written documents as Ucramund in 1178 CE (with another attestation in 1223 CE), although the Slavic tribe of the Ukrani was recorded in the region by Widukind of Corvey in 934 CE.
b_ucramund.etymology_analysis: A German-Slavic hybrid toponym meaning 'mouth of the Uecker', combining the river name Uecker (from the West Slavic tribal/river name of the Ukrani) with German Münde ('river mouth'), where the river empties into the Szczecin Lagoon.

b_gryfino.first_mention_attestation: The settlement of Pyrzyce was first mentioned in written sources in 1124 CE by Bishop Otto of Bamberg during his Pomeranian mission, though the regional tribe of the Prissani was recorded around 850 CE by the Bavarian Geographer.

morphemes.translation: spelt, couch grass, or fertile grain

b_gryfino.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Proto-Slavic *pyrъ ('spelt' or 'wheat-grass'), reflecting the fertile agricultural plain around the stronghold, with the Slavic toponymic suffix -ica (pluralized in Polish as Pyrzyce, German Pyritz).

b_ancona.first_mention_attestation: Founded around 387 BCE by Greek colonists from Syracuse under the name Ankṓn (Ἀγκών) and attested in classical Greek and Roman historiography.
b_ancona.etymology_analysis: Named by its Syracusan Greek founders from Ancient Greek ἀγκών (ankṓn, 'elbow'), referring to the elbow-shaped rocky promontory that shelters the city's natural harbor on the Adriatic Sea.

b_cagli.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Roman antiquity as Cale, a station on the Via Flaminia marked by the Republican-era Ponte Mallio (c. 220 BCE) and Roman itineraries.
b_cagli.etymology_analysis: Evolves from the ancient Roman toponym Cale (pluralized/palatalized in medieval Italian as Cagli), likely from an Italic or pre-Roman root *cal- meaning 'rock' or 'narrow pass' along the Burano valley.

b_gubbio.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Iguvine Tablets (3rd–1st century BCE, written in Umbrian) as Ikuvium, and in Roman sources as Iguvium.

morphemes.translation: ancient Umbrian root of uncertain meaning

b_gubbio.etymology_analysis: Derives from the Umbrian toponym Ikuvium, Latinized as Iguvium and later Eugubium, which yielded medieval and modern Italian Gubbio through apheresis of the initial vowel.

b_camerino.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Livy as Camerinum in 309 BCE, when the Umbrian city concluded a treaty of alliance with the Roman Republic.

morphemes.translation: tribal or topographic root (linked to Camertes)

b_camerino.etymology_analysis: From Latin Camerinum, the town of the Camertes (an Umbrian people), formed with the Latin toponymic suffix -īnum; the name evolved regularly into Italian Camerino.

b_fermo.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the Roman Latin colony of Firmum Picenum in 264 BCE at the start of the First Punic War and attested in Roman histories.
b_fermo.etymology_analysis: Derived from Latin Firmum (Picenum), meaning 'the stronghold' or 'firm place' (from firmus), referring to its fortified hilltop position overlooking the Adriatic coast.

b_ascoli_piceno.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Roman history as Asculum (or Asculum Picenum), becoming a Roman civitas foederata in 268 BCE and playing a central role in the Social War (91–89 BCE).

morphemes.translation: ancient Italic root (possibly linked to ash trees or oak/height)

b_ascoli_piceno.etymology_analysis: Ascoli continues Latin Asculum (of pre-Roman Picene origin), while the qualifier Piceno (from Latin Picenum, the territory of the Picentes) was added to distinguish it from Ascoli Satriano in Apulia.

b_macerata.first_mention_attestation: Macerata was established as a free municipality (comune) in August 1138 CE through the union of two hilltop settlements founded after the decline of nearby Roman Helvia Recina.
b_macerata.etymology_analysis: Derived from Late Latin maceria ('stone wall' or 'ruins'), referring either to defensive dry-stone walls or the stone ruins of nearby Roman Helvia Recina reused on the hilltop.

historical_names.name: Ricina
historical_names.source: Roman imperial inscriptions and itineraries (re-founded as a colony under Septimius Severus, 195–205 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman Ricina lay in the Potenza valley just below the modern hill of Macerata; its inhabitants relocated to the hilltops after late antique invasions.

historical_names.name: Helvia Recina
historical_names.source: Roman imperial inscriptions and itineraries (re-founded as a colony under Septimius Severus, 195–205 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman Ricina lay in the Potenza valley just below the modern hill of Macerata; its inhabitants relocated to the hilltops after late antique invasions.

b_urbino.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Urbinum in Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia (c. 77 CE) and later prominent in Procopius's account of the Gothic War in 538 CE.
b_urbino.etymology_analysis: From Latin Urbinum (specifically Urbinum Mataurense), traditionally explained as a diminutive/adjectival formation from Latin urbs ('city'), meaning 'little city', yielding Italian Urbino.

b_civitas_castelli.first_mention_attestation: Attested in antiquity as Tiphernum Tiberinum by Pliny the Elder (c. 77 CE) and Pliny the Younger; fortified by the Lombards after 601 CE as Castrum Felicitatis before taking the name Città di Castello around 1000 CE.
b_civitas_castelli.etymology_analysis: Italian Città di Castello ('City of the Castle', Latin Civitas Castelli) replaced the early medieval Lombard name Castrum Felicitatis ('Fortress of Felicity') and ancient Tiphernum Tiberinum around 1000 CE.

historical_names.name: Tiphernum Tiberinum
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (c. 77 CE), and early medieval Lombard records
historical_names.notes: Ancient Roman municipium on the upper Tiber, renamed Castrum Felicitatis in the 7th century and Città di Castello c. 1000 CE.

historical_names.name: Castrum Felicitatis
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (c. 77 CE), and early medieval Lombard records
historical_names.notes: Ancient Roman municipium on the upper Tiber, renamed Castrum Felicitatis in the 7th century and Città di Castello c. 1000 CE.

b_pesaro.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the Roman colony of Pisaurum in 184 BCE in the territory of the Picentes and attested in Livy and Roman inscriptions.
b_pesaro.etymology_analysis: Derives from Latin Pisaurum, named after the Pisaurus river (modern Foglia) at whose mouth the Roman colony was founded in 184 BCE.

b_roma.first_mention_attestation: Traditionally founded in 753 BCE and continuously attested in Latin and Greek literary and epigraphic records from the early Roman Republic onward.

morphemes.translation: uncertain root (traditionally linked to Romulus or Etruscan Ruma/Tiber)

b_roma.etymology_analysis: From Latin Rōma, whose ultimate origin is debated among scholars—variously linked to an Etruscan gentilicium *Ruma, an archaic name of the Tiber (*Rumon), or the legendary eponymous founder Romulus.

b_ostia.first_mention_attestation: Historically attested as Rome's fortified port castrum at the mouth of the Tiber by c. 338 BCE (with Roman tradition attributing an earlier foundation to Ancus Marcius).
b_ostia.etymology_analysis: Derived from Latin ōstium ('mouth' or 'entrance', plural ōstia), referring directly to the town's strategic position at the mouth of the Tiber River.

b_vaticano.first_mention_attestation: The Vatican Hill (Mons Vaticanus / Ager Vaticanus) is attested in classical Roman sources from the 1st century BCE/CE, and Old St. Peter's Basilica was built on the site around 326 CE.

morphemes.translation: of Vatica/Vaticum (Etruscan settlement or prophetic root)

b_vaticano.etymology_analysis: Named after Vatican Hill (Latin Mons Vaticanus), derived from the name of an Etruscan settlement (Vatica or Vaticum) in the area the Romans called Ager Vaticanus.

b_palo.first_mention_attestation: The medieval Castello di Palo at Palo Laziale was built in the High Middle Ages around the 12th century CE on the coast near Ladispoli, on the site of ancient Alsium.
b_palo.etymology_analysis: Palo derives from Latin pālus ('stake' or 'palisade', or alternatively palūs 'marsh'), referring to coastal fortifications or wetlands; Laziale was added in modern times to specify its location in Lazio.

historical_names.name: Alsium
historical_names.source: Roman sources on the coastal colony founded at Alsium in 247 BCE (port of Etruscan Caere)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Etruscan port of Caere and Roman maritime colony located directly at modern Palo Laziale.

b_paterno.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE for the medieval settlement of Paterno in Sabina (near Castel Sant'Angelo, Rieti); the nearby Lake of Paterno was known in antiquity as Aquae Cutiliae.

morphemes.translation: paternal, ancestral (from pater 'father', or gentilicium Paternus)

b_paterno.etymology_analysis: Derives from Latin (fundus) Paternus or Paternianus, indicating a Roman rural estate belonging to a landowner named Paternus or a family inheritance.

historical_names.name: Aquae Cutiliae
historical_names.source: Marcus Terentius Varro and Pliny the Elder (1st century BCE–1st century CE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Sabine sacred lake and Roman thermal settlement adjacent to modern Paterno in the province of Rieti.

historical_names.name: Cutilia
historical_names.source: Marcus Terentius Varro and Pliny the Elder (1st century BCE–1st century CE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Sabine sacred lake and Roman thermal settlement adjacent to modern Paterno in the province of Rieti.

b_farfa.first_mention_attestation: Farfa Abbey was refounded around 680 CE by Thomas of Maurienne under Lombard patronage and is extensively documented in early medieval charters from the late 7th and 8th centuries.

morphemes.translation: ancient hydronym of the Farfa stream (a tributary of the Tiber)

b_farfa.etymology_analysis: Named after the Farfa stream (ancient Latin Farfarus, mentioned by Virgil and Ovid), a Sabine-Latin hydronym whose root may be related to Sabine *farfarus ('white poplar' or 'coltsfoot').

b_tivoli.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Roman historical tradition as Tibur from the 5th century BCE (e.g., 446 BCE) and allied with Rome after the Latin War in 338 BCE.

morphemes.translation: ancient Italic toponym (traditionally linked to mythical Tiburtus)

b_tivoli.etymology_analysis: Evolves from Latin Tibur (locative/ablative Tiburi > Tivoli), an ancient Italic city name at the falls of the Aniene River, traditionally attributed to the legendary founder Tiburtus.

b_velletri.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Roman histories as the Volscian city of Velitrae from the early 5th century BCE (494 BCE), and in medieval records from 465 CE via its bishop Adeodatus.
b_velletri.etymology_analysis: Derives from Volscian Velester and Latin Velitrae, associated with an Italic root *vel- meaning 'marsh' or 'swamp', referencing the nearby Pontine wetlands below the Alban Hills.

b_segni.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Roman sources as Signia, where Tarquinius Superbus established a Roman outpost and additional colonists were sent in 495 BCE.
b_segni.etymology_analysis: Evolves regularly from Latin Signia (Greek Σιγνία), an ancient hilltop stronghold in the Lepini Mountains overlooking the Sacco valley.

b_terracina.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 509 BCE in the first treaty between Rome and Carthage under Roman supremacy, and known in ancient sources as Latin Tarracina and Volscian Anxur.

morphemes.translation: Etruscan Tarquinii clan name or pre-Roman coastal root

b_terracina.etymology_analysis: Derives from Latin Tarracina (Greek Ταρρακινή), attributed by scholars either to a pre-Indo-European substrate or to the Etruscan family name Tarchna (Tarquinius), predating the Volscian name Anxur.

b_viterbo.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the 8th century CE as Castrum Viterbii when it was fortified in 773 CE by the Lombard king Desiderius in his campaign against Rome.
b_viterbo.etymology_analysis: Commonly derived from Medieval Latin Vetus Urbs ('Old City', attested as Castrum Viterbii in the 8th century), though folk etymology later connected it to a Roman Vicus Antonii or Etruscan roots.

b_sutri.first_mention_attestation: Attested as the Latin colony of Sutrium founded in the early 4th century BCE (c. 383 BCE) on the road into Etruria, and famously recorded in the 728 CE Donation of Sutri.
b_sutri.etymology_analysis: Continues Latin Sutrium (from an Etruscan substrate name), whose locative form Sutri became the modern Italian name.

b_civitavecchia.first_mention_attestation: Built and attested around 106 CE as Centumcellae by Emperor Trajan (described by Pliny the Younger) as a major imperial port north of Rome.
b_civitavecchia.etymology_analysis: Italian Civitavecchia ('Old City', Latin Civitas Vetus) arose in the 9th century to distinguish the older Roman port of Centumcellae from the nearby refuge town of Leopolis founded by Pope Leo IV.

historical_names.name: Centumcellae
historical_names.source: Pliny the Younger, Epistulae (c. 106–107 CE, describing Trajan's villa and harbor at Centumcellae)
historical_names.notes: Called Centumcellae throughout antiquity and Civitas Vetus ('Civitavecchia') after its 9th-century Saracen sack and temporary relocation to Leopolis.

b_bologna.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the Roman colony of Bononia in 189 BCE on the site of the earlier Etruscan city of Felsina and Boii Gallic settlement, and attested in Livy and Polybius.
b_bologna.etymology_analysis: Derived from Latin Bonōnia, which adapts the Gaulish name given by the Boii (likely containing Celtic *bona 'foundation/settlement' or a tribal/personal root), evolving into Italian Bologna.

historical_names.name: Felsina
historical_names.source: Livy and Roman sources on the 189 BCE founding of Colonia Bononia
historical_names.notes: Etruscan Felsina (6th century BCE) preceded the Boii and Roman Bononia.

b_cona.first_mention_attestation: The settlement of Cona along the Po di Volano near Ferrara is first attested in written documents in 1183 CE.

morphemes.translation: bend, recess, or fork of a river

b_cona.etymology_analysis: Historically derived from a Byzantine Greek hydrographic term (cona) used in medieval Po Delta charters to denote a river bend, recess, or the bifurcation point of the Po di Volano.

b_monte_sole.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Monte Sole is a mountain massif south of Bologna in the Apennines, designated as a regional historical park in 1989 to commemorate the 1944 Marzabotto massacre.
b_monte_sole.etymology_analysis: A descriptive Italian oronym meaning 'Mount of the Sun' (from Latin mons + sōl), referring to the sun-exposed massif between the Reno and Setta valleys.

b_casentino.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE for the valley choronym Casentino, which is documented in the High Middle Ages under the rule of the Conti Guidi.

morphemes.translation: root associated with Etruscan/Roman Clusium or Casinum

b_casentino.etymology_analysis: Regional choronym for the upper Arno valley in Tuscany, traditionally traced to a Latinized form *Clusentinum or *Casentinum from an Etruscan or Italic root.

b_montefeltro.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 9th century CE (including the Roman synod of 826 CE) as the seat of the Diocese of Montefeltro (Mons Feretri), centered on the rocky spur of San Leo.

morphemes.translation: of the bier (feretrum) or Jupiter Feretrius

b_montefeltro.etymology_analysis: From Latin Mons Feretri, referring to the rocky hill of San Leo—either from its shape resembling an ancient funerary bier (feretrum) or from a temple to Jupiter Feretrius—which later shifted to Montefeltro.

b_camaldoli.first_mention_attestation: Founded around 1012 CE by Saint Romuald on land granted by a certain Maldolus, and attested in Bishop Tedald of Arezzo's diploma of 1027 CE as 'Campus Malduli'.

eponym.details: Named after Maldolus (Latin Campus Malduli, 'Maldolo's field'), the 11th-century landowner who donated the mountain site to Saint Romuald around 1012 CE.

b_camaldoli.etymology_analysis: Contracted from Medieval Latin Campus Malduli ('field of Maldolus'), documented in 1027 CE, which evolved through Campo Maldoli into Camaldoli.

b_ferrara.first_mention_attestation: First appears in a document of the Lombard king Desiderius in 753 CE, when he captured the town from the Exarchate of Ravenna, before it was donated to the Papacy in 754–756 CE.
b_ferrara.etymology_analysis: From Medieval Latin Ferrāria, likely denoting a place associated with ironworking or iron trade along the Po river branches (or alternatively linked to a personal/imperial name).

b_pomposa.first_mention_attestation: The earliest documented report of a Benedictine abbey at Pomposa dates to 874 CE (though local tradition attributes its foundation to the 6th–7th centuries).

morphemes.translation: splendid, stately, or from Insula Pomposia

b_pomposa.etymology_analysis: Named after Insula Pomposia, the wooded island between two branches of the Po where the abbey stood; the Latin adjective pompōsa ('stately, splendid') or an earlier personal/estate name underlies the island's name.

b_comacchio.first_mention_attestation: Comacchio Cathedral dates to 708 CE, and the lagoon city is attested in early medieval sources including its 854 CE sack by Venice.

morphemes.translation: small wave (cumaculum) or grouping of mounds

b_comacchio.etymology_analysis: Attested in medieval Latin as Comaclum; its etymology is uncertain, variously derived from Greek-Latin *cumaculum* ('small wave') or an Etruscan substrate word meaning 'grouping of bumps/islets'.

b_ravenna.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Roman historical sources from the early 2nd century BCE (c. 191 BCE) as an allied Umbrian/Etruscan-influenced lagoon city, becoming a Roman municipium in 89 BCE.
b_ravenna.etymology_analysis: The ending -enna strongly points to an Etruscan origin (cf. Clavenna, Felsina), possibly from a root *rav- meaning 'watercourse' or 'marshy depression'.

b_imola.first_mention_attestation: Founded around 82 BCE by the Roman dictator Lucius Cornelius Sulla as Forum Cornelii along the Via Aemilia; the name Imola is attested from the 7th century CE under the Lombards.

morphemes.translation: from a Lombard fortress name (Castrum Imolae)

b_imola.etymology_analysis: The medieval name Imola (replacing Roman Forum Cornelii) emerged in the 7th century CE during Lombard rule, derived from a Lombard fortress or personal name (Castrum Imolae).

b_forli.first_mention_attestation: Founded in Roman times along the Via Aemilia as Forum Livii (traditionally dated to 188 BCE) and attested in classical Roman itineraries.
b_forli.etymology_analysis: Contracted from Latin Forum Līviī ('Market of Livius'), attributed to the Roman consul Gaius Livius Salinator in 188 BCE, which yielded Romagnol Furlè and Italian Forlì.

b_rimini.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the Roman colony of Ariminum in 268 BCE at the mouth of the Ariminus (Marecchia) river and attested in Polybius and Livy.
b_rimini.etymology_analysis: Evolves from Latin Ariminum, named after the nearby Ariminus river (modern Marecchia), through apheresis of the initial vowel and stress shift.

b_avezzano.first_mention_attestation: No verified written attestation <= 867 CE with a confirmed pre-867 date; Avezzano is first clearly mentioned in an undated 9th-century diploma preserved in Leo Marsicanus's late-11th-century Chronica monasterii Casinensis, and coalesced as a town in the 14th century.
b_avezzano.etymology_analysis: Generally derived from the Latin praedial toponym (fundus) Avidiānum, denoting a Roman rural estate belonging to the gens Avidia (attested in nearby Alba Fucens), or alternatively from Ad Vettiānum.

historical_names.name: Alba Fucens
historical_names.source: Livy and Roman histories on the founding of Alba Fucens (304–303 BCE)
historical_names.notes: The Roman colony of Alba Fucens (7 km north) was the regional urban center whose ager included the fundus Avidianus.

b_rieti.first_mention_attestation: Ancient Sabine city of Reate, conquered by the Roman Republic in 290 BCE and frequently attested in Varro, Cicero, and Livy.

morphemes.translation: ancient Sabine toponym (traditionally linked to Rhea or a water/valley root)

b_rieti.etymology_analysis: Continues Latin Reāte (an ancient Sabine city name), which evolved through regular Italian sound changes into Rieti.

b_lanciano.first_mention_attestation: Attested in antiquity as Anxanum (a city of the Frentani and Roman municipium) by Pliny the Elder (c. 77 CE), Ptolemy, and the Antonine Itinerary.

morphemes.translation: ancient Italic root (or Roman gentilicium Anxius)

b_lanciano.etymology_analysis: Lanciano evolved from Latin Anxānum (via *L'Anzano / Lancianum with agglutination of the definite article l'), the ancient Frentanian city and Roman municipium.

b_cluieli.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Roman sources from the late 4th century BCE (c. 304 BCE) as Teate (Teate Marrucinorum), the chief city of the Italic Marrucini.
b_cluieli.etymology_analysis: Chieti derives from Latin Teāte (Greek Theátē), the chief town of the Marrucini, whose initial T- palatalized to Ch- [k-] in regional Romance.

b_agnone.first_mention_attestation: First clearly attested in High Medieval records in 1139 CE when the Borrello family took control of the town (though situated in ancient Samnite territory near the 3rd-century BCE Oscan Tabula Osca).

morphemes.translation: traditionally linked to Aquilonia or Latin angulus ('corner/ridge')

b_agnone.etymology_analysis: Medieval Latin Anglonum (whence Agnone) is traditionally linked by local lore to ancient Samnite Aquilonia, or linguistically to Latin angulus ('corner/ridge') with an augmentative suffix.

b_orvieto.first_mention_attestation: Identified with the major Etruscan city of Volsinii Veteres (Velzna), conquered and destroyed by Rome in 264 BCE, and later attested in late antiquity as Urbs Vetus.
b_orvieto.etymology_analysis: Derived from Late Latin Urbs Vetus ('Old City', attested in Procopius as Οὐρβιβεντός), referring to the ancient Etruscan acropolis after the Roman relocation of Volsinii.

historical_names.name: Volsinii Veteres
historical_names.source: Roman historical accounts of the 264 BCE conquest of Volsinii
historical_names.notes: Etruscan Velzna / Roman Volsinii Veteres, called Urbs Vetus by the 6th century CE.

b_perugia.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Roman history as the Etruscan city of Perusia from 310–309 BCE during Rome's wars in Etruria.
b_perugia.etymology_analysis: Evolves from Latin Perusia, the Romanized form of an ancient Etruscan city name, with regular palatalization of -si- to -gi- in Italian Perugia.

b_spoleto.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Roman historical records for the foundation of the Latin colony of Spoletium in 241 BCE (AUC 513), shortly after the First Punic War.

morphemes.translation: ancient settlement root (possibly related to Umbrian Pola)

b_spoleto.etymology_analysis: Recorded in classical Latin as Spoletium (later Spoletum) and in Greek as Spoletion, the name derives from a pre-Roman Umbrian toponym adapted with the Latin locative/toponymic suffix -ium.

b_assissi.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 77 CE by Pliny the Elder in his Naturalis Historia (Book III), which names the Asisinates among the peoples of Regio VI Umbria, following the Roman municipium Asisium.
b_assissi.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Romanized Umbrian toponym Asisium, attested in Latin inscriptions and Pliny the Elder, which evolved through Old Italian Ascesi into modern Italian Assisi.

b_terni.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Interamna by Marcus Terentius Varro in De Lingua Latina (c. 43 BCE), and also recorded in a Tiberian-era Latin inscription citing its traditional 672 BCE foundation.
b_terni.etymology_analysis: From Latin Interamna Nahars, literally 'between the rivers of the Nar', referring to its position at the confluence of the Nera (ancient Nar) and Serra rivers; Interamna contracted in medieval Italian to Terni.

b_teramo.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 77 CE by Pliny the Elder in Naturalis Historia (Book III.110) as Interamnia Praetuttiorum, the chief center of the Praetutii in Regio V Picenum.
b_teramo.etymology_analysis: From Latin Interamnia Praetuttiorum, meaning '(city) between the rivers of the Praetutii', referencing its site between the Tordino and Vezzola rivers; Interamnia evolved through medieval Teramne into Teramo.

b_atri.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Livy's Ab Urbe Condita / Periochae (Book 11, c. 9 BCE), which records the establishment of the Roman colony of Hatria c. 290–289 BCE, and subsequently by Strabo, Pliny, and Ptolemy.

morphemes.translation: pre-Roman root (linked to the Illyrian deity Hatranus or 'dark' water)

b_atri.etymology_analysis: From ancient Latin Hatria (Hadria, Atria) and Greek Atria, a pre-Roman Picene-Illyrian settlement name whose root is often connected either to the Illyrian god Hatranus or to an Indo-European root for dark/water.

b_ajaccio.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a letter of Pope Gregory I around 600–601 CE (late 6th to early 7th century) as Adjacium, referring to an episcopal see on Corsica.

morphemes.translation: adjacent place / resting place (or pre-Roman root)

b_ajaccio.etymology_analysis: Attested in early medieval Latin as Adjacium (Corsican Aiacciu), the name is variously derived from Latin adiacens ('lying near / adjacent') or a pre-Roman Corsican toponym.

b_calvi.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the fortified settlement of Calvi is first documented in the 13th century (fortified in 1268 by Giovaninello de Loreto and ceded to Genoa in 1278).

morphemes.translation: bald, bare (referring to the barren granite promontory)

b_calvi.etymology_analysis: Derived from Latin calvus ('bald, bare'), referring to the bare, rocky granite promontory on which the medieval citadel was built.

b_bastia.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Bastia was founded in 1378–1380 when Genoese governor Leonello Lomellini built a fortress ('a bastiglia') above Porto Cardo.
b_bastia.etymology_analysis: Named after the Italian/Genoese word bastia ('bastion' or 'fortress'), referring to the citadel erected by Leonello Lomellini in the late 14th century to replace the inland castle of Biguglia.

historical_names.name: Mariana
historical_names.source: Pomponius Mela (De Chorographia, c. 43 CE) and Pliny the Elder (Naturalis Historia, 77 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman colony founded by Gaius Marius c. 93 BCE south of modern Bastia; served as the episcopal see of northern Corsica until its transfer to Bastia in 1570.

b_corte.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Corte first enters documented medieval history in the early 15th century, notably when Vincentello d'Istria fortified its citadel in 1419.

morphemes.translation: court, enclosed courtyard, fortified enclosure (from Latin cohors/cortis)

b_corte.etymology_analysis: From Corsican Corti / Italian Corte, deriving from Latin cohors, cortis ('enclosure, courtyard, royal court'), reflecting its role as an inland fortified stronghold.

b_bonifacio.first_mention_attestation: Founded and attested in 828 CE when Count Boniface II of Tuscany established a fortified coastal citadel in southern Corsica to defend against Saracen raids.
b_bonifacio.etymology_analysis: Named after Boniface II, Margrave of Tuscany, who built the fortress in 828 CE; his Latin name Bonifatius comes from bonum ('good') and fatum/facere ('fate' or 'doer').

b_vecchio.first_mention_attestation: While ancient Portus Syracusanus (c. 150 CE) lay on the gulf, the modern town and citadel of Porto-Vecchio were founded by the Republic of Genoa's Bank of Saint George in 1539 CE.
b_vecchio.etymology_analysis: Italian Porto-Vecchio (Corsican Portivechju) means 'old port', referring to the ancient natural harbor known in Roman times as Portus Syracusanus.

historical_names.name: Portus Syracusanus
historical_names.source: Claudius Ptolemy, Geographia (c. 150 CE)
historical_names.notes: Classical name ('Syracusan Port') attested in Ptolemy's Geographia, reflecting earlier Syracusan and Roman maritime activity at the bay.

b_oristano.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE for Oristano itself; the town of Aristanis / Oristano rose to prominence in 1070 CE when Judge Orzocorre I of Arborea relocated the capital and archdiocese there from Tharros.

morphemes.translation: uncertain toponym (possibly from Greek aristos 'best' or Latin stagnum 'lagoon')

b_oristano.etymology_analysis: Attested in medieval Sardinian and Byzantine Greek as Aristanis (Italian Oristano), the name is variously linked to a Byzantine-era settlement near the lagoon (stagnum) or to the Greek personal/honorific element aristos.

historical_names.name: Othoca
historical_names.source: Claudius Ptolemy (Geographia, c. 150 CE) and the Antonine Itinerary (3rd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Oristano developed adjacent to the Phoenician-Roman town of Othoca (modern Santa Giusta) and succeeded the coastal city of Tharros as capital of Arborea in 1070 CE.

historical_names.name: Tharros
historical_names.source: Claudius Ptolemy (Geographia, c. 150 CE) and the Antonine Itinerary (3rd century CE)
historical_names.notes: Oristano developed adjacent to the Phoenician-Roman town of Othoca (modern Santa Giusta) and succeeded the coastal city of Tharros as capital of Arborea in 1070 CE.

b_isili.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Isili is first documented in medieval Sardinian records as a settlement within the curatoria of Valenza/Siurgus under the Giudicati before passing to Aragon in the 14th century.

morphemes.translation: toponym of uncertain origin (possibly from Latin ilex 'holm oak' or a Paleo-Sardinian root)

b_isili.etymology_analysis: The etymology of Sardinian Ìsili is uncertain; scholars suggest either a Paleo-Sardinian substratum toponym or a derivation from Latin ilex ('holm oak'), reflecting former oak forests in the Sarcidano hills.

b_cagliari.first_mention_attestation: Attested in classical historiography by Polybius (Histories, c. 146 BCE) and Livy (Ab Urbe Condita) as Caralis / Karalis, the chief Punic and Roman port of southern Sardinia.

morphemes.translation: fortress, rock, or town (compare Punic qart)

b_cagliari.etymology_analysis: From Latin Caralis (Greek Karalis), a pre-Roman Phoenician or Paleo-Sardinian name likely meaning 'rocky hill' or 'fortified town', which evolved into medieval Calari and modern Cagliari.

b_iglesias.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; founded as the silver-mining town of Villa di Chiesa by Count Ugolino della Gherardesca after 1258 and first documented in 1272.
b_iglesias.etymology_analysis: Originally named Villa di Chiesa ('Town of the Church') in Pisan Italian in the late 13th century, the name was translated into Spanish as Iglesias ('Churches') during Aragonese-Spanish rule.

b_samassi.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; although an early medieval necropolis exists under San Geminiano, Samassi is first documented in written records in the 13th–14th centuries (sending representatives to the 1355 Sardinian parliament).
b_samassi.etymology_analysis: Of pre-Roman Paleo-Sardinian origin, Samassi (Sardinian Samàssi) preserves an indigenous Campidano root whose exact lexical meaning is unattested.

b_olbia.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 56 BCE in Cicero's letters (Epistulae ad Quintum Fratrem 2.3/2.6) and subsequently in Livy, Pliny the Elder, and Ptolemy as Olbia, an ancient port on northeastern Sardinia.
b_olbia.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Olbía (Ὀλβία), meaning 'happy' or 'prosperous', reflecting Greek colonization or maritime trade in the 7th–6th centuries BCE before Roman annexation.

b_galtelli.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Galtellì is first documented in 1138 CE when Pope Innocent II placed the Diocese of Galtellì under the metropolitan authority of Pisa.
b_galtelli.etymology_analysis: Sardinian Gartèddi (Italian Galtellì) is a pre-Roman Paleo-Sardinian toponym of uncertain etymology, first recorded in 12th-century ecclesiastical documents.

b_sassari.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Sassari emerged in the early 12th century and first appears in written/cartographic records around 1131 CE as Thathari.

morphemes.translation: uncertain root (possibly from a pre-Roman settlement name or Latin saxum 'rock')

b_sassari.etymology_analysis: Recorded in medieval Sardinian as Thathari (modern Sardinian Tàtari, Italian Sassari), the name's origin is debated between a Paleo-Sardinian substratum toponym and a derivation from Latin saxum ('rock').

b_alghero.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Alghero was founded between 1102 and 1112 CE as a fortified port by the Genoese Doria family.
b_alghero.etymology_analysis: From Medieval Latin Aleguerium, meaning 'place of seaweed/algae' (Posidonia oceanica), referring to the dense seagrass deposits along its coast; adapted into Catalan L'Alguer and Italian Alghero.

b_porto_torres.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 77 CE by Pliny the Elder in Naturalis Historia (Book III.85) as Colonia quae vocatur ad Turrem Libisonis, the first Roman colony on Sardinia (founded c. 46 BCE).

morphemes.translation: tower (from Latin turris, referring to Turris Libisonis)

b_porto_torres.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Roman colony Turris Libisonis ('Tower of Libiso'), combined with Italian porto ('port') in the medieval and modern periods.

b_ardara.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Ardara is first documented around 1064–1065 CE as the capital of the Giudicato of Torres in monastic donation charters of Barisone I.

morphemes.translation: pre-Roman toponymic root of uncertain meaning

b_ardara.etymology_analysis: Sardinian Àldara (Italian Ardara) is a pre-Roman Paleo-Sardinian toponym of uncertain etymology, first attested in 11th-century judicial charters.

b_tortoli.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Tortolì is first attested in medieval Pisan fiscal and administrative records of the early 14th century (c. 1316) as Tortohelie.

morphemes.translation: toponymic root of debated origin (possibly linked to Latin Portus Ilii or Paleo-Sardinian)

b_tortoli.etymology_analysis: Attested in medieval Pisan records as Tortohelie (Sardinian Tortuelie), the name's etymology is debated between a Paleo-Sardinian root and a folk/learned association with the classical Portus Ilii.

b_carbonara.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the village was known as Carbonara from at least the 13th century before being repopulated and renamed Villasimius in the 19th century.

morphemes.translation: place where something is produced (charcoal-making site)

b_carbonara.etymology_analysis: The historical barony name Carbonara (Sardinian Crabonaxa) derives from Latin carbonaria ('charcoal-burning site'); in the 19th century the municipality was renamed Villasimius after the nearby medieval village of Simius.

b_torgau.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Torgau is first documented in 973 CE as Turguo (and in 1004 as Torgua), referring to a Slavic settlement and river crossing on the Elbe.
b_torgau.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Sorbian *Torgov (from Proto-Slavic *tъrgъ, 'market'), denoting a Slavic market settlement at an Elbe crossing, Germanized as Torgau.

b_brene.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Brehna is first documented in 1053 CE as a castle and seat of the Counts of Brehna.
b_brene.etymology_analysis: Of Old Sorbian origin, likely derived from Proto-Slavic *brьnьje ('mud, clay, marsh'), referring to the damp lowland terrain around the settlement.

b_duben.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; first documented in 981 CE as the Slavic castle of Dibni on the Mulde River.
b_duben.etymology_analysis: From Old Sorbian *Dǫbny (attested as Dibni in 981), derived from Proto-Slavic *dǫbъ ('oak'), meaning 'oak place' or 'oak grove'; the prefix Bad ('spa') was added in 1948.

b_juterbog.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Jüterbog is first documented in 1007 CE by the chronicler Thietmar of Merseburg as Jutriboc.
b_juterbog.etymology_analysis: First recorded as Jutriboc in 1007, the Slavic name is traditionally interpreted from Polabian/Old Sorbian *jutro ('morning/dawn') and *bogъ ('god'), or alternatively from *bokъ ('side/slope').

b_dahme.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Dahme is first mentioned in a 1186 CE charter as a castle and settlement on the Dahme River.

morphemes.translation: river name (possibly from Sorbian *dub 'oak' or pre-Slavic hydronym)

b_dahme.etymology_analysis: Named after the Dahme River (Lower Sorbian Damna or Dubna), a tributary of the Spree whose name is either a Slavic formation from *dǫbъ ('oak') or an older pre-Slavic hydronym.

b_naumberg.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; known historically in German as Sommerfeld, the town is first documented in 1253 CE (1258 in some charters) and received town rights in 1283.
b_naumberg.etymology_analysis: Modern Polish Lubsko (adopted in 1947) derives from the Lubsza River; its medieval German name Sommerfeld means 'summer field', while Lower Sorbian Žemŕ reflects an earlier Slavic settlement name.

b_forst.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Forst is first documented in the 13th century (with the foundation of St. Nikolai church in 1265 CE) as a German settlement on the Lusatian Neisse.

morphemes.translation: forest, managed woodland (from Old High German forst)

b_forst.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German forst ('forest, woodland'), referring to a settlement cleared in the forested borderland along the Neisse River (Lower Sorbian Baršć).

b_spreewald.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; while the Spree River is attested in 965 CE (Sprewa), settlements in the Spreewald (Spree Forest) such as Lübbenau are first documented in the 12th–14th centuries (1315 CE).
b_spreewald.etymology_analysis: German Spreewald ('Spree Forest', Lower Sorbian Błota 'the swamps') is a regional choronym combining the hydronym Spree with German Wald ('forest').

b_storkow.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Storkow is first mentioned in a 1209 CE deed issued by Emperor Otto IV.

morphemes.translation: path through a swamp / marshy crossing (or Slavic personal name)

b_storkow.etymology_analysis: Derived from the medieval Slavic form Sturkuowe, generally interpreted as 'path through the swamp' (or from a Slavic personal name), later folk-etymologized with German Storch ('stork') on the town's arms.

b_wittenberg.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Wittenberg is first mentioned in historical documents in 1180 CE as a village founded by Flemish colonists under the House of Ascania.
b_wittenberg.etymology_analysis: From Low German witt ('white') and Berg ('hill/mountain'), referring to the light-colored sandy hills along the Elbe River where Flemish settlers established the town.

b_belizi.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Beelitz is first documented in June 997 CE as the Slavic castle district Belizi in the Gau Ploni.
b_belizi.etymology_analysis: Attested in 997 CE as Belizi, the name derives from Slavic *bělъ ('white, bright'), likely referring to light sandy soil or clear water in the Nieplitz valley.

b_cottbus.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Cottbus is first documented in 1156 CE as Chotibuz in a charter naming Heinricus Castellanus de Chotibuz.

morphemes.translation: Slavic personal name ('one who wakes desire/joy')

b_cottbus.etymology_analysis: From Lower Sorbian Chóśebuz (attested 1156 as Chotibuz), meaning 'settlement of Chotěbud', formed from an Old Sorbian personal name with a possessive suffix.

b_kamenz.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kamenz is first documented in a 1225 CE charter as a settlement guarding the Via Regia crossing over the Black Elster.
b_kamenz.etymology_analysis: From Upper Sorbian Kamjenc (Proto-Slavic *kamenь 'stone'), meaning 'stony place', referring to the rocky granite terrain along the Black Elster.

b_lubben.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the castle of Lubin (urbs Lubin) in the March of Lusatia is first mentioned in an 1150 CE document of Nienburg Abbey.
b_lubben.etymology_analysis: From Lower Sorbian Lubin (attested 1150 as urbs Lubin), derived from the Slavic root *ljubъ ('beloved') or a personal name Lub, meaning 'settlement of Lub'.

b_dresden.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Dresden is first mentioned in surviving documents on 31 March 1206 CE as Dresdene in connection with a legal dispute.
b_dresden.etymology_analysis: From Old Sorbian *Drežďany (Upper Sorbian Drježdźany), meaning 'people of the floodplain forest', referring to the Slavic fishing settlement along the Elbe.

b_bischofswerda.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Bischofswerda is first documented in 1227 CE (mentioning Meinhardus de Biscofiswerde) under the Bishops of Meissen.

morphemes.translation: bishop (referring to the Bishop of Meissen)
river island, elevated dry ground in a marsh

b_bischofswerda.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German Bischof ('bishop') and werda/wert ('river island' or 'elevated ground in marshland'), meaning 'the bishop's island' in the Wesenitz wetlands.

b_freiberg.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Freiberg was founded around 1168 CE on the lands of Christiansdorf following the discovery of silver ore in the Ore Mountains.

morphemes.translation: free (referring to mining freedom / tax-free status)
