b_freiberg.etymology_analysis: From Middle High German frī ('free') and berc ('mountain, mine'), meaning 'free mountain/mine', reflecting the free mining privileges granted by Margrave Otto of Meissen after 1168.

b_gorlitz.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Görlitz is first documented in 1071 CE as villa Goreliz in a charter issued by King Henry IV.
b_gorlitz.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1071 as Goreliz (Upper Sorbian Zhorjelc), from Proto-Slavic *gorěti ('to burn'), denoting a settlement established on burned or slash-and-burn cleared land.

b_bautzen.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Bautzen is first documented in 1002 CE by Thietmar of Merseburg as civitas Budusin, the chief fortress of the Slavic Milceni.
b_bautzen.etymology_analysis: Originally Budissin (Upper Sorbian Budyšin, attested 1002 as Budusin), from a Slavic personal name with the possessive suffix -in; officially renamed Bautzen in German in 1868.

b_spremberg.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Spremberg is first documented in a purchase contract dated 3 August 1301 CE.

morphemes.translation: Spree River (or Middle High German sprengen)

b_spremberg.etymology_analysis: German Spremberg combines a reduced form of the Spree River name (or a hill-related root) with Berg ('hill/mountain'), while its Lower Sorbian name Grodk means 'small fortress/town'.

b_meissen.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Meissen was founded in 929 CE as a royal fortress (Misnia) by King Henry I on the Elbe River.
b_meissen.etymology_analysis: Named after the Meisa stream (Upper Sorbian Mišno, Latin Misnia), which flows into the Elbe at the foot of the castle hill.

b_radebeul.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the village of Radebeul is first documented in 1349 CE as Radebůl.
b_radebeul.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1349 as Radebůl, deriving from the Old Sorbian personal name Radobyl with a possessive suffix, meaning 'settlement of Radobyl'.

b_grossenhain.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Großenhain is first documented in 1205 CE as Hayn, developing from a Sorbian settlement on the Große Röder.

morphemes.translation: grove, enclosed wood (Middle High German hagen)

b_grossenhain.etymology_analysis: Originally recorded as Hayn (from Middle High German hagen/hain 'grove, enclosed wood'), with the prefix Großen- ('great') added to distinguish it from smaller places named Hain.

b_naumburg.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Naumburg is first documented in 1012 CE as neweburg, the newly built castle of the Ekkehardinger Margraves of Meissen.

morphemes.language: Old High German / Middle Low German

b_naumburg.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1012 as neweburg ('new castle'), from German neu ('new') and Burg ('castle/fortress'), referring to the Ekkehardinger stronghold founded around 1000 CE.

b_altenburg.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Altenburg is first documented in 976 CE when Emperor Otto II donated the settlement to the Bishopric of Zeitz.
b_altenburg.etymology_analysis: From Old High German alt ('old') and burg ('castle'), meaning 'old castle', referring to the early medieval fortress built over a Slavic stronghold on the Pleiße.

b_eilenburg.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Slavic castle of Eilenburg is first documented in 961 CE as civitas Ilburg.
b_eilenburg.etymology_analysis: First recorded in 961 as Ilburg, combining Slavic *il ('clay, loam', compare Upper Sorbian Jiłow) with German Burg ('castle'), referring to the clay-rich hill overlooking the Mulde.

b_colditz.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1046 CE as the burgward district 'Cholidistcha' on the Zwickauer Mulde when Emperor Henry III granted it to his consort Agnes of Poitou; the town itself is first recorded as a 'civitas' in 1265 CE.

morphemes.translation: member of a community, kin, or personal root

b_colditz.etymology_analysis: Colditz derives from an Old Sorbian settlement name *Koldici, attested in 1046 CE as 'Cholidistcha'. Onomastic scholars link the root to Slavic *kol- (referring to a member of a community or a personal name) combined with the patronymic suffix *-ici denoting the people or settlement associated with that group.

b_devin.first_mention_attestation: First documented for the year 981 CE in the chronicle of Thietmar of Merseburg (written c. 1015) as the Slavic fortress 'urbs Dibni' (also recorded later as 'Dewin' and 'Dybin') at a ford over the Mulde River.
b_devin.etymology_analysis: The modern German name Düben (prefixed with 'Bad' in 1948) corresponds to the Upper Sorbian form Dźěwin and the 981 CE Latinized attestation 'Dibni' (later 'Dewin'). Scholars debate whether the Old Sorbian root derives from *dyb ('pole, stake', yielding *Dybno, as favored by Ernst Eichler and Hans Walther) or from *děva ('maiden') or a personal name *Děva ('settlement of Děva').

b_leisning.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1046 CE as 'Lisnich', designating the burgward centered on Mildenstein Castle above the Freiberger Mulde; the adjacent merchant settlement of Altleisnig is recorded in 1215 CE as 'oppidum novum Liznik'.
b_leisning.etymology_analysis: Leisnig (Upper Sorbian: Lěsnik) derives from Old Sorbian *Lěsnik, attested as 'Lisnich' in 1046 CE. It is formed from Slavic *lěsъ ('forest, woodland') and the suffix *-nikъ, designating a forested settlement or a place inhabited by foresters.

b_reichenbach.first_mention_attestation: First officially documented in 1212 CE as 'Richenbach', with town privileges granted around 1240 CE and a 1271 decree referring to 'civitatis richenbach'; no written attestation exists prior to 867 CE.
b_reichenbach.etymology_analysis: Reichenbach derives from Middle High German 'Richenbach', composed of 'rīhhi' ('rich, abundant') and 'bach' ('stream, brook'), referring to the numerous streams and wetland basins in the valley of the old town. The regional qualifier 'im Vogtland' refers to the historic territory of the Imperial Bailiffs (Vögte).

b_plauen.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1122 CE as 'vicus Plawe' ('Plawen') in the consecration record of St. John's Church under Count Adalbert of Everstein; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_plauen.etymology_analysis: Plauen (Upper Sorbian: Pławno; Czech: Plavno) derives from an Old Sorbian toponym *Plavno, built on the Slavic root *plav- ('to float/raft timber' or 'alluvial flood-meadow') along the White Elster River, Germanized as 'Plawe' and 'Plauen'.

b_gera.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 995 CE as 'Gera' in a border description issued under Emperor Otto III, and in 999 CE when 'provincia Gera' passed to Quedlinburg Abbey; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: wedge-shaped piece of land, bend, or valley section

b_gera.etymology_analysis: Gera originally designated the widened section of the White Elster river valley where the city sits. The name likely predates the Migration Period (akin to Old High German 'gēro', meaning 'wedge' or 'gore of land') and was adopted by Slavic settlers from the 8th century onward before appearing in Latin charters in 995 CE.

b_cheb.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1061 CE under the Latinized name 'Egire' (German: Eger), derived from the Celtic hydronym Agara (the Ohře River); the Czech name 'Cheb' first appeared in the mid-14th century.

morphemes.translation: bend, curve (referring to meanders of the Ohře River)

b_cheb.etymology_analysis: Cheb has a dual toponymic history. Its earliest recorded name, 'Egire' (1061 CE, whence German 'Eger'), derives from the Celtic river name *Agara (the Ohře). The Czech name 'Cheb', attested from the mid-14th century, comes from Old Czech 'heb' (modern 'oheb', meaning 'bend'), referring to the bends of the Ohře River.

b_rehau.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1234 CE as 'Resawe' and granted town rights in 1427 CE; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: place/collective suffix denoting a forest clearing

b_rehau.etymology_analysis: Despite its canting coat of arms featuring a roe deer ('Reh') in a meadow ('Au'), Rehau derives from the West Slavic form *rězava (attested in 1234 CE as 'Resawe'), meaning 'forest clearing' or 'woodland cut'. Over time the medial 's' dropped and the name was folk-etymologized into German 'Reh-Au'.

b_wolkenstein.first_mention_attestation: The lordship 'Herrschaft Wolkenstein' is first documented in 1262 CE (following a 1241 reference to Hugo de Waldenberc in the region), and the town itself is first mentioned in 1293 CE.
b_wolkenstein.etymology_analysis: Wolkenstein takes its name from Wolkenstein Castle, perched on a rocky spur 70 meters above the Zschopau River. Composed of Middle High German 'wolke(n)' ('clouds') and 'stein' ('rock, stone fortress'), the name literally means 'cloud-rock', evoking a crag rising into the clouds.

b_waldenburg.first_mention_attestation: Waldenburg Castle was built between 1165 and 1172 CE, with Hugo von Wartha first styling himself 'Hugo von Waldenburg' around 1199 CE; the town itself is first documented in 1336 CE as 'Waldinberg'.
b_waldenburg.etymology_analysis: Waldenburg is a German compound of Middle High German 'wald' ('forest') and 'burg' ('castle, stronghold'), meaning 'forest castle'—referring to the 12th-century imperial fortress erected to guard the salt trade route crossing the Zwickauer Mulde.

b_aveiro.first_mention_attestation: First documented on 26 January 959 CE as 'Alauario' in the testamentary donation of Countess Mumadona Dias to the Monastery of Guimarães; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_aveiro.etymology_analysis: Aveiro derives from the medieval Latinized toponym 'Averius' (attested as 'Alauario' in 959 CE), which traces back to the Celtic root *aber ('river mouth, estuary', from Proto-Celtic *adberos, cognate with Welsh 'aber'), describing the Vouga River estuary and lagoon.

b_gralheira.first_mention_attestation: Although the area's medieval lords (such as Egas Moniz) are associated with the 12th-century foundation of Portugal, Cinfães is formally documented with its royal charter (foral) granted by King Manuel I in 1513 CE; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: genitive plural of a personal name (possibly Germanic *Sindifans)

b_gralheira.etymology_analysis: Cinfães reflects a medieval Galician-Portuguese toponym derived from the genitive/plural of an early medieval personal name (likely of Germanic or Hispano-Roman origin, comparable to -ães place names in northern Portugal denoting an estate or family holding).

b_lamego.first_mention_attestation: Documented as the episcopal see 'Lameco' in the Suebic Parochiale Suevum (569 CE) and represented by Bishop Sardinarius at the Second Council of Braga in 572 CE, continuing the Roman-era settlement of Lamaecum.
b_lamego.etymology_analysis: Lamego derives from the Romanized Hispano-Celtic toponym 'Lamaecum' (recorded as 'Lameco' in 569 CE), formed from the pre-Roman root *lama ('marsh, wet meadow') or a related agrarian estate name with the Celtic-Latin suffix *-aecum.

b_castelo_branco.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1182 CE when noble Fernandes Sanches donated the estate called 'Vila Franca da Cardosa' to the Knights Templar; the name 'Castel-Branco' first appears in its 1213 CE royal charter (foral), confirmed by Pope Innocent III in 1215 CE.
b_castelo_branco.etymology_analysis: Castelo Branco literally means 'White Castle' in Portuguese (from Latin 'castellum' and Germanic-borrowed 'blancus'), referring to the Templar castle built on the Colina da Cardosa, which replaced the earlier Luso-Roman hillfort name Castra Leuca (Greek/Latin 'white camp').

b_idanha.first_mention_attestation: Recorded in Roman epigraphy since 16 CE as 'Civitas Igaeditanorum', later serving as the Suebic and Visigothic episcopal see of 'Egitânia' (attested in the 569 CE Parochiale Suevum and 572 CE Second Council of Braga) and Arabic 'Exitânia'.
b_idanha.etymology_analysis: Idanha-a-Velha ('Idanha the Old') derives phonetically from Roman 'Igaeditania' / Suebic-Visigothic 'Egitânia' (from the Lusitanian ethnonym Igaeditani, attested epigraphically from 16 CE), with the Portuguese qualifier 'a-Velha' added later to distinguish it from Idanha-a-Nova.

b_abrantes.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1173 CE when King Afonso I donated the Castle of Abrantes to the Order of Saint James of the Sword (following its 1148 capture from the Moors), with 'Aulantes' appearing in 1176 CE and a royal charter (foral) in 1179 CE.
b_abrantes.etymology_analysis: Abrantes is attested in 1176 CE as 'Aulantes' and is commonly derived from a hypothetical Latin *Aurantes (from 'aurum', 'gold'), referring to alluvial gold deposits in the Tagus River; an alternative hypothesis links it to archaic Portuguese 'brança'/'branza' ('pine needles/straw').

b_coimbra.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Aeminium' by Pliny the Elder in Naturalis Historia (4.113, c. 77 CE) and later by Ptolemy; after nearby Conimbriga was abandoned in the 5th–6th centuries, its episcopal see and name ('Conimbria' > 'Coimbra') transferred to Aeminium.
b_coimbra.etymology_analysis: The modern name Coimbra evolved from Latin 'Conimbria' / 'Conimbriga', a Celtic-Latin compound containing *-briga ('hillfort'). Originally belonging to the Roman city 16 km south (modern Condeixa-a-Velha), the name and bishopric were transferred to the Roman city of Aeminium (attested c. 77 CE) in the early Middle Ages.

historical_names.name: Aeminium
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia 4.113 (c. 77 CE)
historical_names.notes: Original Roman name of the exact hilltop city of Coimbra prior to the transfer of the name Conimbria.

b_leiria.first_mention_attestation: Conquered by King Afonso Henriques in 1135 CE and first formally documented under the name 'Leirena' in its royal charter (foral) of 1142 CE; no written attestation of Leiria exists <= 867 CE.
b_leiria.etymology_analysis: Leiria derives from Portuguese 'leira' (medieval Galician-Portuguese 'laria'), from Proto-Celtic *ɸlār-yo- ('floor, flat ground, small farming plot'), referring to the fertile river plots along the Lis and Lena.

historical_names.name: Collippo
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia 4.113 (c. 77 CE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Celtiberian and Roman town located ~7 km away at São Sebastião do Freixo, whose stones were later used to build medieval Leiria.

b_obidos.first_mention_attestation: Captured from the Moors by Afonso Henriques in 1148 CE and granted its first royal charter (foral) by King Sancho I in 1195 CE; no written attestation of Óbidos exists <= 867 CE.
b_obidos.etymology_analysis: Óbidos derives from the Latin word 'oppidum' ('citadel, fortified hilltop town'), reflecting the medieval fortified hill settlement that succeeded the abandoned Roman lagoon town of Eburobrittium nearby.

historical_names.name: Eburobrittium
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia 4.113 (c. 77 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman civitas located near Óbidos, occupied from the 1st century BCE until the late 5th century CE when inhabitants moved to the defensible Óbidos hilltop.

b_viseu.first_mention_attestation: First clearly documented in ecclesiastical records as the episcopal see of 'Veseo' at the Second Council of Braga in 572 CE (and in the Suebic Parochiale Suevum of 569 CE), preceded by a Roman votive altar bearing the indigenous name 'Vissaîegobor'.
b_viseu.etymology_analysis: Viseu (attested as 'Veseo' in 572 CE) continues an indigenous Lusitanian-Roman toponym related to the name 'Vissaîegobor' discovered on a Roman votive altar beneath Viseu Cathedral.

b_trancoso.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 960 CE in the testament of Dona Chamôa (Flâmula) Rodrigues, who donated the Castle of Trancoso ('Castelo de Trancoso') to the Monastery of Guimarães; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: tree trunk, stockade, or steep pass

b_trancoso.etymology_analysis: Trancoso is a Romance toponym formed from Galician-Portuguese 'tronco'/'tranco' (from Latin 'truncus', meaning 'tree trunk, timber, or palisade') and the adjectival suffix '-oso', likely referring to a timbered or palisaded ridge settlement.

b_astorga.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a Roman camp for Legio X Gemina in the late 1st century BCE and attested as 'Asturica Augusta' ('urbs magnifica') by Pliny the Elder in Naturalis Historia (3.28, c. 77 CE).
b_astorga.etymology_analysis: Astorga derives from Latin 'Asturica (Augusta)', named after the Astures, the indigenous people of northwestern Hispania, combined with the Latin suffix '-ica' and the imperial honorific 'Augusta' bestowed under Emperor Augustus.

b_lugo.first_mention_attestation: Founded around 25 BCE by Paullus Fabius Maximus as 'Lucus Augusti' and attested in written sources by Pliny the Elder (Naturalis Historia 3.28, c. 77 CE) and Ptolemy.

morphemes.translation: sacred grove (Latin lucus) or Celtic deity Lugus

b_lugo.etymology_analysis: Lugo derives from the Roman city name 'Lucus Augusti', combining Latin 'lucus' ('sacred grove', likely also echoing or translating a sanctuary of the pan-Celtic deity Lugus) with the honorific 'Augusti'.

b_ourense.first_mention_attestation: Documented as the episcopal see 'Auriensis' at the Second Council of Braga in 572 CE (represented by Bishop Witimer), and also attested in the 6th-century Suebic Parochiale Suevum; its Roman settlement was known as Auria / Aquae Urentes.
b_ourense.etymology_analysis: Ourense (Spanish: Orense) derives from Latin '(civitas) Auriensis', from 'Auria' ('golden', Latin 'aurum'), reflecting the rich Roman alluvial gold mines along the Miño River (an alternative folk etymology links it to 'Aquae Urentes', 'burning waters', after its hot springs).

b_monfortedelemos.first_mention_attestation: First documented in a royal charter of 10 April 1104 CE when Count Fruela Díaz and his wife founded the town at the foot of the hillfort called 'Castro Dactonio' on lands of the Monastery of San Vicente do Pino.

morphemes.translation: of the Lemos (from the Lemavi tribe)

b_monfortedelemos.etymology_analysis: Monforte de Lemos combines Galician 'monte forte' ('strong/fortified mountain', referring to the fortified hill of San Vicente do Pino) with 'de Lemos', derived from the ancient Celtic-Iberian tribe of the Lemavi (whence the comarca Terra de Lemos).

historical_names.name: Dactonium
historical_names.source: Ptolemy, Geography 2.6 (c. 150 CE)
historical_names.notes: Hillfort of the Lemavi tribe attested by Pliny and Ptolemy and located on the San Vicente do Pino hill overlooking Monforte de Lemos.

b_ponferrada.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 928 CE in a donation to the Monastery of San Pedro de Montes of a villa between the Sil and Boeza rivers; the name 'Pons Ferrata' ('Iron Bridge') arose after 1082 CE when Bishop Osmundo of Astorga reinforced the bridge over the Sil with iron.
b_ponferrada.etymology_analysis: Ponferrada derives directly from Medieval Latin 'Pons Ferrata' ('Iron Bridge'), named after the iron-reinforced bridge over the Sil River commissioned in 1082 CE by Bishop Osmundo of Astorga to ease passage for pilgrims on the Camino de Santiago.

b_corunna.first_mention_attestation: The name 'Crunia' (modern A Coruña) is first documented in 1208 CE in a royal charter of King Alfonso IX of León; earlier in the Middle Ages the settlement around the Roman lighthouse was called 'Faro'.

morphemes.translation: meadow or possibly a transferred place name from Historia Turpini

b_corunna.etymology_analysis: The origin of A Coruña (attested as 'Crunia' in 1208 CE) is debated: hypotheses link it to a Celtic root *Clunia ('meadow'), to a Latin *Coronium, or to a medieval borrowing by Alfonso IX from the 12th-century Historia Turpini. Earlier in Antiquity, the port and its Roman lighthouse (Tower of Hercules) were known as Brigantium / Farum Brigantium.

historical_names.name: Brigantium
historical_names.source: Ptolemy, Geography (c. 150 CE); Paulus Orosius, Historiae adversum Paganos (c. 417 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman port city and lighthouse (Tower of Hercules) located on the A Coruña peninsula.

historical_names.name: Flavium Brigantium
historical_names.source: Ptolemy, Geography (c. 150 CE); Paulus Orosius, Historiae adversum Paganos (c. 417 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman port city and lighthouse (Tower of Hercules) located on the A Coruña peninsula.

historical_names.name: Farum Brigantium
historical_names.source: Ptolemy, Geography (c. 150 CE); Paulus Orosius, Historiae adversum Paganos (c. 417 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman port city and lighthouse (Tower of Hercules) located on the A Coruña peninsula.

b_ferrol.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1087 CE as 'sancto Iuliano de Ferrol' near the Monastery of San Martín de Jubia; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: genitive of the personal name Ferreolus ('estate of Ferreolus')

b_ferrol.etymology_analysis: Ferrol most likely derives from the local Galician evolution of the Latin genitive personal name 'Ferreoli' ('property/villa of Ferreolus', attested in 1087 CE as 'sancto Iuliano de Ferrol'). Alternative theories link it to Latin 'ferrum' ('iron') or 'farol' ('lighthouse').

b_mondonedo.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 858 CE during the reign of King Ordoño I of Asturias under the Latinized form 'Mindunietum' (modern Mondoñedo).
b_mondonedo.etymology_analysis: Mondoñedo (Latinized as 'Mindunietum') derives from a pre-Roman/Celtic compound combining *mund- ('hill, mountain') and *onna ('spring, stream') with the collective suffix '-etu', reflecting the sheltered mountain valley rich in springs and rivers.

b_vilalba.first_mention_attestation: Documented in the 12th century (1128 CE) under its earlier medieval designations 'Santa María de Montenegro' and 'Vilarente', before adopting the name 'Vilalba' ('White Town') in the late Middle Ages; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.
b_vilalba.etymology_analysis: Vilalba (Spanish: Villalba) is a Galician-Romance compound from Latin 'villa' ('estate, town') and 'alba' ('white'), literally meaning 'White Town', which replaced the earlier medieval name Santa María de Montenegro.

b_monterrei.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 950 CE as the castle and villa of Count Hermenegildo Gutiérrez (father of St. Rosendo of Celanova), and later recorded in the Cortes of Zamora of 1301 CE; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.
b_monterrei.etymology_analysis: Monterrei (Spanish: Monterrey) is a Galician compound of 'monte' ('hill, mountain') and 'rei' ('king'), meaning 'King's Mountain', referring to the fortified hilltop overlooking the Támega valley.

b_limia.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation of the medieval town Xinzo de Limia exists on or before 867 CE (the modern town developed in the High Middle Ages, with local fairs recorded by the 16th century), although the surrounding valley and Roman civitas of the Limici are attested in Antiquity.

morphemes.translation: from a medieval personal/estate name (possibly Latin Gentius or Genesius)
of the Limia River (classical Limia / Lethes)

b_limia.etymology_analysis: Xinzo de Limia (Spanish: Ginzo de Limia) combines 'Xinzo' (likely from a Latinized personal estate name such as Gentius) with 'de Limia', referring to the Limia River (associated in classical sources with the mythical river Lethe) and the ancient Limici tribe.

historical_names.name: Forum Limicorum
historical_names.source: Ptolemy, Geography 2.6.44 (c. 150 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman administrative center of the Limici people in the Antela/Limia valley.

historical_names.name: Civitas Limicorum
historical_names.source: Ptolemy, Geography 2.6.44 (c. 150 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman administrative center of the Limici people in the Antela/Limia valley.

b_santiago.first_mention_attestation: Following the early 9th-century discovery of the purported tomb of Saint James the Great, King Alfonso II of Asturias ordered the first church built on the site in 829 CE and issued a royal preceptum in 834 CE establishing the shrine, around which the settlement of Santiago de Compostela grew.

morphemes.translation: burial ground (from compositum tella, or folk-etymologized campus stellae)

b_santiago.etymology_analysis: Santiago de Compostela combines Galician 'Sant Iago' (Saint James, from Latin Sanctus Iacobus) with 'Compostela', which modern philologists (Richard A. Fletcher, Joan Coromines, Ramón Menéndez Pidal) derive from Latin 'compositum tella' ('well-ordered burial ground'), later reinterpreted via folk etymology as 'campus stellae' ('field of stars').

b_betanzos.first_mention_attestation: The modern town of Betanzos was formally established in 1219 CE by King Alfonso IX of León on the hill of Castro de Untia (earlier known in the Middle Ages as 'Carunio'); no written attestation of Betanzos exists <= 867 CE.
b_betanzos.etymology_analysis: Betanzos is traditionally explained as a phonetic evolution from Latin/Celtic 'Brigantium' (> 'Breganzo' > 'Betanzos'), though the identification of classical Flavium Brigantium with Betanzos versus A Coruña remains debated among historians.

b_melide.first_mention_attestation: Although the village originated in the 10th century at the junction of the French Way and Camino Primitivo, its earliest specific charter attestation is 1320 CE when Archbishop Berenguel de Landoira of Santiago granted Melide the privilege to build a castle and levy taxes; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: genitive of a personal name (e.g., Mellitus)

b_melide.etymology_analysis: Melide (Spanish: Mellid) is a Galician place name derived from the Latin genitive of a personal estate owner's name such as *Melliti ('estate of Mellitus'), following a common Galician pattern of -ide toponyms.

b_padron.first_mention_attestation: While Roman Iria Flavia (77 CE) lay adjacent, medieval Padrón (Petronum, named after the Pedrón stone) developed from the 10th century and received its royal fuero from Ferdinand II of León in 1164 CE.

morphemes.translation: large stone, pillar (augmentative of pedra 'stone', from Latin petra)

b_padron.etymology_analysis: Padrón derives from Galician 'pedrón' ('large stone', augmentative of 'pedra' from Latin 'petra'), referring to the Roman granite altar dedicated to Neptune (kept in the parish church of Santiago) to which legend says Saint James's boat was moored.

historical_names.name: Iria Flavia
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder / Flavian municipal grant (1st century CE); Parochiale Suevum (569 CE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Celtic-Roman town and early medieval episcopal see, today a parish of Padrón.

b_monte_faro.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation exists on or before 867 CE; the mountain sanctuary of Our Lady of O Faro (in Requeixo, Chantada, Galicia) is first documented in late 13th-century Galician-Portuguese cantigas de romaría by the troubadour Xoán de Requeixo.
b_monte_faro.etymology_analysis: Monte Faro means 'Beacon Mountain' in Galician, combining 'monte' ('mountain') and 'faro' ('beacon, watchtower', from Latin 'pharus'), referring to the prominent 1,187 m summit on the Lugo–Pontevedra border from which all four Galician provinces are visible.

b_tui.first_mention_attestation: Recorded as 'Tyde' / 'Tude' by 1st-century CE classical authors including Pliny the Elder (Naturalis Historia, c. 77 CE), Pomponius Mela, and Ptolemy, and documented as an episcopal see in the 6th century under the Suebi.

morphemes.translation: ancient hillfort settlement name of the Grovii

b_tui.etymology_analysis: Tui (Spanish: Tuy) derives directly from the pre-Roman Gallaecian settlement name 'Tude' or 'Tyde', attested by Pliny the Elder and Ptolemy as the principal city of the Grovii above the Miño River.

b_vigo.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Roman-era epigraphy (1st–3rd centuries CE) from the port settlement of 'Vicus Spacorum' on the Ría de Vigo.
b_vigo.etymology_analysis: Vigo derives directly from Latin 'vicus' ('village, settlement'), specifically the Roman port settlement known as 'Vicus Spacorum' located on the southern shore of the Ría de Vigo.

b_braganza.first_mention_attestation: Documented as 'Vergancia' in the acts of the Suebic Council of Lugo / Parochiale Suevum (569 CE), before receiving its medieval municipal charter (foral) in 1187 CE.
b_braganza.etymology_analysis: Bragança (Mirandese: Bergáncia; English: Braganza) derives from Celtic *Brigantia ('high/fortified place'), attested in 569 CE as 'Vergancia' and Latinized in the Middle Ages as 'Bragança'.

b_miranda_do_duoro.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1136 CE when Afonso Henriques granted a foral charter to Miranda, later renewed by King Dinis on 18 December 1286 CE; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: place to be admired, lookout point (from Latin mirandus)

b_miranda_do_duoro.etymology_analysis: Miranda do Douro combines 'Miranda' (from Latin 'miranda', 'lookout, place with a wide view', referring to its dramatic cliffside position) with 'do Douro' ('of the Douro River').

b_villa_real.first_mention_attestation: Established by King Afonso III on 7 December 1272 CE and granted its municipal charter by King Dinis on 4 January 1289 CE under the name 'Vila Real de Panóias'; no written attestation of Vila Real exists <= 867 CE.
b_villa_real.etymology_analysis: Vila Real literally means 'Royal Town' in Portuguese (from Latin 'villa regalis'), reflecting its royal foundation in 1272–1289 CE within the territory of Panóias.

b_mogadouro.first_mention_attestation: Mogadouro Castle was begun in the 12th century and the town received its first municipal charter (foral) from King Afonso III on 27 December 1272 CE (renewed 1273 CE); no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: boundary stone, cairn, or hill (cf. moio/marcos)
toponymic ending or association with the Douro region

b_mogadouro.etymology_analysis: Mogadouro is a Trás-os-Montes toponym of uncertain pre-Roman or early Romance origin, often linked by regional tradition to boundary markers or hilltop cairns overlooking the Douro and Sabor basins.

b_porto.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the late Roman Antonine Itinerary (c. 3rd–4th century CE) as 'Cale' / 'Portus Cale' at the mouth of the Douro River, and recorded by Hydatius in 456 CE during the Suebic-Visigothic wars.
b_porto.etymology_analysis: Porto derives from Latin 'portus' ('harbor, port'), shortened from the Roman-Celtic compound 'Portus Cale' ('Port of Cale'), which also gave rise to the name of Portugal ('Portucale' > 'Portugale').

b_braga.first_mention_attestation: Founded as 'Bracara Augusta' under Emperor Augustus c. 16 BCE and attested in written sources by Pliny the Elder (Naturalis Historia, c. 77 CE) and Ptolemy (2nd century CE), later serving as capital of the Suebic Kingdom.
b_braga.etymology_analysis: Braga derives directly from Latin 'Bracara (Augusta)', named after the indigenous Celtic-Gallaecian tribe of the Bracari, with the imperial title 'Augusta' added upon its Roman foundation under Augustus.

b_chavez.first_mention_attestation: Attested epigraphically in 79 CE on the 'Padrão dos Povos' inscription of Trajan's Bridge over the Tâmega River as the Roman municipium 'Aquae Flaviae'.

morphemes.translation: Flavian (from the Roman imperial Flavian dynasty; Aquae Flaviae > Flaviae > Chaves)

b_chavez.etymology_analysis: Chaves evolved phonetically from Latin '(Aquae) Flaviae' ('Waters of Flavius', named after the Flavian dynasty in the 1st century CE), with 'Flaviae' undergoing regular Galician-Portuguese palatalization of 'fl-' to 'ch-' ('Chaves').

historical_names.name: Aquae Flaviae
historical_names.source: Padrão dos Povos inscription on Trajan's Bridge (79 CE)
historical_names.notes: Roman thermal city and bishopric on the exact site of modern Chaves.

b_guimaraes.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 950–951 CE (and in the famous testament of 26 January 959 CE) when Countess Mumadona Dias founded the Monastery of São Mamede on her estate of 'Vimaranes'; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

eponym.details: Named after Count Vímara Peres (d. 873 CE), the Galician nobleman who reconquered the Minho–Douro region in 868 CE and founded the fortified estate bearing his name, 'Vimaranes' (later 'Guimaranes' / 'Guimarães').

b_guimaraes.etymology_analysis: Guimarães derives from medieval 'Vimaranes' (attested 950–959 CE), formed from the Germanic-origin personal name 'Vímara' (traditionally identified with Count Vímara Peres, fl. 868 CE) plus the genitive/possessive suffix '-anes', with initial 'v-' shifting to 'gu-' in Portuguese.

b_albarracin.first_mention_attestation: First documented under its current name in the early 11th century (1012 CE) with the establishment of the Taifa of Albarracín by the Berber Banu Razin dynasty ('Ibn Razin' / 'Aben Razin'); no written attestation of the name Albarracín exists <= 867 CE.

eponym.details: Named after the Berber Banu Razin ('Ibn Razin') family, who ruled the Taifa of Albarracín from 1012 to 1104 CE.

morphemes.translation: personal/dynastic name of the Banu Razin

b_albarracin.etymology_analysis: Albarracín derives from Andalusi Arabic 'al-Banū Razīn' / 'Aben Razín' ('the sons/place of Razin'), named after the Berber Banu Razin dynasty that ruled the Taifa of Albarracín in the 11th century (until the 19th century its full Christian title was Ciudad de Santa María de Albarracín).

historical_names.name: Lobetum
historical_names.source: Ptolemy, Geography 2.6.59 (c. 150 CE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Celtiberian/Roman city of Lobetum identified near Albarracín, succeeded by Visigothic Santa María de Oriente.

historical_names.name: Santa María de Oriente
historical_names.source: Ptolemy, Geography 2.6.59 (c. 150 CE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Celtiberian/Roman city of Lobetum identified near Albarracín, succeeded by Visigothic Santa María de Oriente.

b_sierradesanjust.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation exists on or before 867 CE; while lignite deposits in the Sierra de San Just near Utrillas were exploited in Roman times, the medieval settlement of Utrillas is only documented after the Aragonese Reconquista in the 12th–13th centuries.

morphemes.translation: leather wineskin or depression/basin (from Latin uter, utris)

b_sierradesanjust.etymology_analysis: Utrillas is a Spanish/Aragonese toponym likely derived from a diminutive plural of Latin 'uter' or a related pre-Roman/Romance topographic term referring to small basins or depressions in the Cuencas Mineras valley beneath the Sierra de San Just.

b_belchite.first_mention_attestation: First documented in Christian charters around 1118–1122 CE when King Alfonso I the Battler of Aragon established the Confraternity of Belchite (1122 CE) to defend the frontier south of Zaragoza; no written attestation of Belchite exists <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: ancient root shared with the Belli tribe and Belia

b_belchite.etymology_analysis: Belchite reflects a Mozarabic/Aragonese phonetic evolution of the ancient Celtiberian-Roman toponym 'Belia' (or 'Belgeda'), associated with the pre-Roman Belli tribe in the Ebro-Huerva basin.

historical_names.name: Belia
historical_names.source: Ptolemy, Geography (c. 150 CE)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Celtiberian and Roman town in the territory of the Belli, precursor to medieval Belchite.

b_alcaniz.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1157 CE in the municipal charter (fuero) granted by Count Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona following its Christian reconquest, though an Andalusi castle and settlement (al-Qanā'is) existed earlier.
b_alcaniz.etymology_analysis: Derived from Andalusi Arabic al-Qanā'is ('the churches'), likely referring to Christian Mozarabic churches in the settlement prior to or during Islamic rule; an alternative hypothesis links it to Arabic al-qanīṣ ('the hunting ground') or Latin canna ('reed').

b_caspe.first_mention_attestation: Documented in Christian Aragonese charters from 1169 CE after its reconquest by Alfonso II of Aragon, and attested in medieval Andalusi geographical sources as Qasp or Qasb.
b_caspe.etymology_analysis: Attested in Andalusi Arabic sources as Qasp or Qasb (possibly related to qaṣaba, 'citadel'), though philologists also propose a pre-Roman Indo-European or Iberian-Basque origin from *cass- ('oak') combined with the locative suffix -pe ('below' or 'place of').

b_calaceite.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Christian documentation around 1151 CE when Ramon Berenguer IV reconquered the Matarraña valley and enfeoffed the castle of Qal'at Zayd to Aragonese-Catalan knights.
b_calaceite.etymology_analysis: Derived from Andalusi Arabic Qal'at Zayd ('fortress of Zayd'), named after the Muslim Zayd family or clan that held the hilltop stronghold before the 12th-century Aragonese conquest.

b_jaca.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 2nd century BCE on indigenous Iberian silver and bronze coinage inscribed 'Iaka' in Iberian script, and later recorded as Iacca by Strabo (early 1st century CE) and Ptolemy (2nd century CE).
b_jaca.etymology_analysis: Descends from the pre-Roman indigenous town name Iaka (Latinized as Iacca), associated with the Iacetani or Vasconic-Aquitanian linguistic sphere in the central Pyrenees.

b_alto_aragon.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE for the compound regional designation 'Alto Aragón' (Upper Aragon), which is a modern Spanish geographical and cultural term for the northern Pyrenees and Huesca province.
b_alto_aragon.etymology_analysis: A modern Spanish compound combining alto ('upper/high') with Aragón, the name of the river and medieval county/kingdom; Aragón itself is often derived from Basque haran ('valley') or haragona ('good upper valley').

historical_names.name: Aragón
historical_names.source: Early 9th-century Carolingian and Navarrese-Aragonese charters (County of Aragon under Aznar Galíndez I, c. 809–828 CE)
historical_names.notes: The early medieval County of Aragon (Aragone) occupied the Pyrenean valleys of Hecho, Ansó, and Jaca that form the core of Alto Aragón.

historical_names.name: Pagus Aragone
historical_names.source: Early 9th-century Carolingian and Navarrese-Aragonese charters (County of Aragon under Aznar Galíndez I, c. 809–828 CE)
historical_names.notes: The early medieval County of Aragon (Aragone) occupied the Pyrenean valleys of Hecho, Ansó, and Jaca that form the core of Alto Aragón.

b_uncastillo.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 921 CE as 'Unicastello' in a charter of the Monastery of San Juan de la Peña ('ad uenta Unicastello'), during the early Pamplonese fortification of the Cinco Villas frontier.
b_uncastillo.etymology_analysis: Derived from Medieval Latin Unum Castellum / Unicastello ('one castle'), referring to the single prominent hilltop fortress around which the town developed in the 10th century.

historical_names.name: Tarraca
historical_names.source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia 3.24 (77 CE); Ptolemy, Geographia 2.6.66
historical_names.notes: The Roman city at Los Bañales (plausibly ancient Tarraca) lies in the southern part of Uncastillo municipality and remained inhabited on its central hill until the 9th century CE.

b_calatayud.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written history by the Andalusi historian al-Udri recording that in 862 CE the Umayyad Emir Muhammad I ordered the reconstruction of Qal'at Ayyūb, though local tradition places its foundation around 716 CE.
b_calatayud.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Qal'at Ayyūb ('fortress of Ayyub'), traditionally associated with Ayyub ibn Habib al-Lakhmi (governor of al-Andalus in 716 CE) or a later Umayyad commander.

historical_names.name: Bilbilis
historical_names.source: Celtiberian coinage (1st century BCE); Strabo, Martial, and Pliny the Elder (1st century CE)
historical_names.notes: The Celtiberian and Roman city of Augusta Bilbilis lies about 4 km north of Calatayud; its inhabitants relocated to the fortified site of Qal'at Ayyūb in the early Islamic period.

historical_names.name: Augusta Bilbilis
historical_names.source: Celtiberian coinage (1st century BCE); Strabo, Martial, and Pliny the Elder (1st century CE)
historical_names.notes: The Celtiberian and Roman city of Augusta Bilbilis lies about 4 km north of Calatayud; its inhabitants relocated to the fortified site of Qal'at Ayyūb in the early Islamic period.

b_daroca.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written sources in 837 CE as a fortified Andalusi town held by the Banu al-Muhayir family, and recorded in 862 CE under the name Qal'at Darawqa.

morphemes.translation: settlement name adapted into Arabic as Darawqa

b_daroca.etymology_analysis: Adapted from the Andalusi Arabic name Qal'at Darawqa (or Calat-Darawca), which itself likely preserves an earlier pre-Roman or Celtiberian toponym (*Darek or *Darauca).

b_monzon.first_mention_attestation: First securely attested in Christian chronicles in 1089 CE when King Sancho Ramírez of Aragon captured the fortress of Monzón from Muslim rule, though an Andalusi castle (Muntiyūn / Munshūn) preceded it.

morphemes.translation: mountain, hill, or Roman personal name Montius + -one

b_monzon.etymology_analysis: Likely derives from a Latin/Romance formation *Montione (from mons, 'hill/mount', or the Roman gentilicium Montius with the augmentative/locative suffix -ōne), adapted into Andalusi Arabic before becoming Aragonese/Spanish Monzón.

historical_names.name: Tolous
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (late 3rd century CE)
historical_names.notes: The Roman mansio of Tolous, listed in the Antonine Itinerary between Ilerda and Osca, was located near modern Monzón.

b_fraga.first_mention_attestation: Established as Medina Afraga (whence Fraga) following the Moorish conquest in 714 CE near the Roman site of Gallica Flavia and Villa Fortunatus (c. 150 CE).

morphemes.translation: rocky/rough terrain (Latin fraga) or Arabicized pre-Roman form

b_fraga.etymology_analysis: Traditionally linked to Latin fraga ('broken/craggy ground', cognate with fragosus) or an indigenous pre-Roman name adapted into Andalusi Arabic as Ifrāġa (Afrāġa).

historical_names.name: Gallica Flavia
historical_names.source: Ptolemy, Geographia (c. 150 CE) for Gallica Flavia; archaeological Villa Fortunatus (2nd–5th century CE)
historical_names.notes: Ptolemy's Gallica Flavia is frequently associated with Fraga, and the Roman Villa Fortunatus lies just north of the town.

historical_names.name: Villa Fortunatus
historical_names.source: Ptolemy, Geographia (c. 150 CE) for Gallica Flavia; archaeological Villa Fortunatus (2nd–5th century CE)
historical_names.notes: Ptolemy's Gallica Flavia is frequently associated with Fraga, and the Roman Villa Fortunatus lies just north of the town.

b_huesca.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the 2nd century BCE via Iberian coinage reading 'Bolskan' and Roman historical accounts of Praetor Gaius Terentius Varro's 179 BCE campaign, after which the city was refounded as Roman Osca.
b_huesca.etymology_analysis: Spanish Huesca (Aragonese Uesca, Arabic Wašqa) descends from Latin Osca, which itself adapted the pre-Roman Iberian city name Bolskan.

b_barbastro.first_mention_attestation: Attested in early 9th-century Andalusi accounts of the Banu Khalaf (Khalaf ibn Rashid, c. 802 CE), who ruled the region of Barbitanya from the castle of Barbastra (Arabic Barbaštar).
b_barbastro.etymology_analysis: Evolved from Late Latin/Romance Barbastrum (Arabicized as Barbaštar), connected to the regional name Barbitania (itself linked to the pre-Roman/Roman town of Bergidum or Brutina).

b_ainsa.first_mention_attestation: Attested in early 9th-century Marca Hispanica and Andalusi history, when Sobrarbe formed a Christian Pyrenean principality temporarily held for five years by Amrus ibn Yusuf (governor of Zaragoza, d. c. 813 CE).
b_ainsa.etymology_analysis: Derived from Latin Super Arbem ('above Mount Arbe'), referring to the mountainous district north of the Sierra de Arbe; a late medieval legend reinterpreted it via folk etymology as sobre arbre ('upon a tree').

b_ribagorza.first_mention_attestation: First reliably attested in 806–814 CE in early Carolingian Marca Hispanica charters (including those of the Monastery of Alaón), where the territory appears as Ripa Curtia / Ripacurcia.
b_ribagorza.etymology_analysis: Derived from Latin Ripa Curtia ('cut/steep riverbank'), describing the rugged gorge terrain along the Noguera Ribagorzana and Ésera rivers.

b_biescas.first_mention_attestation: First documented between 1020 and 1030 CE in the Cartulary of San Juan de la Peña.
b_biescas.etymology_analysis: Generally traced to a pre-Roman Pyrenean root related to Basque bizkar ('ridge, crest, hill'), reflecting its position in the upper Gállego valley.

b_zaragoza.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the Roman colony Caesaraugusta in 14 BCE (on the site of the Iberian town of Salduie, attested from the 2nd–1st century BCE) and recorded by Strabo, Pliny, and Ptolemy.
b_zaragoza.etymology_analysis: Descends from Latin Caesaraugusta (named for Emperor Caesar Augustus upon its colonial foundation in 14 BCE), which evolved through Andalusi Arabic Saraqusṭa and Old Spanish Çaragoça into modern Zaragoza.

historical_names.name: Salduie
historical_names.source: Roman colonial foundation of Caesaraugusta (14 BCE); earlier Iberian coins of Salduie
historical_names.notes: Salduie was the pre-Roman Sedetani town; Caesaraugusta was its Roman name and Saraqusṭa its Andalusi Arabic name.

historical_names.name: Salduba
historical_names.source: Roman colonial foundation of Caesaraugusta (14 BCE); earlier Iberian coins of Salduie
historical_names.notes: Salduie was the pre-Roman Sedetani town; Caesaraugusta was its Roman name and Saraqusṭa its Andalusi Arabic name.

b_ejea.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the 2nd century BCE as Segia (Iberian script Śekia) on indigenous coinage, and recorded by Pliny the Elder and Ptolemy among the towns of the Vascones/Suessetani.

morphemes.translation: of the Knights (added after 1105 CE conquest)

b_ejea.etymology_analysis: Ejea derives from the ancient toponym Segia (likely from Celtic *sego-, 'victory/strength'), while 'de los Caballeros' ('of the Knights') was appended after its 1105 CE reconquest by Alfonso I of Aragon.

b_zuera.first_mention_attestation: Documented in Aragonese charters following the 1118 CE conquest of the Zaragoza region (as Zufaria), deriving from an Andalusi Arabic settlement name Ṣuḫayra.
b_zuera.etymology_analysis: Derived from Andalusi Arabic Ṣuḫayra ('little rock/crag', diminutive of ṣaḫra), which passed into Romance as Zufaria and later Zuera; local heritage also notes the nearby Roman mansio of Gallicum.

historical_names.name: Gallicum
historical_names.source: Antonine Itinerary (late 3rd century CE)
historical_names.notes: The Roman road station Gallicum on the Caesaraugusta–Osca route was located along the Gállego river near Zuera.

b_sarinena.first_mention_attestation: First documented in January 1100 CE as 'Saragena' in a donation charter of King Peter I of Aragon to the Monastery of Montearagón.
b_sarinena.etymology_analysis: Likely derives from a Hispano-Roman estate name formed from a personal name such as *Sarinius or *Saranus combined with the Latin/Romance toponymic suffix -ēna/-āna.

b_iviza.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the Phoenician-Punic colony ʾbšm (Ibossim) in 654 BCE according to Diodorus Siculus, and later attested as Ebusus by Pliny the Elder and Ptolemy.
b_iviza.etymology_analysis: Derived from Phoenician-Punic ʾbšm ('dedicated to Bes', the Egyptian-Phoenician protective deity), which became Latin Ebusus, Catalan Eivissa, and Spanish Ibiza.

b_palma.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the Roman colony of Palma in 123 BCE by Consul Quintus Caecilius Metellus Balearicus, and attested by Strabo, Pomponius Mela, and Pliny the Elder.
b_palma.etymology_analysis: Named Palma by the Romans in 123 BCE after the palm branch symbol of military victory (following Metellus's conquest of the Balearics), with 'de Mallorca' added later to distinguish it.

b_alcudia.first_mention_attestation: The medieval town of Alcúdia was founded in 1298 CE when King James II of Mallorca purchased the Moorish farmstead (alquería) of al-Kudya near the ruins of Roman Pollentia.
b_alcudia.etymology_analysis: Derived from Andalusi Arabic al-kudya ('the hillock'), referring to the elevated farmstead site adjacent to ancient Pollentia.

historical_names.name: Pollentia
historical_names.source: Strabo, Geographica 3.5.1; Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia 3.77
historical_names.notes: The Roman city of Pollentia, founded in 123 BCE by Q. Caecilius Metellus, lies immediately beside the old town of Alcúdia and remained occupied into the Byzantine period.

b_menorca.first_mention_attestation: Attested in classical Roman geography, including Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia (77 CE), where it is contrasted with the larger island (Insula Maior) as the smaller Balearic island (Insula Minor / Minorica).
b_menorca.etymology_analysis: Derived from Latin Insula Minor / Minorica ('smaller island'), contrasting with neighboring Mallorca (Insula Maior, 'larger island').

b_alarcon.first_mention_attestation: First securely attested in Christian chronicles in 1184 CE when King Alfonso VIII of Castile besieged and captured the Muslim hilltop fortress, though the citadel itself was built during the Islamic period.
b_alarcon.etymology_analysis: Derived from Andalusi Arabic al-Arkūn, likely an Arabicization of an earlier pre-Roman or Latin toponym (*Ilurco / *Arco) referring to the Júcar river bend.

b_ventadelmoro.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written records in the 16th century as a roadside inn (venta) within the alfoz (jurisdiction) of Requena.
b_ventadelmoro.etymology_analysis: Literally Spanish 'Inn of the Moor' (venta + del Moro), originating from a 16th-century roadside inn along the route between Requena and Castile.

b_valeria.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a Roman city between 93 and 82 BCE under proconsul Gaius Valerius Flaccus and attested by Pliny the Elder, Ptolemy, and Visigothic Church Councils.
b_valeria.etymology_analysis: Named after its Roman founder Gaius Valerius Flaccus (proconsul of Hispania Citerior in 93–82 BCE), preserving his gentilicium Valerius.

b_alcazar.first_mention_attestation: First securely attested in Christian records in 1150 CE when the fortress of Alcázar was donated to three knights following the Castilian reconquest, later passing to the Knights of St. John.
b_alcazar.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-qaṣr ('the castle', ultimately from Latin castrum), with 'de San Juan' added after the 13th-century administration of the Order of St. John of Jerusalem.

b_alcaraz.first_mention_attestation: First securely attested in 12th-century chronicles (such as the Almohad campaigns of 1172 CE and Alfonso VIII's conquest in 1213 CE), though it was an important Andalusi fortress earlier.
b_alcaraz.etymology_analysis: Derived from Andalusi Arabic al-Karaz ('the cherry' or an Arabicized pre-Roman toponym for the mountain pass/fortress).

b_huescar.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Cotillas first appears in late medieval Castilian records as an aldea (hamlet) dependent on Alcaraz after the 13th-century Christian conquest.

morphemes.translation: small hillock, slope, or diminutive of cota ('height/coat')

b_huescar.etymology_analysis: A Romance/Castilian plural toponym (Cotillas) likely derived from *cotella / cota ('height, small ridge') or a related medieval agrarian term.

b_segura.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Andalusi history from 781 CE when Muslim forces captured and fortified the stronghold under the name Šaqūra (Saqura).
b_segura.etymology_analysis: Segura derives via Andalusi Arabic Šaqūra from an earlier pre-Roman/Latin toponym, with 'de la Sierra' added in Castilian to designate its location in the Sierra de Segura.

b_reolid.first_mention_attestation: First securely attested in 1226–1227 CE when the Muslim fortress (Castillo de la Estrella) capitulated to Castilian forces and King Ferdinand III donated Montiel to the Order of Santiago.
b_reolid.etymology_analysis: Derived from Late Latin/Mozarabic *Montellus ('little hill'), referring to the fortified hill overlooking the Campo de Montiel.

b_murcia.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 825 CE by the Umayyad Emir Abd al-Rahman II under the name Madīnat Mursiya, as recorded in Andalusi chronicles.

morphemes.translation: place of myrtles or Roman estate name

b_murcia.etymology_analysis: From Andalusi Arabic Mursiya, generally thought to derive from a pre-existing Latin toponym such as *Myrtea ('myrtle grove') or a Roman estate name *Murcia.

b_cartagena.first_mention_attestation: Founded around 227 BCE by the Carthaginian general Hasdrubal as Qart Ḥadašt ('New City') and extensively attested by Polybius and Livy as Carthago Nova.
b_cartagena.etymology_analysis: Descends from Latin Carthago Nova (accusative Carthaginem), translating Punic Qart Ḥadašt ('New City'), which passed through Arabic Qarṭājanna into Spanish Cartagena.

b_aguilas.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the 16th century under King Philip II as 'San Juan de las Águilas', and formally established as a modern port town in 1785 CE under Charles III.

morphemes.translation: eagles (referring to the eagle-beak rock promontory)

b_aguilas.etymology_analysis: Spanish Águilas ('eagles'), named after the coastal rock promontory resembling an eagle's beak (or possibly reinterpreting an earlier Roman/coastal name Aquilae).

b_caravacadelacruz.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Islamic sources from the 10th–12th centuries as a small rural settlement (qarya) dependent on Mula, before entering Castilian records after the 1243 CE Treaty of Alcaraz.

morphemes.translation: settlement name (possibly Qal'at al-Baqar or pre-Roman)
of the Cross (referring to the Vera Cruz relic)

b_caravacadelacruz.etymology_analysis: Caravaca is of uncertain pre-Roman or Andalusi origin, while 'de la Cruz' ('of the Cross') was added in the late medieval/early modern period in honor of the Vera Cruz relic.

b_cieza.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the 11th century by the Andalusi geographer al-Udri as Siyāsa (Madīnat Siyāsa), an Islamic town on the Castle Hill above modern Cieza.
b_cieza.etymology_analysis: Evolved from Andalusi Arabic Siyāsa (Medina Siyâsa), which passed into Castilian as Cieça and modern Cieza.

b_alicante.first_mention_attestation: Attested in antiquity from c. 230 BCE as Akra Leuke (Diodorus Siculus) and as Roman Lucentum (Pliny the Elder and Ptolemy), before appearing as Arabic al-Laqant from the 8th century CE.
b_alicante.etymology_analysis: Derived from Andalusi Arabic al-Laqant, an adaptation of the Roman city name Lucentum (itself possibly from Greek Akra Leuke, 'White Promontory', or an Iberian root).

historical_names.name: Akra Leuke
historical_names.source: Diodorus Siculus (Akra Leuke); Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (Lucentum); 8th-century Arabic sources (al-Laqant)
historical_names.notes: Lucentum (at Tossal de Manises) and Arabic al-Laqant are the direct ancient and early medieval predecessors of Alicante.

b_albacete.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 928 CE in Andalusi sources as al-Basīṭ ('the plain'), and captured by Castilian forces in 1241 CE.
b_albacete.etymology_analysis: Derived from Andalusi Arabic al-Basīṭ ('the plain'), describing the flat topography of the La Mancha plain around the settlement.

b_castellon.first_mention_attestation: Officially founded on 8 September 1251 CE by royal charter of King James I of Aragon, authorizing the transfer of the settlement from the hillside castle of Fadrell to the coastal plain.
b_castellon.etymology_analysis: Means 'Little Castle of the Plain' (Valencian Castelló de la Plana), referring to the 1251 CE relocation of the hillside castle settlement onto the coastal plain.

b_amposta.first_mention_attestation: First attested in Christian chronicles in 1095–1097 CE during Count Ramon Berenguer III's unsuccessful sieges of the Muslim fortress on the Ebro.
b_amposta.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived from Latin Amni Imposita ('placed upon the river'), referring to its strategic position overlooking the Ebro River.

b_segorbe.first_mention_attestation: Attested from 589 CE in the Visigothic Councils of Toledo as an episcopal see (historically identified in medieval ecclesiastical tradition with Segobriga, though modern archaeology locates Celtiberian Segobriga in Cuenca).
b_segorbe.etymology_analysis: Derived from a pre-Roman/Celtiberian compound containing sego- ('victory') and -briga ('fortress/hilltop'), which evolved into Segorbe (Valencian Sogorb).

b_denia.first_mention_attestation: Attested in classical antiquity from the 1st century BCE as Roman Dianium (Cicero, Strabo, Pliny the Elder), succeeding the earlier Greek-Iberian emporion of Hemeroskopeion.
b_denia.etymology_analysis: Derived from Latin Dianium ('sanctuary/town of Diana'), named after the prominent temple of Diana (Artemis), which evolved through Andalusi Arabic Dāniya into Valencian Dénia / Spanish Denia.

historical_names.name: Hemeroskopeion
historical_names.source: Cicero, In Verrem; Strabo, Geographica 3.4.6; Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia
historical_names.notes: Roman Dianium succeeded Greek Hemeroskopeion and became Andalusi Dāniya.

b_almansa.first_mention_attestation: Formally founded in March 1256 CE by royal charter (carta puebla) of King James I of Aragon, consolidating earlier Muslim farmsteads (alquerías) in the valley.
b_almansa.etymology_analysis: Uncertain etymology, most commonly derived from an Andalusi Arabic toponym (such as al-Qawī or al-Quyūṭ) or a hybrid Arabic-Romance formation.

b_teruel.first_mention_attestation: Founded in October 1171 CE by King Alfonso II of Aragon after capturing the Muslim enclave of Tirwal.
b_teruel.etymology_analysis: Derived from the medieval Andalusi toponym Tirwal (possibly from a pre-Roman/Romance *Turbolium or toro/terol), adapted into Aragonese and Spanish as Teruel.

b_maestrazgo.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the regional name Maestrazgo (Valencian Maestrat) arose in the 14th century (after 1317 CE) from the territories governed by the Grand Master of the Order of Montesa and earlier military orders.
b_maestrazgo.etymology_analysis: Derived from Spanish maestre ('Grand Master') + the jurisdictional suffix -azgo, denoting the domains ruled by the Masters of the Templars, Hospitallers, and Order of Montesa.

b_ademuz.first_mention_attestation: First prominently attested in written history in 1009 CE at the outbreak of the Andalusi fitna, when Abd Allah ibn Qasim established the Taifa of Alpuente (Ḥiṣn al-Būnt).
b_ademuz.etymology_analysis: Derived from Andalusi Arabic al-Būnt, an adaptation of Latin Altum Pontem ('high bridge'), later re-Romanceized with the Arabic article as Alpuente.

b_valencia.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the Roman colony Valentia Edetanorum in 138 BCE by Consul Decimus Junius Brutus Callaicus, and attested by Livy and Pliny the Elder.
b_valencia.etymology_analysis: From Latin Valentia ('strength, valor'), awarded to settled Roman veterans in 138 BCE; it passed through Andalusi Arabic Balansiya into Valencian València and Spanish Valencia.

b_murviedro.first_mention_attestation: Attested in classical historiography from 219 BCE when Hannibal besieged Saguntum (sparking the Second Punic War), preceded by Iberian coinage inscribed 'Arse'.
b_murviedro.etymology_analysis: Modern Sagunto revives the classical Roman name Saguntum; in the Middle Ages the town was known as Murviedro / Morvedre (from Latin Muri Veteres, 'old walls').

historical_names.name: Arse
historical_names.source: Polybius, Histories; Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 21 (219 BCE siege); Iberian coinage reading 'Arse'
historical_names.notes: Arse was the pre-Roman Iberian city, known to Rome as Saguntum and in late antiquity/early Middle Ages as Muri Veteres (Murviedro).

historical_names.name: Muri Veteres
historical_names.source: Polybius, Histories; Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 21 (219 BCE siege); Iberian coinage reading 'Arse'
historical_names.notes: Arse was the pre-Roman Iberian city, known to Rome as Saguntum and in late antiquity/early Middle Ages as Muri Veteres (Murviedro).

b_montanejos.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1239 CE in the aftermath of the Aragonese conquest of Valencia, when King James I granted the neighboring alquerías and lands of the Montán valley to Pedro Ximénez de Vallterra.
b_montanejos.etymology_analysis: A Romance diminutive form related to Montán ('little mountains/hills'), reflecting the mountainous terrain of the Alto Mijares gorge.

b_requena.first_mention_attestation: First securely attested in Christian records around 1238 CE during the conquest of Valencia by James I and Castilian forces, though its hilltop alcazaba dates to the Islamic period (10th–11th century).
b_requena.etymology_analysis: Derived from an Andalusi Arabic or pre-Roman toponym (Raqāna), whose deeper root remains uncertain.

b_antwerpen.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Andoverpis in Dado's Vita Eligii (Life of St. Eligius, c. 700 CE), with earlier Germanic forms such as Andhunerbo cited from c. 567 CE and a 726 CE charter.

morphemes.translation: thrown-up mound, wharf, or alluvial bank

b_antwerpen.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Frankish *anda-werp- (denoting land thrown up against the riverbank, a defensive mound, or a wharf along the Scheldt), later folk-etymologized as Dutch handwerpen ('hand-throwing').

b_rosendaal.first_mention_attestation: First documented as Rosendaele in a charter of 1268 CE; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_rosendaal.etymology_analysis: Middle Dutch compound of rosen ('roses', or possibly dialectal 'reeds') and dael/daele ('valley, low-lying ground'), meaning 'valley of roses' (attested as Rosendaele in 1268 CE).

b_breda.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the historical record in 1125 CE when Engelbertus van Breda appeared as a witness to a charter; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_breda.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Dutch brede Aa ('wide Aa'), referring to the widening of the river Aa at its confluence with the river Mark.

b_leuven.first_mention_attestation: Earliest written mention dates to 891 CE (as Loven in the Annales Vedastini) in connection with the Battle of Leuven against a Viking army; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_leuven.etymology_analysis: From Middle Dutch Loven (Latinized as Lovanium), commonly explained by linguists as a Germanic compound of lo ('woodland clearing') and ven ('fen, marshy ground'), though the exact etymology remains debated.

b_brussels.first_mention_attestation: First recorded as Brosella in a 7th-century chronicle noting that Bishop Vindicianus of Cambrai died there of fever in 695 CE, and later attested as Bruocsella in a 966 CE charter of Emperor Otto I.
b_brussels.etymology_analysis: From Old Dutch Bruocsella (later Broekzele/Broeksel), a compound of bruoc ('marsh') and sella ('hall, settlement'), meaning 'home/settlement in the marsh' along the Senne river.

b_turnhout.first_mention_attestation: A hunting castle of the Dukes of Brabant at Turnhout is attested from 1110 CE or earlier in medieval records; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_turnhout.etymology_analysis: Old Dutch compound of Turn- (possibly from Germanic durnum, 'thorn') and -hout (from Germanic hulta, 'wood, forest'), meaning 'thorn-wood'.

b_cambrai.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the mid-4th century CE as Camaracum (written Camaraco) on the Tabula Peutingeriana, serving as the Roman administrative center of the Nervii.
b_cambrai.etymology_analysis: From Latinized Gaulish Camaracum, combining a Gaulish personal name (Camarus or Cambarius, related to cambo- 'curved') with the Gallo-Roman estate suffix -acum.

b_malboden.first_mention_attestation: Attested from 661 CE in connection with the foundation of Maubeuge Abbey (Malbodium) on the Sambre by Saint Aldegonde.
b_malboden.etymology_analysis: Latinized as Malbodium from Old Frankish Malboden, meaning 'assizes/court of Boden', which evolved into French Maubeuge.

b_valenciennes.first_mention_attestation: Earliest written mention appears in a 693 CE royal legal document of Merovingian king Clovis IV (as Valentianas).
b_valenciennes.etymology_analysis: From Latin Valentianae (attested as Valentianas in 693 CE), derived from a Roman personal name such as Valentius or Valentinianus with the adjectival/estate suffix -ianae.

b_mons.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 7th-century hagiographical accounts (c. 653 CE) as Castrilocus/Castriloc when Saint Waltrude founded a monastery on the hill near Saint Ghislain's oratory, later renamed Montes ('hills', modern Mons).
b_mons.etymology_analysis: From Latin Montes ('hills', singular mons), replacing the earlier Roman-era name Castrilocus ('camp-place') in reference to the hill on which the fortress and abbey stood.

historical_names.name: Castrilocus
historical_names.source: 7th-century hagiography of Saint Waltrude and Saint Ghislain
historical_names.notes: Earlier Latin name meaning 'camp-place' before shifting to Montes ('hills', modern Mons).

historical_names.name: Castriloc
historical_names.source: 7th-century hagiography of Saint Waltrude and Saint Ghislain
historical_names.notes: Earlier Latin name meaning 'camp-place' before shifting to Montes ('hills', modern Mons).

b_tournai.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Turnacum in the Antonine Itinerary (c. 280 CE) and as Turnaco on the 4th-century Tabula Peutingeriana.
b_tournai.etymology_analysis: From Latinized Gaulish Turnacum / Tornacum, combining Gaulish turno- ('height, eminence', or a personal name Turnos) with the Gallo-Roman suffix -acum.

b_ath.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Athum in 1076 CE; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_ath.etymology_analysis: Attested as Latinized Athum in 1076 CE, likely of Celtic origin denoting a fortified crossing or ford (cognate with Old Irish áth, 'ford').

b_castrogiovanni.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 5th-century BCE Greek coinage (legend HENNAION) and classical Greek historiography as Henna/Enna, later becoming Castrum Hennae, Arabic Qasr Yanni, and medieval Castrogiovanni.

morphemes.translation: of Henna (ancient Sicel toponym of obscure origin)

b_castrogiovanni.etymology_analysis: Modern Enna revives ancient Greek Henna/Enna (a pre-Greek Siculian toponym of obscure origin). The medieval name Castrogiovanni arose from Latin Castrum Hennae via Arabic Qasr Yanni and Norman Castrum Johannis.

b_agricento.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Akragas in Pindar's Pythian Odes (early 5th century BCE, c. 490 BCE) and in Thucydides, who dates its Greek foundation from Gela to c. 582–580 BCE.

morphemes.translation: name of the local river (and polis)

b_agricento.etymology_analysis: Named Akragas by Greek colonists after the nearby Akragas river, Latinized as Agrigentum, which evolved into medieval Girgenti and modern Italian Agrigento.

b_caltanisetta.first_mention_attestation: First traceable in late 11th-century Norman chronicles (such as Goffredo Malaterra, c. 1086–1099 CE, as Calatenixet) and 12th-century Arabic geography (al-Idrisi); no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: of the women (or adaptation of Byzantine Nissa)

b_caltanisetta.etymology_analysis: Derived from Arabic Qal'at an-Nisa' ('fortress of the women', or an Arabized adaptation of a Byzantine settlement name Nissa), Latinized under Norman rule as Calatenixet / Caltanixettum.

b_malta.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Melite in Greek geographic fragments of Hecataeus of Miletus (c. 500 BCE) and Pseudo-Scylax, and later in Latin as Melita and Malta in the Antonine Itinerary.
b_malta.etymology_analysis: Either from Phoenician Maleth ('haven, refuge') referring to its natural harbors, or from Ancient Greek Melite (derived from meli, 'honey'), Latinized as Melita and later evolving into Malta.

b_messina.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 5th-century BCE Greek historians (Herodotus and Thucydides) as Zancle (founded in the 8th century BCE) and Messene (renamed by Anaxilas of Rhegium in the early 5th century BCE).

morphemes.translation: Messenia (Greek homeland of the 5th-century BCE settlers)

b_messina.etymology_analysis: Originally named Zancle (from a Siculian word meaning 'sickle', referring to its curved harbor), it was renamed Messene by Anaxilas of Rhegium after Messenia in the Peloponnese, becoming Latin Messana and Italian Messina.

historical_names.name: Zancle
historical_names.source: Herodotus and Thucydides (5th century BCE)
historical_names.notes: Founded as Zancle ('sickle'), renamed Messene in the early 5th century BCE, and Latinized as Messana.

b_cefalu.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Kephaloidion (Latin Cephaloedium) in Diodorus Siculus's account of the Carthaginian campaign of 396 BCE, and later in Strabo, Pliny, and Ptolemy.
b_cefalu.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Kephaloidion (Latinized as Cephaloedium), derived from kephale ('head'), referring to the massive rocky headland (La Rocca) overlooking the town.

b_catania.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Katane in Thucydides (5th century BCE), who records its occupation and colonization by Chalcidian Greeks from Naxos around 729 BCE.
b_catania.etymology_analysis: From Siculian katane ('grater' or 'rough/harsh ground', referring to the rugged volcanic basalt landscape near Mount Etna), adapted into Ancient Greek Katane and Latin Catina/Catana.

b_palermo.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Panormos in Thucydides (5th century BCE) and as Zyz on 5th-century BCE Punic coinage.
b_palermo.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Panormos ('all-port' or 'wide haven', Latinized as Panormus), referring to its large natural harbor; adapted into Arabic as Bal'harm and Italian as Palermo.

historical_names.name: Zyz
historical_names.source: Thucydides and 5th-century BCE Punic coinage
historical_names.notes: Phoenician Zyz ('flower') and Greek Panormos ('all-port', Latin Panormus).

b_trapani.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Drepanon / Drepana in Polybius and Diodorus Siculus in connection with the First Punic War (c. 260–249 BCE), when Hamilcar Barca fortified the promontory.
b_trapani.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Drepanon (Latin Drepanum/Drepana), meaning 'sickle', referring to the curving sickle-like shape of its harbor peninsula.

b_calatafimi.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written records in the mid-12th century (1154 CE) by the Arab geographer Muhammad al-Idrisi as Qal'at Fīmī; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_calatafimi.etymology_analysis: Derived from Arabic Qal'at Fīmī ('Fortress of Euphemius', traditionally linked to the 9th-century Byzantine officer Euphemius who invited Aghlabid intervention in 827 CE), with Segesta added to the modern municipality name from the nearby ancient Elymian site.

historical_names.name: Segesta
historical_names.source: Thucydides (History of the Peloponnesian War)
historical_names.notes: The ancient Elymian city of Segesta lies nearby within the modern municipality, predating the medieval Arab-era fortress Qal'at Fīmī.

b_mazara.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Diodorus Siculus (1st century BCE, describing the 409 BCE Carthaginian campaign) as an emporium near the Mazaro river, and later in Stephanus of Byzantium as Mazara.

morphemes.translation: border or fortress (also the name of the Mazaro river)

b_mazara.etymology_analysis: From ancient Mazara (sharing its name with the Mazaro river), variously traced to a Punic/Phoenician root meaning 'border' or 'fortress'; 'del Vallo' was added in reference to the medieval administrative Val di Mazara.

b_syracusa.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Syrakousai in Pindar's Odes (c. 476 BCE) and in Thucydides (5th century BCE), who dates its Corinthian foundation to 733 BCE.
b_syracusa.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Syrakousai (Latin Syracusae), traditionally linked to a nearby Siculian marsh or lagoon named Syrako ('salt marsh').

b_lentini.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Leontinoi in Thucydides (5th century BCE), who dates its foundation by Chalcidian Greek colonists from Naxos to 729 BCE.
b_lentini.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Leontinoi (Latin Leontini), traditionally associated with Greek leon ('lion'), evolving regularly into Sicilian Lintini and Italian Lentini.

b_caltagirone.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1030 CE when the Arab-era fortress was attacked by Ligurian troops under Byzantine general George Maniakes; no written attestation exists on or before 867 CE.
b_caltagirone.etymology_analysis: Derived from Arabic qal'at al-jirār ('castle of [pottery] jars', or qal'at ghīrān), reflecting the town's ancient ceramic and pottery industry.
